Copy as Markdown Intermediate What you'll learn Understand what a checkpoint captures — and what it silently does not Open the rewind menu two ways and pick the right restore action every time Tell 'restore' (undo state) apart from 'summarize' (compress context) Know exactly why checkpoints complement Git but never replace it Last verified: 2026-10-09. Checkpoint behavior, the rewind menu actions, the snapshot cap and retention change between releases — confirm in the official docs. Confirm against the official source.

When you turn Claude loose on an ambitious, wide-scale change, the scariest question is "what if it goes wrong three edits deep?" Checkpointing is the answer: Claude Code automatically snapshots your code before each edit, so you can rewind to any earlier state instead of untangling a half-finished refactor by hand. Think of it as a local undo for the whole session — a safety net that lets you say "yes, try the bold approach" without fear.

You don't create checkpoints — they happen automatically. Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Every prompt that starts a turn = a checkpoint⌄ Each prompt that starts a turn captures the state of your code before Claude's file-editing tools run. No command, no config, no ceremony. ←PreviousNext→ 2Only the 100 most recent are kept⌄ Claude Code keeps file snapshots for the 100 most recent checkpoints in a session. Older ones are discarded, so a very long session cannot be rewound all the way back to its start. ←PreviousNext→ 3They persist across sessions⌄ Checkpoints are saved with the conversation, so you can still run /rewind after resuming a session, not just in the live one. ←PreviousNext→ 4They clean themselves up⌄ A session's file snapshots are deleted in the retention sweep, by default about 30 days after the session last saved one. Rewinding to a checkpoint whose snapshots are gone fails with 'No files were restored' — raise cleanupPeriodDays to keep them longer. ←PreviousNext→

There are two ways in: Guided walkthrough1 of 2 1Run /rewind⌄ Type the slash command from the prompt. Always works. ←PreviousNext→ 2Press Esc twice — but only on an empty input⌄ Double-Esc opens the rewind menu when the prompt box is empty. If there's text in it, double-Esc clears that text instead (the cleared text is saved to input history, so press Up to get it back afterward). ←PreviousNext→ Open the rewind menu CopyOpen in Claude↗ /rewind The menu lists every prompt you sent this session. Pick the point you want to act on, then choose one action.

This is where people get confused. The menu offers two kinds of action: Restore actions change state on disk and/or in the conversation — they undo. Summarize actions never touch your files — they compress conversation to free up context window space. Watch out Restore = undo (reverts code, conversation, or both). Summarize = compress context (files on disk are untouched). Reach for restore when an edit broke something. Reach for summarize when the session is bloated but the code is fine.
documents.s: Restore vs. summarize: the key distinction

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 3 1Restore code and conversation⌄ Revert both your files and the chat history to the selected point — a clean 'rewind time' to that moment. ←PreviousNext→ 2Restore conversation⌄ Rewind the chat to that message but keep your current code. Useful to re-ask a question without losing edits you want to keep. ←PreviousNext→ 3Restore code⌄ Revert file changes but keep the conversation. Undo the edits, keep the discussion about them. ←PreviousNext→ The two code restore options only appear when the selected checkpoint actually has tracked file changes to revert. If no file edits were captured after that point, the menu offers just Restore conversation, the two summarize options, and Never mind (which returns to the message list without changing anything). After restoring the conversation (or choosing "Summarize from here"), the original prompt from the selected message is dropped back into the input field so you can re-send or edit it.

Both compress part of the conversation into an AI-generated summary — like a targeted /compact where you choose which side of the selected message to squeeze. Guided walkthrough1 of 2 1Summarize from here⌄ Messages BEFORE the selected message stay intact. The selected message and everything after it become a summary. Use it to discard a side discussion while keeping early context in full detail. ←PreviousNext→ 2Summarize up to here⌄ Messages BEFORE the selected message become a summary; the selected message and everything after stay intact. You remain at the end of the conversation. Use it to compress early setup chatter while keeping recent work verbatim. ←PreviousNext→ The original messages stay in the session transcript either way, so Claude can still reference the details, and a Summarized conversation marker appears where the compressed messages were. To steer what the summary focuses on, highlight a Summarize option with the arrow keys and type instructions where the row reads add context (optional), then press Enter — picking the option with its number key summarizes immediately with no instructions. For the whole flow, see Context Management — /rewind's summarize actions are a scalpel where /compact is a broad brush. What you'll learn Summarize keeps you in the same session. To branch off and try a different approach while leaving the original session intact, use /branch or claude --continue --fork-session instead.

If you ran /clear earlier in the same Claude Code process, the rewind menu shows an extra entry at the top: /resume <session-id> (previous session). Select it to jump back to the conversation that was active before /clear. Last verified: 2026-10-09. That entry is available only until you exit Claude Code or resume a different session. Once it's gone, run /resume and pick the previous session from the list instead. Confirm against the official source.

Checkpoints feel magical until they don't. These gaps matter: Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Bash changes are invisible⌄ Files touched by shell commands Claude runs — rm, mv, cp, code generators, formatters — are NOT tracked. Only direct edits through Claude's file-editing tools are checkpointed. A deleted file from rm is gone as far as rewind is concerned. ←PreviousNext→ 2Most subagent edits are not restored⌄ A subagent edits with the same file tools, but your session usually doesn't capture those edits. The exception is a foreground forked skill (context: fork with background: false), which edits during your own turn and rewinds normally. Any other subagent — including a background forked skill, the default — needs Git to undo. See /docs/claude-code/subagents. ←PreviousNext→ 3External and concurrent changes are invisible⌄ Manual edits you make outside Claude Code, and edits from other concurrent sessions, are normally not captured — unless they happen to touch the same files the current session edited. ←PreviousNext→ 4Mid-turn messages get no checkpoint⌄ A message you queue while Claude is working that reaches it within the running turn joins that turn instead of starting a new one, so it gets no checkpoint of its own. To undo what followed it, rewind to the prompt that started the turn — which rewinds the whole turn, including work done before your message arrived. ←PreviousNext→ 5Symlinks and hard links are skipped⌄ Restore skips any tracked path that is a symlink or hard link and warns 'Restored the code, but skipped N files'; those files keep their current contents. Dotfile-manager symlinks and pnpm hard links both hit this. Run /debug before restoring to get the skipped paths named in the debug log. ←PreviousNext→ 6It is session-level, not history⌄ Checkpoints are quick, local recovery. They are not commits, not branches, and not shareable with your team. ←PreviousNext→
documents.s: Where checkpoints stop — the limits that bite

documents.t: They solve different problems, so pair them. Checkpoints (/rewind) Git Scope One session Whole project history Granularity Per turn-starting prompt, automatic Per commit, deliberate Tracks bash-made changes? No Yes (once staged/committed) Lifespan Last 100 checkpoints, swept ~30 days after the session Permanent Shareable / collaborative No Yes Mental model "Local undo" "Permanent history" Pro tip Commit working states with Git before a risky, wide-scale run — that's your durable floor. Use /rewind for fast in-session recovery between commits without polluting your Git history. If Claude will run destructive bash (rm/mv), generators, or background subagents, lean on Git — rewind won't save those files.

Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Exploring alternatives⌄ Try a bold implementation, and if you don't like it, restore code and conversation to the fork point and try another. ←PreviousNext→ 2Recovering from a bad edit⌄ An edit introduced a bug three prompts ago? Restore code to just before it instead of debugging the debris. ←PreviousNext→ 3Iterating on a feature⌄ Experiment with variations, always knowing a known-good state is one /rewind away. ←PreviousNext→ 4Freeing context space⌄ A verbose debugging detour ate your context window? Summarize from the midpoint forward and keep your original instructions in full detail. ←PreviousNext→ Check yourself 0/3 Key takeaways Checkpoints are automatic snapshots taken before each turn-starting prompt — a local undo for the session. The last 100 are kept, then swept ~30 days after the session. Open the rewind menu with /rewind or double-Esc on an empty input; it lists every prompt you sent. Restore actions undo state (code, conversation, or both); summarize actions compress context and never touch files. Bash-made, external, concurrent, and most subagent changes are NOT tracked — and symlinked or hard-linked paths are skipped on restore. Checkpoints complement Git, they don't replace it: think 'local undo' vs. 'permanent, shareable history'.

Copy as Markdown Beginner Last verified: 2026-10-06. Locations, load order and import syntax are from the official memory docs ("How Claude remembers your project"), which now describe two mechanisms: CLAUDE.md files you write and auto memory Claude writes itself. Imports resolve to a maximum depth of four hops. Confirm specifics there — these details change. Confirm against the official source. If you do one thing to make Claude Code better, do this. CLAUDE.md is a plain-text file Claude reads at the start of every session — your project's permanent briefing. What you'll learn Why CLAUDE.md is the single highest-leverage Claude Code setting How the memory hierarchy loads, from managed policy down to CLAUDE.local.md How auto memory differs from the CLAUDE.md you write How to generate a starting file with /init and trim it down What belongs in CLAUDE.md — and what to keep out How @imports let you reference docs without duplicating them

Without it, you re-explain your project every session ("we use pnpm, tests are in __tests__, don't touch /generated…"). With it, Claude already knows. Good instructions here improve every future interaction at once.

Claude Code loads memory from several locations and merges them in load order, broadest scope first — so a project instruction lands in context after a user instruction: Managed policy — org-wide instructions your IT/DevOps team ships. Path is per-OS: /Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/CLAUDE.md on macOS, /etc/claude-code/CLAUDE.md on Linux and WSL, C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\CLAUDE.md on Windows. User instructions (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md) — your personal preferences across every project. Project instructions (./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md, committed) — how this repo works. Shared with your team. If your repo uses AGENTS.md, that can load instead of or alongside these. Local instructions (./CLAUDE.local.md) — project-specific notes just for you, like a sandbox URL. Add it to .gitignore. Files in the directory hierarchy above your working directory load at launch; files in subdirectories load on demand, when Claude touches something in that area. Pro tip Outgrown one file? Split instructions into .claude/rules/*.md — one topic per file, discovered recursively. Rules without paths frontmatter load at launch with the same priority as .claude/CLAUDE.md; add paths frontmatter to load a rule only when Claude works on matching files, which saves context.

CLAUDE.md is the half of memory you write. Claude Code also keeps auto memory — notes Claude writes itself from your corrections and preferences, stored per repository and loaded into every session alongside your CLAUDE.md files. CLAUDE.md files Auto memory Who writes it You Claude What it holds Instructions and rules Learnings and patterns Scope Project, user, or org Per repository, shared across worktrees Both are context, not enforcement: Claude treats them as guidance it can weigh, not as configuration it must obey. To hard-block an action regardless of what Claude decides, use a PreToolUse hook instead. Watch out Auto memory loads only its first 200 lines or 25 KB — a bloated MEMORY.md silently truncates. See Context Budget Audit for the full startup cost breakdown.

Guided walkthrough1 of 3 1Run /init in the project⌄ Claude inspects the code and drafts a CLAUDE.md for you automatically. ←PreviousNext→ 2Edit it down⌄ The draft is a starting point, not the finish line. Trim it to what is true and useful. ←PreviousNext→ 3Borrow a template⌄ Grab a ready-made starter from the CLAUDE.md Templates page and adapt it to your repo. ←PreviousNext→ Generate a draft CLAUDE.md CopyOpen in Claude↗ /init Grab a ready-made starter from CLAUDE.md Templates.

What the project is, in two sentences. Tech stack and how to run / test / lint. Conventions Claude can't infer (naming, structure, commit style). Guardrails: "run tests before declaring done", "never edit /vendor", "never commit secrets".

Watch out Claude follows CLAUDE.md literally — stale, vague, or wishful instructions actively hurt. Describe how the project actually works today; short and true beats long and aspirational. Avoid giant pasted docs (use @imports instead), secrets, and rules you don't actually follow. Review it periodically so it stays accurate as the project evolves.
documents.s: What NOT to put in it

documents.t: Pull in existing docs instead of duplicating them — e.g. reference your style guide with an @path/to/file import so there's one source of truth. Relative and absolute paths both work; relative paths resolve against the file containing the import, not your working directory. Imported files can import others, to a maximum depth of four hops. Two syntax traps worth knowing before they bite: Spaces need backslashes. @Design\ Docs/api-conventions.md works; without the backslash the path stops at the first space. Wrapping it in quotes doesn't import the file at all. Backticks opt out. Import parsing skips code spans and fenced blocks, so `@README` stays literal text while @README on its own imports the file. That's how you mention a path without loading it. See the official memory docs for the full reference. Pro tip One source of truth: reference a file with @imports rather than pasting its contents into CLAUDE.md. If a doc already exists, link it — don't copy it. Copies drift out of date.

Check yourself 0/6 Key takeaways CLAUDE.md is the highest-leverage setting: it improves every future session at once. Memory loads broadest-first: managed policy, then user (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md), project (./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md), then local (./CLAUDE.local.md). Subdirectory files load on demand. Auto memory is the other half — Claude's own notes, per repository, loaded every session. Both are context, not enforcement: use a hook to hard-block something. Outgrown one file? Split it into .claude/rules/*.md and scope rules with paths frontmatter. Start with /init, then edit the draft down to what is actually true. Keep it short and true — use @imports (max four hops) for big docs, and never commit secrets.

Copy as Markdown Intermediate Last verified: 2026-10-07. Every command, flag, default and version floor below is from the official CLI reference, read on 2026-10-07. Flags appear and change between releases, and the reference states plainly that claude --help does not list every flag — so a flag missing from --help is not necessarily missing from your build. Check the reference, not the help text, and check your version with claude -v. Confirm against the official source. Most people learn three things about the Claude Code command line — claude, claude -c, and claude -p — and stop. That is a fair place to stop if you only ever sit in front of it. The moment you put Claude Code in a script, a CI job, a background queue, or a teammate's hands, the flags stop being conveniences and start being the difference between a run that costs a dollar and a run that hangs for an hour. This page is not a second copy of the reference table. It is the order to learn the surface in, the flags that materially change what happens, and the four traps that cost people real time. What you'll learn The six kinds of session you can start, and which flag picks each one The five-flag contract that makes an unattended run bounded, answerable, and parseable Why editing --append-system-prompt and re-running --continue appears to do nothing — the recorded-prompt rule How --bare, --safe-mode and --restricted differ, and which one to reach for when Driving background sessions from the shell: agents, attach, logs, respawn, rm, daemon The flag pairs people confuse: --tools vs --allowedTools vs --disallowedTools
documents.s: The claude CLI: Flags That Change Outcomes

documents.t: Every other decision follows from this one. Claude Code can start six materially different things, and the flag that picks one is usually the first thing you type. You want Flag It gives you A conversation you watch (none) Interactive session in this terminal One answer, then exit -p / --print Non-interactive run, output to stdout Work that outlives this terminal --bg / --background A background session; prints its ID and how to manage it An isolated branch to experiment on -w / --worktree A git worktree under <repo>/.claude/worktrees/<name> Work on Anthropic's machines --cloud A cloud session, or a follow-up queued into an existing one To drive this session from your phone --rc / --remote-control An interactive session also controllable from claude.ai or the Claude app Two of these can't be combined: --bg and -p are mutually exclusive, because one returns immediately and the other waits for an answer. If you want a shell command rather than a Claude session in the background, pair --bg with --exec: Run the test suite as a background job, not a Claude session CopyOpen in Claude↗ claude --bg --exec 'pytest -x' And --bg checks workspace trust for the directory before it starts — so a background session in an untrusted repo fails up front rather than halfway through.
documents.s: Start with the question: what kind of session is this?

documents.t: This is the highest-value thing on this page. An unattended claude -p run has three ways to go wrong that an interactive session simply doesn't have: it can stall on permission prompts nobody is there to answer, it can loop far longer than you expected, and it can emit prose when your script needed data. Five flags close all three. Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Run non-interactively — -p⌄ `claude -p "query"` prints the answer and exits. Everything below is print-mode only, so this flag is the gate for the rest. ←PreviousNext→ 2Decide who answers permission prompts — --permission-prompts⌄ The default is `host`, which sends prompts to the Agent SDK host or to a `--permission-prompt-tool`. Pass `--permission-prompts none` when nobody can answer, as in a cron job or CI step: the run stops consulting or waiting on a host, anything that would prompt is denied unless a `PermissionRequest` hook allows it, and Claude is told not to retry. A `-p` run with no host at all already denies those requests; there the flag mainly stops the retries. Requires v2.1.259 or later. Pair it with narrow `--allowedTools` rules so the denials are rare rather than constant. ←PreviousNext→ 3Bound the loop — --max-turns⌄ There is no turn limit by default. `--max-turns 3` exits with an error when the limit is reached. Use it as a tripwire for runaway agentic loops, not as a budget. ←PreviousNext→ 4Bound the spend — --max-budget-usd⌄ `--max-budget-usd 5.00` stops once the client-side cost estimate reaches the cap. Subagent spend counts toward it; once reached, spawning another subagent fails with `Budget limit reached` and running background subagents are stopped. Cap enforcement requires v2.1.217 or later. ←PreviousNext→ 5Make the output parseable — --output-format or --json-schema⌄ `--output-format json` gives you a structured envelope. `--json-schema '<schema>'` goes further: Claude Code validates the final answer against your JSON Schema and errors on an invalid schema up front, so your script never has to regex prose. ←PreviousNext→ A CI step that cannot hang, cannot loop forever, and cannot overspend CopyOpen in Claude↗ claude -p "Review the staged diff and list bugs" \ --permission-prompts none \ --allowedTools "Read" "Bash(git diff *)" \ --max-turns 6 \ --max-budget-usd 2.00 \ --output-format json --max-budget-usd is an estimate, not your invoice Claude Code checks the cap against its own client-side cost estimate, which can differ from what you are billed. When you return to a conversation with --continue or --resume, totals restored from earlier runs do not count toward the cap — so three resumed runs under a $2 cap can spend more than $2 in total. Treat it as a circuit breaker for one run. For a real ceiling on a whole account or project, see Hard Spend Caps. For the full posture around letting a run proceed without a human — what to allow, what to mask, what to log — see Hardening Autonomous Runs and Headless Mode & the Agent SDK. For provider-level ceilings, Hard Spend Caps.
documents.s: The five-flag contract for unattended runs

documents.t: Five flags shape the system prompt. Four set its text; the fifth decides whether the conversation keeps the text it started with. Flag What it does --system-prompt Replaces the entire default prompt with your text --system-prompt-file Replaces it with a file's contents --append-system-prompt Appends your text to the default prompt --append-system-prompt-file Appends a file's contents to the default prompt --system-prompt-snapshot off rebuilds the prompt on every request; on (the default) reuses the recorded one The choice between append and replace is a choice about identity. Appending keeps Claude Code's default tool guidance, safety instructions, and coding conventions, and layers your rules on top — right for per-run instructions, output formatting, or project context. Replacing drops all of that, including the tool guidance, which makes it right only when the surface genuinely isn't a coding assistant: a non-coding agent in a pipeline nobody watches. If you replace, you own whatever the task still needs. You can combine them. Passing an append flag together with a replace flag replaces the default and then appends your text. From v2.1.283 you can also pass a flag together with its own file form — --append-system-prompt and --append-system-prompt-file — and Claude Code uses both, with the file's contents first regardless of the order you typed them. The trap: a resumed conversation reuses the prompt it was born with Claude Code builds the system prompt once, on a conversation's first request, and records it in the session. Until the conversation is compacted, every later request uses that recorded prompt — including after --resume or --continue. So you edit your --append-system-prompt text, re-run claude --continue, and nothing changes. The flag is not broken; the conversation is still using the recording. New text takes effect once the conversation compacts, or in a brand-new conversation. To iterate on wording across --continue runs, pass --system-prompt-snapshot off and the prompt is rebuilt every request. Requires v2.1.257 or later. There is one more trick worth knowing in a replacement prompt that mixes stable instructions with per-run context. Put a line containing only __SYSTEM_PROMPT_DYNAMIC_BOUNDARY__ between them: Claude Code splits at the first such line and removes it, so the part above stays cached while the part below changes. Requires v2.1.275 or later. Why that matters for your bill is the subject of Prompt Caching. And for multi-user scripted workloads, --exclude-dynamic-system-prompt-sections moves per-user context, such as the auto-memory location, out of the system prompt and into the first user message — so the same task on different machines shares one cached prefix. It applies only to the default prompt and is ignored when you set --system-prompt or --system-prompt-file.
documents.s: The system-prompt family, and the trap in it

documents.t: People reach for these interchangeably and then wonder why the symptom didn't move. They solve three different problems. --bare --safe-mode --restricted The problem it solves Startup is too slow for a scripted call My configuration is broken and I don't know which part An eval harness must not touch this shared machine CLAUDE.md, skills, commands, subagents, plugins, MCP, auto memory Not discovered Not loaded Only managed settings and --settings load Built-in tools Bash, file read, file edit Work normally Command/code-running tools and WebFetch removed unless named individually in --tools File access Normal Normal Confined to the working directories bypassPermissions Allowed Allowed Refused Managed policy Applies Still applies, including policy hooks and status line Applies Side effect Sets CLAUDE_CODE_SIMPLE Sets CLAUDE_CODE_SAFE_MODE Refuses to create cloud sessions Read the table as a progression of intent: --bare is about speed, --safe-mode is about diagnosis, --restricted is about containment. One useful detail: skills in a directory you pass with --add-dir still load under --bare, which is how you keep exactly one capability in an otherwise-stripped run. --safe-mode is the one to reach for first when something is misbehaving and you can't tell whether it's Claude Code or your own configuration — including when you're trying to work out whether a customization is what's triggering automatic model fallback. Pair it with claude doctor, which prints read-only installation and settings diagnostics without starting a session at all. (The in-session /doctor command is a different thing: it can also apply fixes.) More symptom-first debugging in Troubleshooting Claude Code. --restricted requires v2.1.248 or later.
documents.s: Three flags that turn things off, and they are not the same

documents.t: Once you start sessions with --bg, the terminal becomes a control plane. The whole lifecycle has a command, and none of it requires opening the interactive UI. Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1See what is running — claude agents⌄ Opens the agent view to monitor and dispatch parallel background sessions. For scripting, `--json` prints active sessions as a JSON array, and `--json --all` includes completed ones. `--cwd <path>` narrows to sessions started under that directory. Opening the view itself needs an interactive terminal; the JSON form does not. ←PreviousNext→ 2Look inside one — claude logs⌄ `claude logs <id|name>` prints recent output from a background session. From v2.1.290 you can pass part of a running session's name instead of its ID — so `claude logs auth` is usually enough. ←PreviousNext→ 3Take it over — claude attach⌄ `claude attach <id|name>` brings a background session into this terminal. Partial-name matching also requires v2.1.290 or later. ←PreviousNext→ 4Restart it — claude respawn⌄ `claude respawn <id>` restarts a session, running or stopped, with its conversation intact. `--all` restarts every running session — the move after upgrading the Claude Code binary. ←PreviousNext→ 5Stop and clean up — claude stop, claude rm⌄ `claude stop <id>` (also `claude kill`) halts a session. `claude rm <id>` removes it from the list; the transcript stays on your machine and is still reachable through `claude --resume`. If removal is refused over the session's worktree, the refusal prints the exact flag to pass next — `--discard-unpushed` (v2.1.260+) or `--force-remove-worktree` (v2.1.268+). ←PreviousNext→ 6When the whole thing is wedged — claude daemon⌄ Background sessions are hosted by a supervisor process. `claude daemon status` prints its state, version, socket directory and worker count, and exits 1 if it isn't running. `claude daemon logs` follows `~/.claude/daemon.log`. `claude daemon stop --any --keep-workers` restarts the supervisor while leaving the sessions alive for the next one to reconnect to. ←PreviousNext→ The counterpart to this from inside a session — how work gets backgrounded, and what carries over when it does — is Background Tasks, /loop & Scheduling.
documents.s: Driving background sessions from the shell

documents.t: Six confusions worth pre-empting --tools restricts which built-in tools exist. --allowedTools says which calls skip the permission prompt. --disallowedTools denies calls. They are three different jobs, and passing the wrong one is the most common cause of "why is it still asking me". --tools does not affect MCP tools at all. To remove those too, add --disallowedTools "mcp__*". A bare name in --disallowedTools removes the tool from Claude's context; a scoped rule like Bash(rm *) leaves the tool available and denies only matching calls. --dangerously-skip-permissions starts in bypassPermissions. --allow-dangerously-skip-permissions only adds that mode to the Shift+Tab cycle, so you can start in plan mode and switch later. The second is almost always what you actually wanted. --add-dir grants file access, but Claude Code does not discover most .claude/ configuration from those directories. Adding a directory is not the same as adopting its config. --desktop takes no prompt and no other flags except --verbose and the --debug flags, because the Desktop app starts the session itself. Requires v2.1.285 or later. One small quality-of-life detail: mistype a subcommand and Claude Code suggests the closest match and exits without starting a session — claude udpate prints Did you mean claude update? rather than opening a conversation you didn't want.
documents.s: The flag pairs people get wrong

documents.t: Check yourself 0/3 Key takeaways Pick the session kind first — the flag that does that constrains every other flag you can pass. An unattended run needs five flags, not one: -p, --permission-prompts none, --max-turns, --max-budget-usd, and a structured output format. Treat --max-budget-usd as a circuit breaker for one run, not as a bill ceiling. It is a client-side estimate and resumed totals escape it. Conversations record their system prompt on the first request. If a prompt edit seems ignored, that is why — use --system-prompt-snapshot off while iterating. --bare is speed, --safe-mode is diagnosis, --restricted is containment. Reaching for the wrong one wastes an afternoon. --help is incomplete by design. The CLI reference is the source of truth, and version floors matter — check claude -v before blaming a flag.

Copy as Markdown Intermediate A Claude Code project accumulates context debt the way a laptop accumulates browser tabs. Every skill you installed adds a line to a listing Claude re-reads on every turn. Every subagent adds a description. Every CLAUDE.md paragraph you wrote in March loads in September whether the task needs it or not. And every npm test dumps up to 30,000 characters into the conversation. None of it is visible until the session starts forgetting instructions or the bill stops matching the work. Context management covers the two commands you use in the moment, /clear and /compact. This page is the audit you run once per project: six places where Claude Code spends context before you type anything or between your turns, the setting that governs each, and the number it defaults to. Everything here is in the official docs as of September 2026, and most of the knobs are newer than the folklore about them. What you'll learn Measure before you cut: read /context, /usage attribution, and /doctor's listing estimate so you fix the biggest line item first Prune the skill listing with /skill-doctor (v2.1.252+) and the four skillOverrides states, and know the 1%-of-window budget the listing is capped at Cap what a shell command or background task returns inline (30,000 and 32,000 characters by default) with bashOutputMaxChars and taskOutputMaxChars Stop paying for CLAUDE.md in every subagent with omitClaudeMd (v2.1.271+) and keep subagent descriptions under the 15,000-token warning line Set the auto-compact window on purpose (/autocompact, autoCompactWindow) and understand the 25,000-token budget that decides which invoked skills survive compaction Cap effort fleet-wide with maxEffortLevel when thinking tokens, not context, are the real bill Last verified: 2026-09-15. Setting names, defaults, ranges, and minimum versions from the Claude Code settings reference (autoCompactWindow, bashOutputMaxChars, taskOutputMaxChars, maxEffortLevel, skillListingBudgetFraction, skillOverrides, disableBundledSkills). /skill-doctor behavior, the 1% listing budget, the 1,536-character description cap, and the 25,000-token re-attach budget from the skills docs. Bash inline limits from the tools reference. omitClaudeMd, the 15,000-token description warning, and what a subagent loads from the subagents docs. CLAUDE.md and cost guidance from Manage costs. Model context sizes are not repeated here; see Models and pricing. Confirm against the official source.

documents.t: Two facts make this diagram actionable. Everything in the left box is paid on every request, because Claude Code sends the full conversation each turn and only the cache-read discount softens it. And the right box is where a single verbose command can add more than the whole left box in one step. The audit below works left to right.
documents.s: What is in the window before you type

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 9 1Measure: /context, /usage, /doctor⌄ Run /context for a live breakdown by category with optimization suggestions, including which CLAUDE.md and auto-memory files loaded. On a Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise plan, /usage attributes recent usage to skills, subagents, plugins, and individual MCP servers as percentages, and flags behaviors (long context, cache misses) that account for 10% or more. /doctor estimates the skill listing's context cost and its biggest contributors. Write the three biggest line items down before changing anything. ←PreviousNext→ 2Prune the skill listing with /skill-doctor⌄ Every skill in the listing costs context on every turn whether or not Claude uses it. /skill-doctor (v2.1.252+) shows each skill's context cost and invocation frequency, flags skills never invoked, and tells you where to turn them off; it also lists plugins you have not used recently. Start with the highest-cost unused ones. Interactive sessions open the report in the /plugin manager's Stats tab; with -p it prints as text. It does not cover bundled or enterprise skills, needs feature-flag fetching, and refuses over Remote Control. ←PreviousNext→ 3Collapse, do not delete, with skillOverrides⌄ Four states per skill: on (name and description listed), name-only (listed without description, still invocable), user-invocable-only (hidden from Claude, still in the / menu), off. The /skills menu writes this for you: highlight a skill, press Space to cycle, Esc to save to .claude/settings.local.json. Plugin skills are managed through /plugin instead. Setting disableBundledSkills: true removes Claude Code's own bundled skills and workflows in one line. ←PreviousNext→ 4Know the listing budget and the description cap⌄ The listing is capped at 1% of the model's context window (skillListingBudgetFraction, default 0.01). When it overflows, Claude Code keeps every name but drops descriptions starting with the least-used skills, which strips the keywords Claude needs to auto-select them. Each skill's description plus when_to_use is also cut at 1,536 characters (skillListingMaxDescChars). Put the key use case in the first sentence. ←PreviousNext→ 5Shrink what loads at startup⌄ Keep CLAUDE.md under 200 lines and move workflow-specific instructions (PR review, migrations) into skills, which load only when invoked. Auto memory loads only its first 200 lines or 25 KB, so a bloated MEMORY.md silently truncates. Subagent descriptions are read every turn: when the combined descriptions of your custom subagents pass 15,000 tokens, Claude Code warns at startup. Move detail into each subagent's system prompt, which loads only when it runs. ←PreviousNext→ 6Cap tool output inline⌄ A successful Bash or PowerShell command returns up to roughly 30,000 characters inline by default; past that Claude gets a short preview plus a file path and reads the file on demand. A failing command returns up to 10,000 characters as a head-and-tail excerpt. bashOutputMaxChars (v2.1.261+, clamped to 4,000–128,000) sets the inline ceiling and read-back window together and makes Claude Code ignore BASH_MAX_OUTPUT_LENGTH. taskOutputMaxChars does the same for background tasks read with TaskOutput (default 32,000, same range). Lower them on projects with chatty build tools; raise them only when Claude keeps opening the saved file anyway. ←PreviousNext→ 7Stop paying for CLAUDE.md in every subagent⌄ A non-fork subagent loads every level of your CLAUDE.md hierarchy plus a git-status snapshot, on top of its own prompt. The built-in Explore and Plan agents skip both. For custom subagents that get everything from the delegation prompt, set omitClaudeMd: true in the frontmatter (v2.1.271+): user, project, and local CLAUDE.md files are skipped; managed policy files still load. Ignored when the agent runs as the main session agent. For large shared instructions in headless runs, pass --append-subagent-system-prompt-file (v2.1.261+) instead of stuffing them into every description. ←PreviousNext→ 8Set the auto-compact window on purpose⌄ autoCompactWindow is a token count from 100,000 to 1,000,000, capped at your model's window; unset means Claude Code picks a window tuned for the model. /autocompact 500k writes it to user settings; --autocompact overrides for one session; CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW overrides both. CLAUDE_AUTOCOMPACT_PCT_OVERRIDE (1–100) can only lower the trigger point. After compaction, invoked skills are re-attached at up to 5,000 tokens each within a 25,000-token total, most recent first, so older skills can be dropped entirely. If a skill must survive, re-invoke it after /compact. ←PreviousNext→ 9Cap effort when thinking is the bill, not context⌄ Thinking tokens are billed as output. maxEffortLevel (v2.1.267+) caps the effort any session can use: one of low, medium, high, xhigh, or max (max = no cap). It applies before every request on every provider, the lowest cap across scopes wins, and a cap below xhigh disables ultracode. Per-model caps go in modelSettings. Deploy through managed settings to enforce for an organization. ←PreviousNext→

Project-local context caps (.claude/settings.local.json) CopyOpen in Claude↗ { "bashOutputMaxChars": 12000, "taskOutputMaxChars": 12000, "skillOverrides": { "legacy-migration-notes": "name-only", "deploy-prod": "user-invocable-only", "old-design-system": "off" }, "autoCompactWindow": 500000, "maxEffortLevel": "high" } Read it top to bottom as decisions, not defaults. The two output caps assume a chatty test runner; drop them back toward the 30,000 / 32,000 defaults if Claude starts opening the saved output file on every run. The three overrides keep the skills reachable without paying for their descriptions. The compaction window is an explicit choice for a 1M-context model where you would rather compact at half than at the model-tuned point. The effort cap is the one line here that changes output quality, so set it last and only after /usage shows thinking tokens dominating. Subagent that does not load CLAUDE.md (.claude/agents/repo-auditor.md) CopyOpen in Claude↗ --- name: repo-auditor description: Audits a repository for dead code and unused exports. Use for read-only sweeps. tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash model: sonnet omitClaudeMd: true --- You are a read-only auditor. Everything you need is in the delegation prompt. Report findings as a table of path, symbol, and evidence. Do not edit files. Run the skill report in a headless session CopyOpen in Claude↗ claude -p "/skill-doctor"
documents.s: A settings block you can paste

documents.t: Watch out Deleting skills instead of collapsing them. name-only keeps a skill invocable at near-zero listing cost; off removes it from the / menu too. Most 'unused' skills should become name-only, not disappear. Raising bashOutputMaxChars to the 128,000 ceiling because one build log overflowed. That makes every future command up to 4× more expensive inline. Filter the log with a PreToolUse hook (grep for FAIL, head -100) instead; the costs docs show the exact hook. Setting autoCompactWindow above the model's context. Claude Code caps it at the window silently, so the setting looks applied and does nothing. Assuming a subagent is cheap because its context is separate. Its startup still includes every CLAUDE.md level and a git snapshot unless it is Explore, Plan, or sets omitClaudeMd. Reading /skill-doctor over Remote Control from a phone. It returns 'Skill usage reports are not available on this connection.' Run it in the terminal where the session lives. Expecting an invoked skill to survive /compact. Only the most recent invocations fit in the 25,000-token re-attach budget, at 5,000 tokens each. Re-invoke the ones you still need.

Check yourself 0/6 Key takeaways Measure first: /context for the live breakdown, /usage for attribution by skill, subagent, plugin, and MCP server, /doctor for the listing estimate. The skill listing is a per-turn tax capped at 1% of the window. /skill-doctor tells you what to collapse; name-only keeps a skill usable at near-zero cost. Tool output is the fastest way to blow a window: ~30,000 characters inline per successful command, 32,000 per background task. Cap with bashOutputMaxChars / taskOutputMaxChars, or filter with a hook. Subagents are not free at startup: every CLAUDE.md level plus git status, unless Explore, Plan, or omitClaudeMd. Keep custom descriptions under 15,000 tokens combined. Compaction keeps only the most recent invoked skills (5,000 each, 25,000 total). Set autoCompactWindow deliberately, and re-invoke what must survive. When thinking tokens dominate the bill, maxEffortLevel caps effort fleet-wide; lowest scope wins and it holds on every provider.

Copy as Markdown Intermediate What you'll learn Tell /clear and /compact apart and pick the right one instantly Understand auto-compaction and why proactive clearing still beats it Apply four techniques to keep long sessions sharp Recognize the symptoms of a full context window and fix them fast Last verified: 2026-07-20. Command names like /compact and /clear and auto-compaction behaviour can change — confirm in the official docs. Confirm against the official source.
Every session has a finite context window. As it fills, older content gets squeezed and Claude can start to "drift." Managing context deliberately is what keeps long sessions sharp.
Two commands cover almost every situation. The trick is matching the command to your intent. Decide with one question: is this a new task or the same one?

When context approaches the limit, Claude Code can auto-compact so work continues without a hard stop. It's a safety net — but proactively /clear-ing between tasks gives better results than relying on it. Pro tip Treat auto-compaction as a backstop, not a strategy. Clearing between unrelated tasks keeps context cleaner than letting the window fill until auto-compaction kicks in.

Beyond the two commands, four habits keep your context lean from the start. Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1One task per session⌄ Don't let an afternoon of unrelated work pile into one context. ←PreviousNext→ 2Delegate heavy reading to subagents⌄ Hand large reads to subagents — they burn THEIR context and return only the conclusion. See /docs/claude-code/subagents. ←PreviousNext→ 3Reference, don't paste⌄ Point Claude at files with @path instead of pasting large blobs, and keep CLAUDE.md lean (see /docs/claude-code/claude-md). ←PreviousNext→ 4Watch the budget⌄ A statusline showing context use tells you when to compact. See /docs/claude-code/statusline. ←PreviousNext→ These map to live docs: subagents, CLAUDE.md, and statusline. :::tip Symptom → fix If Claude starts forgetting an earlier instruction or repeating itself, the window is likely full. /compact (same task) or /clear (new task) usually fixes it instantly. More in Why Did Claude Do That?. If you instead hit Autocompact is thrashing, compaction is working and something oversized keeps refilling the window — see Troubleshooting Claude Code. ::: Key takeaways /clear wipes the conversation for a fresh start — use it for unrelated tasks /compact summarizes the session to free space — use it to continue the same task when the window fills Auto-compaction is a safety net; proactive /clear between tasks gives better results Keep context lean: one task per session, delegate heavy reading to subagents, reference files instead of pasting, and watch the budget via a statusline Forgetting or repetition means a full window — /compact (same task) or /clear (new task) fixes it Check yourself 0/4

Copy as Markdown Intermediate Last verified: 2026-08-27. /design is a research preview (shipped week 34, Aug 17–21, 2026). Version gates, plan availability, and behavior can move — confirm in the Claude Code whats-new digest before relying on any specific detail. Confirm against the official source. Anthropic dropped a slash command into Claude Code that skips coding on purpose. /design publishes a canvas of editable UI artboards from a plain-English brief; you pick one, tweak it, and only then does Claude turn it into real code. It is the first Claude Code feature where the deliverable is not code — the design phase is the artifact. What you'll learn Understand what an artboard is and why it changes the coding-first flow Run /design correctly on the first try (version, plan, prompt shape) Know the three phases: draft → pick+edit → implement Avoid the three known traps: token cost, style drift from your repo, and the free-tier wall Pair /design with the Concise output style that shipped the same week

/design is a skill — not a plain slash command. When you invoke it, Claude Code hands off to Claude Design's artboard workflow and prints a link to a published canvas. An artboard is a working screen you can act on: change the color, move a block, widen a gap. It is rendered on the artifacts runtime, so it lives in your Claude account, not as files in your repo. That distinction matters. The output of /design is a URL, not a diff. Nothing lands in git status until you tell Claude to implement. What you'll learn Availability: Pro, Max, Team, Enterprise. Not free. Requires Claude Code v2.1.233 or later. Ships in both the CLI and Claude Code Desktop. Status: research preview — expect the invocation shape, output format, and included artboard count to shift.

Guided walkthrough1 of 3 1Draft — describe the screen, not the layout⌄ Run /design with a brief that says what the screen is for. Claude publishes several artboard variants side by side, each editable. You get a link; open it in a browser. ←PreviousNext→ 2Pick and edit — iterate on the canvas⌄ Choose the variant closest to what you want. Edit inline (colors, spacing, layout) or keep iterating in the same Claude Code thread with prompts like 'make the hero bolder' — the thread keeps context so you don't restate the brief. ←PreviousNext→ 3Implement — hand off to code⌄ Tell Claude which artboard to implement. It writes the code into your repo, using the artboard as ground truth for layout and copy. ←PreviousNext→

/design rewards briefs that describe purpose and audience, not pixel targets. Two patterns: /design — feature brief CopyOpen in Claude↗ /design a few options for the sign-in screen. Users are engineers on mobile. Optimize for one-hand thumb reach; SSO is the primary path, email/password secondary. Show a state for a locked-out account. /design — redesign an existing surface CopyOpen in Claude↗ /design redesign our composer based on what people actually use it for: drafting long messages, attaching files, and switching model. The current version buries the model picker; make it a first-class control. Two things that quietly do a lot of work in those briefs: Naming the user and constraint ("engineers on mobile", "one-hand thumb reach") pulls Claude off the statistical-average layout it defaults to. Naming a failure state ("locked-out account") forces the artboard to cover empty/error/edge cases, not just the happy path.

1. It is token-hungry. Multiple full-fidelity artboards per invocation eats budget faster than a normal chat turn. Research-preview users report this consistently. Save /design for real decisions, not throwaway sketches. 2. It does not match your codebase. Claude Design generates from a generic aesthetic, not from your existing components. If you want the artboard to feel like the rest of your app, front-load a DESIGN.md at the repo root (fonts, spacing scale, color tokens, existing components) and reference it in the brief — the same trick that keeps /design's implementation phase from re-inventing your button primitives. Reference DESIGN.md before /design CopyOpen in Claude↗ Before you draft anything, read DESIGN.md and list the type scale, spacing scale, and named color tokens you'll use. Then /design a settings screen that respects those tokens. 3. Free-tier wall. /design is gated behind paid plans (Pro and up). If your team pays for Claude Code seats but a contractor is on free, /design silently isn't there for them.

Anthropic shipped the built-in Concise output style the same week (v2.1.237). It makes Claude lead with results and skip preamble — a good pair for /design, because the handoff turn ("implement option 2") does not need narration: ~/.claude/settings.json { "outputStyle": "Concise" } Concise still keeps full detail for error reports, security warnings, and destructive-action confirmations — you lose narration, not safety rails.
documents.s: Pair it with Concise output style

documents.t: Use /design when Skip it when The visual decision is the hard part (new surface, unclear layout) You already know the layout; you just need the code You want to compare 3+ directions cheaply before committing You are iterating on an existing screen's logic, not shape The stakeholder needs a clickable-ish artifact to approve The screen must match an existing design system 1:1 The failure/empty/loading states matter You are prototyping throwaway internal tooling
documents.s: When /design wins vs. writing code directly

documents.t: The canvas URL is shareable. Because artboards live on artifacts, the link works for anyone with access to your Claude account view — you can send it to a designer or PM without exporting anything. Iteration is dual-channel. You can edit on the canvas and keep prompting in the Claude Code thread. Both feed the same context. Implementation still respects your repo. Once you say "implement", Claude Code goes back to normal repo-aware behavior — it will use your Tailwind config, your components, your file structure. The artboard is the target; your codebase is the terrain. Check yourself 0/4

Copy as Markdown Advanced Last verified: 2026-08-08. Dynamic workflows are a fast-moving feature: the trigger keyword, approval options, agent caps, and availability change between Claude Code releases — confirm specifics in the official docs. They require Claude Code v2.1.154+ and a paid plan. Confirm against the official source. What you'll learn Tell a workflow apart from subagents, skills, and agent teams by who holds the plan See one in 30 seconds with the bundled /deep-research command Start your own three ways: the ultracode keyword, /effort ultracode, or a saved command Know what the approval prompt is protecting you from before you press Yes Keep cost and unattended runs under control with slicing and the allowlist A dynamic workflow is a JavaScript script that orchestrates subagents at scale. You describe a task; Claude writes the script; a runtime executes it in the background while your session stays responsive. Where a normal multi-step task lives turn-by-turn in Claude's context window, a workflow moves the plan into code — the loop, the branching, and every intermediate result live in script variables, so your context holds only the final answer. That single shift is what makes workflows scale to dozens or hundreds of agents in one run, where ordinary delegation tops out at a handful.

Claude Code gives you four ways to run multi-step work. The real question is who holds the plan: Subagents Skills Agent teams Workflows What it is A worker Claude spawns Instructions Claude follows A lead supervising peer sessions A script the runtime executes Who decides what runs next Claude, turn by turn Claude, per the prompt The lead, turn by turn The script Where results live Context window Context window A shared task list Script variables Scale A few per turn Same as subagents A handful of peers Dozens to hundreds On interruption Restarts the turn Restarts the turn Teammates keep running Resumable in-session Use a workflow when a task needs more agents than one conversation can coordinate, or when you want the orchestration codified as a script you can read and rerun. Canonical cases: A codebase-wide bug sweep — fan a finder across every module, then have independent agents adversarially verify each finding before it's reported. A 500-file migration — one agent per file, each in its own worktree, with a verification stage. A research question where sources must be cross-checked against each other, not just summarized. A hard plan worth drafting from several independent angles, then weighed against each other before you commit. That last point is the underrated one: a workflow can apply a repeatable quality pattern (adversarial review, multi-angle drafting, majority-vote verification), so you get a more trustworthy result than a single pass — not just more agents.
documents.s: When to reach for a workflow

documents.t: Claude Code ships a built-in workflow so you don't have to write one to try the model. Run it on any question: Try a workflow in one command CopyOpen in Claude↗ /deep-research What changed in the Node.js permission model between v20 and v22? It fans web searches across several angles, fetches and cross-checks the sources, votes on each claim, and returns a cited report with claims that didn't survive cross-checking filtered out. Approve when prompted, then watch it work with /workflows. (It needs the WebSearch tool available.)
documents.s: The fastest way to see one: /deep-research

documents.t: 1. Ask in one prompt. Include the keyword ultracode, or just ask in plain words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow"). Claude writes a script for that single task without changing your session's effort level: Run one task as a workflow CopyOpen in Claude↗ ultracode: audit every API endpoint under src/routes/ for missing auth checks The keyword is highlighted in your input. Didn't mean it? Press Option+W (macOS) or Alt+W (Windows/Linux) to dismiss the highlight for that prompt. :::note Keyword history Before v2.1.160 the literal trigger word was workflow; it was renamed to ultracode so the common word "workflow" wouldn't fire a run. Natural-language requests ("run a workflow") work in both versions. ::: 2. Let Claude decide — ultracode effort. Set the session to ultracode and Claude plans a workflow for every substantive task, deciding on its own when one is warranted: Turn on automatic orchestration for the session CopyOpen in Claude↗ /effort ultracode Ultracode combines xhigh reasoning effort with automatic orchestration. A single request can become several workflows in a row — one to understand the code, one to make the change, one to verify it. Every task then uses more tokens and takes longer, so drop back with /effort high for routine work. It lasts only the current session. 3. Run a saved or bundled command. /deep-research, or any workflow you've saved (below), appears in / autocomplete like any slash command.
documents.s: Three ways to start your own

documents.t: Workflows can spawn a lot of agents, so the CLI shows you the planned phases and asks first: Yes, run it — start the run Yes, and don't ask again for [name] in [path] — start and skip the prompt for this workflow in this project View raw script (Ctrl+G opens it in your editor) — read before deciding No — cancel (Tab lets you tweak the prompt first) Whether you're prompted depends on your permission mode: Default / accept-edits prompts every run (unless you opted out for that workflow); Auto prompts on first launch only; bypass / claude -p / Agent SDK never prompt — the run starts immediately. :::warning The subagents don't inherit your session's mode Whatever your session's permission mode, the agents a workflow spawns always run in acceptEdits and inherit your tool allowlist — file edits are auto-approved. Shell commands, web fetches, and MCP tools not on your allowlist can still pause the run to prompt you. On a long unattended run, add the commands the agents need to your allowlist before starting so it doesn't stall waiting on you. See Hardening Autonomous Runs. :::

The runtime runs the script in an isolated environment, separate from your conversation — intermediate results stay in script variables, never touching Claude's context. The script itself has no direct filesystem or shell access: the agents read, write, and run commands; the script only coordinates them. Every run writes its script to a file under your session directory in ~/.claude/projects/, and Claude gets the path. So you can ask Claude for the script, read the orchestration it wrote, diff it against a previous run, or edit it and ask Claude to relaunch from your edited version. The runtime enforces a few caps so a bad script can't run away: Constraint Why No mid-run user input (only agent permission prompts pause it) For sign-off between stages, run each stage as its own workflow Script has no direct filesystem/shell access Agents do the work; the script coordinates Up to 16 concurrent agents (fewer on low-core machines) Bounds local resource use 1,000 agents total per run Prevents runaway loops

Run /workflows to list running and completed runs, then select one to open its progress view — each phase with its agent count, token total, and elapsed time. Drill into a phase, then an agent, to read its prompt, recent tool calls, and result. Key controls: Key Action ↑ / ↓ Select a phase or agent Enter / → Drill in; Esc backs out f Filter agents by status (v2.1.186+) p Pause or resume the run x Stop the selected agent — or the whole run when focus is on it r Restart the selected running agent s Save this run's script as a command A one-line progress summary also appears in the task panel below your input box; press down-arrow to focus it, Enter to expand. Resume: stop a run and resume it later (p) — agents that already finished return cached results, the rest run live. Resume works within the same session; exit Claude Code mid-run and the next session starts it fresh.

When Claude writes a good orchestration for something you'll repeat — a review you run on every branch — press s in /workflows to save that run's script. Tab toggles where: .claude/workflows/ in your project — shared with everyone who clones the repo ~/.claude/workflows/ in your home — available everywhere, only you see it It then runs as /[name] in future sessions. A saved workflow can take input via an args global, so you parameterize it at call time instead of editing the script: > Run /triage-issues on issues 1024, 1025, and 1030 Claude passes the list as structured data, so the script calls array/object methods on args directly.

A workflow spawns many agents, so one run can use meaningfully more tokens than doing the same task in conversation, and it counts toward your plan's usage and rate limits. Two habits keep this sane: Slice first. Run on one directory (not the whole repo) or a narrow question first to gauge spend; /workflows shows per-agent token usage live, and you can stop anytime without losing completed work. Right-size the model. Every agent uses your session's model unless the script routes a stage elsewhere. Check /model before a large run, and when you describe the task, ask Claude to use a smaller model for stages that don't need the strongest one. See Cost & Latency and Choosing a Model.

Expecting a human-in-the-loop mid-run. There's no mid-run input. If a task needs your sign-off between stages, split it into separate workflows. Forgetting the allowlist on unattended runs. A long workflow stalls the moment an agent hits a non-allowlisted shell command. Pre-authorize what the agents need. Reaching for a workflow when a subagent would do. A few delegated tasks per turn is what subagents are for. Workflows earn their overhead at fleet scale or when you want the orchestration saved as a rerunnable script. Running ultracode effort all session for routine edits. It plans a workflow for everything — great for hard work, wasteful for a one-line fix. Drop to /effort high. Check yourself 0/3 Key takeaways A workflow moves the plan into code — the script holds the loop and intermediate results, so runs scale to dozens or hundreds of agents. Try one instantly with /deep-research; start your own with the ultracode keyword, /effort ultracode, or a saved /command. The approval prompt exists because a run can spawn many agents — Default and accept-edits prompt every run; Auto prompts once; bypass and headless never prompt. Spawned agents run in acceptEdits with your allowlist, so pre-authorize the commands they need before an unattended run. Workflows cost meaningfully more tokens — slice first, right-size the model per stage, and drop ultracode effort back to /effort high for routine edits.

Toggle Dynamic workflows off in /config, set "disableWorkflows": true in ~/.claude/settings.json, or set the CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_WORKFLOWS=1 environment variable. Organizations can disable them in managed settings. When off, bundled workflow commands disappear and ultracode no longer triggers a run or appears in the /effort menu.

Copy as Markdown Advanced Last verified: 2026-09-24. Which features sit behind a fetched flag changes with almost every Claude Code release — features get ungated once a rollout finishes. Treat the feature list below as the shape of the problem, and check the live docs for today's exact membership. Confirm against the official source. Two developers install the same Claude Code version, on the same OS, in the same repo. One of them has a feature the other doesn't, and neither of them gets an error message. This isn't folklore — it's the documented design. Claude Code switches some features on using feature flags it fetches from Anthropic at startup, and several ordinary, well-intentioned configurations turn that fetch off completely. The consequence that surprises people: a purely local operation can depend on a network call. In September 2026 that became a 437-point Hacker News thread, because reading a Markdown file off your own disk turned out to need one. What you'll learn How Claude Code's remote feature flags are fetched, cached, and evaluated The four configurations that silently switch flag fetching off Why DISABLE_TELEMETRY=0 still opts you out — and why DO_NOT_TRACK=0 doesn't The fifteen features you lose with fetching off How to detect gating in two minutes and pin behavior so it can't bite you
documents.s: Feature Flags: Why Your Claude Code Isn't Mine

documents.t: Claude Code ships with a code default for every flag and then tries to fetch the real values. The provider is GrowthBook — there's a dedicated DISABLE_GROWTHBOOK environment variable, and the changelog has entries like a crash fix for "when a GrowthBook feature evaluates to null" (v2.1.214). Four properties of that system explain almost every weird case you'll hit: Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Flags are fetched, not bundled⌄ The binary knows the flag names and a fallback value for each. The values that decide what your session can do come from Anthropic over the network. No fetch means every flag falls back to its code default — which for a feature mid-rollout is usually off. ←PreviousNext→ 2Flags are cached to disk⌄ Fetched values persist between sessions, which is why a feature can appear one run after you expected it. The changelog records this going wrong: v2.1.70 fixed flags read during early startup never refreshing their disk cache, so stale values survived across sessions. ←PreviousNext→ 3Flags are evaluated against your identity and version⌄ Evaluation takes your Claude Code version and your subscription tier into account. v2.1.227 fixed flags being evaluated without the user's tier when a session started on an expired login token — which wrongly prompted Max plan users to enable usage credits. v2.1.261 fixed flags gated to a newer version occasionally applying to an older Claude Code running on the same machine. ←PreviousNext→ 4Flags can go stale mid-session⌄ v2.1.214 fixed feature flags going stale in long-running sessions after the OAuth token rotates. A session that runs for hours is not guaranteed to hold the same feature set it started with. ←PreviousNext→

The docs are explicit about this. Claude Code skips the flag fetch in these sessions: You set one of four environment variables: DISABLE_GROWTHBOOK, DISABLE_TELEMETRY, DO_NOT_TRACK, or CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC. You're on a third-party provider: Amazon Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, or Microsoft Foundry — unless a host platform that embeds Claude Code sets CLAUDE_CODE_PROVIDER_MANAGED_BY_HOST. You're in a Claude apps gateway session. It's your first session after a fresh install or an upgrade — the flags haven't arrived yet. More on this below. Notice what those first two have in common: they're the configurations a security-conscious enterprise picks. The exact population most likely to disable telemetry and route through Bedrock is the population that silently gets the smallest feature set. Watch out Disabling telemetry is not only a privacy choice — it is also a feature switch. The docs say DISABLE_TELEMETRY 'also disables feature-flag fetching with the same effect as DISABLE_GROWTHBOOK'. If you want privacy without losing features, there is no combination that gives you both: every documented way to stop the telemetry also stops the flag fetch. CI runners with an ephemeral HOME are a fresh install on every run, so they land in the no-flags case every single time.
documents.s: The four ways the fetch goes dark

documents.t: This is the part that costs people an afternoon. These variables live in the same family, read as if they do the same thing, and parse their values under three different rules. Variable How it reads the value So =0 means DISABLE_TELEMETRY Any non-empty value turns it on Still opts you out. Unset it to re-enable CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC Any non-empty value turns it on Still disables the traffic. Unset it to re-enable DISABLE_ERROR_REPORTING Any non-empty value turns it on Still opts you out. Unset it to re-enable DISABLE_GROWTHBOOK Standard boolean — set to 1 or true Leaves fetching on DO_NOT_TRACK Standard boolean — set to 1 Leaves telemetry on Read that table twice. DISABLE_TELEMETRY=0 disables telemetry. DO_NOT_TRACK=0 does not. Both are documented, deliberate, and opposite. What you'll learn The docs state the rule directly: some variables 'read only whether you set them at all, so any non-empty value including 0 turns the behavior on'. To undo one of those, you must unset the variable or set it to an empty value — assigning 0 or false is not an off switch. This bites hardest in a Dockerfile or CI config where someone 'turned it off' by flipping 1 to 0.
documents.s: The value trap: three variables, three parsing rules

documents.t: With flag fetching off, fifteen documented capabilities go away. Grouped by what they cost you: Permissions and startup Sessions can't start in auto mode by default on Pro, Max, and Team plans The VS Code extension can't read settings files for the starting permission mode /auto-mode-setup can't draft autoMode.environment entries Anything that reaches beyond the local session Remote Control Messaging sessions on other machines (same-machine messaging still works) Syncing the skills and plugins enabled for your claude.ai account into terminal sessions Reading or replying to comments on an artifact The advisor tool Commands and diagnostics claude import and the /import command /skill-doctor and its report in the /plugin Stats tab Silent behavior changes — the dangerous group MCP: Claude Code stops excluding MCP tools whose input schema the API would reject. It sends the schema anyway, and the request fails with a 400 naming the tool by position MCP: no probing of claude.ai connector servers for protocol revision 2026-07-28, unless you set MCP_PROTOCOL_NEGOTIATION=auto Large pastes are no longer treated as pasted rather than typed text — the content behind a [Pasted text #N] placeholder reaches Claude unmarked On Windows with Git Bash installed, claude.ai and Console accounts don't get the PowerShell tool by default; set CLAUDE_CODE_USE_POWERSHELL_TOOL=1 Claude-drafted feedback is off The last group is the one to internalize. A missing slash command announces itself. A 400 error that names a tool by its position in the array does not look like a telemetry setting, and you will debug your MCP server for an hour before you think to check an env var.

Flag and telemetry settings have leaked into places nobody would predict. Two fixed-but-instructive examples from the changelog: v2.1.108 fixed subscribers who set DISABLE_TELEMETRY falling back to a 5-minute prompt cache TTL instead of 1 hour. A privacy variable was quietly costing money on every long session — a 12× shorter cache window. v2.1.105 fixed CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC set in one project's settings permanently disabling usage metrics for all projects on the machine. Both are fixed. Both show the shape of the risk: these switches cut across subsystems that look unrelated.

This one is worth its own heading because it produces the classic irreproducible bug report. On your first session after installing Claude Code — or after upgrading to a version that adds a feature — a flag-gated feature can simply be missing, and the session can start in Manual mode on a plan that otherwise starts in auto mode. Claude Code fetches the flags during that session, so both are present next time. Two corollaries: It fixes itself, which is exactly why it's hard to report. By the time anyone looks, the second session has the flags. It never fixes itself in ephemeral environments. A CI runner, a fresh container, or any setup with a throwaway home directory is on its first session every time. The docs do note one mitigation: after a fresh install, a non-interactive session such as claude -p, the Agent SDK, or the VS Code extension can still pick the flags up before it chooses the starting permission mode.
documents.s: The first session after an install or upgrade

documents.t: The clearest example of the whole pattern, and the one that made the front page. Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1v2.1.277 adds native AGENTS.md support⌄ The changelog entry: in a project with no CLAUDE.md, Claude Code reads AGENTS.md instead; change it under 'Project instructions' in /config. The entry itself flags that it isn't on Bedrock, Vertex or Foundry yet. ←PreviousNext→ 2The feature ships behind a fetched flag⌄ Because the rollout was flag-gated, sessions that skip the fetch fell back to the code default — off. Reading a Markdown file from the current directory, an operation with no network component whatsoever, became conditional on a network call. ←PreviousNext→ 3It fails silently⌄ No warning, no log line, no error. The instructions simply never reach the model, so the symptom reads as 'Claude is ignoring my AGENTS.md' — which sends you to rewrite the file rather than to check an env var. ←PreviousNext→ 4Issue #95690, 2026-09-20⌄ Filed as 'Claude Code's AGENTS.md Support: A Local Feature Locked Behind a Remote Switch'. Reporters reproduced it on 2.1.278 and 2.1.280, and confirmed that DISABLE_TELEMETRY, DISABLE_GROWTHBOOK and nonessential-traffic-off all block it, plus the very first session after a fresh install. ←PreviousNext→ 5Fixed in v2.1.281⌄ The memory docs now say it plainly: 'Before v2.1.281, some sessions, such as those on Amazon Bedrock or with telemetry disabled, read CLAUDE.md files only. On those versions, update Claude Code.' If you're pinned below 2.1.281, you still have this. ←PreviousNext→ The lesson generalizes past this one bug. Ask of any new Claude Code feature: is this gated? If it is, then your telemetry posture, your provider, and how recently you installed all become inputs to whether it works.
documents.s: Case study: AGENTS.md, a local file behind a remote switch

documents.t: You don't need to guess. Three checks, cheapest first. 1. Ask whether the setting even exists. When AGENTS.md support is unavailable, the Project instructions row doesn't appear in the /config panel at all. A missing setting is itself the diagnosis — the feature isn't off, it's absent. 2. Look at what an interactive session tells you. When it works, Claude Code prints a line in the conversation like no CLAUDE.md found; AGENTS.md loaded: /home/you/repo/AGENTS.md. No line, no load. 3. Run a canary. The technique that cracked the original report: put a word in the file that appears nowhere else, then ask for it in a clean, non-interactive session. If the word comes back, the file reached the model. This works for any instruction file, on any version. Canary test — did the instruction file actually load? CopyOpen in Claude↗ mkdir -p /tmp/canary && cd /tmp/canary echo 'The project codeword is PERIWINKLE.' > AGENTS.md claude -p 'What is the project codeword? Answer with one word.' Run it once with your normal environment, then once with the privacy variables cleared, and compare. Note the empty-string assignment — remember that DISABLE_TELEMETRY=0 would not clear it. Same test with flag fetching allowed — note the empty values, not zeros CopyOpen in Claude↗ cd /tmp/canary env DISABLE_TELEMETRY= CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC= DISABLE_GROWTHBOOK=false \ claude -p 'What is the project codeword? Answer with one word.' 4. If you need the detail, turn on debug logging. Launch with --debug or /debug, and logs land in ~/.claude/debug/<session-id>.txt. One catch: the DEBUG environment variable only accepts the truthy values 1, true, yes, and on — a namespace pattern like DEBUG=express:* left over from another tool will not enable it.

The durable fix is to stop depending on the gate. Two patterns. Pin the setting explicitly. For instruction files, the Project instructions value can go in a settings file under the built-in plugin's ID rather than being left to the default. One important limit: Claude Code ignores this key in project and local settings files — it only reads it from ~/.claude/settings.json, a --settings file, or managed settings. Putting it in your repo's .claude/settings.json will do nothing. Load CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md together — user or managed settings only CopyOpen in Claude↗ { "pluginConfigs": { "agents-md@builtin": { "options": { "instructionFiles": "claude-md-and-agents-md" } } } } Use a path that was never gated. A CLAUDE.md that imports AGENTS.md has worked on every version, every provider, and with telemetry off — because it's ordinary @path import expansion, not a flagged code path. This is the recommendation the docs themselves give for Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry sessions. The one-line CLAUDE.md that has never needed a flag CopyOpen in Claude↗ @AGENTS.md One subtlety if you take this route: an AGENTS.md read through the setting behaves slightly differently from one pulled in by import. InstructionsLoaded hooks don't fire for the setting-based path, but they fire as usual for an AGENTS.md that a CLAUDE.md imports or symlinks to. If you have hooks on instruction loading, the import is the safer path.
documents.s: Pin behavior instead of relying on a flag

documents.t: Check yourself 0/4 Key takeaways Claude Code fetches feature flags from Anthropic (GrowthBook), caches them to disk, and evaluates them against your version and subscription tier — so two identical installs can legitimately behave differently. Four env vars, three third-party providers, apps gateway sessions, and the first session after an install all skip that fetch, costing you fifteen documented features. DISABLE_TELEMETRY, CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC and DISABLE_ERROR_REPORTING treat any non-empty value as on — including 0. DO_NOT_TRACK and DISABLE_GROWTHBOOK are real booleans. Unset, don't zero. The worst losses are silent: unfiltered MCP schemas causing positional 400s, and unmarked pasted text. AGENTS.md was the case study — native from v2.1.277, gated, fixed in v2.1.281. A CLAUDE.md containing @AGENTS.md never needed the flag.
