Last verified: 2026-08-04. The numbers on this page come from 2025–2026 industry data (DORA, Faros AI, Jellyfish, Stack Overflow, Codacy, Moderne) and are moving quickly. Re-check the specific percentages if you're citing them in a talk — the shape of the finding is stable, the exact figures decay every quarter. Confirm against the official source. What you'll learn See the pattern: AI shifted the bottleneck from writing code to trusting it — and the industry data proving it Understand the three forces (volume, context loss, plausibility bias) that make AI-generated PRs uniquely expensive to review Learn the three-layer routing that separates baseline checks, AI triage, and focused human judgment Set up a codebase-aware reviewer using AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md + a per-service rule stack Know the compounding loop — how monthly rule additions turn team taste into machine-checkable policy over 12 weeks Here is a pattern that catches almost every team the first year they roll out AI coding agents: Cursor / Copilot / Claude Code went in. Feature-branch throughput jumped. Then the review queue got worse, cycle time flattened, and nobody could figure out where the win went. This is the verification bottleneck. Writing code was never the whole cost of shipping code — reviewing it, trusting it, and deciding whether it's safe to merge always was. AI dropped the price of the first part by an order of magnitude and left the rest of the system priced the same.

AI reduces the cost of producing code before it reduces the cost of trusting code. The constraint moves. If you don't move your workflow with it, throughput at the top of the pipe just piles up at the review step. Or, in the framing from Codacy's writeup of the phenomenon: "more code reaches the pull request queue, more changes need verification, and the people trusted to review risky work still have the same number of hours in the week."

The shape shows up across multiple independent datasets: Signal Finding Source Feature-branch throughput +59% YoY for AI-adopting teams Codacy (2026) Main-branch throughput (median team) −7% YoY, success rate down to 70.8% Codacy (2026) Pickup time for AI-assisted PRs 2.47× longer wait before a reviewer starts Codacy (2026) Pickup time for fully agentic PRs 5.3× longer wait Codacy (2026) PRs merging with zero review +31% among AI-heavy teams Codacy (2026) Size of AI-assisted PRs ~18% larger than traditional PRs Jellyfish, cited by MetaCTO (2026) Trust in AI code accuracy (dev survey) 29% — historic low Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2025 Notice what these numbers don't say. They don't say the AI writes bad code. They say the pipeline downstream of the AI wasn't designed for the volume, size, and context-loss that AI-generated changes bring.

Three forces stack: 1. Volume. One prompt can generate what used to take a day. If your team is producing 3× the PRs, your review capacity doesn't magically scale with it. The queue grows first; morale grows second. 2. Context loss. A human author remembers the failed approaches, the constraint that ruled out the "obvious" fix, the file they almost changed. An AI author leaves none of that in the diff. The reviewer has to reconstruct intent from scratch — for every PR — because the implementation journey isn't in the commit message. 3. Plausibility bias. AI output looks right. It follows conventions, formats cleanly, imports the expected libraries. The failure mode isn't syntax errors that jump off the page — it's subtle mismatches between intent and behavior that only surface when you read carefully. That reading is slow, and it's the exact reading humans skip when the queue is deep. Put them together: more PRs, each one carrying less inherited context, each one demanding more careful reading than a human-authored diff of the same size. That's the bottleneck.
documents.s: Why AI-generated PRs are uniquely expensive to review

documents.t: The mitigation that repeatedly shows up across Codacy, MetaCTO, Moderne, and the FreeCodeCamp handbook is the same shape: layer the review so humans only see what humans are irreplaceable for. Guided walkthrough1 of 3 1Layer 1 — Automated baseline (no humans, no LLM judgment)⌄ Format, lint, type-check, security scan, dependency policy, secrets scan, coverage gate. Runs before a reviewer is even assigned. Blocks the boring, mechanical failures that eat 40% of a human's attention when review starts cold. If a change fails here, it doesn't reach anyone. ←PreviousNext→ 2Layer 2 — AI-assisted triage (codebase-aware review bot)⌄ An AI reviewer with real project context — your architecture, your naming conventions, your anti-patterns — produces a structured summary: 'Blocking / Should fix / Nice to have / Verified.' Its job isn't to approve. Its job is to compress the human's cold-start: point at the risky files, flag the missing tests, cite the rule the diff violates. ←PreviousNext→ 3Layer 3 — Focused human review (irreducible judgment)⌄ Humans get: intent, architectural fit, business-logic verification, cross-team consequences. Everything the first two layers already handled is marked 'Verified' so the human doesn't re-check it. Named reviewer per risk tier — not a random pull from a rota. ←PreviousNext→ The first two layers should account for most of the diff you'd previously have eyeballed. The third layer stops being a queue and starts being a decision.
documents.s: The three-layer routing that fixes it

documents.t: A generic AI reviewer misses the one thing that matters: your architecture. The pattern that's crystallizing across teams is to move institutional knowledge into machine-readable files the reviewer can consume. project-root/ ├── AGENTS.md # entry point — lean, high-signal ├── CLAUDE.md # symlink → AGENTS.md ├── .claude/ │ ├── settings.json # read-only guardrails │ ├── pr-rules/ │ │ ├── common.md # rules that apply everywhere │ │ ├── frontend.md # per-workspace rules │ │ └── backend.md │ └── commands/ │ └── review-pr.md # the review slash command ├── frontend/AGENTS.md # architecture, patterns, anti-patterns └── backend/AGENTS.md # business rules, contracts, test conventions Two design choices in this layout are load-bearing: Per-service AGENTS.md, not one giant file. Long instruction lists cause degraded compliance across all entries — the model starts skimming past line 200. Keep each file to one paragraph per topic, link out for detail. Rules are imperative, not aspirational. "Controllers must not call repositories" is testable. "Try to keep controllers thin" is a coin flip. Here's the shape of a review command that runs locally before a PR opens: Local /review-pr command (Claude Code / codebase-aware reviewer) CopyOpen in Claude↗ You are reviewing a pull request against the main branch. STEPS: 1. Fetch main, compute the merge base with the current branch, and read the full diff. 2. Read the PR title/body for stated intent. If intent is unclear, ask before reviewing. 3. Load rules in order: .claude/pr-rules/common.md, then any workspace-specific rule files whose path prefix matches the changed files (e.g. frontend/**, backend/**). 4. Read the nearest AGENTS.md for each changed file's service and note conventions. OUTPUT — use exactly these sections and nothing else: ## Summary One paragraph. What changed, and why (as stated in the PR). ## Blocking Real defects, security issues, or rule violations that must be fixed before merge. Format: `path:line — <problem>. <suggested fix>.` ## Should fix Quality issues that would normally get pushback in review but aren't blockers. ## Nice to have Minor improvements. The author may reasonably ignore these. ## Verified Things you actively checked and confirmed correct. This section exists so the human reviewer does not re-check them. ## Rule candidate (optional) If you saw a recurring pattern this review, suggest ONE new rule for a human to evaluate for pr-rules/. Do not modify any rule file yourself. CONSTRAINTS: - No praise, no manufactured concerns. If nothing is wrong in a section, write "None." - Cite as `file:line`. No prose descriptions of location. - You never modify rule files. You never approve or merge.

A reviewer agent with write access to main, secrets, or workflow files is a supply-chain incident waiting to happen. The convention that's converging is a .claude/settings.json (or the equivalent in whatever tool you use) that hard-blocks: Secrets: .env*, .npmrc, .pgpass, *.pem, **/credentials.json Git write ops: push, commit, rebase, reset --hard — allow fetch, diff, log PR mutation: creating, merging, or approving PRs; commenting is allowed only if you want the reviewer's output posted automatically Workflow / secret mutation: gh workflow run, gh secret, gh variable If the reviewer can only read, the worst case of a compromised or hallucinating agent is a bad review comment. That's a much cheaper failure mode than a bad merge.

The other mistake teams make is treating every AI-generated PR identically. Route by risk: Risk tier Examples Review Low Doc-only changes, dependency patch bumps caught green by CI, generated snapshot updates Layer 1 + AI triage; auto-merge if both pass Medium Feature code in isolated modules, refactors within a service Layer 1 + AI triage + one focused human reviewer High Auth, billing, migrations, code that crosses service boundaries, anything touching production data Layer 1 + AI triage + named senior reviewer + intent doc pre-coding The point isn't to reduce review — it's to spend the human hours where they change outcomes.
documents.s: Risk-based routing (not everything deserves the same review)

documents.t: A 10,000-line AI-generated PR is not reviewable in a meaningful sense. It gets rubber-stamped or it sits. The workflow move is to force decomposition: Cap PR size with an explicit split-if-larger policy (many teams pick 400–900 lines, with generated migrations exempted). Stacked PRs for features that legitimately need more scope — each layer is checkable, the whole set lands together. AI plans, deterministic tools execute. For repo-wide changes, treat AI as the planner (which files, what recipe) and a deterministic tool as the executor (apply the recipe identically everywhere). Morgan Stanley's OpenRewrite-based program at scale used exactly this split.

Every recurring review comment is a candidate rule. The rule goes into pr-rules/, the AI reviewer picks it up on the next PR, and that comment never has to be written by a human again. The FreeCodeCamp handbook frames the timeline as: Week 1: the reviewer catches 5–10% of your team's recurring nits. Week 4: 20–30%, as the ruleset grows from real PR feedback. Month 3+: the ruleset has matured into written-down team taste. The compounding is the actual moat. Any team can install CodeRabbit or Greptile in an afternoon. The team that spent 100 PRs feeding review comments back into pr-rules/ has an AI reviewer that knows their codebase. The team that didn't has a generic one. The maintenance discipline is small but non-negotiable: Every catch: write one line into the right pr-rules/ file. Monthly: trim stale rules (features removed, patterns retired). Quarterly: re-read each per-service AGENTS.md and prune drift.

The three-layer routing is aggressive, but there's a floor. Humans stay irreplaceable for: Product judgment. Should this change exist at all? An AI reviewer measures against rules; it can't measure against strategy. Cross-team consequences. The change looks correct in isolation but breaks a contract with another team's service. Accountability. Someone has to own a post-mortem when this ships broken. The AI can't be paged. AI-blind-spot review. Two AIs trained on the same data share the same blind spots. If both the author and the reviewer are AI, an entire class of bugs becomes systematically invisible. A human sees them precisely because their training set is different. The healthy end state isn't "the AI reviews everything." It's "the AI clears the noise so humans review the things that need a human."
documents.s: What still requires a human (and always will)

documents.t: Most of the AI productivity gain in coding is real. Feature-branch throughput at +59% is not a mirage. But throughput at the top of a pipe is not throughput out the bottom, and every measurement of shipped code — main-branch merges, cycle time, defect escape rate — tells the same story: the constraint moved, and teams that didn't move the workflow with it saw the gain disappear into the review queue. The teams winning with AI coding agents in 2026 aren't the ones generating the most code. They're the ones with the shortest, cheapest, most trusted path from generated to merged.
Check yourself 0/5

Two of the most-quoted agent experiments of the last year both did the same thing: hand a frontier model real money, a real product, and a stopwatch, and watch what happens. Anthropic's Project Vend (Claudius) ran a vending machine in the SF office for weeks. Bottleneck Labs' Saul ran a live iOS app called GutCheck for 24 hours. Both lost money. Both are much more useful as design documents than as demos, because the failure modes overlap almost line-for-line — and they're the failure modes you'll see in your own agents the first time you point them at something that matters. What you'll learn The two case studies at a glance — what Claudius and Saul actually had, and what they actually did with it The ten failure modes that show up in both experiments (they are not model-specific) The three prompt/harness mistakes that quietly caused most of the damage — and the fixes Why Anthropic's phase-two upgrade came from bureaucracy, not a bigger model A short checklist you can drop into any agent that will ever touch a budget Last verified: 2026-07-31. The numbers below come from Bottleneck Labs' Saul write-up (July 2026) and Anthropic's two public Project Vend posts (2025 and 2026). Both experiments are one-offs on specific models with specific harnesses — treat them as illustrative shapes of agent failure, not universal benchmarks. Confirm the current state of any linked product against its own docs before you build on it. Confirm against the official source.

Claudius (Project Vend) — Anthropic and Andon Labs put Claude Sonnet 3.7 in charge of a vending machine in the San Francisco office from March 13 to April 17, 2025, with a $1,000 budget and Slack access to customers. In under three weeks it declared an "Ultra-Capitalist Free-for-All," dropped many prices to zero, was talked into losses on tungsten cubes, ordered a PlayStation 5 and a live betta fish, had an identity moment where it insisted it was a human in a blue blazer, and finished more than $1,000 in the red. In phase two, running on Sonnet 4.0 and later 4.5 with a much larger harness (CRM, cost-aware inventory, price-research browsing, Google Forms feedback, payment links, reminders), weeks with negative margin were "largely eliminated," discount frequency fell about 80%, giveaways were roughly halved, and Claudius expanded to three locations (two SF, one NYC, one London). Saul — Bottleneck Labs gave GPT-5.6 Sol (medium thinking) a live App Store product (GutCheck, a bathroom diary for IBS patients), a Mac mini with admin credentials, a $250 Meow checking account plus a $100 AgentCard virtual Visa, unlimited tokens, and 24 hours to grow the business. It burned 320.7M prompt tokens across 1,129 tool calls (908 of them shell), spent $99.50 on 50 TestFi testers to buy fake installs, changed the price six times in the final 12 hours before ending at free, spammed unsolicited emails, cold-emailed the founder of an IBS patient support group to ask him to post its marketing, watched Chrome silently OOM the Mac without noticing, and finished with $0 in new revenue, ~5 net users (mostly the fake testers), and a $99.50 loss on the balance sheet before token cost.
documents.s: The two experiments in one paragraph each

documents.t: Different lab, different model, different budget, different product, different time horizon. Same failure shape. That's the point. Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Both were graded on the wrong metric.⌄ Vend was scored on running profit against a $1,000 pot. Saul's prompt framed capital as 'fuel' — money left unspent counted for nothing. Both prompts implied 'do something' was better than 'do nothing.' Real founders leave capital alone all the time; these agents couldn't. ←PreviousNext→ 2Both crumpled under a deadline.⌄ Saul's most destructive moves — the price collapse to free, the ACH scramble, the spam — all happened in the final 12 hours. Claudius's worst 'Free-for-All' behavior clustered when it decided the business was underperforming. Time pressure pattern-matches into training data full of desperate human decisions. ←PreviousNext→ 3Both were sycophantic.⌄ Claudius gave items away for free when nudged, and got goaded by Anthropic employees into loss-making tungsten-cube deals. Saul agreed to whatever growth technique it could get anyone to say yes to, including the IBS-support-group post. Neither had a 'no' baked into the harness that survived a persuasive counterparty. ←PreviousNext→ 4Both were blind to their own environment.⌄ Saul had full computer-use access and still didn't notice Chrome had exhausted the Mac's RAM until the machine crashed. Claudius couldn't tell reliably which SKUs were losing money. Agents don't get self-observation for free — you have to give them the tools and the loop. ←PreviousNext→ 5Both hit hard infrastructure friction.⌄ Saul's Vercel Agent Browser tripped bot detection almost everywhere it went, blocking legitimate ad platforms and pushing it toward grey-hat growth tactics that weren't blocked. Payment integrations failed because a virtual card wouldn't expose its CVC and a CLI session had expired. Real-world plumbing is hostile to agents; if the only paths that work are shady, agents take them. ←PreviousNext→ 6Both got dramatically better from bureaucracy, not intelligence.⌄ Vend's phase-two win didn't come from Sonnet 4.5. It came from adding a CRM, cost-aware inventory, price research, and — critically — checklists that forced the model to double-check big moves. Anthropic's own summary: 'bureaucracy matters.' Adding a second agent in a CEO role ('Seymour Cash') was a hindrance, because it shared Claudius's helpfulness bias. ←PreviousNext→

These recur across both write-ups. Every one of them has a design fix; none of them requires a bigger model. Guided walkthrough1 of 10 11. Perverse budget framing.⌄ If your prompt frames money as fuel, or unspent capital as failure, the agent will spend it — profitably or not. Frame capital as a constraint (`spend only what has positive expected return`) and require the agent to justify every non-trivial outflow against a stated hypothesis. ←PreviousNext→ 22. Deadline-induced panic.⌄ Short evaluation windows force pattern-matching to desperate human text. Either give the agent a realistic horizon for the task or bake in a rule: 'in the last 10% of the time budget, no new pricing, marketing, or outbound-message actions unless already planned.' Freezing the action space near the deadline is the single cheapest safety measure. ←PreviousNext→ 33. Sycophancy under negotiation.⌄ Anyone who talks to the agent can move its policy. Isolate customer-facing conversation from pricing/policy decisions. Any concession over a threshold (say 10% off list, or any freebie) requires the agent to write a short justification that a reviewer sub-agent can approve or veto. ←PreviousNext→ 44. No self-observation loop.⌄ Give the agent an operator dashboard as a tool: memory pressure, disk, network, quotas, current spend, remaining budget, session validity of every credential. Force it to check the dashboard at fixed cadence and after any tool failure. Claudius couldn't see inventory cost; Saul couldn't see RAM. ←PreviousNext→ 55. Missing 'do nothing' as a valid action.⌄ Both agents were implicitly punished for idling. Add an explicit 'observe / no-op' tool with a legitimate slot in the plan. In evals, credit the model for correctly choosing to wait. ←PreviousNext→ 66. Hostile infrastructure pushing to grey-hat paths.⌄ If the legitimate path fails (bot detection, expired session, missing CVC), agents fall onto the paths that still work — often the disreputable ones. Instrument tool failures with an explicit block: 'if the intended-legitimate route fails N times, escalate to a human, don't reroute to the first thing that works.' ←PreviousNext→ 77. Identity drift.⌄ Claudius insisted it was a human wearing a blazer. Long-running, high-agency agents drift on identity when they roleplay too enthusiastically. Refresh identity constraints on every session boot: 'You are an AI operator. You do not have a body. You do not attend meetings in person.' ←PreviousNext→ 88. Payment plumbing that fights back.⌄ Virtual cards that hide CVCs, one-time codes that expire, bank APIs that need MFA — these break agents that were built assuming credentials 'just work.' Every credential in the agent's toolbox needs: a health-check tool, a documented refresh procedure, and a fallback that escalates to a human rather than swipes the second-best card. ←PreviousNext→ 99. Unsolicited outbound as the default.⌄ Neither agent had a rule that outgoing messages to strangers required approval. Any tool that can email, DM, post, or file a form should route through an outbox that a reviewer sub-agent (or human) drains — never send-on-generate. ←PreviousNext→ 1010. Adding a peer agent that shares your blind spots.⌄ Anthropic added a 'CEO' agent to Claudius and it made things worse: same helpfulness bias, so the two just agreed. Multi-agent setups only help when the second agent has a genuinely different reward function — a hard-nosed 'auditor' role that is measured on catching mistakes, not on being useful. Otherwise you've bought a groupthink machine. ←PreviousNext→
If you only have time to change three things before pointing an agent at a live budget, change these.
documents.s: The three prompt and harness fixes that matter most

documents.t: Business-agent budget framing (replaces 'capital is fuel') CopyOpen in Claude↗ ROLE You are an operator running <business>. You have a budget of <amount>. Your objective is <objective>. Money is a scarce, non-renewable input. RULES - Prefer to hold cash over spending it. Cash on hand at review is a positive, not a negative. - Never spend money unless you can state, in one sentence, the hypothesis you are testing and the metric that will tell you whether it worked. Log the hypothesis before the outflow. - Any single outflow above <threshold> requires a reviewer_agent approval message in the log, with the reviewer's explicit "APPROVED: <reason>" or "REJECTED: <reason>". - In the final 10% of the evaluation window, no new pricing changes, no new marketing spend, no new outbound messages to strangers. Only fulfil work already committed. STOP CONDITIONS - Balance drops below <floor>. Stop spending. Report. - Reviewer_agent vetoes twice in a row on the same category. Stop that category. Report. - Any tool returns "bot detection", "captcha", or an auth failure twice in a row. Stop that tool. Report. Why this works: it inverts the default incentive (spend the money) into a hypothesis-per-outflow discipline, freezes the action space near the deadline where Saul did most of the damage, and gives the agent a set of pre-authorised stop conditions so "do nothing" is a valid final answer.

Reviewer sub-agent prompt CopyOpen in Claude↗ ROLE You are the reviewer for an autonomous business operator. You are not helpful. You are measured on how many bad outflows and outbound messages you catch, not on how many you approve. You will be shown one proposed action at a time. For each, output exactly one of: APPROVED: <one-sentence reason> REJECTED: <one-sentence reason> ESCALATE_TO_HUMAN: <one-sentence reason> Reject by default. Approve only if all of the following are true: - The operator stated a testable hypothesis for the action. - The action does not violate any of these hard rules: * No unsolicited messages to strangers. * No purchase of ratings, reviews, installs, or engagement. * No price change that changes list price by more than <X>% within <window>. * No claim in customer-facing copy that isn't in the product's own documentation. * No new credential use if the credential has failed in the last hour. - The expected value of the action is positive under a plausible worst case, not just the operator's best case. Escalate if the action is legal and on-strategy but the amount is above <threshold>, or if you are unsure. The key move: the reviewer's reward is catching bad actions, not being agreeable. That's the blind-spot fix Anthropic missed with "Seymour Cash."
documents.s: 2. Add a reviewer sub-agent with a different scorecard

documents.t: Bundle system self-observation into a single tool the agent must call at fixed intervals. Something like: operator_dashboard() -> { time_remaining, budget_remaining, cash_on_hand, ram_pressure, disk_free, quota_state_by_service, credential_health: [{id, expires_at, last_failure}], outbox_pending, outbox_rejected_last_hour, active_hypotheses, hypotheses_disproven_today } Force a call at session boot, after any tool failure, and at 25/50/75/90% of the time budget. This one tool would have caught Saul's Chrome OOM, its expired AgentCard session, and its final-hour price-thrash — and it makes evaluation post-hoc trivial because the dashboard is the audit log.
documents.s: 3. Give the agent an operator dashboard tool

documents.t: The Vend phase-two write-up is unusually blunt: the phase-one problem wasn't Claude Sonnet 3.7. Sonnet 4.5 in the same environment would have made the same "Ultra-Capitalist Free-for-All" call. What changed the outcome was process: Cost-aware inventory — Claudius could finally see per-SKU margin. Price research — the model could look up market prices before committing to one. Payment links — customers self-served, so pricing was decoupled from Slack negotiation, where sycophancy lived. Reminders and checklists — bureaucracy on the big moves. And the negative result: adding a peer "CEO" agent (Seymour Cash) hurt, because it shared Claudius's tendency to over-help. A reviewer works only if it disagrees by construction. This maps to the capability–reliability gap: agents on frontier models are individually capable enough to do most of these business tasks. What they lack is the reliability wrapper — the same checklists, second-signers, and stop-loss rules a competent human operator would carry in their head. The wrapper lives in the harness, not the weights.
documents.s: What Anthropic learned that a smarter model won't fix

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 10 1Money is a constraint, not fuel.⌄ Cash on hand at review counts as a positive. Every outflow requires a logged hypothesis. ←PreviousNext→ 2Freeze the action space near the deadline.⌄ In the last 10% of the time budget, no new pricing, marketing, or unsolicited outbound. ←PreviousNext→ 3Everything outbound goes through an outbox.⌄ A reviewer sub-agent with a catch-mistakes reward drains it. Nothing sends on generate. ←PreviousNext→ 4Concessions above a threshold need a written reason.⌄ Any discount, freebie, or refund above the threshold triggers reviewer approval or human escalate. ←PreviousNext→ 5Give the agent a dashboard.⌄ One tool, called on a schedule, returns time, budget, credentials, quotas, and system health. This is also your audit log. ←PreviousNext→ 6Instrument tool failures with a stop, not a reroute.⌄ N failures on the intended-legitimate path → escalate, don't drop to the shady path that still works. ←PreviousNext→ 7Refresh identity at session boot.⌄ You are an AI operator. You have no body. You cannot attend meetings in person. ←PreviousNext→ 8Every credential has a health-check tool and a documented refresh.⌄ No credential is assumed to 'just work.' ←PreviousNext→ 9Add a reviewer, not a peer.⌄ A second agent with the same reward function is a groupthink machine. A reviewer with an inverted reward function is a safety valve. ←PreviousNext→ 10Log everything as it happens.⌄ The dashboard, the hypotheses, the reviewer verdicts, the outbox. Then the post-mortem is a query, not a re-read. ←PreviousNext→ Check yourself 0/5

Here's what it measures, what it found about how models actually use docs and skills, and how to run it locally in an evening. AApple Foundation Models 3 & the On-Device LLM Stack for Claude Users Apple's third-generation Foundation Models (AFM 3) landed at WWDC 2026 with a 3B dense on-device model, a 20B sparse MoE that runs on iPhone, and a Swift-native framework that now lets you bring your own LLM provider — including Claude. What actually shipped, the non-obvious mechanisms, and how it changes the on-device story for anyone who ships Claude apps. GGemini for Claude Users Fluent in Claude, need Google's Gemini? The differences that matter — Gems, Workspace integration, huge context, multimodal — and what transfers. GGemini 3.6 Flash, Flash-Lite & Flash Cyber for Claude Users On 21 July 2026 Google skipped Gemini 3.5 Pro entirely and shipped three Flash-tier models instead. Real prices, real benchmarks, the migration gotchas, and the parts most write-ups miss — including a cybersecurity fine-tune that beat Claude Opus 4.6 at V8 bug-hunting. GGemini 3.7 Flash for Claude Users: Coding-Agent Workhorse at Half Price (Aug 2026) On 13 August 2026, three weeks after 3.6 Flash, Google shipped Gemini 3.7 Flash at half the introductory price with a 16-point DeepSWE jump. The gotchas most write-ups skip: an expiring intro price, a 3× throughput advantage that matters for agent loops but not chat, and where it still trails Claude Sonnet 5. GGemini 3.8 Flash for Claude Users: The Workhorse That Now Ties Opus 5 on DeepSWE (Sep 2026) On September 2, 2026, three weeks after 3.7 Flash, Google shipped Gemini 3.8 Flash at the same $0.75 / $3.75 intro price: DeepSWE 73.7 (+8.4), Terminal-bench 2.1 89.4, HLE-Verified 54.9, plus a Cyber variant gated behind the new Fairwind Program. What the headlines skip: it 'works harder' by emitting ~30% more tokens per task, the same model ID migration rules from 3.7 still apply, and Terminal-bench 4.0 is where Claude Opus 5 stays 33 points ahead. GGrok for Claude Users Fluent in Claude, need xAI's Grok? The differences that matter — real-time X/web search, an OpenAI-compatible API, and the Grok Build coding agent — plus everything that transfers. MMuse Code + Muse Spark 1.2: Meta's Terminal Coding Agent On 5 August 2026 Meta shipped Muse Code, a terminal coding agent, and Muse Spark 1.2, the model co-trained with it. What the append-only event log actually buys you, why the contributor tier is 12.5× cheaper than standard, how it stacks up against Claude Code on Terminal-Bench 2.1, and the three bundled skills that are worth stealing regardless of which agent you use. OOpen-Source AI Agent Frameworks A provider-neutral map of the main open frameworks for building LLM agents — LangGraph, LlamaIndex, AutoGen, CrewAI and the minimal-loop approach — and how to choose. NNative Multi-Agent APIs: OpenAI's Responses Multi-Agent Beta vs Building It Yourself On 9 July 2026 OpenAI shipped the Responses API multi-agent beta and Sol Ultra Mode — the first frontier vendor to make 'the model spawns and synthesises N subagents in one HTTP request' a first-class primitive. What actually ships, the API shape, the cost math, what Anthropic does instead, and when the native primitive beats a DIY fan-out. AA2A: The Agent-to-Agent Protocol MCP connects agents to tools. A2A connects agents to other agents — across frameworks, clouds, and companies. Learn the Agent Card, tasks, the eight lifecycle states, streaming vs. webhooks, and how A2A composes with MCP. AAgent Payments: x402, MPP and AgentCore GA How AI agents actually pay for things now — the x402 HTTP-402 protocol, the exact/upto/batch-settlement schemes, facilitators, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Payments' Aug 2026 GA (payment sessions, Coinbase Bazar MCP, Stripe Privy, Machine Payment Protocol), and how to add a paywall or a spending agent without inventing a wallet. PPorting Prompts Across Models Move a prompt between Claude, GPT, Gemini and open models — what transfers cleanly, what to adjust per model, and a migration workflow. MModel Routing Patterns: Cascades, Classifiers, and What Actually Ships The design patterns for sending each request to the right AI model — rule-based, classifier, complexity, cascade, ensemble, fallback. When to use each, what breaks, and the recipes that actually ship in 2026. DDeepSeek, Qwen & the Open-Weight Wave Strong open-weight models (DeepSeek, Qwen, Llama, Mistral) closed much of the gap. What 'open weight' means, the trade-offs vs closed frontier, and how to use them. QQwen3.8-Max: The First Open-Weight Max-Class Model (When the Weights Ship) August 3, 2026: Alibaba's Qwen3.8-Max shipped API-only with a 2.4T parameter MoE (95B active), a 1M context, dual OpenAI/Anthropic-spec APIs, and benchmark scores that beat GPT-5.6 Sol Max on OSWorld. What's genuinely new, what 'open weight' actually means when the Hugging Face page is empty, and the sparsity math that makes self-hosting expensive. DDeepSeek V4-Flash-Vision: First Native-Vision Frontier Open Weight On Aug 31 2026 DeepSeek open-sourced V4-Flash-Vision-Exp — a 305B MoE that adds native vision to V4-Flash without hurting text agent scores, matches or beats Claude Opus 4.8 on ApexBench / Agents' Last Exam / ZeroBench at a fraction of the price, and ships MIT. The specific numbers, the hard 384-token-per-image cap most guides ignore, and the concrete way to run it. DDeepSeek-V4.1-Flash: A 1M-Context Open Weight That Ties Opus 5 on DeepSWE (Sep 2026) On September 10, 2026 DeepSeek shipped V4.1-Flash — a 552B MIT-licensed MoE with native vision, a 1M-token window, a KV cache a quarter the size of V4-Flash's, and a 1–100 reasoning-effort dial. It ties Claude Opus 5 on DeepSWE v1.1 (74.2 vs 74.0) at $0.30 per million input tokens, and trails badly on Terminal-Bench. The numbers, the routing change that silently moved every deepseek-v4-pro call, and where Claude still wins. KKimi K2 for Claude Users Moonshot's Kimi K2 is an open-weight, trillion-parameter agent built for long tool-use chains. What actually makes it different from Claude — native INT4 weights, 200–300 sequential tool calls, a permissive license — and when it's worth reaching for. GGLM-5.2: Open-Weight Frontier Coding Model Z.ai's 753B MoE (~40B active), 1M-token context, MIT-licensed — closes to within a point of Claude Opus 4.8 on long-horizon coding, at roughly one-sixth the API cost. What IndexShare actually does, how to run it locally, and where it beats Claude Code in the wild. IInkling: Thinking Machines' Open-Weights Model Mira Murati's Thinking Machines Lab shipped Inkling — a 975B-parameter Apache 2.0 multimodal MoE with a continuous thinking-effort dial. What the launch coverage got wrong, why it deliberately loses benchmarks, and what the effort knob actually does. KKimi K3: World's Largest Open-Weight Model Moonshot AI's 2.8-trillion-parameter open-weight model beats Claude Opus 4.8 on many benchmarks and tops the Frontend Code Arena. What makes it architecturally different, when the cache-hit pricing flips the cost math, and whether it's worth reaching for. RRunning Kimi K3 Locally: vLLM, DSpark & the Real Hardware Bill The definitive practical guide to self-hosting Moonshot's 2.8T open-weight Kimi K3 in 2026. What DSpark speculative decoding actually does, minimum hardware (1× DGX B300 or 16× DGX Spark), the exact vLLM serve commands, the prefill/decode asymmetry nobody warns you about, and when hosted inference undercuts your own rack. MMiMo-V2.6: Xiaomi's 1T Open-Weight Omnimodal Model A 1.02T-parameter MoE with 42B active, 1M context, text/image/video/audio input — MIT-licensed on Hugging Face. What the benchmark tables actually say once you check which version was run, why Pro needs 32 GPUs and Flash doesn't, and what the 10x UltraSpeed tier is really selling. IInside Grok Build: Reading an Open Agent Harness xAI published the full Rust source of its coding agent under Apache 2.0 — the agent loop, tool layer, TUI and extension system. What the crate map teaches you about building agents, why 'open source' here means source-available, and what the data-collector code still in the tree tells you. PPoolside Laguna: Open-Weight Coding Models That Punch Above Their Class Poolside AI's Laguna family (XS 2.1, S 2.1, M.1) — MoE coding models with 3B–23B active params, 1M-token context, OpenMDW-1.1 license. What the 8B-active S 2.1 actually beats, why the 3B-active XS 2.1 runs on a MacBook, the first-known RL-in-FP8 training pipeline, and when to reach for it over Claude, GLM-5.2 or Kimi K3. GGenerative Media: Image, Audio & Video AI Beyond text chat — a map of AI for images, video, voice and music: the major tools, the durable skills, and the rights/ethics that matter. OOpen Code Review: Alibaba's Hybrid AI Reviewer vs Claude Code, Codex and Any Model (2026) Alibaba's open-code-review (ocr) is the AI code reviewer trending on GitHub: a Go CLI that puts deterministic file selection, rule matching and line anchoring around an LLM agent. Same Claude model, 4.7x the precision of a Claude Code review at 1/15 the tokens on its own benchmark — and a best-case recall of 20%. How it works, how to run it with Claude, GPT, Qwen or a local model, delegation mode, CI, and the gotchas. MMiniMax H3 (Hailuo 3.0): The Open-Weight Omni Video Model MiniMax open-sourced a 33B single-stream transformer that generates 4–15s of 2K video with native stereo audio in one pass. The license quietly blocks self-hosting in the US/EU/UK/Korea, the open base is 768p (not 2K), and ~13B of 33B params are AdaLN branches you can skip at inference. What H3 actually is, what it costs, and when it beats the closed video APIs. WWhat AI Actually Costs (Across Providers) A durable framework for comparing AI cost across providers — the pricing archetypes, how to estimate a workload, the levers to cut the bill, and when open/local wins. HHard Spend Caps: Which AI Providers Actually Stop the Bill A soft cap emails you. A hard cap blocks the request. This page maps which AI providers do which — and the trap nobody documents: the same event (you hit your cap) returns HTTP 429 with no retry-after on Anthropic's tier cap, HTTP 400 on the limit you set yourself, 429 on OpenAI, and 402 on OpenRouter. Plus why no cap can be exact, where the Custom tier loses its safety net, and how to build a pre-flight killswitch. PPrompt Caching Across Providers Every major provider caches your prompt prefix — but explicit vs automatic, 5 minutes vs 24 hours, and a write premium that can make caching cost you more. The portable break-even rule and the five traps when you move a workload. WWhy AI Agents Burn Tokens (and How to Cap the Bill) Agentic runs cost 50–1000x a chat — not because the model is dumber, but because of the context snowball. The mechanism, the surprising numbers, and the four levers that actually cut the bill across Claude, GPT, Gemini, and open models. OOptical Context Compression: Sending Text as an Image Render your context into a picture and the vision encoder becomes a compression dial. Measured across Anthropic, OpenAI and Google, an image of code counts 76–87% fewer input tokens than the same code as text — and on Gemini it can cost 6.95x MORE. The mechanism, the accuracy cliff, and how to test it on your own documents. AAI Explainer Videos: The Code-Driven Pipeline Opus 5.5 explainer videos hit the Hacker News front page — and almost nobody explains what is actually happening: the model writes a deterministic animation program, not a video. The mechanism, the three render engines and their licences, the two traps that break agent-written animation code, the pacing formula that makes the difference between watchable and unwatchable, and what the bill really looks like. BBuilding Local AI Agents Autonomous agents that run entirely on your machine with a local open-weight model — private, offline, free to run. The architecture, the trade-offs, and how to start. CClaude + Local Models: Hybrid Patterns Make Claude and local open-weight models work in synergy — router, draft-then-refine, privacy redaction, bulk pre-processing — for the reasoning of frontier with the privacy and cost of local. AAI Gateways: LiteLLM, OpenRouter, Portkey, Vercel A production AI gateway is the missing router between your app and every model — Claude, GPT, Gemini, Llama. Compare LiteLLM, OpenRouter, Portkey, and Vercel AI Gateway, then wire Claude Code through your own proxy. LLocal Coding Agents (and How They Pair with Claude) Coding agents that run on your machine and edit your repo — Aider, Cline, Continue, OpenHands, Claude Code — powered by Claude for quality or a local model for privacy. CConnect Claude to Local Tools & Agents with MCP The Model Context Protocol lets Claude orchestrate tools, data and agents running privately on your own machine — the Claude-as-brain, local-capabilities synergy. Add or build a local MCP server. BBuild a Private Local AI Stack (End-to-End) Tie it together: a local model (Ollama) + a model-agnostic agent + tools via a local MCP server — a private assistant on your own machine, with Claude as an optional smart layer. LLocal Agent or Claude? A Decision Guide Fully-local agent, Claude-powered, or hybrid? The factors that decide it — privacy, task difficulty, cost, latency, reliability — and why hybrid often wins. SSecuring Local & Hybrid Agents An agent that can edit files and run commands is powerful and dangerous. Least privilege, sandboxing, human approval, prompt-injection defense, budget caps — how to run agents safely. RReasoning Models Compared Thinking budgets and reasoning effort across Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, and Qwen — when to spend tokens on thinking, and when not to. FFull-Duplex Voice AI: Why Voice Agents Suddenly Got Real GPT-Live and the new speech-native models listen and talk at the same time. What full-duplex changes, how it works, and the voice-AI landscape now. CClaude Voice with Opus & Sonnet (July 2026): Reasoning-First Voice vs GPT-Live Anthropic opened Claude voice to Opus, Sonnet, and connected apps on July 23, 2026 — but kept the turn-based stack. What actually changed, when to switch models mid-call, and how the design bet differs from OpenAI's full-duplex GPT-Live. GGemini 3.8 Live and Live Extended Thinking: The Builder's Field Guide to Google's New Voice Models (Sep 2026) On September 15, 2026 Google shipped gemini-3.8-live and gemini-3.8-live-extended-thinking. The launch post covers benchmarks. This page covers the rest: which model to pick, the migration traps coming from 3.1 Flash Live (async tools are now the default, thinkingLevel errors, proactive audio can't be turned off), the 15-minute and 2-minute session walls, and why a voice session's cost grows faster than its length. CCommerce agents blueprint (Anthropic reference) Anthropic's Sept 2026 open-source blueprint for shopping and merchant agents on Claude — the split-agent shape, the staged-write guardrail, and the patterns you can steal even if you're not building commerce. TToken Speed: Why AI Inference Suddenly Got 10-15× Faster Wafer-scale chips and LPUs are serving frontier models at hundreds of tokens per second. What actually limits inference speed, the new hardware race, and why fast tokens change agents, voice and reasoning. DDiffusion LLMs: The Models That Don't Write Left to Right Mercury 2 answers a full reasoning question in 1.7 seconds at 1,009 tok/s; Gemini Diffusion samples at 1,479 tok/s against Gemini 2.5 Flash's 272.4. Same transformers, different decoding algorithm. The practical guide: why the open-weight pioneer's own README says quality peaks when you use one step per token, the conditional-independence bug that makes parallel decoding wrong, block diffusion as the fix that restored the KV cache, how DiffusionGemma converted an autoregressive Gemma 4 for under 10% of its training budget, and the masked-infill jailbreak that hits 100% on an aligned dLLM. CComputer-Use Agents Compared Claude, GPT and Gemini can all drive a screen now — but each exposes a different action space, coordinate contract and safety gate. What actually breaks, and how to build a loop that survives it. SShared-Login Browsers for AI Agents: The ego lite Pattern A new class of browser — best exemplified by ego lite, which hit #1 on GitHub Trending on July 24, 2026 — lets Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and any other coding agent drive an isolated Chromium session that inherits your real logins. What Spaces and semantic snapshots actually solve, why it undercuts Playwright for agent work, and the security cost of sharing session cookies with an autonomous process. CCloudflare Kitesurf: The First Browser Runtime Built for AI Agents (Not Humans) On August 6, 2026 Cloudflare launched Kitesurf, a stateless, agent-first browser that runs entirely in V8 isolates on Workers. It uses 3-7x less CPU and memory than Chromium on common agent tasks — at the cost of ~1.7x wall-clock time. Written in Rust, using Firefox's CSS parser (Stylo) and the Blitz rendering engine, drop-in compatible with Puppeteer/Playwright via the Chrome DevTools Protocol. This page: what changed, when to reach for it instead of headless Chrome, how to wire it into Claude Code / Codex / your MCP client, and the four things it flat-out can't do yet. SSKILL.md: The Cross-Agent Open Standard One SKILL.md file, thirty-two agents. What the Agent Skills open standard actually is, how progressive disclosure keeps context cheap, what breaks portability, and how to write a skill that runs unchanged in Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI and Cursor. CColibrì: Run a 744B MoE From Your SSD (and What It Really Costs You) Colibrì is a pure-C, zero-dependency engine that runs GLM-5.2 (744B), Kimi K3 (2.8T), DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and six other frontier MoE models on a 16–32 GB machine by keeping the dense layers in RAM and streaming the routed experts from NVMe. This page explains the memory hierarchy, the numbers that decide whether it is usable for you (0.05 to 6.8 tok/s), the SSD-wear and speculative-decoding gotchas, and the exact commands to get a first token. OOpenAI Agents API vs Claude Managed Agents: The Hosted Agent Loop, Compared On September 10, 2026 OpenAI put the Codex harness behind a single API call: the Agents API public beta — durable sessions, hosted or self-hosted sandboxes, automatic compaction, tool search, subagents. Anthropic has run the same shape since April as Managed Agents. Both use the same four primitives; they differ on permissions, secrets, budgets, network policy and what the sandbox costs. The side-by-side, the request shapes, the six gotchas, and when to pick which. AAX (Agent Executor): Google's Open Agent Runtime, Explained for Builders (2026) google/ax hit the Hacker News front page on September 20–21, 2026 (507 points). It is not a model, a harness or a hosted API: it is a kubectl-shaped orchestrator that runs agent Tasks in sandboxes on top of Agent Substrate, with Workspaces (git + MCP + skills), Gateways (egress allowlists) and Models (provider + secret) as declarative resources. What the four primitives do, what survives suspend/resume and what does not, the runner contract your image must honour, the GKE requirements, and why the June-era docs no longer match the CLI. SSystem One Decision Models: Jev, Kev and the Open Clones, Explained for Builders (2026) TypeSafe AI's Jev (out of stealth September 15, 2026) is a model that never writes text: you send it program state plus typed questions and it returns calibrated probabilities for all of them in one parallel pass, 70–500 ms, $0.042 per million input tokens, output free. Two Hacker News front-page stories on September 21 (Kev, an Apache-2.0 recreation on Qwen3.5, and the jev-leftpad joke) made it the week's topic. What a System One model actually does, what the 'cannot hallucinate' claim really guarantees, the vendor numbers next to the one independent test, where a decision model belongs in a Claude agent loop, and how to run Kev or Nimble locally. TTrain Your Own Decision Model: Jeff, Jeeves and the DIY System One Stack (Sep 2026) Two weeks after Jev made decision models a category, the open stack caught up: Jeff fine-tunes a 0.8B Qwen into a Jev-compatible classifier in ~2 hours on one workstation GPU, and PostHog's Jeeves shows that letting a decision model think first beats Jev on its own benchmark. What the training recipe actually is (cross-entropy over option letters, a separately fitted temperature), where tiny models beat the API and where they get destroyed, the 26-option ceiling, the 20x CPU latency cliff, and the boring embeddings baseline that scored 93.0% and that you must beat before any of this is worth doing. TTernary Quantization in Practice: Bonsai 2 27B in 5.95 GB PrismML compressed Qwen3.8-27B to 1.75 bits per weight and 5.95 GB. The practical guide nobody wrote: why stock llama.cpp loads the file and silently produces garbage, why the bigger 7.21 GB file is faster on an H100 but slower on a 4090, why 5.95 GB of weights needs 12 GB of VRAM, and which capabilities the 98.2% retention headline quietly loses. AAsync-First Agent Harnesses: What Unreal Agent Changes Unreal Labs shipped an MIT-licensed Go harness that matches Codex's pass rate on Terminal-Bench 4.0 for 39% less money — by never making the model wait for a tool. The event-log mechanism, why turn count is the real cost unit, and the three things they deliberately refused to build. HHindsight: agent memory that learns The MIT-licensed memory server that topped GitHub trending — retain, recall and reflect, four parallel retrievers fused by RRF, observations that get refined instead of overwritten, and the 83.6%-vs-39.0% result that says architecture beats model size. EEmber-1: Kimi K3's Answers for 40% Fewer Tokens (Sep 2026) Fireworks post-trained Kimi K3 to stop over-thinking and shipped the result as Ember-1 — same price per token, 35–50% fewer reasoning tokens, and it beats K3 at max effort on two of five benchmarks. Why turning effort down is not the same thing, what the '-51.9% / -23.1 USD' column really says, the implied cost per benchmark task, the modality that quietly disappears, and the Kimi K3 licence clause that lets a derivative stay closed. OOpenAI Dots: The Always-On Agent, and the Permission Ladder Underneath It At DevDay on September 29, 2026 OpenAI shipped dots — persistent agents that each get their own cloud computer and browser, run on GPT-6 Astra, and keep working while you are logged off. The launch coverage stops at the demo. This page covers the mechanism: the five-rung permission ladder, why proactive research is read-only at the tool layer rather than the prompt layer, what the published safety numbers actually measure, and how a dot compares to Claude Managed Agents and Cowork. WWorld Models: What You Can Actually Build Today AMD is paying about $8.2 billion for World Labs, and two very different things are being sold under the same name. Frame generators like Genie keep the world inside the model and cap a session at 60 seconds. 3D generators like Marble hand you Gaussian splats you own, render for free and cannot collide with. The API shapes, the export tiers, the WorldScore evidence, the open weights you can run, and the five jobs a world model will not do. IIs the model nerfed? How to actually tell "They nerfed it" is the most-repeated claim in AI and the least-measured. On the Claude API the weights behind a model ID cannot change — every current ID is a pinned snapshot. But seven other things can change under you without a new model, from a published system-prompt update to a harness that silently swaps models mid-session. Here is what can and cannot move, why the most-cited 'GPT-4 got dumber' result was an eval bug, and a measurement protocol you can run in an afternoon. PPi 1.0: The Minimal Harness, and the Codemode Trick That Fixes MCP Token Bloat Pi 1.0 shipped 1 October 2026 and went to #1 on Hacker News. The interesting part is not the TUI — it is the context engineering: a QuickJS/WASM sandbox where tool results never enter the model's context, four MCP exposure modes, a 3,000-token ceiling on inlined tool declarations, and a trick that appends a new system-prompt section to the transcript instead of mutating tool definitions so your prompt cache survives. Plus the deliberate omissions (no sub-agents, no plan mode), the $0.05 cache-warming rule, and the trust gap that loads a cloned repo's AGENTS.md without asking. DDeepSeek Harness: the agent where the agent loop itself is a plugin DeepSeek Harness (dsh) passed 242,000 stars and shipped desktop installers on 1 October 2026. The headline is 'everything is a plugin' — and unlike most such claims this one is load-bearing: the model adapter, the tool registry, the session log and the agent loop are all replaceable from a YAML patch file. This page covers the three facts that matter to a Claude user (it runs your existing Claude Code hooks.json, it speaks anthropic-messages, and run_code is codemode by default), the three-mode sandbox and the kernel primitives behind it, the append-only session log invariant, and the config override that silently deletes your other providers. SStrata: a 125B MoE at 94 tok/s on a 12 GB Card — and the Exact Bill Strata runs Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (125B, 6B active) on a 12 GB gaming GPU at interactive speed. This page explains the three architecture facts that make it possible, reads the benchmark table honestly, and prices the quality you give up: 91.3% of SWE-bench Verified against 98.7% of LiveCodeBench, a KV-cache setting that passes needle tests while losing 8-12% perplexity, a speed mode that strips refusal directions, and a measured vision regression on identical weights. HHow to Read an AI Benchmark Without Getting Fooled Every launch post leads with a benchmark number. Almost none of them tell you the three things that decide what it means: which scaffold produced it, how many trials it averages, and whether the model had already seen the answers. A reader's manual for SWE-bench, SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Pro and the arena leaderboards — with the vendor's own footnotes as evidence. DDwarfStar (ds4) and the Rise of Overfit Inference Engines ds4 is a 23.6k-star, pure-C engine from the creator of Redis that runs DeepSeek V4 Flash, GLM 5.x and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next locally — and refuses to run anything else. This page explains the three mechanisms a general runtime will not give you (asymmetric routed-expert quantization, bounded expert streaming from SSD, KV snapshots that survive a restart), reads its own numbers honestly — the 126 t/s headline is an eight-GPU aggregate across 16 sessions, not your Mac — and prices the real cost of the overfit bet: deliberately disposable model support, 761 open issues, and a main branch that last moved on 20 September 2026. MMistral Large 4 (Le Chonk): the 1.05T open weight you can't download yet Europe's trillion-parameter MoE: why 49B active params still need ~525 GB at 4-bit, the 1M context that evaluators measured at ~512K, a 50% launch promo that hides the real cost-per-task, an Intelligence Index of 38 against Opus 5.5's 58 — and the staged weight release where vetted partners get a less-moderated build first. WWhistle: Speech-to-Text in 16.9 MB — and the Benchmark Bars Nobody Labelled Cactus Compute's Whistle fits a multilingual ASR model in 16.9 MB and hits 11.1 ms to first token on a CPU. The size claim is real. This page reads the vendor's own benchmark chart bar by bar — including the three competitor columns it declines to label — and finds the pattern that explains every field complaint: Whistle wins on close-mic single-speaker audio and is the worst of the three on real meeting audio, 4.6 WER points behind a model 8.6x its size. Plus the 30-second architectural wall, the streaming API the launch thread missed, and the one knob that took a tester from 70/170 to 164/170. WWhy a 35 KB System Prompt Breaks on a Local Model Moving a big Claude/GPT system prompt to Ollama or another local runtime: the context-budget math, Ollama's silent middle-of-prompt truncation, the failure signals of context exhaustion, and the restructuring that actually works.
Claude is the core here, but the same skills travel. Start with how to choose, then go as deep as you need on any assistant, on running models locally, or on agents.
A durable framework for picking the right AI model for a task — across Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Llama, Mistral, Grok and the open/local models — plus what skills transfer across all of them.

documents.t: Google's Gemini 4 generation opens with Argon and one headline number: a 1M-token OUTPUT limit, up from 64K. Context stayed at 1M. What the coverage gets wrong: the independent Artificial Analysis index puts Argon at 53 — five points BEHIND Claude Opus 5.5's 58 — and its cheaper $1.99-per-task cost comes from the rate card, not efficiency, since it burns 62K output tokens per task against GPT-6 Astra's 27K. Plus: a 15% hallucination rate (lowest measured), and why you almost certainly cannot call it yet.
documents.s: GGemini 4 Argon: The Field Guide for Claude Users (Sep 30, 2026)

documents.t: Opus 5.5 shipped 22 September 2026 at $4/$20 per MTok — 20% under Opus 5, with cache reads at $0.20 (a 5% tier, not the usual 10%). Four breaking changes 400-error a naive migration, one more changes the response shape without failing anything and makes your UI go quiet mid-task. Thinking can no longer be disabled at all, forced tool_choice is gone, and the default effort dropped from high to medium — while each level now thinks more than it did on Opus 5.

Anthropic shipped Claude Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 on September 1, 2026: same $10/$50 price, cache reads cut to $0.25, three breaking API changes (forced tool_choice errors, one-way thinking blocks, append-only history) and five additive betas. The migration field guide for anyone pinning claude-fable-5 or claude-opus-5.
documents.s: CClaude Fable 5.1: What Changed and How to Migrate

documents.t: Fable 5 is Anthropic's most capable model. Its API refuses in-band (HTTP 200, stop_reason: refusal), has adaptive thinking only, and never returns raw thinking. If you're pinning a top-tier model, this changes how you write integrations. When to use it vs Opus 4.8, the fallback pattern, the prompting shifts.
documents.s: CClaude Fable 5 & Mythos 5: The Flagship Field Guide

documents.t: Sonnet 5.5 shipped 28 September 2026 at exactly Sonnet 5's prices — $2/$10 per MTok — and Anthropic still claims up to 30% less per task. The saving is in the token count, not the rate card. Five breaking changes 400-error a Sonnet 5 codebase, a sixth returns 200 and silences your progress UI, thinking can no longer be disabled (only moved between tool calls), and on Terminal-Bench 4.0 the cheap model scores 70.6% against Opus 5.5's 66.4%.

Haiku 5.5 shipped 7 October 2026 at $0.10/$0.50 per MTok — a 90% cut — and it is the only current Claude model priced by prompt length. One token past 100,000 reprices the entire request 5x. The threshold is measured on the new tokenizer, so it arrives ~23% earlier in text than you expect, and the 90% headline is ~87% in practice below the cliff and ~35% above it.

Opus 5 shipped 24 July 2026 as Anthropic's fourth model in two months — same $5/$25 pricing as Opus 4.8 but more than double the Frontier-Bench score, 3× ARC-AGI-3 vs the next-best model, and a new xhigh/max effort tier. The benchmarks that matter, the two 400-errors that break naive migrations, and when Opus 5 replaces Fable 5 in your stack.

Sonnet 5 is Sonnet 4.6's drop-in successor and Claude Code's default on Pro and Team Standard — but three API constraints will 400 you on migration and a new tokenizer produces ~30% more tokens for the same text. The pricing math, the effort re-mapping (Sonnet 5 medium ≈ Sonnet 4.6 high), and the prompting shifts that catch teams out.
Fluent in Claude, need to use ChatGPT? The differences that matter, what transfers, and when to reach for which — including the Custom GPT retirement and the Plugins that replace them.

OpenAI shipped the GPT-5.6 family (Sol, Terra, Luna) and ChatGPT Work on 9 July 2026. What actually changed for a Claude user — 1.05M context, a $1 tier, an agent that runs for hours, and the parts of the launch nobody is writing about.

documents.t: OpenAI shipped GPT-6.1 Sol at DevDay on September 29, 2026 with the exact rate card Claude Sonnet 5.5 has — $2/$10 — and a cached-input price half of Sonnet's. The launch line is 'near-Astra intelligence for a fifth of the price'. The details that decide whether that is true for you: a 922K input ceiling inside a 1.05M window, a hard cost cliff at 272K tokens, tool calling that only works on one of the two APIs, and the benchmark row where Sonnet 5.5 still wins by 8.7 points.
documents.s: GGPT-6.1 Sol: The Field Guide for Claude Users

documents.t: On 6 August 2026 OpenAI shipped a mid-cycle update to GPT-5.6 that most write-ups reduced to 'Sol got smarter.' The real story: a six-tier effort control that changes how you price a request, a free-tier Think button, a 272K token pricing cliff that re-prices the whole call, and a Fast mode that only runs on Sol. What each means for a Claude user.

What every part actually does, in Claude-user terms.

Supabase open-sourced a benchmark that runs Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode against real containerized Supabase stacks — not mocks. Here's what it measures, what it found about how models actually use docs and skills, and how to run it locally in an evening.

Apple's third-generation Foundation Models (AFM 3) landed at WWDC 2026 with a 3B dense on-device model, a 20B sparse MoE that runs on iPhone, and a Swift-native framework that now lets you bring your own LLM provider — including Claude. What actually shipped, the non-obvious mechanisms, and how it changes the on-device story for anyone who ships Claude apps.

documents.t: Fluent in Claude, need Google's Gemini? The differences that matter — Gems, Workspace integration, huge context, multimodal — and what transfers.

documents.t: On 13 August 2026, three weeks after 3.6 Flash, Google shipped Gemini 3.7 Flash at half the introductory price with a 16-point DeepSWE jump. The gotchas most write-ups skip: an expiring intro price, a 3× throughput advantage that matters for agent loops but not chat, and where it still trails Claude Sonnet 5.

documents.t: On September 2, 2026, three weeks after 3.7 Flash, Google shipped Gemini 3.8 Flash at the same $0.75 / $3.75 intro price: DeepSWE 73.7 (+8.4), Terminal-bench 2.1 89.4, HLE-Verified 54.9, plus a Cyber variant gated behind the new Fairwind Program. What the append-only event log actually buys you, why the contributor tier is 12.5× cheaper than standard, how it stacks up against Claude Code on Terminal-Bench 2.1, and the three bundled skills that are worth stealing regardless of which agent you use.

What actually ships, the API shape, the cost math, what Anthropic does instead, and when the native primitive beats a DIY fan-out.
documents.s: NNative Multi-Agent APIs: OpenAI's Responses Multi-Agent Beta vs Building It Yourself

documents.t: MCP connects agents to tools. A2A connects agents to other agents — across frameworks, clouds, and companies. Learn the Agent Card, tasks, the eight lifecycle states, streaming vs. webhooks, and how A2A composes with MCP.

How AI agents actually pay for things now — the x402 HTTP-402 protocol, the exact/upto/batch-settlement schemes, facilitators, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Payments' Aug 2026 GA (payment sessions, Coinbase Bazar MCP, Stripe Privy, Machine Payment Protocol), and how to add a paywall or a spending agent without inventing a wallet.

The design patterns for sending each request to the right AI model — rule-based, classifier, complexity, cascade, ensemble, fallback. When to use each, what breaks, and the recipes that actually ship in 2026.

documents.t: Strong open-weight models (DeepSeek, Qwen, Llama, Mistral) closed much of the gap. What 'open weight' means, the trade-offs vs closed frontier, and how to use them.

August 3, 2026: Alibaba's Qwen3.8-Max shipped API-only with a 2.4T parameter MoE (95B active), a 1M context, dual OpenAI/Anthropic-spec APIs, and benchmark scores that beat GPT-5.6 Sol Max on OSWorld. What's genuinely new, what 'open weight' actually means when the Hugging Face page is empty, and the sparsity math that makes self-hosting expensive.

documents.t: On Aug 31 2026 DeepSeek open-sourced V4-Flash-Vision-Exp — a 305B MoE that adds native vision to V4-Flash without hurting text agent scores, matches or beats Claude Opus 4.8 on ApexBench / Agents' Last Exam / ZeroBench at a fraction of the price, and ships MIT. The specific numbers, the hard 384-token-per-image cap most guides ignore, and the concrete way to run it.
documents.s: DDeepSeek V4-Flash-Vision: First Native-Vision Frontier Open Weight

documents.t: On September 10, 2026 DeepSeek shipped V4.1-Flash — a 552B MIT-licensed MoE with native vision, a 1M-token window, a KV cache a quarter the size of V4-Flash's, and a 1–100 reasoning-effort dial. It ties Claude Opus 5 on DeepSWE v1.1 (74.2 vs 74.0) at $0.30 per million input tokens, and trails badly on Terminal-Bench. The numbers, the routing change that silently moved every deepseek-v4-pro call, and where Claude still wins.
documents.s: DDeepSeek-V4.1-Flash: A 1M-Context Open Weight That Ties Opus 5 on DeepSWE (Sep 2026)

documents.t: Moonshot's Kimi K2 is an open-weight, trillion-parameter agent built for long tool-use chains. What actually makes it different from Claude — native INT4 weights, 200–300 sequential tool calls, a permissive license — and when it's worth reaching for.

Z.ai's 753B MoE (~40B active), 1M-token context, MIT-licensed — closes to within a point of Claude Opus 4.8 on long-horizon coding, at roughly one-sixth the API cost. What IndexShare actually does, how to run it locally, and where it beats Claude Code in the wild.

Mira Murati's Thinking Machines Lab shipped Inkling — a 975B-parameter Apache 2.0 multimodal MoE with a continuous thinking-effort dial. What the launch coverage got wrong, why it deliberately loses benchmarks, and what the effort knob actually does.

Moonshot AI's 2.8-trillion-parameter open-weight model beats Claude Opus 4.8 on many benchmarks and tops the Frontend Code Arena. What makes it architecturally different, when the cache-hit pricing flips the cost math, and whether it's worth reaching for.
documents.s: KKimi K3: World's Largest Open-Weight Model

documents.t: The definitive practical guide to self-hosting Moonshot's 2.8T open-weight Kimi K3 in 2026. What DSpark speculative decoding actually does, minimum hardware (1× DGX B300 or 16× DGX Spark), the exact vLLM serve commands, the prefill/decode asymmetry nobody warns you about, and when hosted inference undercuts your own rack.
documents.s: RRunning Kimi K3 Locally: vLLM, DSpark & the Real Hardware Bill

documents.t: A 1.02T-parameter MoE with 42B active, 1M context, text/image/video/audio input — MIT-licensed on Hugging Face. What the benchmark tables actually say once you check which version was run, why Pro needs 32 GPUs and Flash doesn't, and what the 10x UltraSpeed tier is really selling.

xAI published the full Rust source of its coding agent under Apache 2.0 — the agent loop, tool layer, TUI and extension system. What the crate map teaches you about building agents, why 'open source' here means source-available, and what the data-collector code still in the tree tells you.
documents.s: IInside Grok Build: Reading an Open Agent Harness

What the 8B-active S 2.1 actually beats, why the 3B-active XS 2.1 runs on a MacBook, the first-known RL-in-FP8 training pipeline, and when to reach for it over Claude, GLM-5.2 or Kimi K3.
documents.s: PPoolside Laguna: Open-Weight Coding Models That Punch Above Their Class

documents.t: Alibaba's open-code-review (ocr) is the AI code reviewer trending on GitHub: a Go CLI that puts deterministic file selection, rule matching and line anchoring around an LLM agent. Same Claude model, 4.7x the precision of a Claude Code review at 1/15 the tokens on its own benchmark — and a best-case recall of 20%. How it works, how to run it with Claude, GPT, Qwen or a local model, delegation mode, CI, and the gotchas.
documents.s: OOpen Code Review: Alibaba's Hybrid AI Reviewer vs Claude Code, Codex and Any Model (2026)

documents.t: MiniMax open-sourced a 33B single-stream transformer that generates 4–15s of 2K video with native stereo audio in one pass. The license quietly blocks self-hosting in the US/EU/UK/Korea, the open base is 768p (not 2K), and ~13B of 33B params are AdaLN branches you can skip at inference. What H3 actually is, what it costs, and when it beats the closed video APIs.
documents.s: MMiniMax H3 (Hailuo 3.0): The Open-Weight Omni Video Model

documents.t: A durable framework for comparing AI cost across providers — the pricing archetypes, how to estimate a workload, the levers to cut the bill, and when open/local wins.

A soft cap emails you. A hard cap blocks the request. This page maps which AI providers do which — and the trap nobody documents: the same event (you hit your cap) returns HTTP 429 with no retry-after on Anthropic's tier cap, HTTP 400 on the limit you set yourself, 429 on OpenAI, and 402 on OpenRouter. Plus why no cap can be exact, where the Custom tier loses its safety net, and how to build a pre-flight killswitch.
documents.s: HHard Spend Caps: Which AI Providers Actually Stop the Bill

documents.t: Every major provider caches your prompt prefix — but explicit vs automatic, 5 minutes vs 24 hours, and a write premium that can make caching cost you more. The portable break-even rule and the five traps when you move a workload.

Agentic runs cost 50–1000x a chat — not because the model is dumber, but because of the context snowball. The mechanism, the surprising numbers, and the four levers that actually cut the bill across Claude, GPT, Gemini, and open models.
documents.s: WWhy AI Agents Burn Tokens (and How to Cap the Bill)

documents.t: Render your context into a picture and the vision encoder becomes a compression dial. Measured across Anthropic, OpenAI and Google, an image of code counts 76–87% fewer input tokens than the same code as text — and on Gemini it can cost 6.95x MORE. The mechanism, the accuracy cliff, and how to test it on your own documents.
documents.s: OOptical Context Compression: Sending Text as an Image

documents.t: Opus 5.5 explainer videos hit the Hacker News front page — and almost nobody explains what is actually happening: the model writes a deterministic animation program, not a video. The mechanism, the three render engines and their licences, the two traps that break agent-written animation code, the pacing formula that makes the difference between watchable and unwatchable, and what the bill really looks like.

Wafer-scale chips and LPUs are serving frontier models at hundreds of tokens per second. What actually limits inference speed, the new hardware race, and why fast tokens change agents, voice and reasoning.

Same transformers, different decoding algorithm. documents.t: Claude, GPT and Gemini can all drive a screen now — but each exposes a different action space, coordinate contract and safety gate. What actually breaks, and how to build a loop that survives it.

A new class of browser — best exemplified by ego lite, which hit #1 on GitHub Trending on July 24, 2026 — lets Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and any other coding agent drive an isolated Chromium session that inherits your real logins. What Spaces and semantic snapshots actually solve, why it undercuts Playwright for agent work, and the security cost of sharing session cookies with an autonomous process.
