What you'll learn Understand the two-agent split (shopping vs merchant) and why Anthropic did NOT use an intent router or domain subagents Learn the staged-write guardrail: how no model tool call ever moves money or mutates the store — every write ends at a human-approved surface See the three runtime paths (Messages API, Agent SDK, Managed Agents) and how the SAME core code plugs into all three Steal three transferable patterns for any agent that touches a real business system: server-issued IDs, fenced third-party text, and prompt-vs-skill split On September 2, 2026 Anthropic published anthropics/commerce-agents — an Apache 2.0 reference blueprint for building shopping and merchant agents on Claude. It ships two working agents, four vertical examples (retail, travel, telecom, entertainment), and — crucially — a set of guardrail patterns implemented in code, not in prompts. Anthropic states the repo is a reference implementation they will not maintain as a product and does not accept outside contributions. The interesting thing is not that you can now build a shopping bot. The interesting thing is the shape: an unusually opinionated take on how an agent that touches real business systems should be structured. Everything below is transferable to any agent that has to write to a real backend — inventory, customer records, banking, ops tooling.

Anthropic ships one shopping agent (customer-facing) and one merchant agent (staff-facing), each with its own backend interface (StorefrontBackend and MerchantBackend) and its own set of skills. They deliberately did not build: an intent router that dispatches to sub-agents per-domain subagents (a "cart agent" + "returns agent" + "search agent") one monolithic agent that does both consumer and staff work Instead: one unified agent per audience, in a standard agent loop, with skills and tools. Their guidance in the anatomy of effective commerce agents post: "anything the agent needs on most turns generally goes in the system prompt" — so for a shopping agent, catalog search lives in the prompt because it's on nearly every turn. "The rest goes in skills." Customer care, personalization, returns — skills. This is a strong opinion. Intent routers and domain subagents are the default architecture in a lot of tutorials, and Anthropic is telling you: for a single audience with tightly coupled sessions, don't.
documents.s: The split: two agents, not one

documents.t: Pro tip The single most important line in the blueprint: 'No model tool call moves money or changes the business.' Every mutation goes through a server-controlled approval step. If you take one thing from the repo, take this. The blueprint enforces safety in code, not prompts. The mechanism has three parts: Guided walkthrough1 of 3 11. Server issues every ID the model is allowed to reference⌄ The server maintains a per-session record of every product ID, SKU, campaign ID, and price ID it has handed the model. Writes and renders will ONLY accept IDs from that record. If the model hallucinates a SKU, the harness refuses — no prompt engineering required. ←PreviousNext→ 22. Every write is staged, never applied⌄ Order placement, payments, refunds, price changes, and campaign launches all end in a server-generated draft with its own approval ID. The tool call returns the draft ID and a preview. Nothing is live yet. ←PreviousNext→ 33. Approval happens on a real human surface⌄ A staged change only succeeds when the approval ID is signed off through a real UI — a button in the operator's portal, a confirmation in the CLI. The agent cannot self-approve; the approval endpoint doesn't accept model-generated identity. ←PreviousNext→ The blueprint also handles two other classic footguns: Regulated content: for fees, disclosures, and price-shown-to-consumer, the model chooses which product to disclose; the words come from server-supplied approved copy. The model never writes disclosure text. Third-party text sanitization: any user-generated content (reviews, seller notes, messages) is wrapped in "fenced text" markers before it reaches the model, so it can't smuggle instructions into the prompt.

The blueprint places no orders and charges no cards. Checkout is rendered for the host application to complete. In Anthropic's words, this "keeps payment handling, fraud rules and credentials outside the agent." Visa, Mastercard, and Accenture are named partners on the announcement, but the payment step lives in your existing checkout or an agentic payments provider — never in the model's tool surface. This is another opinionated line: if it can lose money in one shot, the model doesn't touch it.

The repo splits every agent into a core package (types, backend interface, prompt, tool contracts) and separate runtime packages that adapt the core to different serving surfaces: Messages API — the reference loop CopyOpen in Claude↗ from shopping_agent import ShoppingAgentConfig from shopping_agent_runtime import ShoppingAgent agent = ShoppingAgent( backend=your_backend, skills_dir=Path("shopping-agent/skills"), config=ShoppingAgentConfig(brand_name="Your Store"), ) async for event in agent.stream_turn(messages, session, state): # yields: text_delta | tool_call | ui | cart_update | turn_complete ... await agent.update_memory(messages, session) Agent SDK — with a local console CopyOpen in Claude↗ python shopping-agent/runtime-agent-sdk/main.py \ --once "a two-person tent under $250" python merchant-agent/runtime-agent-sdk/main.py # prints staged changes and waits for y/n approval Managed Agents (beta) — hosted CopyOpen in Claude↗ scripts/deploy_managed_agent.sh \ shopping-agent/managed-agents/shopping-agent # The manifest declares tools + a storefront MCP server; # Anthropic hosts the loop. The same core/ code runs under all three, which is the actual portable pattern: keep the agent's contract (tools, prompt, backend interface) separate from the serving harness. If you swap Messages API for Managed Agents six months from now, only the runtime package changes.

Long-term memory (preferences, past orders, service notes) is persisted in your existing databases, not in model context. Extraction happens asynchronously after the conversation ends — you don't pay latency to update memory on the hot path. On the next turn, the runtime hydrates relevant memory into the system prompt. This is worth internalizing even if you're not building commerce: shoving conversation summaries into context on every turn is a common performance mistake. The blueprint's shape — write async, read on turn-start — is the cheaper one.

examples/ includes end-to-end demos for four verticals, each with a different structural wrinkle you can copy: Retail — the base case. Standard catalog, cart, checkout. Travel — date-bound inventory (a flight seat expires), itinerary presentation with multi-leg comparison. Telecom — account context ("your current plan is X"), plan matrices, regulated fee disclosure. Entertainment — timed holds on tickets, waitlists, venue seat maps. If your product isn't commerce but has any of these traits (expiring inventory, regulated disclosure, timed holds), the matching vertical is worth reading before you design your own agent.
documents.s: The four verticals (and why they differ)

Copy as Markdown Advanced Every major lab now ships a model that can look at a screen and click on it. Anthropic's computer use tool, OpenAI's computer tool, and Google's computer_use tool all solve the same shape of problem — take a screenshot, decide an action, execute it, screenshot again — and all three are wire-incompatible with each other in ways that are not obvious until your clicks start landing 40 pixels off. This page is the harness-level guide, not the leaderboard. The leaderboard changes monthly; the failure modes below have been the same since the first preview shipped. :::caution Related security reading When the screen an agent drives is a browser, the agent also lands above a boundary the web has relied on for 30 years — see Agentic Browsers Break the Same-Origin Policy for the UW findings on Atlas, Comet, Gemini in Chrome and Claude for Chrome. ::: :::tip Related pattern For the shared-login variant — an agent that drives a real Chromium session with your cookies inherited, via ego lite and its ego-browser skill — the loop above collapses into a JavaScript-per-turn model and the security posture inverts (the agent has your privileges by design). ::: What you'll learn Understand the agent loop all three providers share — and the three places they diverge Fix the coordinate bug that silently breaks most first attempts (Retina, downscaling, and image size limits) Know each provider's safety gate, because it is part of the protocol, not an optional add-on Read OSWorld honestly: what the human baseline actually means Pick reasoning effort correctly — the cheapest setting is not the one you would guess Last verified: 2026-07-14. Model names, beta headers, pixel limits and benchmark scores in this space move fast, and every provider still labels its computer-use surface as preview or beta. The mechanics below are durable; re-check any specific number, header or model id against the provider docs linked in Sources before you ship. Confirm against the official source.

Strip away the branding and all three are the same state machine: Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Send the task plus a screenshot⌄ The model gets your instruction and an image of the current screen. Some providers also want the current URL or a short history of recent actions. ←PreviousNext→ 2The model returns an action, not a result⌄ Click at (x, y). Type this. Scroll here. It is a request for your code to do something — the model cannot touch the machine itself. ←PreviousNext→ 3Your harness executes it⌄ You own this. Anthropic states it plainly: your application must run the tool; Claude cannot run it directly. You implement the screenshot capture, the mouse, the keyboard. ←PreviousNext→ 4Screenshot again, feed it back⌄ The new screen goes back as a tool result. The model sees the consequence of its own action — this is the entire feedback signal. ←PreviousNext→ 5Repeat until no action comes back⌄ Termination is the absence of a further action request, not a 'done' flag. Your loop needs its own step cap and stall detection. ←PreviousNext→ The consequence people miss: the model's only perception of the world is the image you send it. Every failure below is really a failure of that image, or of the coordinate space it implies.

The divergence is not "which one is smarter." It is the contract. Anthropic (Claude) OpenAI (GPT) Google (Gemini) Action space Raw desktop primitives: screenshot, left_click, type, key, scroll, drag, hold_key, wait, plus zoom on the newest tool version Structured UI actions: click, double_click, scroll, type, keypress, drag, move, wait, screenshot Semantic actions: not just click/type but navigate, go_back, go_forward, open_app, long_press — the browser and mobile concepts are first-class Coordinates You send pixel dimensions; the model returns raw pixel coordinates in that space Same pixel contract, with recommended desktop sizes Same, with an intent field explaining the reasoning behind each action Loop plumbing Tool result blocks carrying an image computer_call → computer_call_output keyed by call_id; previous_response_id carries history so you don't resend it Function call → function_result with a fresh screenshot Safety gate Injection classifiers run automatically on screenshots pending_safety_checks you must explicitly acknowledge safety_decision with policy categories Sweet spot General desktop / OS-level control Desktop and browser, plus a code-execution path Browser-first; strong on mobile; explicitly not optimized for desktop OS control That last Anthropic/Google row is the one that decides architecture. Google's action space is semantic — go_back is a concept the model can name. Anthropic's is mechanical — going back means the model must find and click the back button, or press the right key combination. Semantic actions are more reliable inside a browser and useless outside one. Mechanical primitives work anywhere and fail more often. So: porting a computer-use agent between providers is not a model swap. It is rewriting the harness's action executor. Budget accordingly. (Same lesson as Coding Agent CLIs Compared: the harness, not the model, is the thing you're actually married to.)

This is the single highest-value thing on this page, because almost everyone hits it and the symptom looks like "the model is bad at clicking." It is not bad at clicking. Your image and your coordinate space disagree. Three independent causes, which stack:
documents.s: The coordinate bug that eats your first week

documents.t: macOS Retina displays capture screenshots at a device pixel ratio of 2 — the image is twice the resolution of the logical screen coordinates. Send that raw and the model reasons about a 2880-wide image while your click executor thinks in 1440-wide logical points. Every click lands at roughly half the intended position, consistently, in one direction. Fix: downscale by 2 before sending, or halve the coordinates the model returns. Not both.

Models have image size limits — and they differ between models from the same lab. Claude Sonnet 5, Opus 4.8 and Opus 4.7 accept up to 2576 pixels on the long edge; earlier Claude models accept 1568 pixels and roughly 1.15 megapixels total. Here is the trap: if you send something bigger, the API downscales it for you rather than erroring. The model then returns coordinates in the space of the image it saw — and you never learned the scale factor, because the resize happened server-side. Only genuinely enormous images (over ~8,000 px on a side) get rejected outright with a validation error. So the "helpful" behavior is the bug. Always resize client-side, set display_width_px/display_height_px to the dimensions you actually sent, and scale returned coordinates back up yourself.
documents.s: 2. The API silently downscales oversized images

documents.t: On OpenAI's tool, screenshots should use detail: "original" — both "high" and "low" degrade click accuracy for this task specifically. And if you resize without preserving aspect ratio, clicks land in the right region and miss the target. Coordinate scaling — the shape of the fix CopyOpen in Claude↗ # Before sending: shrink to fit the model's image limit, remember the factor. LONG_EDGE_LIMIT = 2576 # check YOUR model's limit; older Claude models: 1568 scale = min(1.0, LONG_EDGE_LIMIT / max(width, height)) sent_w, sent_h = round(width * scale), round(height * scale) # -> send the resized image, and declare display_width_px=sent_w, display_height_px=sent_h # After the model replies: map its coordinates back to the real screen. real_x, real_y = model_x / scale, model_y / scale # On a Retina capture you did NOT pre-downscale, divide by the device pixel ratio too.

Symptom Almost certainly Clicks consistently offset in one direction Your declared display_width_px/display_height_px don't match the image you actually sent Clicks land in the right area but miss small targets Detail lost to downscaling, or aspect ratio distorted on resize Accuracy poor everywhere Resolution too low — try 1280x720 as a floor Model misreads tiny text (tab titles, filenames, line numbers) It needs to zoom, and you didn't enable it Resolution guidance, from the vendors themselves: Anthropic suggests 1024x768 or 1280x720 for general desktop, 1280x800 or 1366x768 for web apps, and explicitly says to avoid going above 1920x1080. OpenAI recommends 1440x900 or 1600x900. Bigger is not better — you pay tokens for pixels and then throw the detail away in the downscale.

Claude's newest computer tool version (computer_20251124) adds a zoom action, off by default — you must set enable_zoom: true. With it on, Claude zooms into a region when it needs to read small text that isn't legible at the screenshot's base resolution: sidebar filenames, tab titles, status-bar text, line numbers, button labels. Non-obvious operational note: if Claude isn't zooming when you expect it to, the fix is usually to ask about a specific region or element rather than about the screen as a whole.

Do not treat this as a bolt-on. In all three APIs, the safety mechanism changes the shape of your loop. Anthropic trained the model to resist prompt injection and runs classifiers over your prompts automatically when the computer-use tools are in play. When a classifier spots a likely injection in a screenshot, it steers the model to ask the user for confirmation before the next action. That is great with a human present and actively wrong for an unattended pipeline — which is why there is an opt-out, gated behind contacting support. OpenAI surfaces pending_safety_checks that your code must explicitly acknowledge (acknowledged_safety_checks) before the loop proceeds. The gate is in your hands, and skipping it is a decision you make in code. Google returns a safety_decision — allowed, require_confirmation, or blocked — driven by policy categories including FINANCIAL_TRANSACTIONS, COMMUNICATION_TOOL, ACCOUNT_CREATION, SENSITIVE_DATA_MODIFICATION and LEGAL_TERMS_AND_AGREEMENTS. Prompt-injection screening of screenshots is available as an opt-in. The threat is real and specific: a screenshot is untrusted input. Text rendered on a webpage, in an image, in a PDF the agent opened — all of it reaches the model through the same channel as your instructions. Anthropic's own docs note that Claude will, in some circumstances, follow instructions found in content even when they conflict with yours. Every provider's mitigation converges on the same three rules: isolate the environment, keep a human on high-impact actions, and treat everything on screen as hostile. If the agent must log in, that risk goes up sharply — credentials plus injectable content is the worst combination in this space. See Securing Local and Hybrid Agents and Prompt Injection for the defensive playbook.
documents.s: Safety gates are part of the protocol

documents.t: OSWorld is the shared yardstick, and it's a good one because it's hard to fake: it drops an agent into a real OS with real applications, and grades with execution-based verification — a script checks whether the file actually got saved, not whether the agent claimed it did. The benchmark spans 369 tasks (361 in the standard evaluation set, since a handful of Google Drive tasks need manual setup) and ships 134 execution-based evaluation functions. OSWorld-Verified is the cleaned-up revision, with community-reported broken examples fixed and evaluation time cut to about an hour on AWS. Two numbers worth holding together: The human baseline is ~72.4%. Not 100%. These tasks are genuinely fiddly, and humans fumble them too. When OSWorld launched, the best model scored 12.24%. Frontier agents now report scores in the 70s and up — which means the headline "agents have reached human level on computer use" is arithmetically defensible and practically misleading. A benchmark score is a model + harness + scaffold result, exactly like a coding benchmark (see The Capability–Reliability Gap). Your harness is not their harness. And a 75% success rate on single tasks compounds brutally: an eight-step workflow where each step is 95% reliable succeeds about 66% of the time. Treat OSWorld as evidence the capability exists, and your own eval set as the only evidence that your product works.

For Claude computer use specifically, Anthropic's internal benchmarking gives guidance that inverts the usual intuition: Opus 4.7: high effort as the default; drop to low for high-throughput or cost-sensitive workloads. Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.6: medium is the best accuracy-to-cost ratio. Avoid max — on UI tasks it adds token cost without improving accuracy. The counterintuitive one: on those models, low effort uses fewer output tokens than disabling thinking entirely. A little thinking prevents mistakes, and mistakes cost you retries — and retries cost far more tokens than the thinking did. So "turn thinking off to save money" is, for computer use, often wrong. Cheapest is a little thinking. One more model-selection wrinkle: mechanical click precision is not the same axis as intelligence. Sonnet 4.6 is more mechanically precise at clicking than Opus 4.6, and more robust when screenshots have been heavily downscaled. Opus 4.7 narrows that gap and raises the pixel limit, so it needs less downscaling in the first place.

Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Sandbox first, always⌄ A container or VM with nothing valuable in it. Every provider says this and they all mean it: the agent will eventually click something you did not intend. ←PreviousNext→ 2Pin the coordinate space⌄ Capture, resize client-side to your model's limit, declare the exact dimensions you sent, and keep the scale factor. Write this once and never think about it again. ←PreviousNext→ 3Cap the loop⌄ Termination is 'no further action returned' — which never fires if the agent is stuck in a modal it can't dismiss. Add a max-step budget and a stall detector (identical screenshots N times running). ←PreviousNext→ 4Decide your safety-gate policy explicitly⌄ Human-in-the-loop, or unattended with an opt-out and a narrower blast radius. Do not discover this by accident when a confirmation prompt deadlocks your cron job. ←PreviousNext→ 5Build a ten-task eval before you build feature two⌄ Execution-verified, like OSWorld does it: check the world changed, not that the agent said it did. This is the only number about your system that means anything. ←PreviousNext→ 6Prefer the API to the pixels where you can⌄ The most reliable computer-use agent is the one that doesn't have to use the computer. If the target has an API, an MCP server, or a CLI, that path is faster, cheaper and orders of magnitude more reliable. Screens are the fallback, not the goal. ←PreviousNext→ That last step is the strategic one. Computer use is the universal adapter for software with no API — legacy desktop apps, vendor portals, anything behind a login with no integration story. It is a magnificent hack, and it is still a hack. Reach for MCP and real tools first. Check yourself 0/5

Copy as Markdown Advanced DeepSeek Harness — the command is dsh — is DeepSeek's open-source agent harness. It appeared on GitHub on 13 August 2026, carries 242,626 stars and 29,081 forks as of today, is MIT licensed and written in TypeScript. On 1 October 2026 DeepSeek added signed desktop installers, which is what put it back on the Hacker News front page. Its one-line pitch is the repository description: "Everything is a Plugin." That phrase is on the README of roughly every agent framework ever published, and it almost always means "we have a plugin folder." Here it means something much stronger and much weirder, stated plainly in docs/architecture.md: the model adapter, the tool registry, the session log and the agent loop itself are plugins, "so each is replaceable from configuration." You can delete the agent loop from a YAML file and drop in your own without forking anything. That design has consequences — some excellent, some expensive. This page is about the ones you cannot read off the landing page. What you'll learn Understand what 'everything is a plugin' buys you here, and what Cordis — the framework underneath — actually guarantees Run your existing Claude Code hooks.json inside dsh, and know which subset survives the bridge Point dsh at Claude, GPT or a company gateway, and know why an OAuth subscription will not work Use PTC mode (run_code) deliberately instead of accidentally Read the three sandbox modes against the kernel primitive each one really uses Avoid the five configuration traps that cost an hour each Last verified: 2026-10-03. Star counts, the npm version and the desktop installer matrix are perishable. The npm latest tag currently resolves to 0.2.0-rc.2 — a release candidate, not a stable release — and SAFETY.md describes the project as "experimental developer-preview software" that "has not undergone a security audit." The README warns of compatibility-breaking changes. Treat every file path, service key and config field below as true for the 0.2 line and re-check against the repository docs before you build on them. The architecture and safety claims here come from the repository's own documentation, not from secondary coverage. Confirm against the official source.
documents.s: DeepSeek Harness: the agent where the agent loop itself is a plugin

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Start it⌄ `npx @deepseek-ai/dsh web` boots the web profile, prints a URL — `http://127.0.0.1:3080` — and opens your browser. No clone, no build. The directory you invoke it from becomes the default workspace root, but a fresh Web UI has no workspace selected until you add one, and the composer stays disabled until you do. ←PreviousNext→ 2Give it a model⌄ Settings → Models. The DeepSeek card takes an API key from platform.deepseek.com. Add a third-party provider and the shipped catalog offers provider ids including `anthropic`, `openai`, `moonshotai` (Kimi) and `zai` (GLM). Model changes apply on the next request — no restart. ←PreviousNext→ 3Understand where it put things⌄ Keys land in `$DSH_HOME/.credentials.yaml`, write-only: the settings page gets a redacted descriptor back, never the secret, and your settings store only a credential reference. Everything else you change in the UI is written to `$DSH_HOME/profiles/web/cordis.patch.yml` — the same file you can hand-edit. ←PreviousNext→ 4Pick an entry mode⌄ `dsh web` is one of five shipped profiles. `dsh --profile headless "run the tests"` runs one persisted session, prints the final answer and exits — that is your CI entry point. `dsh --profile acp` serves automation clients over ACP stdio. `dsh --profile sdk` serves SDK clients over JSON-RPC stdio. The `desktop` name is reserved for the Electron app's own profile and the npm CLI refuses to boot it. ←PreviousNext→ 5Install plugins like npm packages⌄ `dsh plugin --profile web <pnpm args>` forwards straight to pnpm inside the profile directory. Plugins are ordinary packages in the profile's own `node_modules`. Community plugins are discoverable by the `dsh-plugin` GitHub topic. ←PreviousNext→

Underneath dsh is Cordis, a plugin framework vendored into the repository (vendor/) and described in an arXiv paper the project cites — A Programming Paradigm for Spatiotemporal Composability, arXiv:2608.25512, submitted 26 August 2026, from authors at Peking University and DeepSeek-AI. The paper's two ideas map directly onto how the harness behaves at runtime: Temporal composability — a component's side effects can be completely reversed when it is removed. In the harness this is ctx.effect(): prompt sections, tool schemas, model adapters, providers and listeners are all installed as reversible effects, so unloading a plugin unwinds its registrations in order rather than leaving orphans behind. Spatial composability — dependencies resolve reactively. A plugin names the services it needs via inject, and Cordis simply does not start it until those services exist. There is no boot sequence to maintain; load order is a consequence of declared requirements. A service claims a stable key on the shared context. The names are the architecture: Service key What owns it ctx.llm the LLM adapter registry — the model seam ctx.tools the tool registry and its scoped execution pipeline ctx.agentLoop the default agent-loop driver ctx.agents the live agent registry ctx.sessions the append-only SessionEvent log ctx.systemPrompt system-prompt assembly ctx.fs filesystem access ctx.subprocess subprocess execution ctx.sandbox subprocess confinement ctx.subagents subagent delegation ctx.ptcRuntime program execution for run_code ctx.credentials the credential seam The repository calls these capability seams, and splits every one into three roles: the package that declares the service, the packages that implement it, and the packages that consume it. ctx.sandbox is declared by packages/sandbox/sandbox, implemented by sandbox-local and sandbox-windows-acl, consumed by tool-bash and the PTC runtime. Replace the implementation and every consumer follows, with no consumer edits. Communication between plugins is typed events with five declared dispatch modes, and the mode is part of an event's public contract: Mode Awaited Order Returns a value emit no registration order no waterfall no registration order yes parallel yes all at once no serial yes registration order yes bail no registration order, stops at first bail yes waterfall is the interesting one: it is around-middleware. A listener gets (...args, next), calls next() to pass a possibly-wrapped result down the chain, or returns without calling next() to short-circuit. For single-decision events — "may this tool run?" — short-circuiting is the design: a policy listener that owns the decision returns without delegating, while a listener that merely annotates must delegate. If you have written a Claude Code hook that returns a deny decision, you already know this shape; the difference is that here it is the native extension mechanism rather than a shell-out. The agent loop runs turns (zero or more steps) and steps (one model request plus its tool calls), and the published extension sequence is agent/pre-step → agent/request → llm/stream → tools/* → step/end. Those are the hook points. You do not patch the loop; you listen to it.
documents.s: "Everything is a plugin" is a load-bearing claim

documents.t: This is the single most under-reported fact about dsh. packages/hooks ships three packages: hook-protocol (the shared engine), hooks-claude-code and hooks-codex. Point the Claude Code bridge at an existing hooks.json and your hooks run inside dsh when sessions start, prompts arrive, tools run and runs stop. The group README is explicit about what they can do: block prompts or tool calls with model-visible messages, add conversation context, or require the run to continue. The limit is equally explicit, and it is the thing to check before you plan a migration: each integration supports only the command-hook subset documented by its source tool. So your command-type hooks port. Anything that depends on Claude Code behaviour outside that subset does not. If you have a hooks layer you trust — see Claude Code hooks — this is a genuine "bring your guardrails with you" path, not a rewrite.
documents.s: 1. It will run your existing Claude Code hooks.json

documents.t: The provider list shipped in the installed catalog includes anthropic and openai by name. For anything not in the catalog — a relay, a company gateway, a self-hosted server — the custom-provider form asks for a Provider ID, a base URL, a credential and an API protocol, and offers exactly three: OpenAI Chat Completions, OpenAI Responses, and Anthropic Messages. In cordis.patch.yml these are stored as openai-completions, openai-responses and anthropic-messages. Two consequences people trip over: A provider speaks one protocol. A gateway that serves both OpenAI and Anthropic shapes needs two provider entries, not one. OAuth sign-in is not supported. The providers guide states it directly, using Codex as its example: providers that sign in with OAuth "are not supported here yet." That means API-key billing, not a seat you already pay for. If you were hoping to drive dsh off an existing assistant subscription, budget for metered tokens instead — the arithmetic is in what AI costs across providers. There is also a model-discovery button that asks your endpoint which models it serves. Useful, with a caveat worth internalising: a built-in provider is always answered from the installed catalog even when its base URL points at a gateway. So if you want to see what a gateway really serves, you have to add it as a custom provider. Otherwise you are reading DeepSeek's shipped list back to yourself.
documents.s: 2. You can point it at Claude — but not with your subscription

documents.t: packages/ptc-runtime is the capability family behind what the tool registry presents to the model as run_code. The contract: the model writes one program that calls host-provided functions as ordinary async calls, and only the program's printed output and return value come back. Not the intermediate tool results. Not twenty round-trips. The specifics: The TypeScript backend runs each program in a fresh managed Node process under the resolved sandbox policy. Each run starts with no state from earlier programs. There is no implicit REPL session to lean on; carry state through files or the return value. Failures come back as results, not exceptions, so a caller can diagnose them or hand them to the model. An experimental Python backend exists, owning an fd-3 wire protocol between the Node host and a CPython subprocess, for when you genuinely need CPython. If this pattern is new to you, the clearest write-up of why it saves so much context is on Pi 1.0 and the codemode trick: tool results that never enter the transcript cannot inflate it. The same logic applies here. The difference is that in dsh the program runtime is a swappable seam (ctx.ptcRuntime) rather than a fixed sandbox choice.
documents.s: 3. run_code is codemode, and it is a first-class runtime

documents.t: The three modes will look familiar if you have configured Codex: Mode What a subprocess may do to files read-only read only workspace-write write only under the session workspace danger-full-access unrestricted What is more interesting is the backend table, because it tells you what is really enforcing the policy on your machine: Linux — bwrap, then Landlock as the fallback rung. macOS — Seatbelt. Windows — a restricted token, with sandbox-windows-acl as the write-restriction backend: confined children may write only in the workspace and a private temp directory. A denied call can retry through a user-approved one-time escalation, so the policy is a prompt-and-proceed boundary rather than a hard wall. And then the caveat, which the package README states itself and which you should quote to anyone who tells you this is "sandboxed": confinement is same-world only. It shares the host kernel and the host filesystem. Real isolation — containers, microVMs, remote executors — does not register here at all; it replaces whole capabilities instead. SAFETY.md is unusually candid for a 242k-star repository, and worth reading before a first run rather than after. It says the harness can execute model-generated code, load third-party plugins, reach the network and touch processes, credentials and files; that there is no inherent guarantee that sandboxing, approval prompts and permission controls will prevent damage to anything reachable; and that the software "must not be treated as secure or production-ready." Its own recommendations are the boring correct ones: disposable VMs or containers, backups of anything inside the project scope, and no sensitive credentials unless you accept the risk. The same reasoning applies to any harness you run locally — see securing local and hybrid agents and sandboxing and credential masking. There is also a small guard group worth knowing about: timeout-policy and repeat-tool-reminder — the latter being a nudge for the failure mode where a model calls the same tool in a loop.
documents.s: The sandbox: three modes, three kernel primitives, one honest caveat

documents.t: dsh persists sessions as a versioned JSONL file — session.vN.jsonl[.zstd] — with migration chains between versions, through a ctx.sessionPersistence seam whose shipped implementation is session-persistence-jsonl. Committed events include turn/start, step/start, user/message, assistant/message, tool/result and turn/end. The invariant behind it is the part to steal even if you never run dsh: "model-visible means logged." Every input the model saw must be reconstructable from the log. Live events exist separately, for driving UI in real time; they are explicitly not the record of truth. That single rule is what makes the surrounding packages possible: session-query-sqlite — query sessions out of SQLite instead of grepping JSONL. dsh-session-projection with ctx.sessionProjections — fold session state incrementally rather than replaying from zero. llm-replay plus token-meter ("replay token measurement") — replay a recorded session and measure its token cost, which is how you compare two prompt or model changes on identical inputs instead of on vibes. compaction-tool-result-pruner — described as model-free tool-result pruning, i.e. shrinking the transcript without paying a model to summarise it. Compare with Claude's own approach in context compaction. If you have ever tried to debug an agent run and discovered your logs recorded the rendered UI rather than the bytes the model received, you already know why this invariant is worth more than most features.
documents.s: The session log is the product

documents.t: dsh speaks MCP over both stdio and Streamable HTTP, using the official SDK for negotiation, discovery, validation and cancellation. The design choices are unusual enough to list: Servers are opt-in, one plugin entry per server. You configure one @deepseek-ai/dsh-mcp-client entry per server in the Cordis scope you want it visible in. There is deliberately no shared ctx.mcp service: the client is a connection plugin and a consumer of the tool registry. No configured server means no MCP tax. A caller with no visible configured server receives no MCP prompt text and no MCP tools, in native or PTC mode. Zero bytes, not "a small section." That matters more than it sounds — see the real cost of MCP tools. Public tool names include the server name, so identically-named tools from two servers stay distinct. A serverName must be unique inside its registration scope, but separate agent scopes may reuse it. Server instructions join the logged system prompt, bounded by the client's maxInstructionBytes. A verbose server cannot quietly annex your prompt — but note that this is also the channel through which a malicious server speaks to your model. That is the attack surface described in MCP tool poisoning and rug pulls. A failed tool-list refresh retains the previous tool generation rather than dropping your tools mid-session, and there is no product setting that forces a protocol revision — negotiation follows the SDK's supported revisions.
documents.s: MCP here is a per-server plugin, not a global registry

documents.t: A profile directory holds a package.json — out-of-tree plugin dependencies plus a dsh.profile manifest with an ordered bundles list — and a cordis.patch.yml, your own patch layer. The composed tree is built over an empty root in this order: Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Each bundle's patch, in `dsh.profile.bundles` order⌄ Bundles resolve from the dsh installation first — `@deepseek-ai/dsh-base`, `dsh-web-app`, `dsh-headless`, `dsh-sdk-app`, `dsh-sdk-minimal`, `dsh-acp-app` — then from the profile's own `node_modules`, where pnpm installs out-of-tree plugins. `dsh-base` is the shared floor: model adapters, tools, persistence, sandbox policy. A bundle declares itself through a `dsh` field in its `package.json`. ←PreviousNext→ 2Then the profile's `cordis.patch.yml`⌄ `$DSH_HOME/profiles/<profile>/cordis.patch.yml`. For a plain `dsh web` launch the profile is `web`. This is the file the Settings UI writes; you can edit it directly and the adapters re-read it on the next request. ←PreviousNext→ 3Then the home patch⌄ `$DSH_HOME/cordis.patch.yml` — cross-profile overrides. ←PreviousNext→ 4Then `--patch` overlays⌄ Command-line overlays, applied last. `config/examples/` ships opt-in overlays for GitHub review webhooks, memory MCP servers and runtime Cordis tools; they are never part of a default profile. ←PreviousNext→ 5Inspect before you boot⌄ `--dump-default-config` and `--dump-config` print the composed tree without starting anything — the fastest way to answer "which layer set this?" ←PreviousNext→ With HMR enabled in YAML, dsh-hmr watches the profile manifest and both patch files and recomposes every layer through one serialized reload. Without it, changes apply on restart.
documents.s: Configuration: five layers, and the override that eats your providers

documents.t: A Cordis config override replaces the complete entry config. The providers guide spells this out: when you edit an existing override, you must preserve the other fields and other providers yourself. Patch one provider carelessly and you have deleted the rest. This is the single most expensive mistake available in cordis.patch.yml. A Provider ID is permanent. Requests, saved sessions, model defaults and credential references all key off it. Renaming means adding a new provider and deleting the old one. Display name, base URL, protocol, credential and model list stay editable. --dump-config-schema imports plugin code. Unlike the other dump flags, it loads the composed tree's declared plugin schemas to print JSON Schema — so pointing it at untrusted plugins executes their import-time code. The CLI reference has a dedicated safety note on this. Treat it like reviewing third-party code, not like --help. Plugin version compatibility is enforced, and the escape hatch is explicit. Installation and profile startup check declared DSH peer ranges against the runtime version from dsh --version; an incompatible plugin requires an acknowledged exact-version exemption (allow-version, revoke-version). Good hygiene, surprising the first time a plugin refuses to load. A session that has already sent a request keeps the model recorded in its own log. Changing the default model does not retroactively move a live session, and if a saved default names a deleted provider the composer blocks input until you pick another. Both are correct behaviour; both look like bugs at 1 a.m.
documents.s: Five gotchas that will cost you an hour

documents.t: Start the Web UI, then a headless one-shot run — no clone, no build CopyOpen in Claude↗ # Web UI on http://127.0.0.1:3080, workspace defaults to the invoking directory npx @deepseek-ai/dsh web # One persisted session, final answer to stdout, then exit — the CI shape npx @deepseek-ai/dsh --profile headless "summarize this repo and list its main packages" # Serve automation clients over ACP stdio (editor integrations) npx @deepseek-ai/dsh --profile acp # Inspect the composed config tree WITHOUT booting it npx @deepseek-ai/dsh --profile web --dump-config # Manage a profile's plugins (forwards to pnpm inside the profile directory) npx @deepseek-ai/dsh plugin --profile web add some-dsh-plugin Point dsh at a gateway that speaks Anthropic Messages — in $DSH_HOME/profiles/web/cordis.patch.yml CopyOpen in Claude↗ # WARNING: a Cordis config override replaces the ENTIRE entry config. # Include every provider you want to keep, not just the new one. - id: llm-pi-ai config: providers: my-anthropic-gateway: apiKeyEnv: GATEWAY_API_KEY api: anthropic-messages # or openai-completions / openai-responses baseURL: https://gateway.example/v1 models: - id: some-text-model - id: some-vision-model input: [text, image] # omit to inherit the catalog's input types Bring your Claude Code guardrails across CopyOpen in Claude↗ # The Claude Code hook bridge runs your existing command hooks inside dsh. # Only the command-hook subset documented by Claude Code is supported. # Hooks can: block a prompt or a tool call with a MODEL-VISIBLE message, # add conversation context, or require the run to continue. # # Check the bridge's own README for the current config field names before # wiring this up — the 0.2 line is a developer preview and they can move: # packages/hooks/hooks-claude-code/README.md # # Verify enforcement the same way you would in Claude Code: a hook that is # configured but never fires is worse than no hook, because you trust it.

If you are choosing a harness rather than studying one, the honest summary is: dsh is the most architecturally interesting open harness shipping right now and the least ready to be load-bearing. Its own safety file says so. The plugin model is genuinely stronger than its competitors' — ctx.agentLoop being replaceable is not a thing you can do in most harnesses at any price — and the hook bridges mean adopting it is not an all-or-nothing bet. Against that: a release-candidate latest tag, no security audit, promised breaking changes, and a provider story that assumes API keys. For a comparison across the field, see coding agent CLIs compared and local coding agents. For the models you would most plausibly drive it with, see DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. Check yourself 0/7

Copy as Markdown Intermediate For a long time the story of "good AI" was the story of a handful of closed, frontier models you could only rent through an API. That's no longer the whole story. A wave of open-weight models — many from Chinese labs like DeepSeek and Alibaba's Qwen, alongside Meta's Llama and France's Mistral — got good enough, cheap enough, and small enough that downloading and running your own capable model became a real option. This page is the durable map of that landscape: why it happened, what "open weight" actually means, the honest trade-offs versus closed frontier models, and how to actually use these models today. What you'll learn Understand WHY open-weight models became competitive — capability-per-cost and open reasoning Pin down what 'open weight' really means — vs open-source and vs open-data Recognize the archetypes: general chat, reasoning, coding, and small/efficient models Weigh the real trade-offs vs closed frontier — capability gap on the hardest tasks, and owning your own infra and safety Know the two ways to actually use them: a hosted API, or self-hosting via Ollama

Three things shifted at roughly the same time, and together they closed most of the everyday gap. Capability-per-cost collapsed. Better training recipes, data curation, and mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures (where only a fraction of a large model's parameters activate per token) let labs ship models that punch far above their cost. For a large share of real tasks — drafting, summarizing, extraction, classification, routine coding — a good open model is now "good enough," at a fraction of frontier-API cost. Open reasoning models arrived. DeepSeek's reasoning line was a turning point: it showed that the "think step by step before answering" capability — previously the moat of a few closed models — could be trained and released with open weights. Once one lab proved it, the rest of the open ecosystem followed. Small models got genuinely usable. Sub-10B and even sub-1B models became coherent and useful, which means you can run something capable on a laptop or a cheap server. That changes the economics of privacy, latency, and scale. The net effect: the gap to the closed frontier didn't vanish, but for most work it stopped being the deciding factor. The deciding factors became cost, control, and where your data lives.
documents.s: Why open-weight models suddenly got competitive

documents.t: This is the single most-confused point in the whole space. "Open" is doing a lot of work in three different ways, and they are not the same thing. Term What you actually get What you usually DON'T get Open weight The trained model file (the weights). You can download, run, fine-tune, and self-host it. The training data, and sometimes the full training code. Use may be governed by a custom license. Open source (strict) Weights plus training/inference code under an OSI-style license, with freedom to use, modify, and redistribute. Still often not the training data. Open data The actual datasets the model was trained on, openly published. Rare for frontier-scale models; most "open" models are open-weight, not open-data. The practical takeaway: most models people call "open source" are really open-weight. You can run them and adapt them, but you typically cannot reproduce them from scratch, and you must read the license. Licenses vary: Some ship under permissive licenses (Apache 2.0, MIT) that are clean for commercial use — Qwen and Mistral models, for example, have historically used Apache 2.0, and DeepSeek has used MIT for major releases. Some ship under custom community licenses with conditions — Meta's Llama license, for instance, has historically included a clause restricting the very largest companies (by monthly active users) from using it freely. Always check the specific model card for its license before building on it. Neutral but important: a model being open-weight tells you that you can host it yourself; it does not tell you the legal terms, and it does not make the licensing or data-residency questions go away — it relocates them to you. Last verified: 2026-06-28. Exact current model versions, parameter counts, benchmark scores, and per-token prices move fast and are intentionally not asserted as permanent here. The durable shape of the landscape — the labs, the archetypes, and the open-weight vs open-source vs open-data distinction — is stable; the specific leaderboard numbers are not. Check the linked organization pages for what's current. Confirm against the official source.

Open-weight families almost always come as a spread of variants, not a single model. Learn the four archetypes and you can read any lab's lineup at a glance. A single family — Qwen is the clearest example — typically gives you the whole ladder: tiny models for edge and laptops, mid-size models for servers, a large flagship for hardest tasks, plus coding- and reasoning-specialized variants. You pick the rung that fits your hardware and task, not "the model."

Open-weight models are not a strict upgrade. They're a different deal. Here's the trade neutrally. Dimension Open-weight (self-host or cheap host) Closed frontier (hosted API) Hardest-task capability Strong and closing fast, but the closed frontier usually still leads on the very hardest reasoning, long-horizon agentic, and niche tasks Typically the ceiling on the toughest tasks Cost at scale Can be dramatically cheaper, especially self-hosted or via budget hosts Premium per-token; predictable but adds up Privacy / data residency You can keep data fully inside your environment Data leaves your network to the provider Control & customization Full: fine-tune, quantize, pin a version, run offline Limited to what the API exposes; versions can change under you Who owns safety & ops You do — guardrails, abuse filtering, uptime, scaling, and patching are your job The provider runs infra and ships baseline safety That last row is the one people underweight. When you self-host an open-weight model you also inherit the responsibilities a frontier lab normally absorbs for you: content safety and abuse mitigation, keeping the deployment patched, capacity and uptime, and evaluating each new model version yourself. "Open weight" buys you control, and control is a cost as much as a benefit. For cost intuition on the API side of this trade, see Token economy.
documents.s: The honest trade-offs vs closed frontier

documents.t: There are exactly two paths, and most teams use both at different stages. Hosted API — many providers (including the labs themselves and third-party inference hosts) serve open-weight models behind an API, often OpenAI-compatible. You get open-model economics with zero infrastructure work. Best when you want low cost without running servers, but note your data still leaves your network. Self-host — download the weights and run them in your environment. Maximum privacy and control, and the only option when data truly cannot leave your network. The easiest on-ramp is Ollama, which pulls and runs open models with a single command.
documents.s: How to actually use an open model

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Install Ollama⌄ Download it from ollama.com/download (macOS/Windows) or use the Linux install script. This gives you the ollama command and a local background service. Full walkthrough on the Run models locally page. ←PreviousNext→ 2Pick a size your machine can run⌄ Smaller models need less RAM/VRAM. A laptop comfortably runs small variants (a few GB); large flagships need a real GPU or server. Start small to confirm everything works, then scale up if the quality isn't enough. ←PreviousNext→ 3Run it with one command⌄ ollama run <model> downloads the weights on first use (several GB), then drops you into an interactive chat. First run is slow because it's pulling; later runs are instant from cache. ←PreviousNext→ 4Call it from your code⌄ Ollama exposes an OpenAI-compatible local endpoint, so you can point an existing OpenAI-style SDK at localhost instead of the cloud. Now the same code runs against a private, local model. ←PreviousNext→ Pull and run an open model locally with Ollama CopyOpen in Claude↗ ollama run qwen3 That one command downloads a Qwen open-weight model and starts a local chat — no API key, no data leaving your machine. Swap qwen3 for another family (for example a Llama, Mistral, or DeepSeek tag) to compare them on your own task. Picking the right model for a given job is its own skill: see Choosing a model.
documents.s: Try a model locally in four steps

documents.t: Don't pick by leaderboard. Pick by constraint: Data cannot leave your network → self-hosted open-weight is the answer, full stop. High volume, cost-sensitive, "good enough" quality → open-weight (hosted or self-hosted) usually wins on cost. You need the absolute best on the hardest tasks → the closed frontier still tends to lead — use it where it matters and route easier traffic to cheaper open models. You want to fine-tune, quantize, pin a version, or run offline → only open weights give you that control. The most durable move is to run a tiny evaluation on your own real data across one open and one closed candidate. Benchmarks describe someone else's task; your eval describes yours. Check yourself 0/3 Key takeaways Open-weight models closed most of the everyday gap thanks to capability-per-cost, open reasoning models, and genuinely usable small models 'Open weight' = downloadable weights you can run and fine-tune — NOT necessarily open-source code, open training data, or a permissive license; always read the model card Read any lineup by archetype: general chat, reasoning, coding, and small/efficient — most families ship the whole size ladder The trade is real: open buys cost, privacy and control, but the closed frontier usually still leads on the hardest tasks and you inherit safety and infra Two ways to use them: a hosted (often OpenAI-compatible) API, or self-host via Ollama with one command — then evaluate on YOUR data, not a leaderboard

Copy as Markdown Intermediate At 04:00 UTC on September 10, 2026, DeepSeek flipped its API to a new model and published the weights the same day: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, served as deepseek-flash. It is the smallest member of a new architecture family, but it is not a small model: 552 billion parameters, a 1-million-token context, native vision, and a KV cache that costs 890 bytes per token. On DeepSWE v1.1, the long-horizon software-engineering benchmark both Google and Anthropic now headline, DeepSeek reports 74.2, one-fifth of a point above Claude Opus 5. On Terminal-Bench 4.0 it reports 31.2 against Opus 5's 51.8. Both numbers are true, and the gap between them is the whole story. This page is the field guide for a Claude user: what actually changed, the routing change that quietly re-pointed every deepseek-v4-pro request, the effort dial and what it does to your bill, how to run the weights, and the workloads where Claude is still the right call. What you'll learn Read the V4.1-Flash launch numbers the way they deserve: tied with Opus 5 on DeepSWE, far behind on Terminal-Bench, and why that split is not a contradiction Understand the new Causal Encoder-Decoder + CSA2 design well enough to know what the 890-byte KV cache buys you (and what DeepSeek says it has not yet characterized) Use the 1–100 reasoning_effort dial deliberately — 25 vs 100 is an 8-point DeepSWE swing for ~2.5× the output tokens Do the honest cost math: $0.30 / $1.20 peak, half that off-peak, $0.003 per million on an off-peak cache hit — and the UTC peak window that decides which rate you pay Know the September 14 routing change: deepseek-v4-pro now silently serves V4.1-Flash until V4.1-Pro ships Pick a serving path (hosted API, vLLM, SGLang, Docker Model Runner) and the sampling defaults DeepSeek recommends Last verified: 2026-09-15. Model ID, routing dates, and pricing from DeepSeek's September 10 announcement and the API pricing page. Architecture, license, reasoning-effort range, and sampling defaults from the Hugging Face model card. Benchmark comparisons against Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol are DeepSeek's own launch table as reported by VentureBeat on September 10; treat them as vendor-run until an independent harness publishes. The 3.0/4.0 Terminal-Bench gaps come from the same table. DeepSeek's statement that the architecture has "robustness boundaries it has not fully characterized" is quoted from the same coverage. Confirm against the official source.
documents.s: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash: A 1M-Context Open Weight That Ties Opus 5 on DeepSWE (Sep 2026)

documents.t: V4.1-Flash is DeepSeek's first model on a new architecture (a "Causal Encoder-Decoder" with Compressed Sparse Attention 2), released MIT-licensed with native vision, a 1M-token window, 384K max output, and a continuously controllable reasoning effort from 1 to 100. It replaces every V4-era Flash endpoint immediately and, since September 14, also answers every deepseek-v4-pro call at Flash prices until V4.1-Pro lands.

DeepSeek's launch table, in the columns that matter for an agent shop: Benchmark DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash Claude Opus 5 GPT-5.6 Sol DeepSWE v1.1 (resolved) 74.2 74.0 73.0 Terminal-Bench 3.0 30.0 43.3 — Terminal-Bench 4.0 31.2 51.8 — CyberGym 88.1 — — AutomationBench 54.8 — — DeepSWE rewards a model that reads a repository, plans a patch, and lands it: long context, careful retrieval, a few large edits. Terminal-Bench rewards many short, adaptive shell turns where each decision depends on the last tool result. V4.1-Flash has 1M tokens of context and a cheap cache, so the first shape suits it. It runs 8B active parameters per token at prefill and 16B at decode, which is a lot less "thinking per step" than a dense frontier model, so the second shape hurts. If your work looks like a pull request, the parity claim is credible and worth an eval. If your work looks like an interactive terminal session, the 20-point Terminal-Bench gap is the number to budget around. The same split shows up in Google's Gemini 3.8 Flash launch a week earlier, and for the same architectural reasons. The base-model rows tell a quieter story: MMLU-Pro 74.1 (V4-Flash 68.3, V4-Pro 73.5), HumanEval 79.4 (V4-Flash 69.5), GSM8K 93.0 (V4-Flash 90.8). The new "Flash" is a better base than last month's "Pro", which is why DeepSeek was comfortable routing Pro traffic onto it.
documents.s: 1. DeepSWE parity and Terminal-Bench deficit are the same fact seen twice

documents.t: Unlike Claude's effort (low/medium/high/max), V4.1-Flash exposes an integer from 1 to 100. DeepSeek's own ablation on DeepSWE v1.1: effort 25 scores 66.0%, effort 100 scores 74.2%, and the top setting emits roughly 2.5× as many output tokens. They also say the 60–80 band delivers most of the maximum-effort accuracy at less than half the token budget. Every benchmark row above was run at reasoning_effort=100. So the parity number is the expensive number. Reproduce it at 100 first, then walk down to the cheapest setting your evals still pass at. That is the same discipline we recommend for thinking_level on Gemini and effort on Claude in Reasoning models compared.
documents.s: 2. The reasoning-effort dial is a real dial, and it is on your bill

documents.t: From September 10, deepseek-v4-flash and deepseek-v4-flash-vision-exp route to V4.1-Flash, billed at Flash rates. The V4-Flash-Vision-Exp page's numbers now describe the open weights, not the hosted endpoint. From 04:00 UTC September 14, every deepseek-v4-pro request also routes to V4.1-Flash at Flash rates, "until V4.1-Pro launches". If you have evals pinned to deepseek-v4-pro, your production model changed under you on Sunday morning. Re-run the suite. The upside is that the same call now costs roughly a quarter of the Pro rate; the downside is that any Pro-specific behavior you tuned for is gone. This is exactly the failure mode Porting prompts across models warns about when a provider aliases model IDs.
documents.s: 3. Two routing changes happened without a client-side change

documents.t: Spec DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash API model ID deepseek-flash Release September 10, 2026 (API + open weights same day) Parameters 552B total; 8B active at prefill, 16B at decode MoE layout 384 routed + 1 shared expert per MoE layer; 6 routed experts active per token Architecture Causal Encoder-Decoder, Compressed Sparse Attention 2 (CSA2) KV cache 890 bytes per token (FP4, E2M1): ~1/4 of V4-Flash in HBM, ~1/8 in SSD storage; global KV cache lifetime at least 72 hours Context / max output 1M tokens / 384K tokens Vision Native; DeepSeek-ViT trained from scratch, 2D-RoPE, 3×3 pixel-unshuffle downsampling Reasoning control reasoning_effort integer 1–100 License MIT Weights Safetensors in BF16, F32, F8_E4M3, I8 Serving vLLM, SGLang, Docker Model Runner, Transformers; reference inference code in the inference/ folder Recommended sampling temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95 or 1.0, context 1M API concurrency 2,500 The KV-cache line is the architectural headline. A 1M-token conversation at 890 bytes per token is under a gigabyte of cache, which is why DeepSeek can promise a 72-hour cache lifetime and price cache hits at fractions of a cent. Anthropic's answer to the same problem is a cheaper cache-read rate on Claude Fable 5.1; DeepSeek's is to make the cache physically small. Both push you toward the same habit: put the stable prefix first and never edit it mid-run. See Prompt caching.

DeepSeek keeps a two-rate schedule. Peak hours are 01:00–04:00 and 06:00–10:00 UTC, Monday through Friday; everything else is off-peak at exactly half the peak rate. Per 1M tokens Peak Off-peak Input, cache hit $0.006 $0.003 Input, cache miss $0.30 $0.15 Output $1.20 $0.60 Two things follow. First, the "$0.003 per million" headline is the off-peak cache-hit price, the cheapest of six cells; a cold, peak-hour agent run pays 100× that on input. Second, the peak window is defined in UTC and covers the European morning and the tail of the U.S. night. A batch job scheduled at 09:00 UTC pays double what the same job pays at 11:00 UTC. If you can shift, shift. For a framework that puts these cells beside Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google list prices, use What AI costs across providers; current Claude list prices live on Models and pricing.

Hosted is right for almost everyone: the model is enormous, and the API is the cheapest thing on this page. Self-host when data cannot leave your network or when you want the effort dial and 1M window without a rate limit. Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Decide hosted vs self-hosted honestly⌄ 552B parameters in BF16 is over a terabyte of weights; the F8_E4M3 and I8 safetensors halve or quarter that but still need a multi-GPU node. If you do not already run Kimi K3 or Colibrì-class MoEs, the hosted endpoint at $0.30 / $1.20 peak will beat your amortized hardware bill. See the hardware math on Running Kimi K3 locally. ←PreviousNext→ 2Pick a serving stack the card actually names⌄ vLLM, SGLang, Docker Model Runner, and Transformers are the four listed. The card ships no Jinja chat template; it uses a custom encoding implementation, so use the reference code in the repo's inference folder (or the deepseek-recipe toolkit) rather than hand-rolling the prompt format. ←PreviousNext→ 3Set the sampling defaults DeepSeek recommends⌄ temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95 or 1.0, context window 1M. These are the settings the benchmark rows were produced with. Do not port a Claude-tuned temperature of 0.2 over blindly. ←PreviousNext→ 4Start at reasoning_effort=100, then walk down⌄ Reproduce DeepSeek's number on your own eval first. Then try 80, 60, 40 and record accuracy vs output tokens. Most teams will land in the 60–80 band the vendor itself points at. ←PreviousNext→ 5Test long-context retrieval before you trust it⌄ DeepSeek says the new architecture has robustness boundaries it has not fully characterized, specifically sparse retrieval over very long contexts. Run a needle-in-haystack and a multi-hop retrieval test at the context length you will actually use. Treat the 1M number as a ceiling, not a promise. ←PreviousNext→ Hosted call with the effort dial (OpenAI-compatible endpoint) CopyOpen in Claude↗ curl https://api.deepseek.com/chat/completions \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $DEEPSEEK_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "deepseek-flash", "reasoning_effort": 70, "messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": "You are a senior engineer. Reply with a unified diff and one paragraph of rationale."}, {"role": "user", "content": "The test suite in ./tests fails on macOS only. Here is the log and the relevant module: ..."} ] }' Self-hosted with vLLM (shape only; check the model card for the exact flags) CopyOpen in Claude↗ # One node, tensor-parallel across all visible GPUs. # The card names vLLM, SGLang, Docker Model Runner and Transformers as supported. vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 \ --max-model-len 1000000 \ --trust-remote-code # Then hit http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions with the same body as above.

Pro tip Reach for V4.1-Flash: repository-scale coding tasks that look like DeepSWE (read a lot, edit a little), where you can run at effort 60–100 and the cost per resolved issue still undercuts Claude by an order of magnitude. Reach for V4.1-Flash: anything that needs a 1M-token window and a warm cache for days — a 72-hour global cache lifetime and 890-byte-per-token KV make 'keep the whole codebase in context' cheap. Reach for V4.1-Flash: self-hosted or data-residency workloads where MIT licensing matters and you already run a multi-GPU MoE stack. Stay on Claude: interactive terminal agents and any many-short-turns loop. A 20-point Terminal-Bench 4.0 gap (31.2 vs 51.8) is not noise, and it is the shape of most real Claude Code sessions. Stay on Claude: work that needs Anthropic's tool-use loop, prefilled assistant turns, structured-output strictness, or the safety and retention guarantees of a first-party API. The DeepSeek API is OpenAI-shaped and the model has documented, uncharacterized long-context failure modes. Cross-check both: for a coding agent, run your own eval at DeepSeek's effort=100 and Claude's default effort, then at the cheapest passing setting on each. The vendor tables were run at maximum effort; your bill will not be. For the durable framework behind that list, How to choose a model. For what changes when you move a prompt between an Anthropic-shaped and an OpenAI-shaped API, Porting prompts across models. For the Claude-side reference these comparisons hang off, Claude Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.

documents.t: Check yourself 0/5 Key takeaways V4.1-Flash is a repository-shaped model: parity with Opus 5 on DeepSWE, a 20-point deficit on Terminal-Bench 4.0. Match it to work that reads a lot and edits a little. The 1–100 effort dial is the price lever. Every launch number is at 100; DeepSeek's own guidance is that 60–80 keeps most of the accuracy at under half the tokens. Six price cells, not one. The $0.003 headline is off-peak cache-hit input; a cold peak-hour token is 100× that. Peak is 01:00–04:00 and 06:00–10:00 UTC on weekdays. Two silent routing changes: V4-Flash endpoints on Sept 10, deepseek-v4-pro on Sept 14. If you pinned Pro, your model changed — re-run evals. The 890-byte KV cache and 72-hour cache lifetime make long-lived 1M-token contexts cheap, but DeepSeek itself flags long-context sparse retrieval as uncharacterized. Test before you trust.

Copy as Markdown Intermediate At 00:00 UTC on August 31, 2026, DeepSeek quietly pushed a new repository to Hugging Face: deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp. Ten days after the same model went live on their API (August 21), the weights are now MIT-licensed and public. This is the first V4-family model with native vision — not a text model with a bolt-on adapter, but a joint-trained multimodal MoE — and its agent scores on the vision side jumped from 26.2 to 36.5 on ApexBench without moving the text-only agent scores at all. On several agent benchmarks it now matches or edges past Claude Opus 4.8 while the API costs $0.22 per million input tokens. This page is the practical field guide the launch didn't come with: what changed architecturally, the numbers that matter, the one hard limit nobody warns you about, how to run it, and when Claude is still the right call. What you'll learn Understand what 'native vision' means here — the V4-Flash backbone plus a vision encoder + aligner trained together, not stapled on after Read the benchmark table the way the release intends: text-only agents preserved, vision agents up sharply, both within striking distance of Claude Opus 4.8 Know the hard 384-tokens-per-image architectural cap and why it changes how you prompt Do the honest cost math: $0.22 / $0.66 / $0.007 (cached) per million tokens vs Claude Opus 4.8 at $15 / $75 Pick the right serving path — hosted API for almost everyone, vLLM + DSpark for a real self-hosted run
documents.s: DeepSeek V4-Flash-Vision: First Native-Vision Frontier Open Weight

documents.t: DeepSeek V4-Flash-Vision-Exp is a 305-billion-parameter sparse-MoE multimodal model — 13B active per token, 1.048M-token context — that adds joint-trained vision to the V4-Flash text backbone, ships open under MIT on Hugging Face on August 31 2026, and delivers agent-tier multimodal performance at roughly one-fortieth of Claude Opus 4.8's per-token price.

Every open lab that has bolted vision onto a strong text model has paid a tax on text benchmarks. DeepSeek's release table is the flex: on Terminal Bench 2.1 the vision model scores 83.9 (vs 82.7 for the text-only V4-Flash-0731); on DeepSWE it climbs to 59.3 (from 54.4); on Toolathlon-Verified to 75.9 (from 70.3). None of these are vision tasks — they're pure code and tool-use agent evals. The vision variant is better on text-agent work than the text-only checkpoint, not worse. This matters because it's the "prove-out" the field has been waiting for since Chameleon: you can jointly train a giant MoE for text and vision without the multimodal add causing text regression, as long as the vision head lands late enough and the router gets to keep specializing text experts.
documents.s: 1. Vision was added without breaking the text agents — that's the whole point

documents.t: This is the single most important thing to learn before writing your first prompt. The vision encoder in V4-Flash-Vision-Exp allocates at most 384 tokens per image — and that ceiling is architectural, not a commercial policy. There is no "high-detail" mode that unlocks more. Practical consequences: Big screenshots lose fine text. A 2560×1440 dashboard, a dense CSV rendered as an image, or a long PDF page will be encoded at whatever resolution 384 tokens of visual features can express — meaning small-font text will not survive round-trip. Crop, don't scale. If you need to read numbers off a chart, send the chart cropped to the region of interest, not the whole page. Multi-image beats one giant image. Split large documents into per-region tiles; each tile gets its own 384-token budget. This is why Chartography lands at 64.3 (competitive with Claude Opus 4.8's 65.0) but why the model will still miss a footnote in a 12-point font on a full-page screenshot. Every vision-agent workflow you build should assume this ceiling. Last verified: 2026-09-01. This page quotes facts that change over time — treat the date above as its freshness. Confirm against the official source.
documents.s: 2. The vision encoder has a hard 384-tokens-per-image budget

documents.t: Most published MoE recipes activate 8 experts of 32 or 64. V4-Flash-Vision-Exp uses a much wider expert bank: 256 routed experts + 1 shared expert, with only 6 routed experts firing per token — a 2.3% activation ratio. The model has 43 layers, hidden size 4,096, and the hybrid attention stack combines two mechanisms: Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA) — sparse patterns for long-range reads. Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA) — an aggressively compressed form for the deep-context tail. Wrapped over that, Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) replace the standard residual with a constrained-manifold projection, which the paper reports stabilizes signal propagation through the 43-layer stack. Together these are the reason the model can advertise a 1,048,576-token context window without the quadratic attention bill.
documents.s: 3. The MoE routing is unusually sparse — 6 of 256 experts fire per token

documents.t: Sticker prices, all per million tokens: Model Input Output Cached read DeepSeek V4-Flash-Vision-Exp (API) $0.22 $0.66 $0.007 Claude Opus 4.8 $15.00 $75.00 $1.50 Kimi K3 (cache-miss / cache-hit) $3.00 / $0.30 $15.00 $0.30 Cached-read at $0.007/M is not a typo — that is roughly one two-hundredth of a cent per thousand tokens. For any workload where a repeating system prompt or long context is re-sent (agent loops, RAG over a static corpus, chat with a fixed persona) the effective input price collapses. This is the reason V4-Flash-Vision-Exp is showing up in agent-cost tables at a fraction of what Claude Opus 4.8 costs per task, even when the raw quality is within a few points. Last verified: 2026-09-01. Prices, context window and MoE routing are from the official model card at release. See Freshness half-life for how quickly these numbers move. Confirm against the official source.

Benchmark V4-Flash-Vision-Exp V4-Flash-0731 Claude Opus 4.8 Text agents Terminal Bench 2.1 83.9 82.7 85.0 NL2Repo 57.7 54.2 69.7 DeepSWE 59.3 54.4 58.0 Toolathlon-Verified 75.9 70.3 76.2 Multimodal agents ApexBench (Pass@1) 36.5 26.2† 39.4 Agents' Last Exam 27.3 25.2† 25.7 Chartography 64.3 — 65.0 ZeroBench (Pass@5) 35.0 — 34.0 † Prior text-only checkpoint scored on images it couldn't natively read — a floor, not a fair fight. Reading the table straight: On text-agent work, V4-Flash-Vision-Exp is within a few points of Claude Opus 4.8 across the board, and actively beats V4-Flash-0731 on every eval. Vision was added without regression. On multimodal agents, it beats Claude Opus 4.8 on Agents' Last Exam and ZeroBench Pass@5, trails narrowly on ApexBench and Chartography. This is the first open-weight release where "matches Opus on multimodal agents" is not a marketing line. The one benchmark that's not close is NL2Repo (57.7 vs 69.7). Whole-repository code translation is still a place where the closed frontier holds a real gap. Last verified: 2026-09-01. This page quotes facts that change over time — treat the date above as its freshness. Confirm against the official source.
