documents.t: V4-Flash-Vision-Exp launched on the DeepSeek API on August 21, 2026, and only landed on Hugging Face as open weights on August 31. This ten-day gap is DeepSeek's new default. Compare Z.ai (GLM), which has been shipping API + weights simultaneously; DeepSeek is deliberately sequencing. The industry read: labs now agree that big open MoEs are shipping. The remaining question is when in the release cycle the weights arrive. For production planning that means: If you need on-prem from day zero, watch for GLM-family releases. If you can start on the API and cut over to self-hosted a week or two later, DeepSeek is the pattern.
documents.s: The release pattern — API first, weights ten days later

documents.t: There are three realistic paths. Pick by the two constraints that actually matter: whether the weights need to live on your infrastructure, and how much VRAM (or RAM) you can pay for. Guided walkthrough1 of 3 1Path A — DeepSeek's hosted API (default for almost everyone)⌄ OpenAI-compatible endpoint at api.deepseek.com. Model ID is deepseek-v4-flash-vision-exp. Pricing is $0.22 / $0.66 / $0.007 per million tokens. This is the right answer unless you have a data-residency or air-gap constraint. ←PreviousNext→ 2Path B — vLLM on 4× GB300 (single-node self-host)⌄ The vLLM container ships day-0 support and the deepseek_v4 tool-call parser. You need one node with 4× GB300 (or equivalent B300 config). DSpark speculative decoding is enabled via --speculative-config. FP8 KV cache and block-size 256 are both required for the throughput numbers DeepSeek published. ←PreviousNext→ 3Path C — Community GGUF via llama.cpp / Ollama (workstation-class)⌄ unsloth/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp-GGUF ships two dynamic quants: UD-Q4_K_XL at 155 GB and UD-Q8_K_XL at 162 GB. Neither fits a single 24/48/80 GB GPU. What works is a fat workstation with 192 GB+ system RAM and offload, or a small multi-GPU rig with CPU spillover. ←PreviousNext→ Hosted API — Python (OpenAI-compatible) CopyOpen in Claude↗ import openai client = openai.OpenAI( api_key="YOUR_DEEPSEEK_KEY", base_url="https://api.deepseek.com/v1", ) response = client.chat.completions.create( model="deepseek-v4-flash-vision-exp", messages=[ { "role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "text", "text": "What does this chart claim, and what's the one thing it hides?"}, {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": "https://example.com/chart.png"}}, ], } ], ) print(response.choices[0].message.content) Self-host — vLLM on 4× GB300 with DSpark CopyOpen in Claude↗ docker run --gpus all -p 8000:8000 \ vllm/vllm-openai:deepseekv4-flash-vision \ deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp \ --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \ --block-size 256 \ --tensor-parallel-size 4 \ --tool-call-parser deepseek_v4 \ --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","model":"deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp","num_speculative_tokens":3}' Local — Ollama with the community GGUF CopyOpen in Claude↗ ollama run hf.co/unsloth/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp-GGUF:UD-Q4_K_XL # Compact image syntax the model was trained to accept: # <image>path/to/screenshot.png</image> followed by your prompt

Reach for V4-Flash-Vision when: You need multimodal agent quality at roughly Opus-4.8 tier and cost is a factor. Cached-read pricing crushes anything on the closed frontier. The workload benefits from a 1M-token context (long-document VQA, whole-video-frame analysis, big-repo review with screenshots). You need open weights for compliance, air-gapped work, or fine-tuning, and you have (or rent) frontier-class hardware. You're building a chart-heavy or dashboard-parsing pipeline where you can control image tiling. Stay on Claude Opus 4.8 (or Sonnet 5) when: The job is whole-repository code translation or synthesis — NL2Repo is the outlier where the gap is real (57.7 vs 69.7). You need Claude-specific features: Extended thinking under budget, Skills, Sub-agent orchestration in Claude Code, or the Managed Agents session-budget controls. Your prompts contain images with tiny critical text and you cannot tile — you'll hit the 384-token cap and lose accuracy. You want a single vendor / SLA / support contact and are already invested in Anthropic tooling. For a broader model-choice framework, see How to choose a model. For a side-by-side of the whole open-weight wave, DeepSeek, Qwen & the Open-Weight Wave is the durable overview.
documents.s: When to reach for V4-Flash-Vision — and when to stay on Claude

documents.t: You will forget the 384-token cap. The first three vision agents you build will overshoot resolution and quietly lose accuracy on small text. Instrument for it: log per-image dimensions and downscale + tile deliberately. DSpark drops silently if you skip --speculative-config. Without the flag, vLLM will happily serve the model at 1/3 the throughput the release announced. Always pass the speculative config in production. The GGUF is not a laptop model. UD-Q4_K_XL is 155 GB. Community threads that show it "running" on smaller boxes are running it at fractional tokens/s via SSD swap — technically working, not usable. API vs weights version parity is not guaranteed. The API model can be silently updated; the Hugging Face weights are pinned to Vision-Exp. If a benchmark shifts a few points month-to-month on the API, that's why. Exp means experimental. The vision variant is not guaranteed to survive into production V4 releases. Do not build a critical pipeline on the assumption that this specific checkpoint will be around in a year.

Copy as Markdown Advanced Every model on AILmanac so far generates text the same way: one token, then the next, left to right, forever. A different family of models does not. It starts with a blank canvas of masked positions, predicts all of them at once, keeps the ones it is confident about, and repeats. Position 40 can be decided before position 7. The numbers are the reason anyone cares. Inception's Mercury 2 — a reasoning model — reportedly runs at 1,009 tokens/sec on Blackwell GPUs with 1.7 s end-to-end latency, roughly 8–14× faster than comparable reasoning-enabled competitors (The Decoder). Google's experimental Gemini Diffusion samples at 1,479 tokens/sec excluding overhead, against Gemini 2.5 Flash's 272.4 (Techmeme roundup). And yet the README of LLaDA — the 8B open-weight model that proved the approach at scale — tells you its quality peaks when the number of sampling steps equals the response length. One forward pass per token. Exactly like an autoregressive model, but without a KV cache, so slower. Both facts are true. This lesson is the bridge between them: what the algorithm actually does, which knob buys the speed and what it costs, the two structural limits that made early diffusion LLMs unusable and the fix that shipped, and the three gotchas (streaming, length billing, and a jailbreak class that does not exist on autoregressive models) you need before you put one in production. What you'll learn Describe masked-diffusion generation in terms of a canvas, a denoising pass, and a commit decision — and say what bidirectional attention buys and costs Use the steps knob correctly: compute tokens-per-forward-pass, and explain the conditional-independence failure that makes aggressive parallelism wrong rather than merely worse Explain why block diffusion is on every dLLM you can actually call today — it is what restored the KV cache, variable-length output, and token streaming Pick the jobs where a dLLM genuinely wins: infilling and any-order edits, latency-bound voice, and bounded decisions — not 'everything, but faster' Treat an open dLLM endpoint as unaligned at the boundary, because masked-infill prompts bypass alignment in a way autoregressive refusals cannot Last verified: 2026-10-02. Every price, context window, tokens-per-second and latency figure here is perishable — this field is moving monthly and Inception's rate card currently carries promotional discounts. Check the vendor's own model page and the independent leaderboards before quoting any number in a decision. Research claims are cited to their papers; several are preprints, not replicated results. Confirm against the official source.
documents.s: Diffusion LLMs: The Models That Don't Write Left to Right

documents.t: An autoregressive (AR) model's loop is: read the whole prefix, emit a probability distribution over one position (the next one), sample, append, repeat. The KV cache is what makes this cheap — the keys and values for every earlier token were computed once and never change, because attention is causal and nothing to the right exists yet. A masked diffusion LLM inverts that. Attention is bidirectional: every position attends to every other position, in both directions. So in a single forward pass the model produces a distribution for every masked position simultaneously. Generation becomes an iterative refinement of a whole answer, not a walk along it. Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Lay out a canvas⌄ Decide a generation length L. Fill all L positions with a special mask token. On a pure masked dLLM (LLaDA, Dream), L is fixed before the first forward pass — the model does not grow the sequence as it goes. ←PreviousNext→ 2One denoising pass predicts everything⌄ The transformer runs once over prompt + canvas and returns a distribution for every masked slot at once. Not 'the next token' — slot 3, slot 17 and slot 240, in the same pass. ←PreviousNext→ 3Commit a subset (this is the whole game)⌄ You unmask some of those predictions and freeze them as real tokens. Which ones, and how many, is the decoding policy: random order, highest top-1 confidence, largest top1−top2 margin, or lowest entropy. Everything else stays masked. ←PreviousNext→ 4Re-run with the committed tokens as context⌄ The next pass sees the frozen tokens and re-predicts the remaining masks — and because attention is bidirectional, a token committed at the END of the answer conditions the tokens still missing from the middle. This is what AR models cannot do. ←PreviousNext→ 5Stop when the canvas is full⌄ Total cost = (number of passes) × (one full forward pass). So tokens per forward pass = L / steps. That ratio, not the hardware, is where the headline tokens/sec comes from. ←PreviousNext→ That last line is the one worth memorising. An AR model is pinned at one token per forward pass. A diffusion LLM lets you choose. DiffusionGemma, Google's open-weight entry, reports roughly 20 tokens per forward pass while refining blocks of 256 in parallel, which is how it reaches ~1,500 output tokens/sec on a single H100 (DiffusionGemma Technical Report).
documents.s: The mechanism, in one diagram you have to imagine

documents.t: Dream 7B exposes the knob explicitly. Its diffusion_generate() documents steps as "diffusion timesteps" where max_new_tokens / steps tokens are produced per step, and notes plainly that fewer steps are faster but coarser (DreamLM/Dream, Apache-2.0). So why not always use few steps? Because the error it introduces is not noise — it is a specific, nameable bug. A single forward pass gives you, for each masked slot, a marginal distribution: the probability of a token at that position, averaged over everything still unknown. If you commit two slots from the same pass, you are sampling from the product of their marginals, not from their joint distribution. Any dependency between them is silently discarded. The Fast-dLLM authors state the root cause directly: generation quality degrades under parallel decoding because masked diffusion models sample tokens independently from marginal probabilities when the true joint distribution has dependencies (Fast-dLLM, arXiv:2505.22618). The intuition: ask for a city and two adjacent slots might score "New" and "Delhi" as the most likely token for their own position, because "New York" and "New Delhi" are both plausible. Commit both in one pass and you get neither. The failure mode of over-parallel decoding is not vaguer prose, it is confidently assembled nonsense at the seams. The fix that made the field practical is confidence-aware parallel decoding: compute a confidence per masked slot (typically the max softmax probability), commit only the slots above a threshold, and if none clear it, commit the single highest so the loop still makes progress. Tokens that are nearly independent get decoded together; tokens that depend on each other wait. Fast-dLLM reports up to 27.6× throughput improvement on LLaDA and Dream across benchmarks with minimal accuracy loss — training-free, just a decoding change. That is the shape of this entire research area: the parallelism is free, the independence is not, and the work is in detecting which tokens can safely go together. What you'll learn A confidence threshold is a quality dial you can actually reason about: higher threshold means fewer tokens committed per pass, more passes, slower, closer to AR quality. Fast-dLLM v2 reports a 2.6× speedup on GSM8K at threshold 0.9 with minimal accuracy loss — that is the kind of setting to start from, not 'commit everything'.
documents.s: The steps knob, and why cranking it is wrong rather than just lossy

documents.t: LLaDA's own repository lists its efficiency constraints without euphemism: fixed context length for sampling, no KV-cache support, and degraded performance when sampling steps drop below the response length. The authors frame it as deliberate — they wanted to find the ceiling of the approach before optimising it (ML-GSAI/LLaDA, MIT, ~4k stars, Base and Instruct weights plus LLaDA 1.5, LLaDA-MoE-7B-A1B and iLLaDA variants). Stack those up and a pure masked dLLM is nearly unusable as a product: No KV cache. Bidirectional attention means every pass can change any token's context, so cached keys and values are invalid. You recompute the whole sequence every step. Fixed output length. You must pick L before generating. Too small truncates; too large wastes compute on positions you will throw away. Latency worse than AR. Points 1 and 2 together can make a "parallel" model slower end-to-end than the sequential one it replaces. Block diffusion resolves all three by refusing to be pure. Generate in blocks: condition on previous blocks autoregressively, run diffusion inside the current block. That gives flexible sequence length and KV caching between blocks — the BD3-LM formulation, an ICLR 2025 oral (arXiv:2503.09573, kuleshov-group/bd3lms). Fast-dLLM v2 (arXiv:2509.26328) shows what a tuned version looks like, and the details are worth knowing because they explain the vendor behaviour you will observe: Hybrid attention mask. Block-diagonal (bidirectional) within a block, block-causal (left-to-right) between blocks. Bidirectional context where it helps, AR semantics where the cache lives. Two cache levels. A block-level cache holding finished blocks as clean prefix context, plus a sub-block cache (DualCache) for the recomputation that intra-block decoding still needs. Complementary masking in training. Each sample is duplicated into two views with masks m and 1 − m, so every token is supervised both as a mask target and as context. Reported results. Up to 2.5× faster than standard AR decoding; 1.8× at batch size 64 on H100s; a 7B average benchmark score of 60.3 against Dream's 57.6, including HumanEval 63.4 vs 57.9 and GSM8K 62.0 vs 39.2. And the training cost is the detail that reframes the field: Fast-dLLM v2 reports fine-tuning from an AR model on roughly 1B tokens — about 500× less than Dream's 580B — a 7B trained in ~12 hours on 64 A100s.
documents.s: The two structural limits — and block diffusion, which is why you can call one today

documents.t: DiffusionGemma makes that point unmissable. It is not trained from scratch: it fine-tunes Gemma 4, a mixture-of-experts model with 3.8B activated and 25.2B total parameters, into a diffusion model using fewer than 10% of the starting AR model's total training token budget — supervised denoising fine-tuning, then reinforcement learning and sampler distillation (arXiv:2608.00146, CC-BY-4.0 weights). What survives the conversion is the surprising part. The report states it retains the base model's thinking mode, multimodal inputs and long contexts — and keeps the ability to generate autoregressively with only minor degradation. One set of weights, two decoding modes. If that result holds up, "diffusion LLM" stops being a distinct product category and becomes a serving option: the same family, with a parallelism dial on the inference side. That is a far more consequential claim than any single tokens-per-second record, and it is the reason to learn the mechanism now rather than when a provider flips a flag on a model you already use.
documents.s: Diffusion is a decoding mode you can retrofit, not a separate species

documents.t: Speed is the headline and the weakest part of the case, because speed is contested — specialised AR hardware is also delivering hundreds of tokens per second (see Token Speed). The durable advantages are the ones that follow from the shape of the algorithm. Any-order generation and native infilling. Because you choose which slot to commit, you can leave a hole in the middle of a sequence and have the model fill it with full context on both sides. Dream exposes this as the alg parameter — origin (random order), maskgit_plus (top-1 confidence), topk_margin (top1 − top2 margin), entropy — plus alg_temp to add randomness to those strategies. For code edits, template completion, or filling fields in a fixed JSON skeleton, that is a structurally better fit than asking an AR model to re-emit a whole file to change line 40. Latency-bound interaction. Inception's Mercury Voice advertises time-to-first-token under 170 ms on a 128K context, priced at $0.20/$1.50 per million input/output tokens at the time of writing. Voice is the clearest case where latency is the product; our full-duplex voice AI page covers why that threshold matters. End-to-end reasoning turnaround. Mercury 2's reported 1.7 s for a complete reasoning answer is a different claim from throughput — it is the number an agent loop actually feels, turn after turn. Bounded answers instead of prose. Inception's Mercury Decide returns a choice, a score, or a yes/no with a calibrated probability read off the model rather than written out as text — reported at up to 14 decisions per second, which makes "run it on every case and escalate the unsure ones" affordable. The category and its caveats are covered in depth on System One decision models; the diffusion backbone is an implementation detail there, not the point. Price pressure. Mercury 2.5 currently lists a 260K context at $0.04/$0.15 per million input/output tokens (promotional, off $0.20/$0.75) with cached input at $0.004 per million. Treat promo pricing as temporary and model your bill at list.
documents.s: What a diffusion LLM is actually better at

documents.t: Watch out Tokens/sec is measured at the vendor's chosen parallelism. Your quality bar may require more steps, which costs you the speedup. Benchmark on your own prompts at your own accuracy threshold. Output is not final left-to-right. Only block boundaries are monotonic; inside a block, slots can still be masked or revised. Any UI or parser that assumes 'token N will never change' is wrong. A pure masked dLLM bills and computes a length you chose in advance. Block diffusion reduces that to per-block granularity — it does not remove it. The third one deserves more than a bullet, because it is a security property and it has no autoregressive analogue. An AR model's alignment has a structural advantage: the refusal happens first. If the model decides to decline, every subsequent token is conditioned on "I can't help with that." A diffusion LLM has no such moment. There is no left-to-right point at which a refusal takes over the rest of the generation — masked slots get filled to be consistent with whatever is already on the canvas. DIJA ("The Devil behind the mask", ICLR 2026, arXiv:2507.11097, ZichenWen1/DIJA) turns that into an attack. The adversarial prompt puts the harmful intent in unmasked tokens and leaves masked spans for the model to complete in a contextually consistent way. The reported results: up to 100% keyword-based attack success rate on Dream-Instruct, surpassing the strongest prior baseline by up to 78.5% in evaluator-based ASR on JailbreakBench and by 37.7 points in StrongREJECT score — while requiring no rewriting or obfuscation of the harmful content. The authors' conclusion is that existing alignment mechanisms do not protect dLLMs against context-aware masked-input prompts, because the model cannot filter an unsafe generation mid-inference the way a sequential one can. A follow-up (arXiv:2602.00388) argues the picture is two-sided — diffusion confers a safety blessing in some settings that then breaks under context — which is a reason to measure rather than to assume either way. Practical takeaway: if you expose an open-weight dLLM, do not treat its instruction tuning as a guardrail. Filter and classify at the boundary, on both the request and the response, exactly as you would for a base model. Our securing local and hybrid agents page covers the boundary pattern.
documents.s: Three gotchas before you ship one

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Hosted, zero setup⌄ Inception serves Mercury through an OpenAI-compatible API, and the models are listed on OpenRouter (for example openrouter.ai/inception/mercury-2). Point an existing OpenAI-SDK script at it and change the model string — nothing about the request shape is diffusion-specific. ←PreviousNext→ 2Open weights, local⌄ LLaDA-8B-Instruct (MIT) and Dream-v0-Instruct-7B (Apache-2.0) both ship inference code on Hugging Face. DiffusionGemma's weights are CC-BY-4.0. Note that a pure masked dLLM has no KV cache, so plan VRAM for recomputing the full sequence every step. ←PreviousNext→ 3Run the steps sweep⌄ The single most informative experiment: hold the prompt fixed, vary steps, and plot wall-clock against a task metric you care about. You will find your own quality cliff, and it will not be where a benchmark table put it. ←PreviousNext→ 4Then test the seams⌄ Use prompts whose answers contain multi-token units — proper nouns, numbers with units, identifiers, JSON keys. Those are where conditional-independence errors show up first, and where a confidence threshold earns its cost. ←PreviousNext→ Call a hosted diffusion LLM with the OpenAI SDK (nothing changes but the model string) CopyOpen in Claude↗ # Inception serves an OpenAI-compatible API; OpenRouter also lists the models. # Check the provider's model list for the current slug before you hard-code one. curl https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENROUTER_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "inception/mercury-2", "messages": [ {"role": "user", "content": "Rewrite this function to stream its output, and explain the two failure modes you introduced."} ], "stream": true }' # What to watch for, beyond the content: # - time to first token vs time to last token (the diffusion win is usually in the gap) # - whether the stream arrives in chunks that look like BLOCKS rather than words The steps sweep on Dream 7B — find your own quality cliff CopyOpen in Claude↗ import time, torch from transformers import AutoModel, AutoTokenizer NAME = "Dream-org/Dream-v0-Instruct-7B" tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(NAME, trust_remote_code=True) model = AutoModel.from_pretrained( NAME, torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, trust_remote_code=True ).to("cuda").eval() PROMPT = "List the five largest cities in Germany with their populations." MAX_NEW = 256 # steps == MAX_NEW is the authors' best-quality setting: one token per # forward pass. Each halving doubles tokens-per-pass and doubles the # number of independence assumptions you are making. for steps in [256, 128, 64, 32, 16]: inputs = tok.apply_chat_template( [{"role": "user", "content": PROMPT}], return_tensors="pt", return_dict=True, add_generation_prompt=True, ).to("cuda") t0 = time.perf_counter() out = model.diffusion_generate( inputs.input_ids, attention_mask=inputs.attention_mask, max_new_tokens=MAX_NEW, steps=steps, temperature=0.0, alg="entropy", # commit the lowest-entropy slots first alg_temp=0.0, ) dt = time.perf_counter() - t0 text = tok.decode(out[0][len(inputs.input_ids[0]):], skip_special_tokens=True) print(f"--- steps={steps} tokens/pass={MAX_NEW/steps:.0f} {dt:.2f}s ---") print(text.strip()[:400]) # Read the OUTPUTS, not just the timings. The numbers and the city names are # the multi-token units that break first when too many slots are committed # from one pass. That corruption is the conditional-independence bug, visible.

Key takeaways A diffusion LLM's speed comes from one ratio — generation length divided by denoising steps, i.e. tokens committed per forward pass. An AR model is fixed at 1. Everything else is a consequence of that dial. Over-parallel decoding is wrong, not just coarse: committing correlated slots from one pass samples the product of marginals instead of the joint. Confidence-threshold decoding is the fix, and Fast-dLLM reports up to 27.6x throughput with minimal accuracy loss. Pure masked diffusion has no KV cache and a fixed output length. Block diffusion (AR between blocks, diffusion inside) is what restored caching, variable length and streaming — it is why every callable dLLM today is a block model. DiffusionGemma converted an autoregressive Gemma 4 MoE into a diffusion model for under 10% of its original training token budget while keeping thinking mode, multimodality and AR generation. Diffusion is looking more like a decoding mode than a separate species of model. Pick it for infilling and any-order edits, sub-200 ms voice turns, fast bounded decisions and end-to-end turn latency — and assume its alignment does not hold, because masked-infill prompts reach up to 100% ASR on an aligned open dLLM. Check yourself 0/5 New to the underlying machinery? What is an LLM and Tokens and context cover the autoregressive baseline this page departs from, and Token Speed covers the hardware and software multipliers that attack the same latency problem from the other side.

Copy as Markdown Advanced What you'll learn Understand what an "overfit" inference engine is, why a narrow runtime can roughly double a general one on identical hardware, and why that stopped being an expensive bet in 2026 Learn the three mechanisms ds4 uses that a general GGUF runner will not give you — asymmetric routed-expert quantization, a bounded expert cache streamed from SSD, and KV snapshots that survive a restart Read ds4's own published numbers correctly: which figure is a single Mac, which is eight GPUs sharing 16 sessions, and which is a 178 GB model running on a 128 GB machine Price the real cost of the bet: model support that is designed to be withdrawn, a main branch you should check the date on, and a security posture that assumes you read C Decide when narrow beats llama.cpp for your job — and the three cases where it clearly does not On 2 October 2026 a link titled "From the creator of Redis; run LLM locally with ds4" reached the Hacker News front page and settled at 362 points and 104 comments. The surprising part is not the project. It is that the project was already five months old — antirez/ds4 was created on 6 May 2026 — and had quietly accumulated 23,582 stars, 2,268 forks and 761 open issues before the wider audience noticed. What it got noticed for matters more than the engine itself. ds4 is the most-starred member of a category that barely existed a year ago and now has at least six entries: the overfit inference engine. A runtime built for one model on one class of hardware, that will not run your other models, and whose author intends for it to be thrown away. If you have read Colibrì or Strata here, you have met two points on this map already. This page is about the third point and the map.
documents.s: DwarfStar (ds4) and the Rise of Overfit Inference Engines

documents.t: ds4 picks a short list of mixture-of-experts models, writes Metal, CUDA and ROCm kernels for those specific architectures, crushes only the routed experts to roughly two bits while keeping the per-token path at higher precision, and ships its own CLI, coding agent and HTTP server around them — buying speed and polish on six models at the price of running nothing else.

The category name comes from a deliberate analogy to overfitting a model: the runtime is tuned so tightly to one target that it generalises badly on purpose. The published roster, as of early October 2026: Engine Hardware target Model target DwarfStar (ds4) Metal 96 GB+, CUDA (DGX Spark, Ada/L40S), ROCm (Strix Halo) DeepSeek V4 / V4.1 Flash, V4 PRO, GLM 5.2/5.3, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next Strata Consumer NVIDIA, 12 GB+ Qwen3.8-Flash-Next ninfer RTX 5090 Qwen checkpoints Splash Apple Silicon M3+ Qwen family llamAmpere RTX 3090 / 3090 Ti Qwen3.8-27B gufo AMD Strix Halo a curated set The one measurement in public that compares a narrow engine against a tuned general one, on the same box, is a developer's RTX 4070 (12 GB, 64 GB DDR5) running Qwen3.8-Flash-Next: 27 tok/s on best-tuned llama.cpp against 53 tok/s on Strata at 60K context. Roughly 2x. Take that number with the caveat its own author attaches: the quantizations and settings differed, so it is not a controlled experiment. It is a real-world delta, not a benchmark. That distinction is exactly the kind of thing this whole category is bad at printing, and it is worth internalising before you read any engine's README — the same discipline reading an AI benchmark asks for.

Three arguments, and the third is the non-obvious one: Generality costs throughput. Supporting many models and backends forces defensive branches and shared allocators that constrain how aggressively any single path can be scheduled. Coding agents collapsed the cost of writing kernels. A single competent systems programmer with an agent can now write, benchmark and fix GPU kernels at a pace that used to require a team. ds4's own author has described the project as built with heavy model assistance, with humans leading the ideas, testing and debugging. Inference optimisation has an unusually crisp objective function. Fixed inputs, a reference output to match, and one number to maximise. That is a loop an agent can be pointed at and left to run — which is why argument 2 bites here and not everywhere.

The headline that sounds impossible — a 284B-parameter model on a laptop — is not uniform compression. An MoE model touches only a small slice of its weights per token, and those slices are not equally fragile. ds4 exploits that asymmetry per tensor type. The Qwen3.8-Flash-Next configuration is the one the repo documents in exact terms, and it is worth reading closely: Component Treatment Size Main + MTP weights imatrix IQ2_XXS gate/up experts, padded Q2_K down projections 41.73 GiB Original BF16 n-grams read directly from disk, never resident 95.37 GiB Two things to take from that table. First, the quantization is chosen per tensor role — gate and up projections get a different scheme from down projections, because they tolerate different damage. Second, the single largest artifact on disk is not multiplied per token at all: an n-gram embedding is a lookup, so it stays on the SSD and never competes for RAM. Strata exploits the same property on the same model; the file size and the memory requirement are simply not the same number. The repo states which models survive this treatment: DeepSeek V4 Flash and PRO, and GLM 5.2, "tolerate aggressive routed-expert quantization." That is a per-architecture empirical claim, not a general law — which is precisely why the engine's model list is short.
documents.s: 1. Asymmetric quantization: crush the experts, keep the path

documents.t: The flag is --ssd-streaming, and what it actually does is narrower than the phrase suggests. From the project's own SSD_STREAMING.md: SSD streaming keeps a bounded cache of routed experts and reads missing experts from the GGUF. So: non-routed weights stay in RAM. Only routed experts page in and out of a bounded cache. The documentation is explicit that this does not remove the memory needed for other weights, activations, scratch and the context — a caveat worth noting, because the natural reading of "streaming" is that RAM stops mattering. The headline result here is the genuinely surprising number on this page. On an M5 Max with GLM 5.3 Flash Q4 — a 177.77 GiB model on a 128 GB machine: Phase Measured Prefill (initial / continued) 121 t/s / 104 t/s Generation 11.9–14.9 t/s Read it with the warning the docs attach: "Generation is usually more sensitive to cache misses than prefill. A large model that starts successfully can still be too slow for interactive work." Twelve tokens a second is fine for a batch summarisation job and painful for a coding agent you sit and watch. There is a counter-intuitive tuning trap too: making the expert cache bigger can make decoding slower, because an oversized cache displaces the non-routed weights that are touched every single token. More cache is not monotonically better. For the deeper treatment of expert streaming as an architecture — NVMe bandwidth as the real ceiling, SSD wear, O_DIRECT — see Colibrì, which is built entirely around that idea.
documents.s: 2. SSD streaming that streams experts, not everything

documents.t: This is the mechanism most likely to change how your day feels, and the one almost nobody writes about. ds4 stores session KV state and conversation history under ~/.ds4/kvcache, and the documented promise is that "compatible local KV snapshots avoid rebuilding the prompt." The session verbs: Command Effect /save Persist the current session /list List saved sessions /switch <sha> Resume a specific session with its KV state /strip <sha> Drop the KV payload, keep the text /del <sha> Delete the session Why it matters: a long-running agent re-sends a growing prefix on every turn. If the engine rebuilds that prefix from scratch each time, prefill dominates your wall clock on exactly the workload you care about. Commenters on the HN thread singled this out — append-only message history that preserves KV reusability — as the kind of detail a general runtime typically leaves to the caller. It is the local-engine analogue of prompt caching across providers: same economics, different layer. One documented limit: sessions containing images cannot yet be saved.
documents.s: 3. KV snapshots: the detail that makes agent loops cheap

documents.t: Four binaries ship, and the division of labour is the point: Binary What it is for ds4 Interactive multi-turn CLI with conversation history ds4-agent A native coding agent that calls inference directly — no HTTP hop ds4-server HTTP server on http://127.0.0.1:8000, for external clients ds4-eval Embedded capability regression tests against a real GGUF ds4-server is the integration surface, and the repo names its intended clients directly: Pi, OpenCode, Codex CLI, or Claude Code. That makes ds4 a plausible local backend for the hybrid setups described in Claude plus local models and local coding agents. Note what the repo says about ds4-eval, because it is unusually honest: these are "DwarfStar integration checks, not official leaderboard scores." It answers "did this build regress?", not "is this model good."
documents.s: It is a stack, not just a runtime

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Pick your build target⌄ Metal on Apple Silicon is the primary path and the default. CUDA has two targets — one tuned for DGX Spark, one generic for Ada/L40S-class cards. ROCm targets Strix Halo systems such as the Framework Desktop. You are choosing a compile-time target, not a runtime flag. ←PreviousNext→ 2Check the RAM floor before you download anything⌄ The Metal path wants 96 GB and up for the Flash-class models; the PRO variant is a 256 GB-plus machine. SSD streaming lowers the floor but, as the numbers above show, buys you single-digit-to-low-teens generation speed on the biggest models. Decide which side of 'interactive' you need to be on first. ←PreviousNext→ 3Build⌄ A plain make for Metal; make cuda-spark, make cuda-generic or make strix-halo otherwise. Pure C with platform kernels — the repository is roughly 8.7 MB of C, 4.5 MB of CUDA, 2.3 MB of Objective-C and 1.4 MB of Metal, with no runtime dependency on another inference library. ←PreviousNext→ 4Download a model by tag, not by URL⌄ The helper script takes short tags such as ds4f-q2, qwen38-q2, qwen38-q4k and qwen38-vision. These are project-specific GGUF builds — this is the step where 'not a general GGUF runner' becomes concrete. A checkpoint you already have on disk for Ollama or llama.cpp is not expected to work. ←PreviousNext→ 5Run the CLI first, the server second⌄ Verify quality and speed interactively with ds4 before wiring anything to it. Then start ds4-server and point your client at port 8000. Check the server and client guides in docs/ for the current API shape — the README defers it, and this is the surface most likely to have moved since this page was written. ←PreviousNext→ 6Save a session once you have a prompt you like⌄ Run /save, then /list. This is the step that turns a slow prefill into a one-time cost, and it is the single highest-leverage habit on this engine. ←PreviousNext→ Build, fetch and run — Apple Silicon CopyOpen in Claude↗ git clone https://github.com/antirez/ds4.git cd ds4 make ./download_model.sh ds4f-q2 ./ds4 The other three build targets CopyOpen in Claude↗ make cuda-spark # DGX Spark make cuda-generic # Ada Lovelace / L40S-class, multi-GPU make strix-halo # ROCm on Strix Halo (e.g. Framework Desktop) Serve it to Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenCode or Pi CopyOpen in Claude↗ ./ds4-server # listens on http://127.0.0.1:8000 by default # see docs/SERVER.md for the API surface and multi-session handling, # and docs/CLIENTS.md for per-client setup Flags worth knowing on day one CopyOpen in Claude↗ --ctx 32768 # context window size --prefill-chunk 1024 # prefill batch size --ssd-streaming # bounded routed-expert cache, rest read from GGUF --mtp # speculative decoding (GLM, Qwen) --nothink / --think # reasoning off/on; V4.1 uses --think-level 1-100 --temp 0 # greedy --vision FILE # load a vision encoder --prefix-file FILE # preload conversation pairs --power 100 # throughput/GPU-load trade (V4.1 and GLM require 100)

The repo reports "about 126 t/s aggregate generation with 16 sessions" on an eight-L40S deployment. That is aggregate throughput across sixteen concurrent sessions on eight datacentre GPUs — roughly 8 t/s per session if you divide it out. It is a serving-capacity number. It tells you nothing about how fast a single reply streams on your laptop, and it is the figure most likely to be quoted at you out of context. The general version of this trap is covered in fast inference and token speed.
documents.s: 1. The 126 t/s figure is not your Mac

documents.t: The repo's stated philosophy: "Model support is intentionally opportunistic." Models are added and removed based on relevance to 128 GB laptops and 256/512 GB workstations. The project describes itself as "a working template for the biggest use cases" rather than universal coverage, and encourages users to modify the codebase with coding agents for their own hardware. Read that as a dependency warning. If you build a workflow on ds4 plus DeepSeek V4 Flash, the supported combination is explicitly not a commitment. Pin a commit.
documents.s: 2. Model support is designed to be withdrawn

documents.t: As of 6 October 2026, the most recent commit on main is dated 20 September 2026, about two weeks earlier, against 761 open issues. The commits themselves look like careful engineering work rather than abandonment — test-suite guards for ROCm and Metal, QA preflight documentation. But the category's own chronicler predicts that by April 2027, at least four of the six engines listed above will have gone 60 days without a commit, as model architectures move underneath them. That is a forecast, not a fact. The reason it belongs on this page is that it is a checkable one, and checking it takes ten seconds before you adopt any engine in this class. The commit date is the maintenance column that none of these READMEs print.
documents.s: 3. Check the commit date yourself — and know what the category predicts

documents.t: A commenter on the Hacker News thread reported that the ROCm builds are "absolutely untested". The repository's own commit log from 19 September 2026 says the opposite in specific terms — a commit message describes verifying warning-free ROCm application and test builds on Strix Halo, with placement, memory, session, server and agent tests passing. Both are reported here rather than resolved, because they may both be true of different moments or different Strix Halo configurations. If you are on AMD, treat ROCm as the least-trodden of the three backends and verify on your own box before committing to it.
documents.s: 4. A contradiction worth knowing about on ROCm

documents.t: ds4 is "deliberately narrow, not a general GGUF runner" and requires its own GGUF builds. Separately: the project site at dwarfstar.sh was criticised in the HN thread as marketing-heavy — one commenter called it "pure slop" — with the technical substance living in the repository's docs/ directory instead. Read the repo, not the landing page.
documents.s: 5. Custom GGUFs, and a website the thread disliked

documents.t: These are young, largely single-maintainer projects with native GPU access and few external reviewers, and the whole category shares that shape. The standing advice from people tracking it: build from source, pin commits, and run them on hardware you would not mind losing. If a local engine is going to sit behind an agent with tool access, the threat model in securing local and hybrid agents applies to the runtime as much as to the model.
documents.s: 6. The security posture assumes you read C

documents.t: Choose an overfit engine when your model is on its list and will stay there for the duration of the project; your hardware is on its list; the workload is long-running with a reusable prefix, so KV snapshots pay for themselves; and you are able to build from source and read a diff. Stay on llama.cpp or Ollama when you switch models often, you want one runtime across machines you do not control, you need a model nobody has overfitted for yet, or the thing you are optimising is your own time rather than tokens per second. The general runtime is also your reference baseline: measure it first, or you will never know what the narrow engine actually bought you. Run models locally with Ollama is the right starting point if you have not set that baseline. Use a hosted API when the job needs frontier capability rather than locality. This came up in the HN thread directly: a commenter noted that frontier cloud models remain faster for actual coding work. Local inference buys privacy, cost control and offline operation — not parity. Local or Claude agent? walks that decision properly. The emerging consensus in the local-AI community is a two-tier ecosystem rather than a winner: general runtimes for breadth and portability, disposable overfit runtimes for maximum performance on the model you are actually running this quarter. You are expected to have both installed. Check yourself 0/6 Last verified: 2026-10-06. This page quotes facts that change over time — treat the date above as its freshness. Sources: antirez/ds4 README and docs/SSD_STREAMING.md; GitHub API for antirez/ds4 (23,582 stars, 2,268 forks, 761 open issues, MIT, created 2026-05-06, latest main commit 2026-09-20) and its languages endpoint; Hacker News item 49936575 via the HN API (362 points, 104 comments, posted 2026-10-02) and its comment thread; carteakey.dev, 'The Rise of Overfit Inference Engines', for the category roster and the RTX 4070 comparison. All performance figures are the respective projects' own measurements, not independent benchmarks. This repository describes itself as beta and fast-changing: flags, model tags, RAM floors and the supported-model list will drift — re-read the README and docs/ before relying on any flag or model name here.

Copy as Markdown Intermediate On September 23, 2026 Fireworks published Ember-1: not a new architecture, not a new pre-train — Kimi K3 with its reasoning habit re-trained. Same 2.8-trillion-parameter body, same 1M context, same price per token. It just stops thinking so much. Fireworks reports 35–50% fewer reasoning tokens with no loss of accuracy, and on two of five published benchmarks Ember-1 outscores K3 running at its maximum effort setting while costing less. Four days later it was the top AI story on Hacker News. The interesting part is not the model — it is the claim underneath it: the cheapest way to run a reasoning model is no longer to tell it to think less. This page takes that claim apart, shows you the arithmetic the launch table implies but never prints, and gives you a way to test it on your own traffic in an afternoon. What you'll learn Separate the two things that make an agent expensive: price per token, and number of tokens — Ember-1 changes only the second Read the launch table honestly, including the benchmark where effort buys literally nothing and the one where every model scores under 22% Derive the cost per task the blog does not print (and discover a single benchmark run costs $5–$535) Understand why a 71% cut in reasoning tokens produced only a 39% cut in total tokens — and what that ratio tells you about your own bill Measure reasoning-token share on your workload with one field most SDK wrappers throw away Know the fine print before you migrate: research-preview status, no released weights, a lost input modality, and the revenue-tiered Kimi K3 licence underneath it all Last verified: 2026-09-28. Benchmark table, training description, token-reduction figures and pricing are Fireworks' own announcement of September 23, 2026 — vendor-run, on vendor-chosen benchmarks, with no independent replication published yet. Context window (1,048,576), model id and rates were cross-checked against the Fireworks model page and the OpenRouter model API on 2026-09-28. Ember-1 shipped as a Research Preview with two weeks of serverless access, kept permanently "based on community demand" — availability is the most perishable fact here; check before you build on it. Licence clauses are quoted from the Kimi K3 LICENSE on Hugging Face. Confirm against the official source.
documents.s: Ember-1: Kimi K3's Answers for 40% Fewer Tokens (Sep 2026)

documents.t: Kimi K3, like every reasoning model, spends most of its generated tokens on internal reasoning — Fireworks puts it at sometimes more than 90%. In a multi-turn agent that reasoning is replayed into every later call, so context grows roughly quadratically with turn count and early thinking gets re-billed for the rest of the run. Fireworks' customers asked for K3's coding quality at lower cost; turning reasoning_effort down gave up too much quality, so Fireworks trained the behaviour instead — over 50 training runs and 200+ evaluations — teaching the model to keep the self-reflection that recovers from mistakes and drop the rest. The result is served as accounts/fireworks/models/ember-1 at exactly K3's rates: $3 / M uncached input, $0.30 / M cached input, $15 / M output.

This is the part that reframes how you should think about model cost. Ember-1's rate card is identical to Kimi K3's, on Fireworks and on OpenRouter alike ($3 input / $15 output per million, 1,048,576-token context on both). There is no discount. Every dollar saved comes from tokens that are never generated in the first place — and, in an agent loop, from those same tokens never being replayed as input on the next nineteen turns. That has a practical consequence: $/token is the wrong number on your dashboard. Two models at the same list price can differ 2× on the same task, and the model with the higher list price is regularly the cheaper one per finished task. AILmanac's What AI costs across providers makes the same point from the pricing side; Ember-1 is the cleanest natural experiment for it yet, because the price variable is pinned and only the token count moves.
documents.s: 1. Nothing got cheaper. The model just buys less.

documents.t: K3 exposes reasoning_effort at low, high and max. Fireworks ran all three as separate arms, which is what makes their table more useful than most launch tables: Benchmark N K3 low K3 high K3 max Ember-1 Ember-1 vs K3 max Terminal Bench 2.1 89 76.4% 77.6% 80.9% 82.0% −51.9% / −23.1 USD SWE-bench Verified 500 80.4% 86.0% 93.2% 92.2% −15.5% / −68.1 USD SWE-Interact 75 6.7% 13.3% 21.3% 20.0% −32.5% / −60.8 USD DeepSWE 1.1 113 55.8% 62.8% 66.4% 75.2% −23.7% / −126.9 USD τ-2 Bench Airline 50 64% 64% 64% 66% −5.9% / −0.3 USD Read down the K3 columns before you read the Ember column. On SWE-bench Verified, dropping from max to low costs you 12.8 points — that is the "give up too much quality" Fireworks is talking about, and it is why an effort dial alone could not solve their customers' problem. Ember-1 lands above K3 high on every row and above K3 max on two of five, at a lower cost than max on all five. Against K3 low it is strictly better on both axes. Two rows deserve separate attention: τ-2 Bench Airline: 64% / 64% / 64%. Three effort levels, one score. On this benchmark every extra thinking token K3 generates is pure waste — you pay max prices for low results. If your production workload looks like τ²-bench (a scripted customer-service policy, short turns, tool calls against a fixed API), the effort dial is a cost setting with no quality meaning, and you should have measured that rather than defaulted to it. The general habit — sweep effort on your eval before trusting a default — is in Effort tuning and Reasoning models compared. SWE-Interact: nobody breaks 22%. The same models that resolve 92–93% of SWE-bench Verified resolve one task in five when the benchmark requires interacting with a user mid-task. SWE-bench Verified is close to saturated and tells you almost nothing about a frontier model any more; the interactive variant is where the actual capability gap lives. Keep both in mind whenever a launch post leads with a 90-something SWE-bench number. This is the capability–reliability gap showing up as two columns in one table.
documents.s: 2. Turning effort down is not the same thing, and the table proves it

documents.t: Fireworks never labels the two figures in that last column. Read as relative cost reduction and absolute dollars saved over the whole run, they are internally consistent — and dividing one by the other recovers a number nobody publishes: what it costs to run these benchmarks once. The arithmetic below is ours, not Fireworks' — it is inference from their two published figures, so treat it as an order of magnitude, not a quote: Benchmark N Implied K3-max run cost Implied cost per task Terminal Bench 2.1 89 ~$44 ~$0.50 SWE-bench Verified 500 ~$439 ~$0.88 SWE-Interact 75 ~$187 ~$2.49 DeepSWE 1.1 113 ~$535 ~$4.74 τ-2 Bench Airline 50 ~$5 ~$0.10 A single DeepSWE 1.1 sweep on K3 at max effort runs to roughly half a thousand dollars — for 113 tasks. That is the real reason "just run your own evals on every model" is advice people nod at and do not follow, and it is worth knowing before you promise a stakeholder a five-model bake-off. It is also the number that makes a 24% saving matter: repeated nightly, that one benchmark is a $46,000-a-year line item.
documents.s: 3. The "−51.9% / −23.1 USD" column tells you what a benchmark run costs

documents.t: Fireworks' internal validation reports 71.3% fewer reasoning tokens and 39% fewer total tokens on the same traffic. The gap between those two numbers is the most useful thing in the announcement, and it generalises to any efficiency claim you are ever pitched. Reasoning tokens are a share of generated tokens. The rest of your bill is made of things an efficiency post-train cannot touch: System prompt and tool definitions, re-sent every turn (often the largest single block in an agent). Tool results — file contents, search results, HTTP responses — which arrive from the outside world at their own size. The final answer, which you actually wanted. Prior turns, replayed as input. So the ceiling on any "fewer thinking tokens" saving is your reasoning-token share, not the vendor's. An agent whose turns are 80% tool output will see a fraction of the advertised win; a chat workload with a short prompt and long deliberation will see most of it. Before you migrate anything, measure the share — the next section shows how. Why agents burn tokens covers the other three lines in that list. Watch out A vendor's token-reduction percentage is measured on the vendor's traffic mix. Your saving is bounded by your own reasoning-token share — measure it before you estimate anything.
documents.s: Why 71% off reasoning was only 39% off the bill

documents.t: Fireworks returns the model's thinking in a reasoning_content field (the content that would otherwise sit inside think tags) rather than in content. Many OpenAI-compatible wrappers drop unknown fields, which is how teams end up unable to answer "what share of our output is thinking?" — and, worse, how they silently break multi-turn quality. Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Capture reasoning_content, do not discard it⌄ Log the length of reasoning_content next to the length of content for every assistant message, for a day of real traffic. The ratio is your reasoning-token share and the ceiling on any efficiency saving anyone can sell you. ←PreviousNext→ 2Pass reasoning_content back on the next turn⌄ Fireworks is explicit: if you build the assistant message yourself as a dict and omit reasoning_content, the model loses access to its own previous reasoning. Passing message objects through unchanged handles this for you. A harness that strips the field will look like a quality regression that has nothing to do with the model. ←PreviousNext→ 3Run the same 20 real tasks on K3 max and on Ember-1⌄ Not a benchmark — your tasks, your tools, your system prompt. Record pass rate, total tokens, wall-clock, and dollars. Twenty tasks is enough to see a 35% token difference; it is not enough to see a 1-point quality difference, so treat quality as a gate, not a ranking. ←PreviousNext→ 4Add K3 at low effort as a third arm⌄ This is the arm most teams skip, and it is the one that tells you whether you need an efficiency-trained model at all. If K3-low already passes your gate, you were never going to pay for max in the first place. ←PreviousNext→ 5Compare on cost per completed task, never on $/M tokens⌄ Divide total dollars by tasks that passed your gate. A model that fails 10% more often is more expensive than its token count suggests, because failures are re-run by a human or by the agent. ←PreviousNext→ One call against Ember-1 on the OpenAI-compatible endpoint CopyOpen in Claude↗ curl https://api.fireworks.ai/inference/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $FIREWORKS_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "accounts/fireworks/models/ember-1", "max_tokens": 8192, "messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": "You are a senior engineer. Reply with a unified diff and one paragraph of rationale."}, {"role": "user", "content": "The test suite in ./tests fails on macOS only. Log and module attached: ..."} ] }' | jq '{ reasoning_chars: (.choices[0].message.reasoning_content // "" | length), answer_chars: (.choices[0].message.content // "" | length), usage: .usage }' The A/B you actually want: same task, three arms, one table CopyOpen in Claude↗ # Arm 1 — the incumbent at full effort MODEL="accounts/fireworks/models/kimi-k3" EFFORT="max" ./run-evals.sh > k3-max.jsonl # Arm 2 — the cheap way people try first MODEL="accounts/fireworks/models/kimi-k3" EFFORT="low" ./run-evals.sh > k3-low.jsonl # Arm 3 — the efficiency post-train (no effort setting to choose) MODEL="accounts/fireworks/models/ember-1" ./run-evals.sh > ember.jsonl # Then the only comparison that matters: # dollars spent / tasks that passed the gate jq -s 'group_by(.arm)[] | {arm: .[0].arm, passed: (map(select(.passed)) | length), usd: (map(.usd) | add), cost_per_pass: ((map(.usd) | add) / (map(select(.passed)) | length))}' *.jsonl
documents.s: Measure it on your own traffic in an afternoon

documents.t: It is a Research Preview. Fireworks ships new research models with two weeks of serverless access and makes them permanent "based on community demand". Do not put an unbudgeted migration behind that. Build the A/B, keep K3 as the fallback path, and re-check availability before you cut over — this is exactly the case server-side fallbacks and model routing patterns exist for. The weights are not released, and that is legal. The most-upvoted confusion in the Hacker News thread was some version of "they trained on open weights and are not releasing theirs — can they do that?" They can. The Kimi K3 licence grants the right to "use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense, and/or sell copies of the Software; to run, deploy, fine-tune, or otherwise modify the Software and create derivative works from it" — with no copyleft obligation to publish what you build. What it does attach are two revenue-tiered conditions, and they are worth knowing whether or not you care about Ember-1: Model-as-a-Service above $20M. If you (and affiliates) run a MaaS business — giving third parties access to model inference or fine-tuning, e.g. via API, with meaningful control over inputs, parameters or training data — whose combined revenue exceeds $20 million over any consecutive 12 months, you must enter a separate agreement with Moonshot AI before commercial use of the Software or its derivative works. Attribution above 100M MAU or $20M/month. A product or service built on it that passes 100 million monthly active users or $20 million in monthly revenue must display "Kimi K3" prominently in its user interface. Internal use that does not expose the model or its capabilities to third parties is exempt from the MaaS clause. The practical reading: an open-weight licence can be MIT-shaped at the top and still gate the two situations a serious business ends up in. Read the licence before the benchmarks — the same advice applies to every "open" frontier release on DeepSeek, Qwen and the open-weight wave. Check your input modalities. OpenRouter lists Kimi K3 as text+image+video and Ember-1 as text+image. Fireworks' own model page advertises image input for Ember-1 and says nothing about video. If any part of your pipeline sends video frames to K3, verify that path explicitly before switching — a modality that silently disappears is a much worse failure than a quality dip, because it usually surfaces as a malformed request in production rather than a lower score in an eval. Check your sampling parameters too. OpenRouter's parameter list for Ember-1 omits seed and min_p, both of which it lists for K3. If your eval harness pins a seed for reproducibility, confirm the behaviour on the endpoint you will actually call rather than assuming the parent model's surface carried over. Porting prompts across models has the broader checklist.
documents.s: The fine print before you migrate

documents.t: Ember-1's other headline — "sets a new Pareto frontier on Bedside Bench across open and closed models including GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5" — comes from the Specialized Intelligence Index, which Fireworks launched on September 22, 2026, one day before Ember-1. Same company runs the index and ships the model. That is not automatically disqualifying, but it changes how you read it. What the SII does better than the usual leaderboard: Benchmarks come from practitioners, not academia — Doximity's BedsideBench (500 physician-validated clinical cases) for healthcare, Harvey's legal agent benchmarks for law, Sierra's τ-Banking and τ-Voice and Decagon's DuetBench for support, Rogo for finance, Novee's PWNBench and depthfirst's dfbench for security, and a software cluster including Datacurve's DeepSWE and Proximal's FrontierSWE V2. It reports cost per task and wall-clock duration next to score, from provider rate cards — the axes this whole page argues for. It labels every result by who can reproduce it: anyone, Fireworks-with-partner, or partner-only. That single label is the most useful piece of leaderboard metadata published this year; treat a partner-only row as a vendor claim with a nicer table around it. It refuses a composite score. No rollup across domains, no single "intelligence" number — which is the right call, and rare. What to hold in mind anyway: the benchmark suite, the arms chosen, the effort settings, and the model that wins are all selected by the same party. Compare its rows against an index run by someone with no model to sell before you quote them in a design doc. The general discipline is in The verification bottleneck.

Agentic coding on K3 at max effort, at volume: run the A/B this week. This is the exact workload Ember-1 was trained on, the reported savings are 15–52% of cost, and DeepSWE 1.1 suggests you may gain accuracy rather than trade it. Already running K3 at low or high because max was too expensive: strong candidate. Ember-1 beats K3 high on all five published rows and dominates low outright. Workloads shaped like τ²-bench (short turns, scripted policy, heavy tool output): expect modest savings — the effort dial was already doing nothing for you, and your reasoning-token share is small. Anything needing video input, a pinned seed, or a guaranteed 12-month endpoint: stay on K3 for now and re-evaluate when the preview converts. Not on Kimi K3 at all: the transferable lesson is the measurement, not the model. Find your reasoning-token share, sweep the effort dial on your own eval, and start reporting cost per completed task instead of $/M tokens. Every provider's version of this question is the same question. Check yourself 0/6

Copy as Markdown Intermediate On September 1, 2026 Anthropic shipped Claude Fable 5.1 (claude-fable-5-1) and its Glasswing-only twin Claude Mythos 5.1 (claude-mythos-5-1). If you skim the launch you'll file it as "Fable, but better" and move on. Don't. This is the first Claude point release where a plain model-ID swap can return 400s in production: forced tool_choice is gone, thinking blocks are now bound to the model and the conversation that produced them, and editing conversation history is enforced as an error for new accounts. It is also the first release where the cheapest line on the pricing table is the interesting one: cache reads dropped from $1 to $0.25 per MTok, which is why Anthropic can claim typical workloads cost about 25% less and heavily agentic ones up to 45% less at an unchanged $10 / $50 list price. This page is the migration field guide: what changed, what breaks, what you get, and a checklist you can run in an afternoon. What you'll learn Know the three breaking changes that turn a claude-fable-5 → claude-fable-5-1 swap into a 400, and the fix for each Use the five additive features: per-message effort, turn-scoped system messages, progress updates, cheaper cache reads, content provenance Recognize the seven behavior shifts that show up with no code change (fewer parallel tool calls, less narration, denser prose, whole-file rewrites) Read the launch benchmarks against Fable 5, Opus 5, and GPT-5.6 Sol without being sold to Decide Fable 5.1 vs Opus 5 vs Fable 5 for your workload, then run the migration checklist Last verified: 2026-09-14. Model IDs, pricing, breaking changes, beta headers, and behavior notes are from Anthropic's official "What's new in Claude Fable 5.1", the model overview, the migration guide, and the pricing page, all read on September 14, 2026. Benchmark numbers are Anthropic's own from the launch announcement. The three betas named here can change shape; re-check the headers before shipping. For the live model table see Current Models & Pricing. Confirm against the official source.
documents.s: Claude Fable 5.1: What Changed and How to Migrate

documents.t: Fable 5.1 is the successor to Fable 5, same Mythos-class tier above Opus, same 1M-token context, same 128K max output, same $10 in / $50 out, same tokenizer, same always-on adaptive thinking, same in-band stop_reason: "refusal" behavior, same 30-day retention requirement (no ZDR). Anthropic's own guidance is unchanged in spirit: start with Opus 5 for most work, reach for Fable 5.1 "for demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work, or when your evals on Claude Opus 5 at higher effort still fall short." What is new: three breaking changes, five additive features, a 75% cheaper cache read, and a set of behavioral shifts you should know about before your eval suite tells you.
These are the reasons you cannot just flip the ID. Each is a 400, not a silent degradation.

tool_choice: {"type": "any"} and {"type": "tool", "name": "..."} now return a 400 invalid_request_error: tool_choice: type "tool" and "any" are not supported for this model. The reason is instructive: thinking is always on, and a forced tool call would skip it, so the model would do its working-out inside the tool arguments and argument quality would drop. The check applies on the Messages API, the Message Batches API, and the token-counting endpoint. auto (the default) and none are unchanged. The fix is a two-line change: keep tool_choice at auto, set strict: true on the tool with additionalProperties: false in the schema, and say in the prompt when the tool applies. Anthropic's note is that Fable 5.1 "follows explicit tool instructions reliably." If what you actually wanted was schema-valid JSON rather than a tool call, move to structured outputs instead. Forced tool call → strict tool + explicit instruction CopyOpen in Claude↗ # Before (Fable 5) — now a 400 on Fable 5.1 "tool_choice": {"type": "tool", "name": "record_summary"} # After (Fable 5.1) "tools": [{ "name": "record_summary", "description": "Record the structured summary of the document.", "strict": true, "input_schema": { "type": "object", "properties": {"summary": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["summary"], "additionalProperties": false } }], "tool_choice": {"type": "auto"}, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize: The meeting moved to Thursday. Call the record_summary tool with your result."}]
documents.s: 1. Forced tool use returns an error

documents.t: Every thinking block now records which model produced it, and preservation is one-directional: Fable 5.1 can read thinking blocks from Opus 5, Fable 5, Mythos 5, and every earlier Claude; none of those can read Fable 5.1's. A conversation that moves onto Fable 5.1 keeps its reasoning. A conversation that moves off it (a router, a fallback to Opus 5, a cost-saving downgrade mid-session) loses the Fable 5.1 turns' reasoning. The API handles this by dropping blocks the target model can't read before the model sees them. Dropped blocks aren't billed and don't count toward input_tokens. Without the thinking-binding-controls-2026-08-01 beta header the drop is silent; with it, the drop is reported in a top-level input_transformations array. If you route between models, send the header and log that array. Silent reasoning loss is exactly the kind of thing that shows up as "the model got dumber after step 12" in a bug report.

This is the one to read twice. Modifying anything before a Fable 5.1 thinking block, meaning the system prompt, the tools array, or any earlier message, invalidates every later thinking block. Where the check is enforced, the next request is rejected with a 400 whose message says The block is bound to a different conversation. Enforcement rules as of today: Accounts created on or after August 31, 2026: enforced. Older accounts: the API records the mismatch but acts on it only when you set thinking.block_binding.prefix_mismatch_behavior yourself. Mythos 5.1 does not run this check at all. Claude Code, claude.ai, Managed Agents, and the Agent SDK keep the prefix intact for you. Only hand-built messages arrays are at risk. Anthropic's own list of what invalidates blocks, paraphrased, is a list of common agent-harness habits: Invalidates every later thinking block Keeps them valid Editing, reordering, or removing an earlier turn while keeping later ones Removing a leading run of thinking blocks, oldest first Injecting a per-request reminder or status line into an earlier turn, then removing it next request Server-side compaction or context editing trimming history Rebuilding the top-level system or tools between requests in one conversation Moving cache_control markers An image or document URL that serves different bytes later (the check is on bytes, so a rotating signed URL for the same file is fine) Changing effort between requests The fixes all reduce to one rule: treat the conversation as append-only. Per-turn reminders become turn-scoped system messages (below). Tool and instruction changes become mid-conversation system messages and tool changes. Trimming becomes server-side compaction. To continue instead of erroring, send the thinking-binding-controls-2026-08-01 header with prefix_mismatch_behavior: "drop_block"; the drop is then reported in input_transformations with reason: "prefix_binding_mismatch". Anthropic frames this partly as an anti-distillation measure: the launch post says new API accounts can no longer manually edit prior context while preserving the transcript, which closes a publicly documented distillation technique. The practical upside for you is that the same discipline also keeps the prompt cache warm.
documents.s: 3. Editing earlier turns invalidates thinking blocks

documents.t: You can now change effort mid-conversation without invalidating the prompt cache. Raise it for the hard step, lower it for the routine ones. Send the mid-conversation-output-config-2026-07-01 beta header and insert an effort-only system message; the new level takes effect from the next user turn. Supported on Fable 5.1, Mythos 5.1, and Opus 5 on the Claude API and Google Cloud. Drop effort for a summary turn without breaking the cache CopyOpen in Claude↗ { "model": "claude-fable-5-1", "max_tokens": 4096, "output_config": {"effort": "high"}, "messages": [ {"role": "user", "content": "Plan a migration from SQLite to PostgreSQL in three short steps."}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "1. Export the SQLite data. 2. Create the PostgreSQL schema. 3. Import the data and verify row counts."}, {"role": "system", "content": [], "output_config": {"effort": "low"}}, {"role": "user", "content": "Summarize the plan in one sentence."} ] } # header: anthropic-beta: mid-conversation-output-config-2026-07-01 This pairs with the effort guidance in Thinking & Effort and Effort tuning: the default is high, and "one level for the whole session" is now the lazy option, not the only one.

Set clear_at: "next_user_message" on a role: "system" message and it carries system-prompt authority for the current turn only, then stops rendering once a later user message exists. You keep sending it back verbatim, so nothing earlier changes, the cache keeps matching, later thinking blocks stay valid, and a cleared message costs no input tokens. Header: mid-conversation-system-clear-at-2026-08-21. { "role": "system", "clear_at": "next_user_message", "content": "Results have landed in your inbox. Check it before running more code." } This is the sanctioned replacement for the "inject a reminder, delete it next request" pattern that breaking change 3 now punishes.

Fable 5.1, like Fable 5, writes short progress notes between tool calls, each as its own thinking block right before the call. Under the default thinking.display: "omitted" those come back empty, so a long agentic turn looks silent to your users. New: display: "updates" (header thinking-display-updates-2026-08-18) returns the progress notes as text while reasoning stays hidden. Any thinking block with non-empty text is then a status line you can render. "summarized" returns them too, mixed with summarized reasoning. Raw chain of thought is still never returned.

Base input 5m cache write 1h cache write Cache read Output Fable 5 $10 $12.50 $20 $1.00 $50 Fable 5.1 $10 $12.50 $20 $0.25 $50 Cache reads are 0.025× base input on Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 versus 0.1× on every other Claude model. Writes and the 512-token minimum cacheable prompt are unchanged; batch is still 50% off ($5 / $25). For a long agent loop that re-reads a big cached prefix on every turn, this is where the launch post's "up to 45% cheaper" comes from. Cross-model note: OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra, launched three days later at the same $10 / $50 list price, charges $1.00 for cache reads, four times Fable 5.1's rate; see the Astra field guide.

All Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 text carries Anthropic's statistical text watermark on every platform. Files Claude produces (via code execution, for example) carry signed C2PA Content Credentials when retrieved through the Files API. Anthropic states the watermark adds no tokens or hidden characters, carries no information about you or your org, and needs no request changes. Context: Anthropic signed the EU AI Act Code of Practice on transparency of AI-generated content in July 2026, and a detection API is in private preview for regulators, fact-checkers, researchers, and enterprises that need verification.
Anthropic documents these openly, and each has a prompting fix in the official Prompting Claude Fable 5.1 guide. Watch for them in evals before your users do.
documents.s: Seven behavior shifts you'll see with no code change

documents.t: If you already wired Fable 5 correctly, all of this carries over untouched: Adaptive thinking is always on. thinking: {"type": "enabled"} with budget_tokens, and {"type": "disabled"}, both return 400. Omit thinking or send {"type": "adaptive"}. thinking.display defaults to "omitted"; raw chain of thought is never returned. Interleaved thinking is automatic, no beta header. Prefill returns 400. Non-default temperature, top_p, top_k return 400. Refusals arrive as HTTP 200 with stop_reason: "refusal" and a stop_details.category; you're not billed for a refusal that arrives before any output. Permitted fallback targets are Opus 5 and Opus 4.8, and fallback credit refunds the prompt-cache cost of the switch. Full pattern in Refusals & Safety. 30-day retention is mandatory; a request from an org or workspace without it returns 400. Both models are Covered Models. One divergence worth knowing: neither Fable 5.1 nor Mythos 5.1 is supported on Priority Tier. Fable 5 is. If you bought priority capacity, that's a reason to stay on Fable 5 for now.
documents.s: What stays exactly the same as Fable 5

documents.t: Anthropic's numbers, Anthropic's harnesses. Comparisons against GPT-5.6 Sol are the ones OpenAI would dispute first, and OpenAI's own GPT-6 Astra shipped three days later, so treat this as the state of play on September 1, not September 14. Benchmark Fable 5.1 Fable 5 Opus 5 GPT-5.6 Sol Terminal-Bench 4.0 55.8% (Mythos 5.1: 60.9%) 42.0% 52.3% 37.3% Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1 52.6% 24.7% 29.0% 22.4% GDPval-AA v2 (Elo) 1853 1723 1824 1711 OSWorld 2.0, partial / strict 77.9% / 41.7% 72.9% / 36.1% 75.4% / 39.6% — Humanity's Last Exam, no tools / with tools 60.9% / 65.0% 57.8% / 63.8% 56.6% / 63.6% — AutomationBench 31.4% 17.1% 26.9% 19.6% CursorBench 3.2.0 73.4% 70.5% 70.0% 67.2% Three readings that matter more than any single row: The Fable 5 → 5.1 jump is largest on long-horizon agentic work (Terminal-Bench-Science doubled, AutomationBench nearly doubled). That's consistent with Anthropic's own "use it when Opus 5 at higher effort still falls short" positioning: the win is on hours-long runs, not on chat. Opus 5 is closer than the headline suggests on several rows (Terminal-Bench 4.0: 52.3 vs 55.8; GDPval: 1824 vs 1853) at half the list price. Anthropic keeps telling you to start with Opus 5 for a reason. Customer quotes are about tokens, not just accuracy. Cognition, Rogo, Browserbase, and Block all cite fewer tokens for equal or better results. Combined with $0.25 cache reads, "Fable 5.1 is cheaper than Fable 5 for the same job" is the more defensible claim than "Fable 5.1 is smarter." The science examples in the launch post (protein binders with ~50% hit rate across 12 targets versus a typical 10–15%, a 2–3 km resolution Venus elevation map from 30-year-old Magellan radar data, 2.5× speedups on seven open-source genomics models) are Anthropic-reported research results, not benchmarks. Interesting signal for research workloads, not a procurement input.

Your situation Pick Why Most production work, cost-sensitive Opus 5 Anthropic's own default recommendation; half the price; reads Fable 5.1 thinking blocks if you ever route up Hours-long autonomous coding, research, or document/spreadsheet/slide builds where Opus 5 at high effort still misses Fable 5.1 Largest deltas are exactly here; cache reads make long loops cheaper than on Fable 5 You depend on Priority Tier Fable 5 (for now) Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 aren't on Priority Tier You force tool_choice and can't change the harness this sprint Fable 5 Fable 5.1 returns 400; migrate the harness first, then the model You route or fall back between models mid-conversation Any, but send the thinking-binding header Downgrading off Fable 5.1 silently drops its reasoning otherwise Zero data retention is contractual Opus 5 Fable 5.x and Mythos 5.x require 30-day retention Defensive cyber or life-science research needing fewer classifier interventions Mythos 5.1 via Glasswing, if approved Same model, different safeguard configuration; US organizations, verification programs required
