documents.t: Gemini 3.8 Flash is the same-tier successor to 3.7 Flash, model ID gemini-3.8-flash, 1M-token context, 64K max output, thinking_level of low / medium (default) / high, priced at $0.75 in / $3.75 out per 1M tokens through December 31, 2026 and $1.50 / $7.50 from January 1, 2027. It is live in the Gemini API, Google AI Studio, Antigravity, Android Studio, Stitch, Gemini Enterprise, the Gemini app (AI Pro and Ultra), AI Mode in Search, and Google Sheets. Alongside it, Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber replaces 3.5 Flash Cyber for vetted defenders through the new Fairwind Program. The cadence is the story again. 3.6 Flash on July 21, 3.7 on August 13, 3.8 on September 2: Google is iterating its workhorse tier every three weeks while the flagship stays quiet (The Register notes 3.5 Pro missed its June date). Read that as a fast developer feedback loop at the tier most teams actually pay for. Anthropic's answer this month is Claude Fable 5.1 at the top of the stack, not a cheaper Sonnet; OpenAI's is GPT-6 Astra.

Google's evaluation report, the rows a Claude shop should care about (higher is better): Benchmark 3.8 Flash 3.7 Flash Claude Opus 5 Claude Sonnet 5 GPT-5.6 Sol DeepSWE v1.1 (real bug fixes) 73.7% 65.3% 74.0% 53.8% 72.7% Terminal-bench 2.1 89.4% — 89.1% — 88.8% Terminal-bench 4.0 19.1% 11.2% 51.8% 12.4% 37.3% OSWorld-2.0 (computer use) 59.0% 50.6% 75.4% 42.6% 62.6% HLE-Verified 54.9% 53.6% 54.4% 31.0% 54.5% GDPval-AA v2 (Elo) 1545 1482 1824 1584 1710 Vals Finance Agent v2 61.4% 59.0% 58.6% 53.9% 53.8% Harvey Legal Agent 10.0% 8.8% 6.7% 5.0% 2.5% BioMysteryBench (hard) 56.5% 43.5% 49.4% 34.1% 44.7% Three reads. First, the DeepSWE +8.4 is the load-bearing number, exactly as the +16.3 was for 3.7 Flash: Google keeps pouring the workhorse's gains into repository-scale coding. Second, Terminal-bench 2.1 vs 4.0 is the same split we flag on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash the following week: a cheap model can saturate the older suite while the harder one, with longer adaptive shell sessions, still separates Opus 5 by more than 30 points. Third, on the domain-agent benchmarks (finance, legal, biology) 3.8 Flash now leads every column, including Opus 5. If your work is a finance or legal agent, that row is worth an eval on its own. If your work is an interactive coding session, the 4.0 row is the one to budget around.
documents.s: 1. Parity with Opus 5 on two headline benchmarks, a 33-point gap on the third

documents.t: Google's own description of the change: on complex tasks the model "exhibits greater diligence — executing extra reasoning steps, and calling tools iteratively." The launch post also says developers can "utilize lower effort levels to minimize token overhead," which is a polite way of saying the default now spends more. Emergent's read of the evaluation report puts it at roughly 30% more output tokens per task; Artificial Analysis measured $0.58 per Intelligence Index task, about 40% more than 3.7 Flash, at the same per-token sticker. For a Claude user this is the familiar effort trade-off wearing a different name: the model reaches for more tool calls and more thinking before it answers. The sticker did not move; the bill per task did. Budget on task cost, not token price. And re-run any latency SLO you had on 3.7 Flash: more iterations means more wall-clock, even at Flash speed. The physics is on Why agents burn tokens.
documents.s: 2. "Works harder" is a token-usage decision Google made for you

documents.t: Artificial Analysis puts 3.8 Flash at 59 on its Intelligence Index (at high reasoning), tied with GPT-5.6 Sol at extra-high and Grok 4.6 at medium, versus Claude Opus 5 at 63 and Claude Fable 5.1 at 66 (both at max). Its cost-per-task figure for Fable 5.1 is about $3.76, roughly 6× 3.8 Flash's $0.58. Against Opus 5 on list price, Vellum's arithmetic is about 6.7× cheaper on both input and output. Against Sonnet 5 the gap is far smaller, and Sonnet 5 still leads on GDPval-AA v2 (1584 vs 1545). So the honest comparison is: 3.8 Flash is a Sonnet-tier price with DeepSWE and domain-agent scores that now reach Opus territory, and Terminal-bench 4.0 / OSWorld scores that do not. Current Claude list prices are on Models and pricing.
documents.s: 3. Still cheap next to Claude, but the ratio depends on which Claude

documents.t: Spec Gemini 3.8 Flash Model ID gemini-3.8-flash Release September 2, 2026 Context window 1M input tokens Max output 64K tokens Thinking levels low, medium (default), high; minimal not supported Modalities in text, image, audio, video Modalities out text Knowledge cutoff March 2026 (some domains limited to January 2025) Removed parameters temperature, top_p, top_k, candidate_count (since the 3.6 line) Intro price (through Dec 31, 2026) $0.75 in / $3.75 out per 1M tokens Standard price (from Jan 1, 2027) $1.50 in / $7.50 out per 1M tokens Availability Gemini API, Google AI Studio, Antigravity, Android Studio, Stitch, Gemini Enterprise, Gemini app (AI Pro/Ultra), AI Mode, Google Sheets The knowledge cutoff line is new information versus the 3.7 page and worth a second look: March 2026 headline, but the model card says some domains are limited to January 2025. If you rely on the model knowing a 2026 library API, verify with a grounding tool or paste the docs. That is the same advice we give for any model in Freshness half-life.

The API surface is unchanged from 3.7 Flash. The list of things that break a Claude port is also unchanged, and it keeps catching people. Guided walkthrough1 of 7 1Swap the model ID⌄ Use gemini-3.8-flash. The 3.7 endpoint keeps working, but the benchmark deltas and the 'works harder' behavior only arrive with the new ID. ←PreviousNext→ 2Re-benchmark thinking_level, and this time watch tokens, not just accuracy⌄ Default is medium. Because 3.8 Flash reaches for more reasoning and more tool calls on hard tasks, the same level costs more per task than on 3.7. For extraction and classification, try low first and measure both accuracy and output tokens. ←PreviousNext→ 3Replace thinking_budget with thinking_level if you still carry it⌄ thinking_budget is deprecated in favor of the string enum. A call that still passes a numeric budget is running on legacy behavior. ←PreviousNext→ 4Delete temperature, top_p, top_k, candidate_count from Claude-shaped calls⌄ These sampling knobs have been gone since the 3.6 line. Depending on the SDK they fail or are silently dropped — either way your carefully tuned temperature is doing nothing. ←PreviousNext→ 5Stop prefilling the assistant turn⌄ Conversations ending on a non-empty model turn are rejected. Anthropic-style prefill steering has to become a user-turn instruction or a structured-output schema. ←PreviousNext→ 6Include call_id and name in every FunctionResponse⌄ Required on the generateContent API. A Claude tool_result carries an id; map it explicitly rather than relying on ordering. ←PreviousNext→ 7Budget on the 2027 price and the new task cost⌄ $1.50 / $7.50 from January 1, 2027, times roughly 1.3× the tokens per task 3.7 Flash used. That is the number to put in the Q1 forecast. ←PreviousNext→ Minimal 3.8 Flash call (Python SDK) CopyOpen in Claude↗ from google import genai client = genai.Client() # reads GOOGLE_API_KEY resp = client.models.generate_content( model="gemini-3.8-flash", contents="Review this diff. List the 3 riskiest hunks as file:line with a one-sentence reason each.", config={ "thinking_level": "low", # start low on 3.8 Flash; it already 'works harder' at medium # no temperature / top_p / top_k / candidate_count "tools": [{"function_declarations": [...]}], }, ) print(resp.text)

Alongside the general model, Google released Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber, replacing 3.5 Flash Cyber. Google's numbers: CWE-Bench patching at 47.2% pass@1 against "a leading frontier model" at 47.8%; a vulnerability-discovery success rate above 70% across 20 programming languages; 2.6× more correct patches to Chrome vulnerabilities than the best commercial models per Chrome Security; and, per Wiz, 7.5–9.7 points higher recall at 2.3–5.2× lower cost. You almost certainly cannot call it. Access runs through the Fairwind Program, limited to "trusted government authorities, as well as critical infrastructure operators and software maintainers," by application. This is the same shape as OpenAI gating GPT-6 Astra's exploit capability behind a vetted program (see the Astra field guide) and Anthropic's treatment of Mythos-class models. For a Claude user the practical takeaway is that the frontier's cyber capability now ships as a separate, gated SKU on all three stacks, and the general models are deliberately not it. Our security section covers what that means for the agents you can call.
documents.s: Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber and the Fairwind Program

documents.t: Pro tip Reach for 3.8 Flash: repository-scale coding that looks like DeepSWE, where 73.7 vs Opus 5's 74.0 at a sixth of the task cost is a real trade. Reach for 3.8 Flash: finance, legal, and life-science agent workflows — it now leads every column on Vals Finance Agent v2, Harvey Legal, and BioMysteryBench, including Opus 5. Reach for 3.8 Flash: long-video and chart understanding (LVBench 87.8, CharXiv 86.2) where Claude has no equivalent input path. Stay on Claude Opus 5: interactive terminal agents and computer use. Terminal-bench 4.0 (51.8 vs 19.1) and OSWorld-2.0 (75.4 vs 59.0) are the widest gaps on the table. Stay on Claude for knowledge work where GDPval-AA v2 matters: Opus 5 at 1824 and even Sonnet 5 at 1584 are ahead of 3.8 Flash's 1545. Stay on Claude for anything built on prefilled turns, temperature control, or Anthropic's tool-use loop — you will fight the Gemini API rather than use it. Cross-check both, at the effort you will ship: 3.8 Flash's table is at default or high thinking and costs ~30% more tokens per task than 3.7; Claude's is at max effort. Neither is your production setting. For the broader framing, Gemini for Claude users; for the coding-specific comparison, Claude vs GPT vs Gemini for coding; for the durable decision framework, Choosing a model.
documents.s: When to reach for 3.8 Flash, and when to stay on Claude

documents.t: Check yourself 0/5 Key takeaways DeepSWE +8.4 to 73.7 is the load-bearing number: a Sonnet-priced model now within 0.3 of Opus 5 on repository-scale bug fixing. Terminal-bench 4.0 (19.1 vs 51.8) and OSWorld-2.0 (59.0 vs 75.4) are where Opus 5 stays far ahead — interactive agents and computer use stay on Claude. 'Works harder' means ~30% more tokens per task at the same sticker. Budget per task, start thinking_level at low, and re-check latency SLOs. The 3.6-era API removals (temperature/top_p/top_k/candidate_count, no prefill, call_id + name on FunctionResponse) still break Claude ports; the migration list has not shrunk. 3.8 Flash Cyber is a separate, Fairwind-gated SKU — the third stack this month to ship frontier cyber capability as something you cannot simply call.

Copy as Markdown Intermediate On September 15, 2026 Google released two speech-to-speech models: Gemini 3.8 Live (gemini-3.8-live) and Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (gemini-3.8-live-extended-thinking). Both are generally available today in the Gemini API and Google AI Studio. Google's launch post is mostly benchmarks and demos. If you are building a voice agent, the details that matter are in the developer docs: tools now run asynchronously by default, one config field now returns an error, and one feature is always on and billed while the model listens. This page collects those details in one place. What you'll learn Pick between the two models using the real API differences, not the marketing names Migrate a gemini-3.1-flash-live-preview agent without hitting the thinkingLevel, affective-dialog, and blocking-tool traps Design around the session walls: 15 min audio-only, 2 min audio+video, ~10 min per WebSocket connection Estimate what a voice session really costs, and why cost grows faster than minutes Ship a browser client without leaking an API key Last verified: 2026-09-15. Launched today. Model IDs, GA status and feature list come from the Gemini API changelog (September 15, 2026). Prices come from the Gemini API pricing page. Token limits and the migration list come from the gemini-3.8-live model page. Thinking, tool-scheduling and VAD details come from the Live API capabilities and tools guides. Session limits come from the session-management guide. Billing gotchas come from the Live API best-practices guide. Benchmarks and consumer availability come from Google's launch post. One discrepancy: the launch post says the models detect and switch between 97 languages mid-conversation, while the Live API overview still says live translation covers "70+ languages." Before quoting either number, check which feature it refers to. Confirm against the official source.
documents.s: Gemini 3.8 Live and Live Extended Thinking: The Builder's Field Guide to Google's New Voice Models (Sep 2026)

documents.t: Use gemini-3.8-live as the default for low-latency voice agents. Use gemini-3.8-live-extended-thinking when the caller asks hard, multi-step questions and a short delay is acceptable. Both cost $3.00 / 1M audio input tokens (~$0.005/min) and $12.00 / 1M audio output tokens (~$0.018/min), plus $0.75 / $4.50 for text. Both have a 131,072-token input window and 65,536-token output limit, and both have a free tier in the Gemini API.

gemini-3.8-live gemini-3.8-live-extended-thinking Google's positioning "Default option for most low-latency voice agent experiences" "High-reasoning audio-to-audio model supporting background reasoning during live audio interactions" Thinking Interleaved reasoning; thinkingLevel is not accepted thinkingLevel = low / medium / high (no minimal); includeThoughts: true for summaries Function calling Async by default (NON_BLOCKING); BLOCKING still available; scheduling INTERRUPT / WHEN_IDLE / SILENT Async only, with no blocking mode and no scheduling control Consumer surfaces Search Live Gemini Live app; Docs, Gmail, Keep for subscribers Headline numbers (Google) 2nd on Artificial Analysis' Speech Agent Arena 82.6 Speech-to-Speech Quality Index (1st); 68.6% τ-Voice; 35.1% τ-Voice-banking; 97.7% Big Bench Audio Look at the 35.1% on τ-Voice-banking, the number Google chose to publish. Even the top-ranked voice model completes only about a third of realistic banking tasks by voice. Treat that as the ceiling for unattended voice agents that handle money, and put confirmation gates on anything consequential (the same rule as in Full-duplex voice AI). Every audio output is watermarked with SynthID. If your product records or re-publishes model speech, AI-audio detectors can identify it.
documents.s: What shipped, and what Google claims

documents.t: Extended Thinking does not go silent while it thinks. Google says it "reasons and speaks simultaneously." It gives early verbal cues ("let me check that") and narrates progress while reasoning continues in the background. That changes how your client decides when the model is finished. On this model turnComplete: true does not mean the session is idle. Background reasoning can still be running. Check interaction_status instead (IN_PROGRESS vs IDLE) before you end a call, hand off to a human, or start the next scripted step. This is the same "fast talker, slow thinker" split OpenAI introduced with GPT-Live. The difference is that Google puts both roles in one model, where GPT-Live delegates the reasoning to a separate frontier model.
documents.s: 1. The "thinking" model narrates while it reasons

documents.t: Google's migration notes for gemini-3.1-flash-live-preview → gemini-3.8-live include four changes that alter what your code does: Remove thinkingLevel. 3.1 Flash Live defaulted to minimal. 3.8 Live does not accept the field, so a config copied from 3.1 must drop it. Tool calls are now asynchronous by default. On 3.1 Flash Live, "the model will not start responding until you've sent the tool response." On 3.8 Live the model keeps talking while your function runs. That is good for latency, but a tool that must finish first (an identity check, a payment) now needs behavior: BLOCKING set explicitly. The Extended Thinking model has no blocking mode, so those flows need a gate in your own code. Proactive audio is always on. The model can decide not to respond when speech isn't addressed to it. You cannot turn this off, and the best-practices guide notes that you are billed input tokens while it listens. Affective dialog is gone. If your agent relied on enableAffectiveDialog to adapt to the caller's tone, remove it and test the new default behavior. Two changes help you. send_client_content now works for the whole session, so you can inject text context (CRM data, a transcript of a transfer) mid-call. Turn coverage now defaults to TURN_INCLUDES_AUDIO_ACTIVITY_AND_ALL_VIDEO.
documents.s: 2. Upgrading from 3.1 Flash Live changes behavior, not just the model string

documents.t: Audio accumulates at roughly 25 tokens per second (about 1,500 per minute). That is where the per-minute prices come from: 1,500 × $3/1M ≈ $0.0045 in, and 1,500 × $12/1M = $0.018 out. The trap is that each turn re-processes the entire accumulated context, not only the new audio. The best-practices guide says so directly. Two smaller costs stack on top: enabling transcription bills text output on top of audio output, and proactive audio bills input tokens while the model listens. A rough illustration (our arithmetic, not a Google figure): take a 10-minute call with 20 turns. The context grows from 0 to about 15,000 tokens, so the average turn re-reads about 7,500 tokens of input. That is about 150,000 input tokens (~$0.45), compared with ~$0.045 if only new audio were counted. Longer calls cost more per minute, not just more in total. Context window compression, which you need anyway to get past the 15-minute wall, also limits this cost growth.
documents.s: 3. A voice session's cost grows faster than its length

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Know the three limits⌄ Without compression, audio-only sessions stop at 15 minutes and audio+video sessions at 2 minutes. Separately, each WebSocket connection lasts around 10 minutes. The 2-minute video limit catches most screen-share demos. ←PreviousNext→ 2Enable context window compression⌄ Set ContextWindowCompressionConfig with a sliding window and a token trigger threshold. This removes the session-length limit and also stops per-turn input cost from growing without bound. Choose the trigger deliberately: compression discards the oldest turns, so pin anything the agent must remember (policy, caller identity) in the system instruction or re-send it with send_client_content. ←PreviousNext→ 3Enable session resumption⌄ Configure SessionResumptionConfig and store the latest handle from each SessionResumptionUpdate. A handle stays valid for 2 hours after the session ends, so a dropped connection can resume with its state instead of starting a new call. ←PreviousNext→ 4Handle GoAway before the connection drops⌄ The server sends GoAway with a timeLeft field before it disconnects. Use that time to finish the current sentence and reconnect with the resumption handle, so the caller never hears a gap. ←PreviousNext→ 5Discard buffered audio on interruption⌄ When the server flags an interruption (barge-in), clear your client-side playback buffer immediately. Otherwise the caller hears the model finish a sentence it has already abandoned. ←PreviousNext→ 6Send small, correctly formatted chunks⌄ Input is raw 16-bit PCM at 16 kHz little-endian; output is 16-bit PCM at 24 kHz. Resample microphone input (usually 44.1 or 48 kHz) down to 16 kHz and send 20–40 ms chunks. Large buffers add latency no model can remove. ←PreviousNext→
documents.s: The session walls, and how to design around them

documents.t: Live sessions work best when the client connects directly to Google, because proxying real-time audio through your backend adds latency. The safe way to do this is an ephemeral token. Your server mints it, and the client uses it once. Defaults: the token expires 30 minutes after creation, it must be used to start a new session within 1 minute, and it allows 1 use. You can lock it with liveConnectConstraints to a specific model, response modality and resumption settings, so a stolen token cannot be used for anything else. Ephemeral tokens work only with the Live API and only on v1beta. System-instruction skeleton for gemini-3.8-live (async tools, always-on proactive audio) CopyOpen in Claude↗ You are Ava, a voice assistant for Northwind Travel. You are SPEAKING, not writing. RESPOND IN ENGLISH. YOU MUST RESPOND UNMISTAKABLY IN ENGLISH. Style: - Short sentences, one idea each. Never read lists, markdown, or URLs aloud. - If speech is clearly not addressed to you (TV, side conversation), stay silent. Tools: - lookup_booking: invoke ONLY after the caller has given BOTH booking reference AND last name. - While a lookup is running, tell the caller you are checking. Do not guess the result. - change_booking: before invoking, read back the exact change and wait for a clear spoken "yes". Safety: - Repeat back every number, date, and name before acting on it. - If audio is unclear, say what you think you heard and ask. - Anything involving refunds or payment details: offer a human agent instead. The skeleton follows Google's own guidance for Live agents: state the output language explicitly in capitals, and give each tool a precise condition for when to call it. That second rule matters more with async tools, because the model talks while the tool runs and will fill the silence with a guess unless you tell it not to.
documents.s: Browser and mobile clients: never ship the API key

documents.t: vs Claude. Claude's voice features remain turn-based: voice mode in the Claude apps, push-to-talk in Claude Code. A common hybrid uses a Live model as the conversational front end and calls Claude as a tool for heavy reasoning or coding. Async function calling suits this pattern well, since the call can keep going while the tool runs. vs OpenAI. GPT-Live is a speech-native, full-duplex ChatGPT product. For developers, OpenAI's offering is gpt-realtime on the Realtime API (see Full-duplex voice AI for the landscape). Early community reports (Hacker News launch thread, unverified). Commenters praised latency, voice quality, accent handling and live translation. Others said Extended Thinking reasoned inconsistently and that the model "invents additional requirements" in agentic flows. These are anecdotes, not measurements, but they match the 35.1% banking score: test your own task end to end before trusting it. Check yourself 0/5 Key takeaways Two GA models, one price: gemini-3.8-live is the low-latency default; gemini-3.8-live-extended-thinking reasons in the background while it keeps speaking. Migrating from 3.1 Flash Live changes behavior: remove thinkingLevel, mark must-finish tools BLOCKING, expect always-on proactive audio (billed while listening), and drop affective dialog. Plan for the limits up front: 15 min audio-only, 2 min audio+video, ~10 min per connection. Compression, resumption handles and GoAway handling are required for production. Cost grows faster than call length because every turn re-reads the whole context. Compression is both the session-length fix and the cost fix. Even Google's best score on voice banking tasks is 35.1%. Keep spoken confirmation gates on anything that moves money or data.

Copy as Markdown Intermediate Google opened the Gemini 4 generation on September 30, 2026 with a single model, Argon, and a number nobody else has: a 1 million token output limit, up from the previous 64K. Not the context window — that stayed at 1M. The output ceiling went up 16x. It landed at the top of Hacker News and stayed there. It also landed in a strange place commercially: Google's own post says Argon "leads or ties for the highest score in more categories than GPT-6 Astra or Claude Opus 5.5," while the independent Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index published the same week puts Argon at 53 against Claude Opus 5.5's 58. Both statements are accurate. They measure different things, and the gap between them is the most useful thing on this page. This lesson is for a Claude user deciding whether Argon changes anything about their routing. It covers what the 1M output limit actually buys, how to read two contradictory benchmark stories, the per-task economics that the "40% cheaper" headlines invert, and why your access request will probably be declined. What you'll learn Separate the 1M output limit from the 1M context window — they are different ceilings and only one of them moved Reconcile Google's '13 of 18 categories' claim with the independent index that places Argon 5 points below Claude Opus 5.5 Price a task properly: why 62K output tokens against Astra's 27K means Argon's advantage is its rate card, not its efficiency Read the 15% hallucination rate for what it is — an abstention behaviour, not a knowledge win Understand what the Fairwind Program gates, what it requires of your org, and why Argon is effectively uncallable for most readers Last verified: 2026-10-01. Launch date, the "1M tokens, up from the previous 64K" output figure, introductory and standard pricing, the internal use-case numbers (quantum 40%, 300+ TiB, Fuchsia Zircon 800K lines, libgav1 32K lines / 2.7x) and the Wiz partnership come from Google's launch post. Fairwind eligibility and the access terms come from the Fairwind Program page; the cyber-specific benchmarks from DeepMind's Gemini cyber page. The Intelligence Index scores, 62K-vs-27K output tokens per task, AA-Omniscience hallucination rates and per-task costs are Artificial Analysis' figures as reported by The Decoder and Trending Topics. The 18-benchmark comparison table is Google's own evaluation report as reproduced by VentureBeat. Two discrepancies, both unresolved and both load-bearing. (1) Artificial Analysis' index is quoted as 53 by The Decoder and as 52.6 by Trending Topics, and Opus 5.5 as 58 and 57.6 respectively — the same numbers rounded or not. We use the unrounded pair where precision matters. (2) Google's framing and the independent index disagree on whether Argon leads the frontier; we present both rather than pick. No API model ID has been published — Google's docs do not yet list an Argon identifier, so anyone showing you one is guessing. Pricing is introductory and explicitly scheduled to double; re-check before you budget. Confirm against the official source.
documents.s: Gemini 4 Argon: The Field Guide for Claude Users (Sep 30, 2026)

documents.t: Gemini 4 Argon is Google's new frontier model, 1M-token input context and a 1M-token output limit (up from 64K), priced at an introductory $2 in / $10 out per 1M tokens with cached input at 95% off, rising to $4 / $20 after the introductory period. It is not generally available: it is rolling out to vetted cyber defenders through the Fairwind Program, then to paid API customers and Google AI Ultra subscribers. On Google's own 18-benchmark set it leads or ties in 13 categories; on the independent Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index it scores 53, tying GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 and sitting five points below Claude Opus 5.5.

Almost every summary of this launch says "1 million tokens" and leaves the reader to assume a context window. The context window did not change. Gemini has been at 1M input tokens since the 3.x line — Gemini 3.8 Flash has the same 1M window and a 64K output cap. What moved is the output ceiling, from 64K to 1M. These are separate limits and they fail in separate ways: Limit What it governs Gemini 3.8 Flash Gemini 4 Argon Input context How much you can send — files, transcripts, repo 1M 1M Max output How much the model can emit in one response, including reasoning tokens 64K 1M The practical consequence is about where a long task breaks. With a 64K output cap, a genuinely long-horizon job — refactor this subsystem, draft this filing, triage this codebase — has to be chunked by you, and every chunk boundary is a place where the model loses its own working state. Google's pitch is that Argon can hold a single uninterrupted chain of reasoning and execution across the whole job instead. Three things to keep in mind before you treat that as free: Reasoning tokens come out of the same budget. On Gemini, thinking tokens are output tokens. A 1M output allowance is not 1M tokens of deliverable; it is 1M tokens of thinking plus deliverable. Output is the expensive side. At introductory pricing, output costs 5x input ($10 vs $2). A response that actually used the full million output tokens would cost $10 on its own, and $20 once standard pricing lands. Nothing obliges the model to use it. A raised ceiling changes what is possible, not what is typical. Argon averages 62K output tokens per Intelligence Index task — around 6% of its ceiling.
documents.s: The number that is not what it looks like

documents.t: This is the part worth slowing down for, because the same pattern will repeat at every launch for the rest of the year. Story one — Google's evaluation report. Across 18 disclosed benchmarks, Argon leads or ties in 13 (12 outright leads, 1 tie): Benchmark Argon GPT-6 Astra Claude Opus 5.5 Harvey Legal Agent 19.6% 5.4% 3.8% GraphWalks 84.2% 71.8% 66.8% Vals Finance Agent v2 65.4% 53.5% 58.6% AutomationBench 51.3% 41.4% 42.5% LVBench (long video) 91.7% 87.5% 83.7% DeepSWE v1.1 77.9% 74.1% 74.2% CWE-bench v1 68% 68% (tie) 67% Gray Swan IPI (attack success — lower is better) 0.7% 8.5% 1.0% FrontierSWE v2 55.0% 65.5% — Terminal-Bench Science 0.1 57.6% 68.1% — Terminal-bench 4.0 57.4% — 66.4% PostTrainBench 45.3% — 49.3% Story two — Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index, an independent aggregate run the same week: Model Intelligence Index Claude Opus 5.5 58 (57.6) Claude Sonnet 5.5 56 Gemini 4 Argon (High) 53 (52.6) GPT-6 Astra (max) 53 Claude Fable 5.1 53 GPT-6.1 Sol (max) 52 Argon ranks #8 of 224 models on that index — excellent, and five points behind Anthropic's flagship. Neither source is lying. They diverge for reasons you can name: Benchmark selection is a choice. Google picked 18 benchmarks that include three domain-agent evals (legal, finance, automation) where Argon's margins are enormous. An aggregate index weights a different basket. Change the basket, change the winner. The losses cluster. Argon's four clear losses — FrontierSWE v2, Terminal-Bench Science, Terminal-bench 4.0, PostTrainBench — are all interactive, multi-turn, tool-driven agent work. Its wins cluster in single-shot domain reasoning and long-context retrieval. That is a shape, not noise, and it maps cleanly onto routing decisions. Absolute numbers matter more than ratios. Harvey Legal Agent is the launch's most quoted row: 19.6% against 5.4%, a 3.6x lead. It is also a score of 19.6% — Argon fails roughly four out of five tasks on that benchmark. "Best available" and "good enough to deploy unsupervised" are different claims. Vendor benchmarks are not production behaviour. Trending Topics cites Bloomberg reporting that, per Google employees, the model performs worse in practical coding use than its scores suggest. Treat that as a single unverified report — but it is the kind of gap the is the model nerfed? protocol exists to measure. Pro tip When a launch post says 'leads or ties in N of M categories,' the load-bearing question is who chose M. Go find an aggregate index you did not have to be invited into, and compare the two baskets before you re-route anything.

Several outlets led with Argon being around 40% cheaper than GPT-6 Astra. The rate card supports that. Per-task cost tells a more interesting story, because Argon is a heavy token spender. Artificial Analysis measured average output per Intelligence Index task: Gemini 4 Argon: ~62,000 output tokens GPT-6 Astra: ~27,000 output tokens Argon emits roughly 2.3x more tokens to reach the same index score. Its cheaper bill is a pricing artefact, not an efficiency win. The measured cost per task: Model Cost per Intelligence Index task Index score GPT-6.1 Sol (max) $0.74 52 Gemini 4 Argon (intro pricing) $1.99 53 GPT-6 Astra (max) $3.26 53 Gemini 4 Argon (standard pricing) $3.98 53 Claude Opus 5.5 (max) $5.98 58 Read that table twice. Three separate conclusions fall out of it: Argon's advantage over Astra is scheduled to expire. At $2/$10 it costs $1.99 per task against Astra's $3.26 — a 39% saving. When pricing doubles to $4/$20, it costs $3.98, which is more than Astra. The entire cost argument lives inside the introductory window, and Google has not said how long that window is. GPT-6.1 Sol is the actual value pick on this table. One index point below Argon at 37% of Argon's intro cost and 19% of Opus 5.5's. If your work is not in Argon's strong domains, the cheap tier is where the ratio lives — the same lesson as every other month. Opus 5.5 costs 3x Argon's intro price for 5 more points. Whether that is worth it is entirely workload-dependent, which is the honest answer and also the reason choosing a model is a framework rather than a leaderboard. Measure tokens-per-task yourself before trusting any per-task cost claim CopyOpen in Claude↗ For the same 20 representative tasks from my own workload, I want to compare two models on cost, not on benchmark score. For each model, log per task: - input tokens, output tokens (split reasoning vs final answer if the API reports it) - wall-clock latency - a 0-5 quality score I assign blind, without knowing which model produced it Then compute, per model: - mean output tokens per task - mean cost per task at CURRENT list price - mean cost per task at the post-introductory price, if one is announced - cost per quality point Flag any model whose cost advantage disappears at post-introductory pricing. Do not quote vendor benchmark scores back to me — I only want my own 20 tasks.
documents.s: The economics are the opposite of the headline

documents.t: On AA-Omniscience, the component of the index that measures whether a model asserts false things, Argon posts a 15% hallucination rate against 51% for GPT-6 Astra and 54% for GPT-6.1 Sol. That is not an incremental improvement; it is a different regime, and it is the most under-reported number in the launch. The mechanism matters. Artificial Analysis' characterisation is that Argon is far more likely to admit it does not know than to produce a confident wrong answer. So the win is in calibration and abstention, not in knowing more. Practical consequences: For retrieval, research and compliance work this is the headline feature, well ahead of any coding number. A model that says "not in the provided documents" is worth more than one that scores two points higher and invents a citation. It will read as less helpful in casual use. A model tuned to abstain refuses to guess, and users experience refusal-to-guess as hedging. Expect "it keeps saying it doesn't know" complaints from exactly the same capability that makes it trustworthy. It does not transfer to your prompts automatically. Abstention is a trained disposition interacting with your instructions. Tell a well-calibrated model "always give a definitive answer" and you have spent the advantage.

This is where most readers' interest ends in practice. Argon is not a public endpoint. It is gated behind the Fairwind Program, the same mechanism Google introduced for Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber — but this time it gates the flagship, not a cyber-specific SKU. Fairwind prioritises governments and national cyber authorities, critical-infrastructure operators (healthcare, telecoms, energy, finance) and core technology platforms, and vets applicants for "a proven track record of ethical operations and research." Accepted organisations must agree to: Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1User-level authentication with phishing-resistant MFA⌄ Not an org-level API key. Each human using Argon must be individually authenticated behind phishing-resistant MFA, plus applicable access controls. That rules out the usual pattern of one service credential shared by a team or embedded in a deployment. ←PreviousNext→ 2Restrict access to specific internal teams⌄ Only internal cybersecurity, incident response or penetration testing teams may be granted access. Not the platform team, not the product org, not a general-purpose internal assistant. ←PreviousNext→ 3Track employee access and use⌄ The org must maintain records of who accessed Argon and what for. Plan for an audit trail as a deliverable, not an afterthought. ←PreviousNext→ 4No sharing, redistribution or resale⌄ You cannot wrap Argon in a product and sell access, or pass it to a subsidiary or client. This is why no gateway or proxy legitimately offers it — see our note on gray-market AI proxies. ←PreviousNext→ 5Stay inside the dual-use boundary⌄ Authorized threat simulation, reverse engineering and malware analysis for defensive and academic research only. Malware creation and offensive use are prohibited. ←PreviousNext→ 6Then wait for the general rollout⌄ Google says paid API customers and Google AI Ultra subscribers come first after Fairwind, then developers, enterprises and consumers 'as soon as possible.' No date has been given. ←PreviousNext→ For trusted defenders, Fairwind can pair Argon with CodeMender, Google's code-security agent that automates vulnerability fixes, and grants a build of Argon without the cyber guardrails that the eventual public model will carry. The cyber case is strong on its own numbers: real-world vulnerability discovery at 85.8% (against 71.0% for Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber), the Wiz penetration-test benchmark at 70.9% (from 58.2%), CWE-bench v1 at 68%, and the best measured prompt-injection resistance of any frontier model — 0.7% attack success at k=15 on Gray Swan's indirect prompt-injection suite, against 1.0% for Claude Opus 5.5 and Fable, and 8.5% for GPT-6 Astra. That last number deserves its own sentence. An 8.5% success rate means roughly one in twelve indirect injection attempts lands; 0.7% means about one in 143. If you build agents that read untrusted web content, that is a twelve-fold difference in exposure — and it is measured at k=15, meaning fifteen attempts per target, not one. Worth reading alongside prompt injection and coding agents under attack. Watch out Because Fairwind forbids sharing, redistribution and resale, any gateway, proxy or 'unlocked Argon' reseller claiming to offer it is either misrepresenting a different model or violating the program terms. Treat an Argon endpoint you did not get from Google as untrustworthy by default.

The launch post's internal case studies are more informative than its benchmark table, because they describe long-horizon work with verifiable outcomes: Quantum algorithm optimisation — beat the published baseline for spacetime resource cost by 40%. Fleet memory profiling — found optimisations freeing over 300 TiB, with an estimated 500 TiB to 1 PiB total once applied. C/C++ to Rust migration — including 800K+ lines of the Fuchsia Zircon kernel. libgav1 video decoder — replaced 32K lines of hand-written SIMD, producing code 2.7x faster than the Rust port while emitting bit-identical output. The libgav1 result is the most instructive one on the list. "Bit-identical output" is the detail that makes it credible: there was a mechanical oracle for correctness, so the model's work could be verified rather than reviewed. That is the shape of task where a 1M output budget genuinely pays — large, mechanical, and checkable by a machine. It is also the shape of task most teams do not have, which is worth being honest about before extrapolating from these numbers to your own backlog.
documents.s: What Google says it did with it internally

documents.t: Short answer for most readers: no, because you cannot call it. When it opens up, here is the honest split based on where the benchmarks cluster. Work Where it should go Why Interactive coding agents, terminal work, computer use Claude (Opus 5.5 / Sonnet 5.5) Argon's four clear losses are all in this family — Terminal-bench 4.0 57.4 vs 66.4, FrontierSWE v2 55.0 vs Astra's 65.5 Legal and financial document reasoning Argon, with review Harvey 19.6% vs 3.8–5.4%, Vals Finance 65.4% — but 19.6% absolute means supervision, not automation Long-video and long-context retrieval Argon LVBench 91.7%, GraphWalks 84.2% Research where a wrong citation is worse than no answer Argon 15% hallucination rate against 51–54% Defensive security, autonomous patching Argon via Fairwind, if you qualify 85.8% vuln discovery, CWE-bench 68%, lowest injection susceptibility High-volume everyday work GPT-6.1 Sol or a Flash/Sonnet tier $0.74 per task for one index point less than Argon Anything you are budgeting past the intro window Re-price it first $2/$10 becomes $4/$20; cost per task goes $1.99 to $3.98 Check yourself 0/5 Key takeaways The 1M is the OUTPUT limit (up from 64K), not the context window, which stayed at 1M. Reasoning tokens spend that budget, and output costs 5x input. Google's '13 of 18 categories' and Artificial Analysis' 53-vs-58 are both true about different baskets. Argon's losses cluster in interactive multi-turn agent work; its wins cluster in single-shot domain reasoning and long-context retrieval. Argon burns ~62K output tokens per task against Astra's ~27K. The cheaper bill is the rate card, not efficiency — and at standard pricing cost per task goes $1.99 to $3.98, above Astra's $3.26. The 15% hallucination rate against 51–54% is the most under-reported number here, and it comes from abstention. It is the strongest argument for routing research and compliance work to Argon, and the first thing a 'always answer definitively' instruction destroys. You almost certainly cannot call it: Fairwind gates it to internal cyber/IR/pentest teams with per-user phishing-resistant MFA and no redistribution. No API model ID has been published. Any third-party 'Argon' endpoint is suspect.

Copy as Markdown Beginner You already think in Claude. Now a project lives inside Google Workspace, a teammate shares a custom Gem, or you need to drop a two-hour video and a stack of PDFs into one prompt — and the natural tool is Google's Gemini. Good news: almost everything you know transfers. This page maps your Claude mental model onto Gemini, flags the handful of things that genuinely work differently, and tells you when Gemini tends to be the better reach. What you'll learn Translate Claude concepts to their Gemini equivalents (Gems, the Gemini app, Workspace integration, AI Studio + the Gemini API) Know which of your Claude prompting habits carry over unchanged (most of them) Spot the few things you genuinely have to adjust Know when Gemini tends to shine — Google-ecosystem tasks, huge context, and native multimodal Last verified: 2026-09-22. Exact model names and version numbers, plan tiers, file/upload limits, context-window sizes, and prices change constantly at Google. This page teaches the durable mental model and concept-mapping; for any specific name, limit, or price, check Google's own current docs (linked in Sources) rather than trusting a number here. Confirm against the official source.

If you only read one section, read this. Here's how the things you know in Claude line up with Gemini: In Claude you call it… In Gemini's world it's… Same idea? Claude.ai (the chat app) The Gemini app at gemini.google.com Yes — the consumer/assistant surface Claude Projects (workspace + files + instructions) + reusable Custom Styles Gems (a saved, reusable assistant with instructions + knowledge files) Close — see the distinction below Account preferences / "how I want you to respond" Gem instructions + your account settings Yes — same idea Artifacts / file context Knowledge files attached to a Gem (incl. from Google Drive) Close Model selector (Opus / Sonnet / Haiku) Gemini's model picker (Pro for depth, Flash for speed) Yes — same idea, different names The Console / API + the prompt workbench Google AI Studio + the Gemini API Yes — dev surface to prototype and get a key Tool use / function calling (API) Function calling Yes — same loop, different JSON details The takeaway: there's almost no new concept to learn. It's mostly renaming and relocating things you already understand — plus two areas where Gemini genuinely leans further than Claude does: Google ecosystem integration and native multimodal + very large context.

A Gem is a customizable assistant you build once and reuse: you give it a name, write instructions, and optionally attach knowledge files for it to reference. If you've ever saved a Claude system prompt or built up a Claude Project around reference docs, a Gem is the same instinct in one object. Last verified: 2026-09-22. Google describes a Gem as a customizable assistant defined by instructions (commonly framed as persona, task, context, and format) plus optional uploaded knowledge files (PDFs, Word/Google Docs, Drive files); the exact creation flow, file limits, and supported types change — verify on Google's current help page. Confirm against the official source. The instruction structure Google recommends will feel native to a Claude user, because it's just good prompting: Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Persona⌄ Who the Gem is — its role and voice. The same 'You are a…' framing you use in a Claude system prompt. ←PreviousNext→ 2Task⌄ What it should do. State the goal in one clear sentence. ←PreviousNext→ 3Context⌄ Background it should assume — and the knowledge files it can reference, including live documents from Google Drive. ←PreviousNext→ 4Format⌄ The shape of the output: a table, a list, JSON, a structured doc. Exactly like asking Claude for a specific format. ←PreviousNext→ A subtle thing worth getting right: a Gem packages instructions + reference material into one reusable assistant, much like a Claude Project's instructions and files, but it's framed as a shareable specialist a team can run, not just your private workspace. When a Gem can reference Drive files, it tends to read the most recent version — a small but real difference from pasting a static snapshot into a chat. Last verified: 2026-09-22. Google has described sharable Gems and the ability to reference Drive files (using their latest version) for Workspace subscribers; availability, sharing scope, and file limits change — check Google's current announcements. Confirm against the official source.
documents.s: Gems are the "reusable Claude" you already wish for

documents.t: This is where Gemini diverges most from your Claude habits, and usually in a good way for the right task. The Gemini app is wired into Google Workspace — Gmail, Docs, Drive, Calendar, and more — so it can pull context and act across your Google data without you copy-pasting it in. Last verified: 2026-09-22. Google describes Gemini integrating with Workspace apps (Gmail, Docs, Drive, and others) to surface and summarize your content; which apps are connected, and admin/account controls over that access, change — verify on Google's current Workspace docs. Confirm against the official source. For a Claude user, the mental shift is this: instead of bringing the material to the model, you can often point the model at material that already lives in your Google account. That changes the workflow more than it changes the prompting. The prompt is still "summarize this, extract that, draft this" — but the "this" can be a live Drive doc or a thread in your inbox rather than a paste. Pro tip If your work already lives in Gmail/Docs/Drive, Gemini's integration removes the copy-paste step that Claude would require. Treat what Gemini can access as account- and admin-controlled — verify current permissions rather than assuming. Still scope it: point at the specific doc or thread you mean, not your entire Drive, for the same reason you don't dump everything into a Claude prompt.
documents.s: The Workspace integration is the real headline

documents.t: Two capabilities are where Gemini often genuinely earns the reach over a habitual Claude workflow: Native multimodal input. Gemini models are built to take text, images, audio, and video together in a single request — not just images bolted on. If your task involves watching a video, listening to audio, or reasoning over a mix of media at once, that's a Gemini sweet spot. Last verified: 2026-09-22. Google documents Gemini accepting multiple input modalities (text, images, and — for many models — audio and video) in one request; which modalities each specific model supports changes per model — verify on Google's current model and vision docs. Confirm against the official source. Very large context windows. Many Gemini models accept extremely large inputs — Google frames this as processing entire codebases, multiple long documents, or hours of media in one shot, reducing the need for chunking or retrieval workarounds. The exact token ceiling is volatile and model-specific, so don't hard-code it; the durable point is that "drop the whole thing in" is a more viable strategy here than you may be used to. Last verified: 2026-09-22. Google describes many Gemini models as having large context windows (it cites models capable of 1 million or more tokens) enabling long documents, large codebases, and long video/audio in a single request; the precise per-model limit changes — verify on Google's current long-context docs. Confirm against the official source. The habit to adjust: with Claude you may instinctively trim, chunk, or build retrieval before you even try. With a large-context Gemini model, it's often worth trying the whole document (or video) in one prompt first, then optimizing only if you hit a real limit.
documents.s: Native multimodal + huge context — lean into it

documents.t: When you move from chatting to building, Claude users have a clean analogy: Google AI Studio is the prototyping workbench — the fastest way to test prompts, try multimodal inputs, tune parameters, and get an API key. Think of it as the place you'd go to experiment before wiring anything up. Last verified: 2026-09-22. Google positions AI Studio as the developer environment to prototype with Gemini, test multimodal inputs, adjust parameters, and obtain an API key; its exact features and free-tier terms change — verify on Google's current AI Studio page. Confirm against the official source. The Gemini API is what you call from your code once you've prototyped — the equivalent of moving from a console playground to production calls. One framing difference to keep straight: the Gemini app (gemini.google.com) is the polished assistant with Workspace integration; AI Studio is the developer surface for testing model behavior and getting keys. They're different doors, and a Claude user occasionally conflates them the way one might conflate Claude.ai with the API console. Pick the door by the job: assistant work → the app; building → AI Studio then the API.
documents.s: AI Studio + the Gemini API — the developer surface

documents.t: If you've done tool use with Claude, Gemini's function calling will feel immediately familiar, because the loop is the same: Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Declare your functions⌄ You describe each function with a name, a description, and a JSON-schema of its parameters (types, which are required). Same idea as a Claude tool definition. ←PreviousNext→ 2Model requests a call⌄ Given the prompt and the declared functions, the model returns a structured function call — the name plus arguments — instead of (or alongside) text. It does not execute anything itself. ←PreviousNext→ 3You execute it⌄ Your application extracts the name and arguments and runs the actual function. The model proposes; your code disposes. ←PreviousNext→ 4Return the result⌄ You feed the function's output back to the model. ←PreviousNext→ 5Model answers⌄ It uses the result to produce the final response — and may request more calls before finishing. ←PreviousNext→ What's identical: the describe → model-requests → you-execute → return-result → answer loop, and the principle that the model never runs your code. Gemini also supports parallel calls (several independent functions in one turn) and compositional calls (chaining functions where later calls depend on earlier results) — concepts you already know from Claude. Last verified: 2026-09-22. Google documents declaring functions via name/description/JSON-schema parameters and a define → call-model → execute-locally → return-result loop, plus parallel and compositional (sequential) calling; exact field names, response shapes, and options change — verify on Google's current function-calling guide. Confirm against the official source. What differs and will trip you up if you copy-paste: the exact JSON field names, how function calls and results are represented in the message list, parameter/schema conventions, and the specific endpoint shape. As a rule across providers, prompting and architecture transfer; wire-format details do not — always re-check the per-provider schema. (The same caution applies if you're coming from ChatGPT for Claude Users: the loop is universal, the JSON is not.)
documents.s: Function calling — same shape, different JSON details

documents.t: Your hard-won Claude habits are not wasted. These carry over essentially unchanged: Prompt structure — clear role, explicit task, examples, requested output format → Prompting Basics Giving context deliberately — scope it; point at the right material (now possibly a live Drive doc) Asking for a specific output format — tables, JSON, steps; works the same Iterating in place — refine via follow-ups The tool-use loop — describe tools, let the model call them, return results → Tool Use Choosing a model by task difficulty — Flash for fast/cheap, Pro for deep, same judgment call as Opus/Sonnet/Haiku Provider-neutral system prompt — drop into a Gem's instructions or a Gemini API system prompt CopyOpen in Claude↗ You are a {role}. Goal: {one clear sentence}. Rules: - Use ONLY the context I provide or the files attached; if the answer isn't there, say "I don't know". - Be concise. No preamble. - Output format: {exact format — e.g. a markdown table with columns X, Y, Z}. When you need information you don't have, ask one focused question instead of guessing.

A short, honest list of things that are actually different: Integration changes the workflow, not the prompt. With Gemini you can point at live Google data instead of pasting it. Verify what it's allowed to access — that's account- and admin-controlled. Default to "whole thing in" for big inputs. Large context and native multimodal mean you can often skip the chunking/retrieval reflex and try the full document or video first. Two doors for builders. The Gemini app (assistant) and AI Studio (developer playground + keys) are separate; don't go looking for an API key inside the chat app. Wire-format for tools. The function-calling concept is identical; the JSON details are not — never reuse Claude's exact tool JSON verbatim. Volatile specifics. Model names, version numbers, tiers, context limits, and prices move fast. Build the habit of confirming at the source, exactly as you should for Claude too.

Both are excellent general assistants and the gap on any given task is often small and shifting — so treat this as tendencies, not laws, and let your own eval on your own data decide: Google-ecosystem tasks. If the work already lives in Gmail, Docs, Drive, or Calendar, Gemini's native Workspace integration removes friction Claude can't match without manual paste. Huge single-shot context. Enormous documents, whole codebases, or long media you want reasoned over at once — lean toward a large-context Gemini model and skip the retrieval scaffolding. Native multimodal. Video and audio understanding, or mixed-media prompts, are a structural Gemini strength. A team that already runs on Google. If your collaborators share Gems and live in Workspace, meeting them there beats friction. The honest answer most of the time: whichever you (or your team) are already set up in. The skill is portable; the setup cost is the real switching cost. For the provider-neutral way to choose, see Choosing a Model and Which Claude Should I Use?. Check yourself 0/3 Key takeaways There's almost no new concept — the Gemini app ≈ Claude.ai, a Gem ≈ a reusable system prompt + Project files, the model picker (Pro/Flash) ≈ Opus/Sonnet/Haiku, function calling ≈ tool use. The real differences are leverage, not relearning: deep Google Workspace integration, very large context, and native multimodal (image/audio/video). Adjust your reflexes: point at live Google data instead of pasting; try 'whole thing in' before chunking; remember the app and AI Studio are separate doors. Your prompting, context discipline, output-format, and tool-loop habits transfer unchanged — only the tool-call JSON details differ. Names, versions, tiers, context limits, and prices go stale fast — verify specifics at Google's docs, just as you should for Claude.

Copy as Markdown Beginner Most of AILmanac is about AI that writes and reasons — text models like Claude. But a whole other branch of AI makes media: pictures, video, voices and music from a prompt. This page is a provider-neutral map of that landscape: the archetypes, the notable tools (each verified to exist), how they differ from text LLMs, the skills that carry over, and the rights-and-ethics rules you can't skip. What you'll learn Know the main archetypes of generative media — image, video, voice/music, speech-to-text — and a real tool in each Understand how media models differ from a text chat model like Claude Learn the durable skills: prompting for media, iteration, and reference inputs Respect the non-negotiables: usage rights, provenance/watermarking, and deepfake/consent ethics Last verified: 2026-06-28. Specific model versions, capabilities, resolutions, prices and which tool is "best" change almost monthly in generative media — even faster than in text. Treat any version number or price here as perishable. This page teaches the durable parts (archetypes + skills + ethics); for today's specifics check each tool's own page (linked in Sources) or an independent tracker like Artificial Analysis. Note also that products get renamed, merged, or discontinued — for example, OpenAI's standalone Sora app was wound down even while its video model lived on through the API. Confirm against the official source.
documents.s: Generative Media: Image, Audio & Video AI

documents.t: If you've only used a chat model, four differences matter: Different output, different "correct." A text model returns one mostly-deterministic best answer. A media model returns an artifact (an image, a clip, a voice take) where there is no single right answer — only ones you like more or less. You generate several and pick. You usually can't edit the output by editing the prompt alone. Tweaking one word can change the whole image. Real control comes from reference inputs (a starting image, a style image, a reference voice) plus tool-specific controls, not just words. Seeds and variation are part of the workflow. Many tools let you re-roll, vary, or lock a "seed" for reproducibility. Iteration is the norm, not a failure. The cost unit is different. Text bills by tokens; media bills by image, second of video, or character/minute of audio — and video especially can get expensive fast. Pro tip Mental model: a text model is a writer who gives you the answer; a media model is a slot machine with a steering wheel — you pull, then steer with references and re-rolls until it's right. Generate a batch and curate. Your taste — knowing which of 4 outputs is best — is half the skill.
documents.s: How media models differ from a text LLM

documents.t: Think in archetypes — the lineups shuffle constantly, the categories are stable. Every tool named below was verified to exist with a real URL (in Sources); specific versions are intentionally left vague because they churn.
documents.s: The map: archetypes and notable tools

documents.t: Turn a text prompt — and optionally reference images — into a still picture. Midjourney — closed, hosted; known for a strong default aesthetic and style/reference controls. OpenAI image generation (the DALL·E / GPT Image line) — closed, hosted; tightly integrated into ChatGPT and the API. Google's Gemini image generation ("Nano Banana") and Imagen — closed, hosted; wired into Gemini and Google Cloud. Adobe Firefly — closed, hosted; built for creative workflows and trained with commercial use in mind (see rights, below). Stable Diffusion (Stability AI) and FLUX (Black Forest Labs) — open-weight model families you can download and run yourself, the backbone of the local/open image ecosystem.

Generate short clips — increasingly with synchronized audio — from a prompt or a starting image. OpenAI Sora — a frontier video model (note: the standalone consumer app was discontinued; the model continued via API — a textbook example of why versions/availability go stale). Google Veo — frontier video, with native audio in recent versions. Runway — a creative suite built around its Gen-series video models. Kling (by Kuaishou) and Pika — fast-moving video tools popular for social/short-form content.

ElevenLabs — closed, hosted; lifelike text-to-speech and voice tools (voice cloning has real consent implications — see ethics). Suno and Udio — generate full songs (vocals + instrumentation) from a text prompt. OpenAI Whisper — the other direction: speech-to-text (transcription). It's open-weight (MIT-licensed), so you can run it yourself or call a hosted API. Speech-to-text is the quiet workhorse behind captions, voice notes, and meeting transcripts. Pro tip The single biggest fork (same as for text models): CLOSED hosted tools (often the best quality, least setup) vs OPEN-WEIGHT models like Stable Diffusion, FLUX and Whisper that you can self-host for privacy, control, and lower cost at scale. Don't pick by leaderboard. For your actual look/sound, generate a few real examples in 2-3 tools and judge with your own eyes and ears.

The workflow is more like a photo shoot than a Google search. These steps are tool-agnostic: Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Describe subject, then context⌄ Lead with the main subject, then add setting, action, and mood. 'A red fox' is weak; 'a red fox curled asleep in fresh snow, soft morning light' gives the model something to work with. ←PreviousNext→ 2Specify the medium and style⌄ Say what KIND of image/video/voice it is: photo vs illustration vs 3D render; camera/lens or art style; for audio, the genre, tempo, and emotional tone. Style is where most of the look lives. ←PreviousNext→ 3Add reference inputs when you can⌄ A starting image, a style-reference image, or a reference voice clip controls the result far more reliably than adjectives. This is the durable skill text-only prompters miss. ←PreviousNext→ 4Generate a batch, then curate⌄ Produce several variations. Pick the closest one — your taste is part of the tool. Don't expect the first roll to be the keeper. ←PreviousNext→ 5Iterate narrowly⌄ Change ONE thing at a time (lighting, or pose, or palette) and re-roll, or use the tool's edit/vary/inpaint features. Rewriting the whole prompt every time loses what was working. ←PreviousNext→ 6Check rights and provenance before you ship⌄ Confirm the license covers your use (commercial?), and keep/attach provenance (Content Credentials) so the asset is traceable. Disclose that it's AI-generated where that matters. ←PreviousNext→ Example image-generation prompt (medium → subject → style → details) CopyOpen in Claude↗ A cinematic wide-angle photograph of a lighthouse on a rocky cliff at golden hour, waves crashing below, dramatic storm clouds parting. Style: moody, high dynamic range, shot on a 24mm lens, shallow depth of field. Mood: hopeful, epic. Aspect ratio 16:9. Tip: if the result is close, change ONE element next pass (e.g. "blue hour" instead of "golden hour") and re-roll — or add a reference image to lock the look.
documents.s: How to get a good result from a media model

documents.t: Media AI raises issues text chat usually doesn't. Treat these as part of the job, not an afterthought. Usage & commercial rights. Every tool has its own license, and they differ a lot. Some restrict commercial use, some grant it only on paid tiers, and outputs can resemble copyrighted or trademarked work. Adobe Firefly, for instance, leans on training data chosen with commercial safety in mind — but you should still read the actual license for the tool and tier you're on rather than assume. Provenance & watermarking. A growing standard, C2PA / Content Credentials, attaches tamper-evident "nutrition label" metadata recording how an asset was made and edited. Many major image and video tools now embed it. Keep that provenance intact, and prefer tools that support it — it's becoming the norm for trustworthy media. Deepfakes, voices & consent. Realistic face- and voice-generation can impersonate real people. Don't clone a voice or likeness without explicit consent, never use generated media to deceive, and follow the law in your jurisdiction. Voice-cloning consent and disclosure of AI-generated content aren't just etiquette — increasingly they're legal requirements. Watch out Generated media can carry usage-rights limits and deepfake/consent risks — check each tool's license and disclose AI-generated content.

Good news: a lot of what you already know carries over. Clear, specific prompting — being concrete about what you want beats vague wishes, in every modality. Iteration over one-shot — the same "draft, critique, refine" loop you'd use with Claude applies, just with re-rolls and reference images instead of follow-up messages. See Prompting basics. Choosing the right tool for the task — the framework from Choosing a model (constraints first, then a tiny real-world test) works just as well for media. Understanding what the model actually is — knowing these are pattern-learners, not magic, keeps your expectations and your ethics straight. See Foundations.
documents.s: What transfers from your text-AI skills

documents.t: Check yourself 0/4

Key takeaways Generative media is a separate branch of AI from text chat: it makes images, video, voice and music, and you steer it with references and re-rolls, not just words. Think in archetypes — image, video, voice/music, speech-to-text — and remember the closed-vs-open-weight fork (e.g. Midjourney vs Stable Diffusion/FLUX; hosted TTS vs open Whisper). The durable skills transfer from text AI: specific prompting, iteration, and choosing the right tool for the task. Rights and ethics are part of the work: check the license for your tool and tier, keep provenance (C2PA/Content Credentials), get consent for voices/likenesses, and disclose AI-generated media. Specifics rot fast — verify versions, prices and capabilities against each tool's own page before relying on them.
