Copy as Markdown Advanced Last verified: 2026-09-29. Every accuracy, latency and training-time figure on this page is self-reported by the project that published it, on benchmarks that project chose. Nothing here has been independently replicated. Both repositories are days old and moving fast — star counts, model names, checkpoint ids and CLI flags are the most perishable facts here; read the current README before you copy a command. Neither project is affiliated with or endorsed by TypeSafe, the makers of Jev. Sources: README of firelex/jeff (created 2026-09-28, 895 stars at time of writing) and PostHog/jeeves (created 2026-09-29, 107 stars); denis-pplx/autojev README; Hacker News items 49883844 (Jeff, 536 points / 204 comments) and 49891290 (Jeeves, 105 points / 44 comments). What you'll learn Explain the actual training recipe behind an open decision model — cross-entropy over option letters, one epoch, and a temperature fitted afterwards — and why calibration is a separate step from accuracy Read the published benchmark tables honestly: the three rows where a 0.8B model beats the commercial API, and the two rows where it loses by 20–26 points Decide between four options — hosted API, zero-shot open weights, your own fine-tune, or a plain embeddings classifier — using the one baseline number that kills most of these projects Train and serve a Jev-compatible model yourself in an afternoon on a single GPU, including the checkpoint-selection rule that keeps the result honest Know when adding reasoning back to a decision model is worth 11x the latency, and how a confidence threshold buys most of the accuracy for a third of the wait System One decision models explained the category: you send program state plus typed questions, and you get calibrated probabilities back instead of text. That page ended where the open recreations were in mid-September — Kev, Nimble, a logprob shim. In the last week of September the story changed shape. The question stopped being "can we clone the API" and became "should you train your own?" On September 28 a project called Jeff shipped 0.8B and 2B fine-tunes that land within four points of Jev's overall benchmark score and run in ~22–28 ms on a laptop-class GPU, trained in about two hours on one workstation card. It was the top AI story on Hacker News that day. Twelve hours later PostHog published Jeeves, which does the opposite thing — bolts reasoning onto a decision model — and reports beating Jev on Jev's own hard tier. Both are MIT code with Apache-2.0 weights. Both are honest enough in their READMEs to publish the rows where they lose. This page is about what those rows mean for you.
documents.s: Train Your Own Decision Model: Jeff, Jeeves and the DIY System One Stack (Sep 2026)

documents.t: Date (2026) What shipped Why it matters Sep 15 Jev (TypeSafe AI), API-only Defined the category and the /v1/systemone request shape Sep 21 Kev, Nimble, openjev-sglang Proved the interface was reproducible on open weights — AutoJev (denis-pplx) The recipe: full-weight SFT of Qwen3.8-27B, 73,000 examples, one H200, 84.60% vs a 69.83% base Sep 28 Jeff (firelex) Shrank it — 0.8B/2B students, ~2 h on one workstation GPU, MLX serving, game evals Sep 29 Jeeves (PostHog) Reversed the premise — a thinking decision model, LoRA + RL on Qwen3.5-9B The through-line: in two weeks a category went from a closed API with undisclosed training to a recipe you can run overnight. AutoJev is the hinge — it published the loss function, and everything after it is a variation on that one idea.
Strip the marketing and a decision model is a startlingly small change to a normal LLM.

The model is not taught to "make decisions". It is taught to put probability mass on a single letter token — A, B, C — at one specific position. You lay the options out as a lettered panel, you train with plain cross-entropy on the correct letter, and at inference you read the logits for the letter tokens and renormalise them over just the options you offered. That one implementation detail explains the headline limitation. Jeff caps you at 26 options, and the README is blunt that positions past that are "effectively never selected" — because the alphabet ran out, not because of anything architectural. (Jev itself advertises up to 255 options, which tells you it encodes options differently.) Jeeves takes the other road: a pointer head that scores a projected hidden state against each option's embedding with a scaled dot product. No letters, no alphabet ceiling. It marks the structure with rare tokens borrowed from Qwen's tokenizer that real text essentially never uses — <|fim_prefix|> for state, <|fim_middle|> for questions, <|box_start|>/<|box_end|> around options, <|fim_suffix|> at the decision point. Reusing dead tokens as delimiters is the cheap trick that avoids growing the vocabulary or colliding with content.
documents.s: 1. The loss is cross-entropy over option letters

documents.t: This is the part people skip, and it is the part that makes the output trustworthy. Accuracy and calibration are different properties. A model can rank the right answer first almost every time and still say "91%" when it is right 75% of the time — the independent BANKING77 pilot on Jev found exactly that shape of over-confidence. So all three projects fit a single scalar temperature on a held-out development set after training, and ship it alongside the checkpoint. Divide the logits by it, softmax, done. AutoJev publishes what that buys, and it is the cleanest before/after in the whole stack: Metric Base Qwen3.8-27B AutoJev-27B Accuracy 69.83% 84.60% ECE (expected calibration error — lower is better) 0.06483 0.04282 Brier score (lower is better) 0.40834 0.22027 Note that all three moved, but by different amounts. Accuracy climbed ~15 points while ECE fell ~34% — training made the model both righter and more honest, and the honesty is measurable separately. If you train your own and only report accuracy, you have not finished.
documents.s: 2. The calibration is a separate, one-parameter stage

documents.t: One epoch. Batch 256. Full-weight (Jeff, AutoJev) or LoRA r=16 (Jeeves). Checkpoint selection on a development set, never on the benchmark panel — Jeff states this explicitly, and it is the single line that separates a credible small-model result from a leaked one. Jeff also keeps at least half of each training family in the same panel layout it will see at inference, which matters more than it should; see the wording section below. Train a 0.8B decision model (Jeff's own recipe) CopyOpen in Claude↗ # 1. Build the training mix from public datasets uv run autojev-mix ... # 2. One epoch, full-weight, lr 5e-6 scripts/train.sh RUN data/mix/public.jsonl data/mix 5e-6 40 Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B <revision> --epochs 1 # 3. Evaluate the SELECTED checkpoint against a held-out panel uv run autojev-evaluate --data data/panel.jsonl --local \ --checkpoint checkpoints/RUN/selected --output runs/eval/RUN.json Reported cost of step 2: ~2 hours for 0.8B, ~3.5 hours for 2B, on one RTX PRO 6000. That is the number that made this a front-page story.

Here is Jeff's published panel — 4,599 questions across five public datasets plus JevBench's hard tier — with the commercial API in the last column. Read it by row, not by the overall line. Benchmark Jeff-0.8B Jeff-2B Jeff-Gemma4-E2B Jev (API) Overall 79.1% 83.1% 81.6% 83.0% Financial PhraseBank 96.4% 96.3% 96.1% 77.0% RAGTruth 86.1% 88.9% 87.4% 77.3% WinoGrande 68.6% 79.0% 77.4% 90.7% JudgeBench 62.6% 64.6% 60.6% 78.6% BBH 64.0% 68.0% 66.4% 94.3% JevBench Hard 47.6% 53.3% 48.6% 73.3% The overall scores are nearly tied. The rows are not close at all: Where the tiny model wins, it wins big. Financial PhraseBank: 96.4% against 77.0% — a 0.8B model beating a commercial API by 19 points. RAGTruth (does this answer stay faithful to the retrieved passage?): 86.1% against 77.3%. Both are narrow, high-volume, pattern-shaped jobs — sentiment on a fixed vocabulary, groundedness on a supplied passage. If your agent's hot path is that shape, a local 0.8B is not a compromise, it is the better tool. Where it loses, it is not close. BBH is 30 points down. JevBench Hard is 26 points down. Those are the rows that need multi-step reasoning, and the README says so plainly: small decision models give you "fast, calibrated choices between the options you describe" and no reasoning chain. The overall number is the average of those two facts and therefore describes nothing. This is the most transferable lesson on this page, and it is not specific to decision models: any single headline score is a weighted average over a benchmark mix that is not your mix.

Jeff also evaluated zero-shot game play — 20 episodes each of Doom, Frogger and Pac-Man — and the result is uncomfortable enough that publishing it earns trust: Model Doom (kills) Frogger (crossings) Pac-Man (pellets / 98) Random −0.05 0 11.2 Hand-coded rule bot 6.55 10.25 94.1 Jeff-0.8B 6.55 10.3 57.0 Jeff-2B −0.9 6.0 41.2 The 2B is worse at all three games than the 0.8B it outscores on every benchmark row. The README's read is that the bigger model came out more risk-averse. Whatever the cause, the pairing of those two tables is the point: benchmark rank did not predict behaviour in a loop. And the hand-coded rule bot still wins Pac-Man by 37 points — the reminder that "can a model do it" and "should a model do it" are different questions.
documents.s: The games table is the honest one

documents.t: Median latency per decision, ~200-token questions: Model RTX PRO 6000 Apple M4 Max (MLX) CPU (32 threads) Jeff-0.8B 22 ms 28 ms 463 ms Jeff-2B 24 ms 60 ms 708 ms Jeff-Gemma4-E2B 29 ms — 1.0 s Two things to take from this: "Tiny model" does not mean "runs anywhere fast." The same 0.8B checkpoint is 22 ms on a GPU and 463 ms on 32 CPU threads — a 21x gap. A decision model is only a decision model at GPU latency; on CPU it is a slow API call you happen to host. If your plan was "sprinkle these calls everywhere in the request path", the CPU column is the plan's budget. 2.5x the parameters cost 2 ms on the big GPU. 22 → 24 ms. At this size a single forward pass over ~200 tokens is dominated by overhead and memory bandwidth, not by arithmetic, so on a fast card the 2B is nearly free relative to the 0.8B — while on the M4 Max the same step costs you 2.1x (28 → 60 ms). Pick your model per deployment target, not from the parameter count. Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Serve one locally before you train anything⌄ Install with uv, pull a checkpoint from Hugging Face, start the server. You want the zero-shot number on YOUR data before you decide training is necessary — the most common outcome reported by practitioners is that zero-shot is not good enough, and that is much cheaper to discover in twenty minutes than after a training run. ←PreviousNext→ 2Build a labelled dev set of a few hundred real examples⌄ Real traffic, real label distribution, including the ambiguous ones you would normally throw out. This set does double duty: it selects your checkpoint and it fits your temperature. It must never overlap the panel you report numbers on. ←PreviousNext→ 3Measure the boring baseline first⌄ Embeddings plus a logistic-regression head, on the same dev set. On BANKING77 this approach was reported in the Jeff discussion at 93.0% with a model roughly 15x smaller. If it wins on your data, stop here — you have saved yourself a fine-tune and a GPU. ←PreviousNext→ 4Fine-tune only the gap you measured⌄ One epoch, batch 256, cross-entropy over the option letters, lr around 5e-6. Keep at least half your training examples in the exact panel layout you will use at inference. Select the checkpoint on the dev set. ←PreviousNext→ 5Fit the temperature, then report both numbers⌄ One scalar on the dev set, stored with the checkpoint. Then publish accuracy AND calibration error to yourself. An uncalibrated decision model is a classifier with a confidence field you are not allowed to trust — which defeats the entire purpose of the category. ←PreviousNext→ 6Set the threshold from the reliability curve, not from a round number⌄ Find the confidence at which observed accuracy is actually good enough to skip a human or a frontier model. Everything below it escalates. That number is a property of your data and will not be 0.9 just because 0.9 looks tidy. ←PreviousNext→ Serve a Jev-compatible model locally and send it a real request CopyOpen in Claude↗ # Apple silicon (MLX backend) uv sync --no-default-groups --extra mac uv run --no-default-groups hf download mstrasser/Jeff-Qwen3.5-0.8B --local-dir checkpoints/jeff-0.8b JEFF_BACKEND=mlx JEFF_CHECKPOINT=checkpoints/jeff-0.8b PORT=8765 \ uv run --no-default-groups --extra mac jeff-serve # Two independent questions, one request, one parallel pass curl -s localhost:8765/v1/systemone -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{ "model": "jeff-latest", "state": "Refund request: the customer says the parcel arrived crushed and wants their money back.", "questions": { "route": {"type": "choice", "instructions": "Which team should handle this?", "criteria": {"1": "Refunds and payments", "2": "Damaged or lost parcels", "3": "Account and login problems"}}, "angry": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Is the customer angry?"} } }'

The sharpest criticism in the Hacker News thread was not that Jeff performs badly. It was structural: if you have to fine-tune it on your own labelled data anyway, you have not bought a zero-shot classifier — you have bought a somewhat awkward way to train a classifier, and the field already has cheaper ones. The numbers in that thread support taking it seriously. A commenter reported testing the 0.8B zero-shot on job-ad classification and finding it unusable, with the 2B still missing categories. Another reported that plain embeddings plus a logistic-regression head reached 93.0% on BANKING77 using a model about 15x smaller than the decision models being compared — against the 87.4%-confidence/75.3%-accuracy shape the independent Jev pilot found on the same dataset. So the honest decision table: Situation Use Handful of fixed labels, plenty of examples, latency matters Embeddings + logistic regression. Smallest, fastest, trains in seconds. Beat this before considering anything else. Labels change often, or questions are written in prose per request Zero-shot decision model — the schema is the interface, which is the actual product One high-volume domain, you have labels, you have a GPU for an afternoon Fine-tune. Jeff's chess run went 15.5% → 55.8%; a voice-navigation fine-tune on ~11,000 examples went 31.7% → 95.8% in under 30 minutes Genuinely hard, multi-step judgements Reasoning — Jeeves, or a frontier model behind a cascade You need it working this afternoon and the volume is low Hosted API. Your own GPU is not free either The general rule underneath: a decision model earns its place when the schema is the valuable part — arbitrary typed questions, in prose, resolved in one pass. When your label set is fixed and known, you are paying model-shaped costs for classifier-shaped work.
documents.s: The uncomfortable question: do you need a model at all?

documents.t: Jev's founding pitch was that this class of model does not generate text. PostHog's Jeeves tests that premise directly by letting a decision model think first, then decide, on Qwen3.5-9B with LoRA r=16 and a pointer head. Training runs in three stages: SFT (19,126 questions from 12 public datasets plus synthetic policy data, half carrying reasoning chains, 2 epochs / 596 steps on 8 GPUs), then CISPO reinforcement learning (9,992 questions, 8 rollouts each at temperature 1, thinking capped at 2,560 tokens — a 624-step schedule deliberately stopped at step 402 because calibration was degrading past it), then the same scalar temperature fit. Reported results: Benchmark Jeeves Jev Kev-9B Test overall 0.889 0.857 0.822 JevBench overall (231 items) 0.935 0.866 0.715 JevBench hard (111 items) 0.865 0.730 0.451 And the ablation that matters more than any of those rows: 0.804 without reasoning, 0.840 with it. Thinking is worth about 3.6 points on this model. Now price it. On one H100, Jeeves answers in ~0.3 s with reasoning off and 3.3 s median with it on — 17.1 s at p90. That is roughly 11x the median latency and a tail an order of magnitude worse, for 3.6 points. The README's own mitigation is the interesting engineering: cap thinking at 2,560 tokens and add a 0.9 confidence threshold that stops early when the model is already sure, which brings the median to 2.0 s. Reasoning becomes something you spend only on the items that need it. Two caveats Jeeves publishes about itself: it is worse than Jev on knowledge-heavy tasks (MMLU 0.793 vs 0.900) — reasoning does not add facts — and its reasoning chains were never rewarded for language consistency, so they are not reliably readable. If you wanted the chain as an audit trail, check that it is legible before you promise anyone it is.

Wording consistency beats wording quality. Jeff reports Frogger crossings going from 15 to 23 purely by phrasing every option the same way as its siblings. Options are compared against each other in one pass — asymmetric phrasing is a thumb on the scale. Keep keys short and put the description in the text. Prompt formats do not port between decision models. Jev's bearing-number style did not transfer to Jeff; consequence-focused wording was needed instead. Treat a switch of decision model as a re-tuning job, exactly like porting prompts across models. The 26-option ceiling is silent. Nothing errors. Options 27+ simply never win. Chunk large label sets into a two-stage decision instead. English, text-only for Jeff. AutoJev accepts base64 images; Jeff does not. Zero-shot quality is workload-shaped and often disappointing. Multiple practitioners reported the small models being unusable on their own real classification tasks. Measure on your data on day one. Training-data leak filtering is your job. Jeff generates synthetic data locally with leak filtering precisely because a decision model trained near its eval panel produces a number that means nothing. Both repos are days old. Flags, checkpoint names and defaults are moving. Nothing here substitutes for the current README. Check yourself 0/5

Copy as Markdown Intermediate "How much does AI cost?" has no single answer — it depends on which pricing archetype you're buying and how much you actually use it. The dollar figures churn every few months; the structure of the cost barely moves. This page teaches the durable shape: the three ways AI is priced, how to estimate a workload before you build it, the levers that cut the bill, and the real fork between renting an API and self-hosting. What you'll learn Tell apart the three cost archetypes: per-token API, flat subscription, and open/self-hosted Estimate any workload's cost from tokens × rate × volume — before you ship it Pull the big levers that cut spend without hurting quality Know when open/self-hosted beats API on cost, and when API wins Know which numbers go stale fast — and where to check today's truth Last verified: 2026-10-08. Per-token rates, subscription tiers, cache and batch discounts, and which model is cheapest change almost monthly — treat every specific dollar figure as perishable. This page teaches the durable model (archetypes + how to estimate + the levers); for today's numbers check each provider's own pricing page (linked in Sources), an independent tracker like Artificial Analysis, and run the math in our Cost Calculator. Confirm against the official source.

Almost every way you can pay for AI collapses into one of three shapes. Learn the shapes, not the prices. Per-token API (usage-based). You call a hosted model over an API and pay per token — and input and output are priced separately, with output almost always the more expensive of the two. Bigger/smarter models cost more per token; smaller models cost far less. Most providers also offer discounts: a reduced rate for cached input you re-send, and a flat batch discount for non-urgent async jobs. This is how you pay when you build a product on Claude, GPT, or Gemini. Cost scales directly with usage — pennies at small scale, the dominant line item at large scale. Flat consumer/seat subscription. A fixed monthly fee for a chat app or IDE assistant (the Claude / ChatGPT / Gemini consumer plans, Copilot-style seats). You don't see tokens; you get a usage allowance and rate limits. Predictable and cheap for a human at a keyboard — but it doesn't scale to programmatic/high-volume work, and per-seat costs add up across a team. Open / local (self-hosted). You run an open-weight model (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek) on your own hardware or a rented GPU. There's no per-call price — you pay for the hardware (or hourly GPU rental) + electricity + ops, whether the model is busy or idle. The marginal cost of one more call is effectively near-zero at scale, but you carry fixed cost and operational burden. See Run Models Locally with Ollama. Pro tip The key split: API and subscriptions are MARGINAL cost (you pay per use); self-hosting is mostly FIXED cost (you pay to keep capacity up, used or not). On the API, the single biggest surprise is that OUTPUT tokens usually cost several times more than input — verbose answers cost real money. A flat subscription is the right tool for a human chatting; the per-token API is the right tool for an app calling the model in a loop.

You can size an API bill before writing a line of production code. The whole model is one formula: cost ≈ (input tokens × input rate) + (output tokens × output rate), per call × number of calls Rates are quoted per million tokens, and input and output have different rates — so estimate the two halves separately and add them. A rough token rule of thumb: ~1 token ≈ 4 characters of English, or ~0.75 words. For exact counts, use the Token Estimator area and read Tokens & Pricing. The full mechanics of where tokens hide live in The Token Economy. Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Size ONE call's tokens⌄ Add up the input: system prompt + tools + retrieved context + history + the user turn. Then estimate the output you ask for. Count input and output separately — they're priced differently. ←PreviousNext→ 2Multiply each side by its own rate⌄ input tokens × input rate, plus output tokens × output rate. Use today's per-million numbers from the provider's pricing page (don't trust a figure you memorized — see VerifyNote). ←PreviousNext→ 3Scale by real volume⌄ Multiply the per-call cost by calls per day × days. A cost that's trivial per call (fractions of a cent) becomes your top line item at millions of calls — model your ACTUAL traffic, not one request. ←PreviousNext→ 4Apply the discounts you'll actually use⌄ If a big chunk of input repeats every call, price it at the CACHED rate, not full input. If the job is offline, apply the BATCH discount. These change the answer dramatically at scale. ←PreviousNext→ 5Sanity-check against a tracker, then cut⌄ Compare your per-token assumptions to an independent tracker and our Cost Calculator, then attack the bill with the levers below. ←PreviousNext→ Back-of-envelope estimate (fill in today's rates) CopyOpen in Claude↗ Per call: input_tokens = system + tools + context + history + user_turn output_tokens = the answer you ask for call_cost = (input_tokens * input_rate_per_million / 1e6) + (output_tokens * output_rate_per_million / 1e6) Per month: monthly_cost = call_cost * calls_per_day * 30 Then adjust: - cached repeated input -> use the (lower) cache-read rate for that slice - offline / non-urgent -> apply the batch discount to the whole job Rates change monthly — pull today's numbers from the provider's pricing page.
documents.s: How to estimate a workload's cost

documents.t: Most real workloads carry dead weight. These levers, roughly in order of leverage, cut spend without touching quality — pull the cheap structural ones first. Right-size the model. Don't pay a flagship rate for a job a small/cheap model does fine. Classification, extraction, routing, and simple formatting usually run great on the smallest tier at a fraction of the per-token price. Reserve the big model for genuinely hard reasoning, and consider routing: cheap model handles the easy majority, escalate only the hard cases. See Choosing a Model. Trim the context you send. The cheapest token is the one you never send. Prune bloated system prompts, compact long histories into a running summary, and expose only the tools the task needs — every one is input you re-pay each call. RAG instead of stuffing huge context. Pasting a 50-page document to answer one question pays for 50 pages every call. Retrieval fetches only the few relevant passages — far fewer input tokens for the same (often better) answer. Reach for a giant context window only when you genuinely need the whole corpus in view at once. Prompt caching. If many calls share a large unchanging prefix (system prompt, tool catalog, reference doc), caching processes it once and re-serves it at a steep discount on every later call. The single highest-leverage structural change for chat and agent workloads, because it pays back every turn. Batch the non-urgent. Evals, bulk labeling, summarizing an archive — anything where you don't need the answer in seconds — runs through an async batch path at a flat discount on most providers. Trade immediacy for a materially lower bill. Shorten the output. Output is the pricier side. Ask for JSON or a tight schema instead of a chatty paragraph: fewer output tokens and no downstream parsing guesswork. Smaller / open models for the easy slice. For the high-volume, low-difficulty majority of calls, an open or small model can be dramatically cheaper per call — sometimes near-free if you already self-host. Keep the frontier model for the cases that actually need it. Pro tip These stack multiplicatively: cached input × right-sized model × terser output × batch discount compounds into a large total cut on an easy task — with quality unchanged. Pull the structural levers (right-size, cache, RAG, batch) before micro-optimizing wording — they move the bill far more. Always MEASURE the change against the real bill, not a guess. The deep playbook is The Token Economy.
documents.s: The big levers to cut cost

documents.t: This is the decision that actually moves your AI budget. It's a fixed-vs-marginal-cost crossover, and volume is the variable that decides it. Open / self-hosted wins at HIGH, steady volume. Once you're running enough calls to keep a GPU busy most of the time, the near-zero marginal cost per call beats paying per token forever. You amortize the fixed hardware/rental cost across a huge number of calls, gain data privacy and full customization — and accept the operational burden (provisioning, scaling, uptime, MLOps) as the price of admission. API wins at LOW or SPIKY volume, or with no infra. If traffic is small, bursty, or unpredictable, paying per token means you pay only for what you use and nothing when idle — no GPU sitting warm at 3 a.m. You also skip all the ops. For most teams shipping a product, prototyping, or with traffic that comes in spikes, the API is both cheaper and far less work. Watch out Self-hosting is rarely 'free.' The model weights may be free, but GPUs, electricity, and the engineer-hours to keep it running are not — count them honestly before claiming a saving. Idle GPUs are pure loss: fixed-cost infra only beats per-token pricing when utilization is HIGH. Low or spiky traffic favors the API every time. The crossover point moves whenever API prices drop or hardware gets cheaper — re-run the math periodically, don't decide once and forget. Check yourself 0/3 Key takeaways Three archetypes: per-token API (usage-based, input vs output priced separately), flat subscription (predictable, doesn't scale to high volume), and open/self-hosted (fixed cost, near-zero per call). Estimate before you build: (input × input rate) + (output × output rate), per call × volume — then apply cache and batch discounts. Biggest levers: right-size the model, trim context, RAG over huge context, prompt caching, batch the non-urgent, shorten output. Self-hosting wins at HIGH steady volume (amortize fixed cost); API wins at LOW/spiky volume or with no infra (pay only for use). Every dollar figure goes stale fast — verify at the provider's pricing page and a tracker, and run your own numbers in the Cost Calculator.

Copy as Markdown Intermediate What you'll learn Understand what is actually inside 16.9 MB — and which part of the 9x size headline is architecture versus a quantization choice the comparison does not hold constant Read the vendor's own WER chart including the competitor bars it never labels: Whistle wins 5 of 8 head-to-heads and loses the three that look most like real life Know why 30 seconds is a wall in the encoder rather than a setting, and build the VAD segmentation it forces on you Find the streaming API the launch discussion concluded did not exist, and understand why its real latency is not the 11.1 ms time-to-first-token Use keyword biasing as the primary accuracy lever, not a nicety — it is the difference between 41% and 96% on a closed vocabulary Decide between Whistle, Whisper, Parakeet and a cloud API for your specific audio On 8 October 2026 a blog post titled "Whistle: Speech to Text in 16.9 MB" reached 768 points on Hacker News. The number in the title is the whole pitch, and it is true: the entire multilingual speech recognition model is a single 16.9 MB file that runs on a CPU with no GPU and no dependencies. The discussion that followed split cleanly in two. People who read the benchmark chart were impressed. People who pointed a microphone at it were not — one tester reported 70 correct out of 170 utterances. Both groups were right, and the reason they were both right is printed in the vendor's own chart. It is just in the bars that carry no number.
documents.s: Whistle: Speech-to-Text in 16.9 MB — and the Benchmark Bars Nobody Labelled

documents.t: Whistle buys its size by quantizing a small encoder–decoder ASR model to 2–4 bits and band-limiting its front end to 250–3500 Hz, which costs it almost nothing on close-microphone single-speaker speech — where it genuinely beats Whisper base — and costs it a great deal on far-field, overlapping or accented speech, where it is the worst of the three models in its own comparison.

Component Detail Front end 25 ms window, 10 ms hop, 80 log-mel bins, band-limited 250–3500 Hz Stem 128-channel convolutional, downsamples to one frame per 80 ms Encoder 8 Simple Attention blocks, Monarch Hadamard MLP Decoder 8 laddered Simple Attention blocks, width 512, 8 query heads to 2 KV heads Vocabulary 8,192 text pieces plus 7 language tokens Output ceiling 320 tokens per clip Input ceiling 480,000 samples — 30 s at 16 kHz mono Container .cact, Cactus Quants, 2–4 bit Licence Apache-2.0 Three of those rows do more work than the rest, and two of them are the ones people skip.
documents.s: What is actually in the 16.9 MB

documents.t: The comparison everyone quotes is 16.9 MB against Whisper base's 145.3 MB. That is one ninth the size — but the vendor's own footnote says Whistle is measured at 2 to 4 bit while Whisper is fp32 in memory on the CPU. Those are 8–16x apart in bits per weight before a single architectural decision is made. The honest apples-to-apples row in the same chart is Moonshine tiny v2 at 41.9 MB in int8. Whistle is 2.5x smaller than that, not 9x. The remaining 2.5x is real and is where the architecture earns its keep — but if you repeat the 9x number you are mostly repeating a quantization choice. This is the same trap covered in how to read an AI benchmark without getting fooled: the number is not wrong, the comparison is not held constant.
documents.s: The 9x size headline does not hold precision constant

documents.t: The front end keeps 250–3500 Hz and throws away everything else. That is roughly telephone band, and it is a sensible choice for a model meant to run on a wearable — most speech energy lives below it. Most, not all. The acoustic-phonetics literature is specific here: 3–4 kHz is enough bandwidth for intelligible vowels but not for most voiceless fricatives, whose spectra are concentrated above 4 kHz. English s has its greatest energy concentration in roughly the 5–10 kHz range, peaking near 8 kHz — more than twice Whistle's cutoff — and sh centres near 4 kHz with energy extending to 8. Cutting at 3500 Hz does not make those sounds inaudible. It removes the band that separates them from each other most cleanly. So before you run a single test you can predict the error class: confusions and dropped word-endings on fricatives, worst on speakers whose rhythm or accent gives those consonants less duration to compensate with. The field reports in the launch thread — Spanish output with "non-existent words and terrible typos", Mexican and Venezuelan accents not detected, heavy accents degrading sharply — are that prediction arriving on schedule.
documents.s: Band-limiting to 3500 Hz is a design decision with a predictable error class

documents.t: Here is the part worth the page. Whistle's chart plots word error rate across nine test sets for three models. It prints a number on every Whistle bar and on none of the others. The bars are still there, drawn to a linear scale. Whistle's printed labels calibrate that scale exactly — 6.867 pixels per WER point, consistent to ±0.01 across all nine — so the competitor values are recoverable from bar height. Doing that produces the table the chart stops just short of giving you. Test set What it is Whistle Whisper base ≈ Moonshine tiny v2 ≈ LibriSpeech test-clean Read audiobooks, clean 4.31 4.89 4.51 LibriSpeech test-other Read audiobooks, harder 10.49 11.00 11.71 SPGISpeech Financial calls 7.65 — 7.70 Earnings-22 Earnings calls, accented 19.01 — 21.25 AMI Meetings, far-field, overlapping 26.07 21.50 22.78 AMI cleaned Same, cleaned refs 22.87 — — TED-LIUM Conference talks 7.61 4.99 5.64 FLEURS Multilingual read speech 21.39 24.50 — MLS Multilingual audiobooks 24.90 23.10 — Lower is better; bold marks the winner of each row. Whistle's column is the vendor's printed figures. The other two columns are read off the chart's bars — the vendor states they are Whisper's and Moonshine's own published numbers, and declines to print them. Whistle wins five of the eight rows where a comparison exists. For a model 2.5x smaller than its nearest-precision rival that is a genuine result, and the FLEURS row — 3.1 points better than Whisper base on multilingual read speech — is the most impressive thing in the chart. Now look at what it loses: AMI, by 4.57 points to Whisper base. Far-field microphones, multiple speakers, overlap, interruption. Whistle is not merely behind here, it is the worst of the three, losing to a model 8.6x its size. TED-LIUM, by 2.62 points. Single speaker, but a large room, a stage mic and unscripted delivery. MLS, by 1.80 points. Multilingual long-form, averaged over six non-English languages. The pattern is not subtle once the numbers are side by side. Every row Whistle wins is close-microphone and effectively single-speaker. Every row it loses has either distance between the mouth and the microphone or more than one person in the room. Read-audiobook and dictation audio is exactly the profile a 16 kHz band-limited front end with a tiny encoder handles well. Reverberation and overlapping talkers are exactly what it cannot afford the capacity to disentangle. That single sentence reconciles the two halves of the launch thread. Everyone who tested dictation into a phone held near their face liked it. Everyone who pointed it at a film clip, a meeting or a room disliked it. Nobody was measuring wrong. :::tip The number to carry away 4.31 and 26.07 are the same model on the same weights. If you only remember one WER figure for Whistle, remember the spread, not the headline. :::

The most-quoted field result in the thread — 70 correct out of 170, against 168/170 for a much larger Qwen ASR model — is a real measurement, but it is a measurement of stock settings on a closed vocabulary. The same tester reported 164/170 after tuning. What changed is the subject of the next section, and it is the most under-sold feature on the model card.

Whistle decodes with five beams scored by length-normalised log probability, and it will accept a list of words you expect to hear and favour them during that search, matched with an Aho-Corasick automaton. In a general-purpose ASR model this is a convenience. In a 16.9 MB model with an 8,192-piece vocabulary it is closer to load-bearing. The model has very little capacity to spend on an implicit language model, so proper nouns, product names, place names and domain jargon are precisely what it gets wrong — and precisely what a keyword list fixes. Going from 70/170 to 164/170 is 41% to 96% on the same weights. Transcribe with the two arguments that matter CopyOpen in Claude↗ import needle r = needle.transcribe( "clip.wav", keywords=["Kubernetes", "Grafana", "Prometheus", "Aoife", "Nguyen"], word_timestamps=True, language="en", # skip detection when you already know ) print(r["text"]) for w in r["words"]: print(w["word"], w["start"], w["end"], w["probability"]) Three things in that snippet are worth stating plainly: keywords is not a post-processing filter. It changes the beam search, so it can recover a word the decoder would otherwise never have placed. language="en" removes a failure mode, not just latency. Automatic detection across seven languages on a short or noisy clip is one more thing that can go wrong. If your app knows the language, say so. Every word carries its own probability. That is your confidence gate — see the handoff pattern below. Watch out A keyword list that is too long dilutes the bias and starts pulling the decoder toward words nobody said. Keep it to the vocabulary your users actually produce in this context — the current screen, the current contact list, the current document — not your entire product glossary.
documents.s: Keyword biasing is the primary accuracy lever

documents.t: 30 seconds at 16 kHz is 480,000 samples. After the convolutional stem that is one frame per 80 ms, so 375 encoder frames, and the decoder tops out at 320 output tokens. Those are fixed shapes in a 16.9 MB tensor file. There is no flag that raises them, and a launch-thread tester who recorded past the limit got a runtime error rather than a truncated transcript. So any clip longer than 30 seconds means you own the segmentation — and segmentation is where long-form ASR accuracy actually lives, because a cut through the middle of a word or a clause is an error the model cannot recover from. Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Resample and downmix first⌄ 16 kHz mono is not a recommendation, it is the input contract. A 44.1 kHz stereo file needs converting before it reaches the model; the base install handles 16 kHz WAV and raw samples, and the [mic] extra adds resampling and microphone capture. ←PreviousNext→ 2Segment on silence, not on a timer⌄ Run a voice-activity detector and cut in the gaps. Fixed 30-second slices will eventually cut mid-word, and that error lands in your transcript permanently. Target 10–25 second segments so you keep headroom for a long final clause. ←PreviousNext→ 3Overlap the segments by about a second⌄ Give consecutive passes a shared region so you can stitch on agreement instead of trusting a hard boundary. The cost is re-decoding a second of audio; at 1,319 tokens/s decode that is not your bottleneck. ←PreviousNext→ 4Stitch with the word timestamps, not the text⌄ Every word comes back with a start and an end, so dedupe the overlap region by time rather than by string matching. This is the only reliable way to drop a doubled word without dropping a legitimately repeated one. ←PreviousNext→ 5Gate on probability and hand off⌄ Average the per-word probabilities over each segment. Low-confidence segments are your queue for a bigger model — on-device for free, off-device when it matters. Do not re-run everything. ←PreviousNext→
documents.s: The 30-second wall is in the encoder, not in a config file

documents.t: The model card makes a specific and welcome claim: silence and steady noise return an empty transcript rather than an invented sentence, because silence detection runs before the beam search. That is a direct fix for Whisper's most notorious failure — confidently hallucinating subtitles over nothing. Read the claim precisely. It covers silence and steady noise. It does not cover quiet, distant or overlapping speech, and the thread contains exactly that failure: a tester reported the model emitting "Thank you." repeatedly for over a minute while real dialogue was playing, and another found a negation flipped — "can handle" for "can't handle" — plus a word invented outright. Those are the classic artefacts of training on web video captions, where "Thanks for watching" occupies an enormous share of the text, and they survive the silence gate because the gate was never aimed at them. If a dropped n't would change what your application does, a per-word probability check is not optional.
documents.s: Silence is handled; low-SNR speech is not

documents.t: A recurring complaint in the discussion was that Whistle cannot do live transcription, because the demo showed no partial text while speaking. The demo did not; the library does. needle.stream(chunks) takes live microphone input and commits words that consecutive overlapping passes agree on. That policy — decode an overlapping window repeatedly, emit only the prefix two passes agree on — is the LocalAgreement family of streaming ASR, and knowing that tells you the thing the spec sheet will not: Your perceived latency is not the 11.1 ms time-to-first-token. It is the agreement delay: how long a word has to wait before a second pass confirms it. TTFT is a decode-speed measurement on a complete 10-second clip. In a streaming loop the user-visible number is set by your window stride and how long you are willing to wait for stability, and it will be hundreds of milliseconds, not eleven. Fast is still fast — 11.1 ms against Whisper base's 73.2 ms and Moonshine's 22.8 ms, and 1,319 tokens/s decode against 266 and 262, measured on 10 s of audio on an Apple M4 Pro CPU. Just do not promise a product manager 11 ms of live captioning.
documents.s: Streaming exists — the launch thread concluded it did not

documents.t: Every depth from two layers up is a deployable model, selected at load time with --audio-depth. You download one 16.9 MB blob and choose your accuracy/latency point on the device, which is the right place to choose it — a watch and a phone can run the same artifact at different depths. For scale, the sibling Needle text model decodes at roughly 4,000 tokens/s at two layers and 400 at twenty on a Raspberry Pi 5.
documents.s: The decoder is laddered, so one file is a family

documents.t: The encoder output is available directly: one row per 80 ms frame, via needle.Whistle().embed(audio). That is wake-word spotting, command matching, audio deduplication and "find where in this recording someone said this" — without decoding text, without a language model, and without the error classes discussed above, because you never ask it to spell anything. For a lot of embedded jobs ("did the user say one of these eleven things?") this is the correct tool and transcription is the detour. Run it from the CLI, including the built-in three-way comparison CopyOpen in Claude↗ pip install cactus-needle # microphone playground needle whistle playground # put Whistle next to Whisper and Moonshine on YOUR audio needle whistle compare my-clip.wav # air-gapped / embedded: fetch a platform engine and the weights needle download macos-arm64 needle download whistle ./macos-arm64/needle --model whistle.cact --audio clip.wav --audio-word-timestamps The compare subcommand deserves a mention: the vendor ships the tool that checks its own claims against your audio. Given how sharply the WER spread above depends on recording conditions, running it on a representative clip of your audio is worth more than any table on this page.
documents.s: embed() gives you speech matching with no transcript at all

documents.t: The engine reads no environment variables. Every behaviour is a compiled default or an explicit flag. That means the same blob plus the same flags scores the same on any machine, which is a property most inference stacks cannot claim and which matters enormously when you are trying to work out whether last week's eval regressed or last week's shell did.

Your situation Pick Why Dictation on a phone or wearable, close mic, offline, 7 supported languages Whistle This is the design centre. 16.9 MB, no GPU, word timestamps, and it beats Whisper base on exactly this audio profile Wake words or fixed command sets on a microcontroller Whistle embed() Skip transcription entirely; match encoder frames Meeting recordings, multiple speakers, room mics Not Whistle Its own chart puts it last on AMI. Use a full-size Whisper, Parakeet, or a cloud ASR with diarization Any language outside the seven Not Whistle English, German, French, Spanish, Italian, Dutch, Polish only. No Chinese, despite being the most-requested addition in the launch thread Best open-weight accuracy-per-second on a GPU, English Parakeet NVIDIA's parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v2 was the practitioner favourite in the thread; CC-BY-4.0 Audio you cannot send anywhere, and accuracy matters more than size Whisper large, local Still the accuracy reference. You are trading ~100x the footprint for it Medical, legal or financial transcripts of record Cloud ASR with a human in the loop The negation-flip failure mode above is disqualifying on its own A hybrid is usually the right answer, and it is the same shape as every other local/remote split on this site: run the small model on everything, use the per-word probabilities as the gate, escalate the uncertain fraction. See Claude plus local models for the general pattern and a private local AI stack for where a transcription step belongs in it.
documents.s: Choosing: Whistle, Whisper, Parakeet, or a cloud API

documents.t: Whistle is a good instance of a pattern now showing up across small models: the capability is real and the operating envelope is narrow, and only the first half fits in a headline. The 2-bit quantization is not a cheat — the model genuinely works — but it buys its size by spending the capacity that would have handled hard audio, and the vendor's chart shows exactly where that bill lands while labelling only the rows where it does not. The practical rule generalises past ASR: when a small model publishes a wide benchmark spread, the spread is the specification. Find the row where it does worst, work out what that test set has that the others do not, and check whether your real input looks like that row. For Whistle the answer is distance and overlap. For a quantized language model it is usually long context — see what "98.2% retention" hides. Check yourself 0/6 Last verified: 2026-10-09. This page quotes facts that change over time — treat the date above as its freshness. Sources: Cactus-Compute/whistle Hugging Face model card (README.md and assets/whistle-benchmarks.svg, Apache-2.0, 210 likes, 5,558 downloads); cactuscompute.com/blog/whistle (published 2 October 2026); cactus-compute/needle on GitHub (13,669 stars, Apache-2.0); cactuscompute.com/blog/needle-supported-devices for platform folders and runner flags; Hacker News thread 50008427, 'Whistle: Speech to Text in 16.9 MB', 768 points and 153 comments, submitted 8 October 2026, for all field reports. Whistle's WER figures are its own printed labels. The Whisper base and Moonshine tiny v2 columns are derived from the chart's bar heights against the scale Whistle's labels establish (6.867 px per WER point, self-consistent to ±0.01 — the derived AMI-cleaned value reproduces the printed 22.87 as 22.86); the vendor states these are the respective authors' published figures. Star counts, download counts and the model's API surface will drift — re-read the model card before relying on a flag or argument name.

Copy as Markdown Intermediate A chat turn costs a fraction of a cent. The same question handed to an agent — one that reads files, calls tools, and loops until done — can cost dollars. Teams are discovering this the hard way: a coding agent left running racks up a bill that a human at a keyboard never would. The scary part isn't the average; it's that you can't predict it in advance, and the cost of the same task can swing wildly. This page explains why agents burn tokens (the mechanism is not what most people guess), shows the numbers that surprise even experienced builders, and gives you the four levers that actually cut the bill — the same levers whether you're on Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, or a home-grown loop over any model. What you'll learn Explain the context snowball — why agent cost grows roughly QUADRATICALLY with steps, not linearly Cite the real multipliers: agentic tasks ~1000x a chat's tokens, and the SAME task varying up to 30x Know when a second agent is worth it — and the benchmark showing it usually isn't Pull the four cost levers that work: budget caps, prompt caching, model-tier routing, context pruning Diagnose a runaway agent bill and put a hard ceiling on it Last verified: 2026-07-15. Per-token prices, per-developer monthly spend, and which model is cheapest change almost monthly — treat every dollar figure here as perishable and illustrative. The mechanism (context snowball, re-read tax) and the levers are durable; the exact ratios come from 2026 benchmarks and research linked in Sources. Confirm today's rates on each provider's pricing page before quoting a bill to anyone. Confirm against the official source.
documents.s: Why AI Agents Burn Tokens (and How to Cap the Bill)

documents.t: Here's the trap. A chat is one turn — one input, one output, done. An agent is a loop: it reads a task, takes an action, reads the result, takes the next action, and so on until the job is finished. The catch is that on every step, the model re-reads the entire accumulated conversation so far — the original prompt, every prior action, and every tool result — before deciding what to do next. So the input grows on every step, and you pay for the whole snowball again each time it rolls forward: Step 1 processes the prompt. Step 2 re-reads the prompt + step 1's action + result. Step 3 re-reads all of that + step 2's action + result. …and so on. Add up the input across a run and the total scales roughly with the square of the number of steps, not linearly. The Stanford Digital Economy Lab found agentic tasks to be "uniquely expensive, consuming 1000x more tokens than code reasoning and code chat" — and crucially, it's the input tokens that dominate, not the output. The agent isn't writing more; it's re-reading more. What you'll learn The cost driver is re-reading, not thinking. Each loop step re-processes the full transcript, so a 20-step run pays for early context ~20 times over. This is why 'just let the agent figure it out' is expensive: every extra step it takes multiplies against everything before it. Output-heavy tasks (write me an essay) are cheap by comparison; input-heavy loops (explore this repo, then fix the bug) are where the money goes.
documents.s: The context snowball: why cost grows quadratically

documents.t: Three figures reset most people's intuition: ~1000x. Agentic tasks can consume roughly a thousand times the tokens of an equivalent chat or code-completion, per the Stanford analysis — driven by the snowball above, not by a bigger model. Up to 30x variance on the same task. The same agent, run on the same task, can cost up to 30x more one time than another — because the path it takes (how many tools it calls, how far it wanders) is non-deterministic. You genuinely cannot know the bill until it's done. This is why "result-based pricing" for agents is so hard: you only see the cost after everything runs. More agents rarely pay for themselves. 2026 production benchmarks found that a multi-agent setup added only ~2.1% accuracy at 2x the cost versus a well-configured single agent on 64% of tasks. A hierarchical-supervisor pattern pushed a document task from 85% → 95% accuracy — but at roughly $0.15/task vs $0.003 for the single agent (~50x). More agents buys a little accuracy for a lot of money. Watch out Because the same task varies up to 30x, an average-based budget WILL be blown by the tail. Cap the ceiling, don't budget the mean. Adding agents to 'be safe' usually multiplies cost far faster than it adds accuracy. Reach for a second agent only when the task genuinely decomposes into parallel, independent subtasks.

Before the loop even starts, how the agent reaches its tools sets a floor on cost. Connecting a set of MCP servers can inject tens of thousands of tokens of tool definitions into every step of the snowball. A rough comparison many builders hit: a plain CLI command averages ~200 tokens, while the equivalent MCP operation can cost 32k–82k tokens once tool schemas and wrapping are counted. That gap rides along on every loop step. That doesn't make MCP wrong — it's the right choice for auth, multi-tenancy, and governed access. It means the tool surface is a cost lever you chose at design time. AILmanac has a dedicated deep-dive: The MCP Token Tax covers Tool Search, deferred loading, and code execution as the three fixes.
documents.s: Your tool surface is part of the bill

documents.t: Optimization advice is endless; only four levers move the number materially. In rough order of leverage: Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Cap the budget — a hard ceiling, not a hope⌄ Set a per-run or per-user token/dollar cap that HARD-STOPS the agent. Because the same task can cost 30x more on a bad run, a ceiling is the only thing that bounds the tail. Most agent harnesses expose a max-tokens or max-steps limit — use it. This is the single most important control. ←PreviousNext→ 2Cache the stable prefix⌄ The system prompt, tool definitions, and house rules are re-sent on every loop step (the snowball). Prompt caching charges those repeated tokens at a fraction of the input rate. On a long agentic run this is often the biggest single saving, because the cached part is exactly what gets re-read the most. ←PreviousNext→ 3Route by model tier⌄ Don't run one frontier model for the whole loop. Use a cheap, fast model (Haiku-class, or a small open model) for the grunt work — reading files, formatting, routine tool calls — and reserve the expensive frontier model for the hard reasoning or the orchestrator role. Orchestrator-worker splits with cheaper workers cut cost 40–60% in production benchmarks at near-parity accuracy. ←PreviousNext→ 4Prune the context aggressively⌄ The snowball is the problem, so shrink it. Compact old turns, drop tool outputs the agent no longer needs, summarize instead of carrying raw transcripts, and start fresh sub-tasks with a clean context instead of one ever-growing thread. Every token you remove is a token you stop paying for on EVERY remaining step. ←PreviousNext→ Audit a runaway agent (paste your run's token breakdown) CopyOpen in Claude↗ You are a cost engineer. Here is a token-usage breakdown of one agentic run (input vs output tokens per step, tool calls, model used). Diagnose where the money went, in priority order: 1. Is input or output driving cost? (Agents are almost always input-heavy.) 2. Which repeated content should be prompt-CACHED (system prompt, tools, rules)? 3. Which steps could run on a CHEAPER model without losing correctness? 4. Where is context snowballing — what can be pruned, compacted, or summarized? 5. What is a safe per-run token CAP that stops the worst tail without hurting the median run? Give me the estimated % saving per fix and the ONE change to make first.
documents.s: The four levers that actually cut the bill

documents.t: The cheapest agentic run is the one you don't make. If a task is a single, well-specified transformation — summarize this, classify that, rewrite this — a plain chat/completion call does it at a fraction of the cost, with no snowball at all. Reach for an agent when the work genuinely requires reading, deciding, acting, and re-checking in a loop against a changing environment (explore a repo, debug across files, drive a browser). If you can write the exact steps yourself, script them — don't pay a model to re-derive them every run. Check yourself 0/3
documents.s: When an agent is the wrong tool

Copy as Markdown Intermediate On September 28, 2026 AMD announced it is acquiring World Labs for about $8.2 billion in stock — its second-largest deal ever, behind only Xilinx — and Fei-Fei Li will join as executive vice president and chief scientist reporting to Lisa Su. A day later OpenAI's DevDay took the front page. Between them, "world model" became the phrase of the week. Here is the problem with the phrase. Two products that share it are architecturally opposite. One keeps the world inside the model and streams you frames as you move; it is interactive, it cannot be exported, and a session is capped in seconds. The other generates a 3D scene you download, own and render yourself for free; it is persistent, engine-ready, and completely inert. Picking the wrong one is not a preference mistake, it is a re-architecture. This page is the practical split: what each family really produces, the verified API and export details, the one benchmark that settles a common assumption, the open weights you can run on your own GPU, and the five things neither family will do for you. What you'll learn Tell the two families of world model apart, and pick by what you need to persist Know the real limits: the 60-second wall, the physics disclaimer, the export tier that gates commercial rights Read the World API correctly — async operations, the WLT-Api-Key header, and which splat formats come out Use the WorldScore evidence instead of vibes when choosing between a video model and a 3D model Run an open world model yourself, and understand why inverse dynamics is the part worth $8.2 billion Last verified: 2026-09-30. Deal terms from AMD's own newsroom release: approximately $8.2 billion, all stock, announced September 28, 2026, expected to close by the end of 2026 subject to regulatory approval — so it is not closed, and product roadmaps may move once it is. Project Genie access, Marble plan tiers and World API pricing are all live commercial surfaces that change without notice; the resolution and frame-rate figures for Genie 3 come from third-party reporting, not from Google's Project Genie post, which states only the 60-second generation limit. WorldScore leaderboard positions move as teams submit. Read the linked primary sources before you quote any number here. Confirm against the official source.

documents.t: Frame generators 3D generators Examples Genie 3 / Project Genie, driving world models Marble (World Labs) What it outputs A video stream, frame by frame, conditioned on your actions A scene: Gaussian splats, panoramas, optionally a mesh Where the world lives Inside the model's rolling context In a file you download Interactive? Yes — that is the whole point No. You navigate it, but it does not react Exportable? No geometry to export Yes — SPZ, PLY, GLB, collider meshes Cost shape Per second of interaction, per viewer, forever Once at generation. Rendering is then yours Fails by Drifting, forgetting, running out of session Being static and not simulating anything If you need a world that responds — a player pressing a key, a robot policy taking an action and seeing what happens — you need a frame generator. If you need a world that persists — an asset in your game, a set in your render pipeline, a scene five users load next month and see identically — you need a 3D generator. Almost every confused "why can't it just…" question on this topic is someone holding one and asking for the other.

Google's Project Genie went from research preview to a public-ish product on January 29, 2026. The access shape is narrow and worth knowing before you plan around it: Google AI Ultra subscribers, United States only, 18+, and explicitly not available on Google AI Ultra for Business. Google calls it an "experimental research prototype". The limit that teaches you the most is Google's own: generations are limited to 60 seconds. That is not a billing decision, it is a state problem. In a frame generator the world is not stored anywhere — it is implied by the model's context. Every frame is predicted from the prompt, the accumulated frames and your actions. Consistency is therefore bounded by the same thing that bounds a long chat: how much history the model can hold and keep coherent. Walk away from a wall and back, and whether the wall is still there is a memory question, not a rendering one. Google's stated caveats are the rest of the honest spec sheet: generated worlds "might not look completely true-to-life or always adhere closely to prompts or images, or real-world physics", and characters "can sometimes be less controllable, or experience higher latency in control". Read that physics line carefully if you were planning to use a frame generator as a simulator. It is a plausibility engine, not a solver. Nothing guarantees momentum is conserved between frame 300 and frame 301.
documents.s: The frame generators, and the 60-second wall

documents.t: Interactive generation at the commonly reported 24 fps gives you about 41.7 ms per frame, end to end, including your input reaching the server. That single number explains most of the product decisions in this family: why sessions are short, why access is gated to a paid tier, why there is no public API yet, and why the cost curve is per viewer-second rather than per asset. You are not buying a file. You are renting a GPU that must beat a 42-millisecond deadline for as long as someone is looking.

World Labs' Marble turns text, an image, a panorama, multiple views or a video clip into a navigable 3D scene. The important engineering fact is the representation: the output is 3D Gaussian splats, not a mesh. Splats are millions of small, oriented, semi-transparent blobs with colour and view-dependent shading. They photo-reconstruct beautifully and render fast on commodity GPUs. They also have no surfaces, no edges and no faces — which is why the next section matters more than it looks. What Marble's own export docs say you get: Export Availability Gaussian splats — SPZ and PLY Standard plan 360 panoramas Standard plan Collider meshes Standard plan Textured mesh (GLB) + commercial rights Pro plan only Anything at all Not on Free — generate only Two gotchas live in that table. First, collider meshes are a separate export — you need them because you cannot raycast, collide or do physics against splats directly. The splats are what the player sees; the collider mesh is what the engine tests against. Ship only the splats and your beautiful world has no floor. Second, commercial rights are tied to the Pro tier, not to the act of exporting. Check the plan before you put a generated world in a product. Marble's docs also note that lower-resolution exports are "optimized to be as perceptually similar as possible to the higher-resolution files" — a hint that you should test the small tier before paying to ship the big one.
documents.s: The 3D generators, and what you actually receive

documents.t: A detail several write-ups get wrong: SPZ is Niantic's format, open-sourced by Niantic Spatial, not a World Labs invention — Marble simply exports to it. It is worth using anyway. SPZ stores each spherical-harmonics coefficient as an 8-bit signed integer with optional further quantisation, landing at roughly 10× smaller than the equivalent PLY with no perceptible quality loss. Niantic's own testing puts around 5 bits as the sweet spot for most scenes, with essentially-zero MSE at 8 bits and about 18× compression at 3. SPZ 4, released in 2026, splits compression into six parallel ZSTD streams — one per attribute class — for roughly 3–5× faster compression and 1.5–2× faster end-to-end loading at the same ~10× size advantage. If you are shipping splats over the web, that is the difference between a scene that loads and one that does not.
documents.s: SPZ: the 10× that is not World Labs'

documents.t: The World API exposes Marble's generation to your own code. The verified shape, from World Labs' docs index and its official Python client: Inputs: text, images, panoramas, multi-view inputs, video. Outputs: splats in SPZ, PLY, SOGS, KSPLAT and SPLAT. Auth: an API key passed in the WLT-Api-Key header; the Python client reads WORLDLABS_API_KEY from the environment. Execution model: asynchronous. You submit a generation, get an operation back, and poll until it is done. There is also a credit-balance endpoint, media upload/retrieve, and world create/retrieve/list/export/delete. Client: worldlabsai/worldlabs-api-python, Python 3.12+. A CUDA GPU is only needed for local rendering, not for API use. Pricing: usage-based. Generate a world from text and poll for it CopyOpen in Claude↗ # github.com/worldlabsai/worldlabs-api-python (Python 3.12+) # export WORLDLABS_API_KEY=... from worldlabs_api.client import WorldLabsClient from worldlabs_api.models import WorldTextPrompt, WorldsGenerateRequest client = WorldLabsClient(api_key="your-key-here") request = WorldsGenerateRequest( display_name="Mystical Forest", world_prompt=WorldTextPrompt(text_prompt="A mystical forest"), ) op = client.generate_world(request) # returns an operation, not a world done = client.poll_operation(op.operation_id) # poll until done is true world = done.response Design your integration around that async boundary from day one. World generation is a job, not a request — the same lesson as batch inference or video generation. If your handler waits inline for a world, you will rewrite it.

World Labs also maintains Spark, an MIT-licensed 3D Gaussian splatting renderer for THREE.js / WebGL2, so a generated world can ship as a web page. It loads .PLY, .SPZ, .SPLAT, .KSPLAT and .SOG, fuses splats with ordinary meshes in the THREE.js pipeline, and targets the ~98% of devices with WebGL2. Spark 2.0 (April 15, 2026) is the release that makes big scenes viable in a browser: a level-of-detail splat tree that renders a fixed number of splats per frame regardless of scene size, a streaming .RAD format that supports HTTP Range requests so a coarse proxy appears almost instantly and refines progressively, and virtual splat paging against a fixed GPU memory pool so scenes larger than GPU memory still render — including on phones and Quest 3. Put a generated world on the web CopyOpen in Claude↗ npm install @sparkjsdev/spark three # docs and live examples: https://sparkjs.dev # repo: https://github.com/sparkjsdev/spark # # Export from Marble as .spz (≈10x smaller than .ply), serve it as a # static file, and load it into a THREE.js scene with Spark. # For scenes over a few hundred MB, convert to .RAD so the viewer can # range-request a coarse proxy first. Note what just happened to your cost curve. After generation, you are serving a static file from a CDN and rendering on the user's GPU. Serving the world is free. That is the inverse of the frame-generator model, where every viewer-second is inference.
documents.s: Rendering it without a game engine

documents.t: "Just use a video model" is the most common shortcut here, and there is now a benchmark that answers it. WorldScore (Stanford, arXiv:2504.00983) is a unified benchmark for world generation across 3D, 4D, text-to-video and image-to-video models — about 3,000 examples, with metrics for controllability, consistency, perceptual quality and motion, and explicit 3D consistency and camera-control measures. The result that should change a decision: on WorldScore-Static, dedicated 3D scene generators lead — WonderWorld at 72.69 and LucidDreamer at 70.40 — clearly above the video models. If your requirement is a geometrically consistent world you can move a camera through, a video model is the wrong tool even when its individual frames look better. Two caveats. The leaderboard is live and moves as teams submit. And WorldScore-Static measures exactly what its name says — a static world; strong static consistency tells you nothing about dynamics.

You do not need a vendor's API to have a world model. NVIDIA published Cosmos 3 — an open omnimodel for physical AI — with weights on Hugging Face: Model Size Runs on nvidia/Cosmos3-Edge 4B Edge devices, robots, vision agents nvidia/Cosmos3-Nano 16B = 8B reasoner + 8B generator Workstation class, e.g. RTX PRO 6000 nvidia/Cosmos3-Super 64B = 32B reasoner + 32B generator Hopper / Blackwell, large-scale synthetic data Architecturally it is a Mixture-of-Transformers handling text, image, video, audio and action in one model, pairing an autoregressive subsequence for reasoning with a diffusion subsequence for generation. It is wired into Hugging Face Diffusers, so the entry point is ordinary Python. Run an open world model locally CopyOpen in Claude↗ pip install --upgrade diffusers transformers accelerate # Cosmos3-Nano is 16B (8B reasoner + 8B generator); check the model # card on Hugging Face for the licence and the exact torch version # before you build on it. import torch from diffusers import Cosmos3OmniPipeline pipe = Cosmos3OmniPipeline.from_pretrained( "nvidia/Cosmos3-Nano", torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16 ) Now the part that explains the price tag. Cosmos 3's task table is not a list of video tricks: Input Output What it is Text / image / video Video Video generation Text / video Text Vision-language reasoning Action + image + text Video Forward dynamics — "if I do this, what happens?" Text + video Action Inverse dynamics — "what actions produced this?" Image + text Video and action Policy generation Inverse dynamics is the quiet one. It turns footage into labelled actions — which means ordinary video becomes robot training data, and a generated world becomes a place to train and evaluate a policy without hardware. AMD's own release describes World Labs as building models that "generate, reconstruct and simulate interactive 3D environments" plus technology for "robotic learning and simulation", and frames the deal around reasoning, robotics, simulation and physical AI informing its future silicon roadmap. Read as a compute story rather than a graphics story, $8.2 billion for a training-environment flywheel is a different kind of bet than $8.2 billion for a text-to-3D tool.
documents.s: Open weights: Cosmos 3, and what AMD actually bought

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1It is not a reasoning model, and your prompting does not transfer⌄ None of your chain-of-thought, XML-tag or tool-use technique carries over. Conditioning a world model is closer to directing a camera than to instructing an assistant: what matters is the input image, the viewpoint, the described lighting and the action sequence. The one habit that does transfer is source discipline — a clean, well-framed conditioning image beats an elaborate paragraph. ←PreviousNext→ 2It will not give you physics you can trust⌄ Google states plainly that generated worlds may not adhere to real-world physics. Cosmos-style forward dynamics predicts a plausible next observation, which is not the same as solving for one. Use a world model to generate scenarios and a real physics engine to adjudicate them. If a wrong answer costs money or safety, a solver has to be in the loop. ←PreviousNext→ 3Splats will not collide, and a mesh export is a separate thing⌄ Gaussian splats have no surfaces. Raycasts, character controllers, navmeshes and physics all need geometry, which is why Marble exports collider meshes separately and gates high-quality textured GLB to the Pro tier. Plan for two assets per world — the one you see and the one you hit — and budget the mesh export in the tier you actually pay for. ←PreviousNext→ 4A frame-generated world cannot be saved, diffed or versioned⌄ There is no file. The world exists for the length of the session and then it is gone, and a re-run of the same prompt is a different world. That rules out the whole class of workflows built on persistent state: reviewing a level, shipping a fix to it, having two users load the same scene, or asserting in a test that the scene has not changed. If you need any of those, you need exportable geometry. ←PreviousNext→ 5It will not tell you which plan you are allowed to ship on⌄ The export matrix is the licence. Free generates but cannot export at all; splats, panoramas and colliders sit on Standard; textured mesh and commercial rights sit on Pro. For open weights the equivalent step is reading the Hugging Face model card's licence before shipping, not after. This is the cheapest failure on the list to avoid and the most expensive to discover late. ←PreviousNext→
documents.s: Five jobs a world model will not do for you

documents.t: Game or product asset, multiple users, must look the same tomorrow → 3D generator. Export SPZ for the web or GLB for an engine, and remember the collider. Interactive exploration, one user, novelty is the point → frame generator, and design inside a 60-second session. Training or evaluating a policy → open weights with forward and inverse dynamics, on your own GPU, with a real simulator for anything safety-relevant. A camera moving through a consistent scene → not a video model. WorldScore says so.
Check yourself 0/5

Copy as Markdown Beginner One of AI's most meaningful uses gets the least attention: as an assistive tool. Claude can adapt information to you — your pace, your format, your language — which can be genuinely leveling.
documents.s: Accessibility: Claude as an Assistive Tool

documents.t: Dyslexia / reading load — "rewrite this in short, simple sentences," "summarize the key points," "explain this in plain language." Low vision — pair with voice mode to listen and dictate; ask for clean, well-structured text that screen readers handle well. If you use the CLI, Claude Code has a dedicated screen reader mode and accessibility settings. Neurodivergence / focus (ADHD, etc.) — "break this into a checklist," "what's the one next step?", turn a wall of text into a clear plan, draft the email you're stuck on. Language learners — translate, simplify, explain idioms, practice conversation, or get the same idea at different difficulty levels. Anxiety around writing — get a non-judgmental first draft to react to, lowering the barrier to starting.

Rewrite this so it's easy to read: short sentences, simple words, one idea per line. Keep all the meaning. Text: {paste} Turn this into a step-by-step checklist with the single most important step marked. {paste} Explain this in {your language}, then give me 3 phrases to practice.

It's an aid, not a clinician. For health/medical/legal decisions, consult a professional — verify anything important (Responsible Use). Voice and mobile make it available wherever you are (Voice Mode, Mobile). Your data is yours — share only what you're comfortable with (Privacy). :::tip The site itself AILmanac aims to be accessible too — clear language, level badges, keyboard-navigable, good contrast. Found an accessibility issue? Tell us. :::

Copy as Markdown All levels For founders and small teams, AI is leverage: it does the work of a junior marketer, analyst, and assistant at once. Direct it well and keep judgment on the things that matter.

Positioning & messaging — nail the value prop, then derive copy from it. Marketing content — landing pages, emails, ads, social, FAQs (see Writing). Customer comms — draft replies, handle complaints, write announcements. Research — market/competitor scans (verify!), customer-interview question sets. Planning — turn goals into prioritized, time-boxed plans. Docs & ops — SOPs, job posts, meeting summaries.

Before any copy, get the one-liner right: Write 3 versions of a value proposition using: for {audience} who {need}, {product} is a {category} that {key benefit}, unlike {alternative}. Then critique each in one line. Everything downstream (ads, emails, landing pages) gets easier once this is sharp.

:::warning Don't fabricate proof, and mind the claims Never invent testimonials, metrics, case studies, or awards — use [insert real number] placeholders and fill them with real data. Watch regulated or unsubstantiated claims (health, finance, "#1", guarantees). Verify market facts and figures before acting (Hallucinations). Protect data — don't paste customer PII or confidential numbers into unvetted tools (Privacy). :::
Turn your best prompts into reusable assets — a Project with your brand voice and docs, or the Business & Marketing skill pack so the standards apply automatically.
