Copy as Markdown Advanced Last verified: 2026-09-23. Runner concurrency caps, queue timeouts and merge-queue settings are platform limits that GitHub changes without much noise. The mechanisms below are stable; re-check the exact numbers against the limits page before you size a pipeline on them. Confirm against the official source. What you'll learn Know why the merge queue — not the runner budget — is the first thing that breaks under agent PR volume Do the batching arithmetic: how a few points of failure rate collapse speculative merging Rank the four levers correctly, because 'add more runners' is the weakest one Ship a gate that proves an agent's test actually fails without the agent's fix Quarantine flakes on evidence instead of vibes, and know the caching gotcha that silently poisons CI Your coding agents work. That is the problem. A team that merged 5 pull requests a day and now merges 40 has not changed its test suite, its runner budget, or its branch protection rules. It has changed the arrival rate into a queueing system that was tuned for the old one. Everything downstream — merge queue, flaky-test noise, runner concurrency, review attention — was sized for human throughput, and queueing systems do not degrade gracefully. They hold, hold, hold, then fall over inside a week. This page is the pipeline side of the verification bottleneck. That page asks who checks the code. This one asks whether your CI can physically absorb the volume, and what to do when it can't.

−7.2%. DORA's 2024 Accelerate State of DevOps report modelled a 25% increase in AI adoption and estimated a 7.2% decrease in delivery stability alongside a 1.5% decrease in throughput. Individual productivity and job satisfaction went up. Delivery-level outcomes went down — the report ties this to larger changesets and weaker batching discipline. The 2025 follow-up reframes it: AI is an amplifier, magnifying whatever your delivery system already is. A pipeline that was fragile at 5 PRs/day becomes unusable at 40. 19%. METR's randomised trial (July 2025) took 16 experienced open-source maintainers and 246 real issues from their own repositories, randomising whether AI tools were allowed. With AI, tasks took 19% longer. The gap that matters for CI planning is the perceptual one: developers predicted a 24% speed-up, and after the slowdown still believed they had been sped up by 20%. Nobody on your team will tell you the pipeline is the constraint, because nobody experiences it as one — they experience it as "waiting", which feels like weather. 1.5% / 16% / 84%. Google's published flakiness data: roughly 1.5% of test runs report a flaky result; about 16% of their 4.2M tests have shown flakiness at some point; and around 84% of observed pass→fail transitions involve a flaky test rather than a real regression. Hold onto that 1.5% — it is small enough to ignore at 5 PRs/day and load-bearing at 40.
documents.s: Three numbers that frame the whole problem

documents.t: Most teams assume the ceiling is compute. It isn't. It's the merge queue, and the reason is a mechanism most people have never read the docs for. GitHub's merge queue does speculative checking. Queue PRs #1, #2, #3 and it builds temporary branches: main + #1, main + #1 + #2, main + #1 + #2 + #3 — and tests all of them in parallel. If every check passes, all three land in one round. That is the whole value proposition: batching turns N serial validations into one. Now read the failure path. When a check fails for the group containing PR #1, GitHub removes #1 from the queue — and every group behind it contained #1's changes, so those groups are invalid and get rebuilt without it. One bad PR does not cost you one slot. It costs you the rest of the batch's CI round. That makes queue throughput a function of your pass rate, and it's steeper than intuition suggests. Model it: batch size N, each PR independently failing with probability p, and you merge the run of PRs up to the first failure. Expected merges per round is a geometric expectation: E[merges] = (1 − p) · (1 − (1 − p)^N) / p With N = 10: Per-PR failure rate p Expected merges per round Rounds to clear 10 PRs 2% 8.9 ~1.1 5% 7.6 ~1.3 10% 5.9 ~1.7 20% 3.6 ~2.8 30% 2.3 ~4.4 Two consequences most teams get backwards: A flaky suite is a throughput tax, not a nuisance tax. Flakiness adds directly to p. Going from 5% real failures to 5% real + 5% flake takes you from 7.6 merges per round to 5.9 — roughly 23% of your merge capacity, lost to tests that were never testing anything. Raising the batch size is the wrong lever when p is high. Bigger N only helps when (1 − p)^N stays near 1. At p = 0.2, a batch of 10 delivers 3.6 merges; the fix is lowering p, not queueing more optimism. And agent volume pushes p the wrong way — DORA's stability finding is exactly a statement about p rising.
documents.s: Why the merge queue breaks first

documents.t: Do this on a napkin before you buy runners. Assumptions stated, because they're what make it wrong for your team: Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Count job-minutes, not wall-clock⌄ A 45-minute suite fanned out into 15 parallel jobs still costs ~45 job-minutes. Parallelism buys latency, never cost. Take your suite's total job-minutes from a recent run, not from the slowest job. ←PreviousNext→ 2Multiply by validations per PR, not by PRs⌄ With a merge queue every PR is validated at least twice: once on the PR branch, once inside a merge group. Reruns and rebuilds from the p-math above add more. Budget 2.5x as a floor, not 1x. ←PreviousNext→ 3Divide by the burst window, not the day⌄ 40 PRs x 2.5 validations x 45 job-min = 4,500 job-minutes. Spread over 24 hours that is trivial. It does not arrive over 24 hours — it arrives in two or three hours around review time. 4,500 job-min into a 2-hour window needs ~37 sustained concurrent jobs. ←PreviousNext→ 4Compare against your plan's hard ceiling⌄ GitHub-hosted standard runners cap total concurrent jobs at 20 (Free), 40 (Pro), 60 (Team) and 500 (Enterprise). The napkin above quietly exceeds Free and sits on top of Pro — during the burst, which is the only window that matters. ←PreviousNext→ 5Find the silent failure⌄ A queued job is cancelled after 24 hours. On a saturated queue this shows up as jobs that never ran rather than jobs that failed, which is far harder to notice and does not page anyone. ←PreviousNext→ The takeaway is not "buy Enterprise". It's that the constraint is burst concurrency, and the daily-average number that makes your pipeline look fine is the number hiding the problem.

Teams reach for these in almost exactly the reverse of the useful order. 1. Lower p (highest leverage, lowest cost). Every point of failure rate removed pays off nonlinearly in the batching math. Concretely: make agents run the fast suite locally before opening a PR, require a green pre-merge check before a PR is allowed into the queue, and quarantine flakes aggressively (below). This costs no compute. 2. Cut the work per validation — test selection. This is the only lever that changes the exponent rather than the constant. Instead of running everything, run what the change can plausibly break: Develocity Predictive Test Selection builds a model from your own Build Scan history plus cross-project patterns, and ships a simulator so you can measure the savings and the missed-failure rate before enabling it. Two safety details worth stealing even if you never buy it: you can pin must-run tests by class pattern or annotation, and it always selects recently flaky tests, because a flaky test is by definition unpredictable from the change. Pair it with a "remaining tests" run post-merge or nightly so nothing is skipped forever. Bazel / Buck2 get this structurally: the build graph knows which targets depend on the changed files, so bazel test on affected targets is target determination for free. No build graph? Python has pytest-testmon, which records which tests cover which code and re-runs only the affected ones. Jest ships --changedSince out of the box. Test selection, three ecosystems CopyOpen in Claude↗ # Bazel — test only what the diff can reach bazel test $(bazel query "rdeps(//..., set($(git diff --name-only origin/main)))" --output=label 2>/dev/null) # Python — coverage-based impact analysis pip install pytest-testmon pytest --testmon # first run builds the DB, later runs select # Jest — built in, no plugin npx jest --changedSince=origin/main 3. Cache aggressively — and know the gotcha. Remote caching stores action results keyed by a hash of inputs, command line and whitelisted environment. Bazel's own docs flag the trap: tools outside the workspace are not tracked, so two machines with different compiler versions can get a cache hit on work that would have produced different outputs. Whitelist what matters with --action_env, and keep write access to CI only — developer machines should read: Remote cache, CI-writes-only CopyOpen in Claude↗ # CI: read and write bazel test //... --remote_cache=grpcs://cache.internal:443 # Developer machines: read only, never poison the shared cache bazel test //... --remote_cache=grpcs://cache.internal:443 \ --remote_upload_local_results=false 4. Add runners (last). Linear cost, linear benefit, and it does nothing about p. Do it after the first three, when you actually know your burst concurrency number.

Everything above applies to any high-volume pipeline. This one is specific to agent-written code, and it is the gap most CI setups have. When the same agent writes the fix and the test for the fix, "tests pass" carries much less information than you think. Two failure shapes show up constantly: The test asserts the behaviour of the implementation rather than the requirement — it passes because it was written by reading the code it is testing. The agent, when a pre-existing test fails, edits the test to match the new behaviour instead of fixing the code. The diff is green and the regression shipped. That behaviour has a name and a literature — see reward hacking in coding agents for why models do it and which defenses have measured effect sizes. What follows is the pipeline-side control, not the model-side one. The cheap structural gate: a new test must fail against the pre-change code. That's the red-green discipline of TDD turned into a machine check, and it's what mutation testing formalises at scale. You do not need a mutation-testing framework to get most of the value — you need one CI job: CI gate: new tests must fail without the change CopyOpen in Claude↗ #!/usr/bin/env bash # must-fail-first.sh — run in CI on PRs that add tests set -euo pipefail NEW_TESTS=$(git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD -- 'tests/**' 'test/**') [ -z "$NEW_TESTS" ] && { echo "no new tests, skipping"; exit 0; } # Keep the new tests, revert everything else to the base commit git stash push --keep-index -- $NEW_TESTS git checkout origin/main -- src/ git stash pop # The new tests MUST fail now. If they pass, they prove nothing. if pytest $NEW_TESTS -q; then echo "FAIL: new tests pass against unmodified source — they do not test the change." exit 1 fi echo "OK: new tests fail without the fix." Two honest caveats. It only works when source and tests live in separate trees, and a test that fails for the wrong reason (import error, missing fixture) passes this gate. It is a floor, not a proof — but it catches the single most common way an agent-authored PR is green and worthless. The complementary review-side control is a reviewer that doesn't share the author's context: see the hybrid AI code reviewer and the PR-review GitHub Action.
documents.s: The AI-specific failure mode: the agent grades its own homework

documents.t: Given 84% of pass→fail transitions are flakes, "rerun it" is the default human response and it is the most expensive one available — it burns a full validation on a test that was never going to tell you anything. Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Measure before you judge⌄ A flaky test is one that produces different results on the same commit. Run the suite N times on an unchanged main and record per-test failure counts. That is your evidence; developer memory is not. ←PreviousNext→ 2Quarantine on a threshold, not an argument⌄ Anything above your threshold moves to a non-blocking job that still runs and still reports. It stops gating merges immediately — that is the throughput win — and it stays visible so it does not become dead code. ←PreviousNext→ 3Cap the quarantine and give it an owner⌄ An uncapped quarantine is a graveyard. Fixed budget (say 1% of tests), a name attached, an expiry date. Over budget means the next flake evicts the oldest one back into blocking. ←PreviousNext→ 4Never let test selection skip a flake⌄ This is the counter-intuitive rule Develocity encodes: recently-flaky tests are always selected, because the model cannot predict them from the diff. Selecting away your flakes hides the signal you need to fix them. ←PreviousNext→ 5Re-derive p after each round⌄ Recompute your per-PR failure rate monthly and put it on the dashboard next to merge-queue throughput. It is the one number that tells you whether the pipeline is getting better or the agents are just getting louder. ←PreviousNext→
documents.s: Flake quarantine that survives contact with agents

documents.t: merge_group is not automatic. GitHub's docs are explicit: you must add the merge_group event to your workflow triggers, or your checks never fire inside the queue and merges fail on missing required checks. This is the single most common merge-queue misconfiguration. The 24-hour queue cancellation is silent. Saturated queue → jobs vanish rather than fail. Alert on queue depth, not just on red builds. Matrix jobs cap at 256 per workflow run. Generated matrices (a common agent-scaffolding pattern) hit this without a useful error. Cross-machine cache hits can be wrong. Untracked external toolchains produce false hits. Pin toolchains, whitelist environment with --action_env. Branch protection with wildcard patterns is incompatible with merge queues. If your protection rules use wildcards, the queue will not engage. Agent PRs touching CI are a security boundary, not a style question. A PR that can edit workflow files can exfiltrate CI secrets — see GitHub issue → CI secrets and hardening autonomous runs.
documents.s: Gotchas that cost a day each

documents.t: There is no configuration that makes a pipeline absorb unbounded agent output. What the levers above buy you is a system whose cost grows with the size of the change rather than the number of pull requests — test selection and caching are sublinear, runners are linear, and merge-queue batching is only sublinear while your pass rate stays high. Which puts the real constraint back where DORA's 2025 framing puts it: AI amplifies the delivery system you already have. If small batches, fast suites and low flakiness were already your practice, agents make you much faster. If they weren't, agents find out. Check yourself 0/6 Key takeaways The merge queue breaks before the runner budget does. Speculative batching is a bet on your pass rate, and one failing PR invalidates every group behind it. Compute E[merges] = (1 − p)(1 − (1 − p)^N)/p once for your real numbers. It turns 'CI feels slow' into a decision about which lever to pull. Flakiness is throughput, not hygiene. At Google's published rates the noise is bigger than the signal — 84% of pass→fail transitions are flakes. Size for burst concurrency, never daily average. The daily number is the one hiding the problem, and a saturated queue cancels jobs silently at 24 hours. Test selection is the only sublinear lever: Bazel/Buck2 target determination, Develocity PTS with its simulator, pytest-testmon, or jest --changedSince. When the agent writes both the fix and the test, green means less than you think. Gate on the test failing against pre-change source. DORA's framing holds: AI amplifies the delivery system you already have. Small batches, fast suites and low flake were always the advice — agents just made ignoring it expensive.

Copy as Markdown All levels What you'll learn Know what AI coding is genuinely great at — explain, generate, refactor, debug, translate, review Run the golden loop: context in, plan, generate, read, run — and loop failures back as fresh context Reach for prompts that pull their weight instead of vague one-liners Internalize the two hard rules: verify by running, and never paste secrets Whether you're learning to code or shipping production software, AI changes the loop. The winners treat it as a fast, knowledgeable pair — and verify everything it produces.

Explain unfamiliar code or errors in plain language. Generate boilerplate, tests, and first drafts of functions. Refactor for clarity, and debug by reasoning about a stack trace. Translate between languages/frameworks. Review a diff for bugs and smells. For real codebases, do this in your repo with Claude Code, which can read files, run tests, and edit with your approval.

Give context — the relevant code, the error, what you expected vs. got. Vague in, vague out. Ask for a plan on non-trivial changes before edits (Plan Mode). Generate the change. Read it — understand before you accept. You own the code. Run it — tests/lint/build. Never trust "this works" without running it. The step that separates good results from bad ones is the arrow back to the top: when a test fails, you don't patch blindly — you feed the failure back in as fresh context.

Explain code + spot the edge cases CopyOpen in Claude↗ Explain what this function does and any edge cases it mishandles: {code} Generate tests CopyOpen in Claude↗ Write tests for {function}. Cover the happy path and the edge cases. {code} Debug from a stack trace CopyOpen in Claude↗ This throws {error}. Here's the code and stack trace. Find the root cause and propose a minimal fix. {context}

:::warning Verify, and protect your secrets Run and review generated code — it can be subtly wrong or invent APIs that don't exist. Never paste secrets/keys into a prompt (Privacy). For agentic/automated coding, lock down permissions and read Securing Agents. ::: Check yourself 0/3 Key takeaways Treat AI as a fast, knowledgeable pair — then verify everything it produces by actually running it Context in, quality out: give the code, the error, and expected-vs-actual, never a vague ask Ask for a plan before non-trivial edits so you review the approach before any code changes Read generated code before accepting — it can be subtly wrong or invent APIs that don't exist Never paste secrets or keys into a prompt, and lock down permissions before letting an agent code on its own

Copy as Markdown All levels What you'll learn Describe a dataset the way a model needs it — columns, types, and the grain Run the five-step safe workflow: describe, ask, generate, execute yourself, interpret Treat any number the model did not compute as unverified State the four assumptions that silently change a result: nulls, dedup, time zones, currency Keep sensitive data out of tools you have not vetted You don't need to be a data scientist to get answers from data with AI — but you do need to keep it honest. AI writes the query and explains the result; you confirm the numbers are real.

Write SQL / spreadsheet formulas / pandas from a plain-language question. Explain what a query or result means in business terms. Clean & transform messy data (describe the mess, get steps). Suggest the right chart for the question. Interpret output and propose the next question.

Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Describe your data⌄ Columns, types, and the GRAIN — one row equals what, exactly? Don't assume the model can guess your names or that order_id is unique. Most wrong queries are wrong about the grain, not the SQL. ←PreviousNext→ 2State the question the analysis should answer⌄ In business terms, with the time range and the filter spelled out. 'Monthly revenue from completed orders in 2025' is answerable; 'how are sales doing' is not. ←PreviousNext→ 3Get the query plus a one-line explanation of what it does and its assumptions⌄ The explanation is the part you review. If the stated assumptions don't match your data, the query is wrong no matter how clean it looks. ←PreviousNext→ 4Run it yourself on the real data⌄ This is the non-negotiable step. A model that reports a result without executing against your data is guessing at a plausible number. ←PreviousNext→ 5Bring the results back for plain-language interpretation and caveats⌄ Paste the actual output. Now the model is reading numbers instead of inventing them, which is the one thing it is reliably good at here. ←PreviousNext→ Describe the grain, then ask — SQL with stated assumptions CopyOpen in Claude↗ My table orders has columns: order_id, customer_id, created_at, total_eur, status. One row per order. Write SQL for monthly revenue from completed orders in 2025, and explain any assumptions. Hand the output back — interpretation with caveats CopyOpen in Claude↗ Here is the result of that query. Interpret it in business terms in under 120 words, then list anything that could make these numbers misleading — nulls, duplicate rows, time zone of created_at, mixed currencies, or partial months. Label each as "checked" or "unverified". Result: [paste the rows]

:::warning Never trust numbers it didn't compute If the AI states a result without running the query on your data, that number may be invented. Run queries yourself; treat any figure you didn't compute as unverified. And remember correlation ≠ causation — ask it to flag associational claims. See Hallucinations. ::: Sanity-check magnitudes — implausible result? investigate, don't publish. State assumptions (nulls, dedup, time zones, currency). Don't paste sensitive/PII data into tools you haven't vetted (Privacy). Those four assumptions are listed in a specific order because that is roughly how often they bite. Nulls silently shrink a denominator; duplicate rows silently inflate a sum; a timestamp stored in UTC and read as local time moves revenue across a month boundary; and a total column that mixes currencies produces a number that is arithmetically correct and economically meaningless. Pro tip Ask for the query AND a second query that sanity-checks it — a row count, a date range, a sum you can eyeball. Two cheap queries beat one elegant one you cannot verify. When a result surprises you, suspect the join before you suspect the business. A fan-out join is the most common source of a number that is suddenly 3× too big. For spreadsheet work, ask for the formula plus one worked example cell. If the example is wrong, you have found the bug without touching your real file.
Check yourself 0/3

Key takeaways Describe columns, types, and the GRAIN first — grain errors beat syntax errors for frequency and cost Always ask for the query's assumptions, and review those before the SQL Run it yourself. A number the model did not compute is unverified by definition Hand the real output back for interpretation — reading numbers is the part AI is reliably good at Nulls, duplicate rows, time zones, and mixed currencies are the four quiet result-changers Sanity-check magnitudes and row counts; suspect the join when a total jumps Keep PII out of tools you have not vetted

Copy as Markdown Advanced Last verified: 2026-07-24. Anthropic's evaluation guide is the source of truth for methodology (SMART criteria, exact-match, LLM-graded Likert/binary). Agent-trajectory eval is an emerging discipline — treat framework names as illustrative and confirm APIs at each vendor's docs. Confirm against the official source. What you'll learn Understand why agent evals differ from prompt evals — trajectory matters, not just the final answer Build a golden set of 20–100 real cases with clear pass criteria Score four layers: tool-call correctness, trajectory quality, task success, production drift Use LLM-as-judge safely: rubric first, calibrate against humans, spot-check verdicts Ship an eval that runs in CI and fails a bad change before it reaches users An agent eval answers a harder question than "did the prompt return the right words?" It asks: did a model running in a loop pick the right tools, in the right order, with the right arguments, arrive at the right outcome — and stay within budget and safety bounds? Skip this step and you'll ship a "helpful" agent that quietly regresses every time you tweak the system prompt.

A single-prompt eval scores one input → one output. An agent produces a trajectory: a chain of reasoning, tool calls, intermediate observations, and revisions across many turns. Two failure modes make this hard: Right answer, wrong path. The agent stumbles onto the correct output after wasteful loops, unsafe actions, or lucky guesses. Final-answer-only evals mark this a pass; production won't. Wrong answer, plausible path. Every step looks reasonable in isolation, but the agent misused a tool, ignored a constraint, or hallucinated an intermediate fact. You need to look at the trace, not just the reply.
documents.s: Why agents need their own evals

documents.t: Layer them cheapest-first so a bad change fails fast without waiting for expensive graders. Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Layer 1 — Tool-call correctness (deterministic)⌄ For each expected step, check tool name matches, required parameters are present, and types validate. Pure code, milliseconds, no model needed. Catches 'called search when it should have called write_file' before anything else runs. ←PreviousNext→ 2Layer 2 — Trajectory quality (rubric + LLM-judge)⌄ Score the full trace: did the agent take a sensible path, or wander, loop, or backtrack? Number of steps vs. minimum needed, redundant calls, retries after tool errors, whether it stopped when done. Use an LLM judge with an explicit rubric here. ←PreviousNext→ 3Layer 3 — Task success (end-to-end)⌄ Did the goal get met? Deterministic where possible (schema valid, file written, test passes), LLM-judged where fuzzy (summary faithful, answer helpful). This is your headline number. ←PreviousNext→ 4Layer 4 — Production drift & safety⌄ In prod, sample real traces and re-grade a slice. Watch intervention rate (how often a human had to step in), refusal rate, and cost per successful task. When these shift, your model, tools, or inputs changed underneath you. ←PreviousNext→

Not every metric belongs on the dashboard. These five drive shipping decisions in 2026: Metric What it measures Why it matters Task success rate % of golden-set cases the agent finishes correctly The headline. Everything else is diagnostic. Cost per successful task $ / passing case (tokens in + out, tool costs) Success at 10× the cost is a regression. Latency (p50 / p95) Wall-clock per task, tail included p95 is what real users feel — averages lie. Tool-call accuracy % of expected tool calls with correct name + args Predicts trajectory quality; cheap to compute. Intervention rate % of tasks needing human takeover in prod The autonomy number. Rising = trust falling. Track them together — one moving without the others is usually a leading signal, not noise.

Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Mine real inputs⌄ Pull 20–100 tasks from actual usage (logs, support tickets, user requests). Cover the frequent easy path, the tricky middle, and the edge cases that already bit you. ←PreviousNext→ 2Write pass criteria per case⌄ For each: what does 'done' look like? Exact expected output, required facts, valid JSON schema, files that must exist, or a rubric for fuzzy cases. If you can't write the criterion, the case is unusable — cut or clarify it. ←PreviousNext→ 3Annotate the ideal trajectory⌄ For a subset, sketch the tool sequence a good agent would take. This is what Layer 1 checks against. ←PreviousNext→ 4Freeze it, version it⌄ Commit the set to your repo. Never edit a case in place — add v2 alongside v1 so score history stays comparable. ←PreviousNext→ 5Grow it from failures⌄ Every prod bug becomes a new eval case before you fix it. That's how the set stays predictive instead of decaying. ←PreviousNext→

Grading fuzzy outputs by hand doesn't scale. A capable model reading against an explicit rubric does — Anthropic's own eval methodology guide recommends this pattern for tone, faithfulness, helpfulness, and safety. Judges have well-documented biases: they prefer longer answers, the first option shown, and outputs that echo their own phrasing. Three habits keep them honest: Rubric, not vibes. "Rate helpfulness 1–5" is useless. Anchor every point on the scale to observable behavior. Calibrate on a human-labeled sample. Have humans grade 30–50 cases; measure judge-vs-human agreement (aim for Cohen's κ ≥ 0.6). If it disagrees, tighten the rubric. Use a different model as judge. Grading with the same model that produced the output leaks bias in both directions. Spot-check verdicts weekly. Read 10 random judge scores and their reasoning. It's the cheapest way to catch drift. LLM-as-judge rubric template CopyOpen in Claude↗ You are grading an AI assistant's response against a rubric. Be strict. Cite exact evidence from the response. <task>{task}</task> <response>{response}</response> Rubric (rate 1–5 per dimension): - Task completion: 1 = ignored task; 3 = partial; 5 = fully done, no gaps. - Faithfulness: 1 = contains false claims; 3 = mostly grounded, one soft claim; 5 = every claim traceable to input/tools. - Efficiency: 1 = wandered/looped; 3 = extra steps; 5 = minimum viable path. Output JSON only: {"task_completion": N, "faithfulness": N, "efficiency": N, "evidence": "<quote>", "verdict": "pass"|"fail"} Trajectory review prompt (Layer 2) CopyOpen in Claude↗ You are auditing an AI agent's tool-call trajectory. The goal was: {goal} Expected minimum steps: {n_min} <trajectory> {list of tool_name(args) -> result, in order} </trajectory> Answer in JSON: {"steps_taken": N, "wasted_steps": N, "wrong_tool_calls": [<indices>], "unsafe_actions": [<indices>], "verdict": "pass"|"fail", "reason": "<one sentence>"} Adversarial case generator (grow the set) CopyOpen in Claude↗ Generate 5 new eval cases that are likely to break an agent whose current failures cluster around: {failure_pattern}. For each case give: input, expected output OR pass criterion, ideal tool sequence, and why this case is hard. Return YAML.
documents.s: LLM-as-judge — cheap, fast, but calibrate it

documents.t: The eval only pays off when it blocks regressions automatically. Wire it into CI as a check on every prompt / model / tool change: # tests/eval_gate.py — runs on every PR import json, sys from anthropic import Anthropic from my_agent import run_agent client = Anthropic() golden = json.load(open("evals/golden.v3.json")) results = [] for case in golden: trace = run_agent(case["input"]) layer1 = tool_calls_match(trace, case["expected_tools"]) # deterministic layer3 = judge(client, case, trace.final_output) # LLM rubric results.append({"id": case["id"], "layer1": layer1, "layer3": layer3["verdict"]}) pass_rate = sum(r["layer3"] == "pass" for r in results) / len(results) tool_acc = sum(r["layer1"] for r in results) / len(results) # Gates — tighten over time assert pass_rate >= 0.85, f"Task success dropped to {pass_rate:.0%}" assert tool_acc >= 0.90, f"Tool-call accuracy dropped to {tool_acc:.0%}" print(f"PASS: task={pass_rate:.0%} tools={tool_acc:.0%}") Store per-run scores so you can chart the trend. A drop of 3+ points between merges is a real regression, not noise. Anti-patterns that make evals under-deliver Judging the final answer only — misses every trajectory bug. Score Layers 1 and 2 too. Static golden set — if it doesn't grow with every prod failure it stops predicting prod. Budget time monthly. Same model as agent and judge — bias in both directions. Rotate to a different model for grading. No cost or latency in the gate — a prompt tweak that adds 8 tool calls can 'pass' the eval while 10×-ing the bill. Vibes-only scoring — 'feels better' is not a metric. If you can't diff two numbers, you can't ship confidently. Key takeaways Agents produce trajectories, not answers — evaluate the path, not only the outcome Layer cheapest-first: tool-call correctness → trajectory quality → task success → production drift The five metrics that ship decisions: task success rate, cost per success, p50/p95 latency, tool-call accuracy, intervention rate LLM-as-judge scales, but only with an explicit rubric, a different model, and calibration against human labels A golden set that doesn't grow from prod failures stops predicting prod — grow it monthly Wire the eval into CI as a hard gate — the check that catches a regression before users do

Copy as Markdown All levels AI can be the patient, infinitely-available tutor most of us never had — if you use it to understand, not to outsource thinking. The difference between learning and cheating is the workflow.

Explain like I'm new. "Explain [concept] simply, with one analogy and one example." Then go deeper in layers. Socratic tutoring. "Don't give me the answer — ask me questions that lead me to it." Teach-back. Explain it, then you restate it; the AI corrects your gaps. This is where real learning sticks. Quiz me. "Generate 5 questions on [topic], then grade my answers and explain the misses." Study plan. "I have 2 weeks for [exam]. Build a plan and drill my weak spots."

Tutor me on {topic}. Start by asking what I already know, then teach one step at a time and check my understanding before moving on. Don't just give answers. I'll explain {concept} back to you. Point out anything wrong or missing, kindly and specifically. Here's my explanation: {your attempt}

:::warning For graded work, get guidance — not the answer key If you paste homework and copy the output, you didn't learn it (and may break your school's rules). Ask for hints, checks, and explanations that get you to the answer. Own the result. ::: Verify facts — tutors can be confidently wrong; cross-check key claims (Hallucinations). One concept at a time — depth beats breadth. Spaced practice — come back and re-quiz; that's what makes it stick.
documents.s: Use it to learn, not to cheat

documents.t: For dyslexia, language learning, or focus differences, AI can rephrase, simplify, translate, and pace patiently — see Accessibility.

Copy as Markdown Beginner Five things almost anyone can use today. Each comes with a starter prompt — paste it, swap the brackets, refine in plain language.

"Here's an email I received. Draft a polite, concise reply that [accepts the meeting but proposes Thursday instead]. Keep it under 80 words. Email: [paste]" Follow-ups that help: "more formal," "add a line thanking them," "give me two versions."

"Summarise this in 5 bullet points a busy manager could read in 30 seconds, then list any decisions or action items separately. Text: [paste]" Works on articles, meeting notes, threads, and reports. For very long inputs, ask for the summary first, then drill in.

"I need to [organise a 30-person team offsite] by [October]. Give me a step-by-step plan with rough timing, and flag the 3 things most likely to go wrong." Great for project plans, checklists, and turning a vague goal into next actions.

"I'm deciding between [option A] and [option B] for [situation]. Lay out the trade-offs in a table, then tell me what else I should consider before deciding." Use it as a sparring partner — ask it to argue the opposite case to pressure-test your thinking.

"Write a first draft of [a LinkedIn post announcing our new feature]. Match this voice: [paste a paragraph you wrote]. Then suggest a punchier opening line." Giving a sample of your writing is the secret to outputs that don't sound generic.

:::tip Give context, then iterate Every prompt above names the goal, format, and constraints — that's Prompting Basics. And none of them have to be right first try; refine in plain language. ::: :::warning Verify anything factual Dates, numbers, names, quotes, and "facts" can be confidently wrong. For anything that matters, check it — see Hallucinations. :::

Copy as Markdown All levels What you'll learn Use the five research moves that actually pay off — summarize, compare, map, extract, pressure-test Write a grounded prompt that forbids outside knowledge and demands a supporting quote per claim Spot a fabricated citation before it reaches your document Run the five-step research flow, from gathering sources to spot-checking the critical facts Keep stated facts and model inference visibly separate in your notes AI is a superb research accelerator — and a dangerous one if you trust it blindly. Used right, it compresses hours of reading into minutes; used carelessly, it confidently invents sources. Here's the disciplined version.

Summarize a long document/paper into key points + implications. Compare multiple sources into a table (what they agree/disagree on). Build a landscape — map the players, approaches, or arguments on a topic. Extract specific facts/figures from a document (with citations). Pressure-test — "what's the strongest counterargument to this?"

Grounded summary — quote-per-claim, 'not stated' allowed CopyOpen in Claude↗ Using ONLY the text I provide, summarize the key findings and quote the exact sentence supporting each one. If something isn't in the text, say "not stated." Text: """[paste]""" Feed it the sources. Don't ask it to recall facts from memory for anything important — paste the material or use a tool that retrieves it (RAG). Demand citations. "Quote the sentence that supports each claim." Unsupported claims become visible. Separate fact from inference. Ask it to label what's stated vs. interpreted. The third one is the move most people skip, and it is the cheapest. A summary that mixes "the paper reports X" with "which suggests Y" reads fine and is useless for checking, because you can no longer tell which half you need to verify. Fact vs. inference — force the two apart CopyOpen in Claude↗ From the text below, produce two separate lists: STATED — claims the text makes explicitly, each with the exact supporting sentence. INFERRED — anything you concluded that the text does not say outright, each with what it is based on and how confident you are. Put nothing in STATED that you cannot quote. Text: """[paste]""" :::warning Fabricated citations are the classic trap Models invent realistic-looking papers, authors, and URLs. Verify every citation exists before you rely on it. See Hallucinations. ::: A fabricated citation rarely looks wrong. It looks exactly right: a plausible author pair, a real-sounding journal, a year that fits. Which is why the only reliable check is mechanical — resolve the citation, don't evaluate it. Three signals that something needs resolving before you cite it: a DOI or URL that 404s, a title you cannot find anywhere but the model's answer, and a paper quoted for a claim that is slightly too perfect a fit for your argument.

Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Gather sources yourself⌄ Collect the material, or point a retrieval tool at it. This is the step that decides whether the rest of the work is grounded or improvised. ←PreviousNext→ 2Summarize each with grounding + citations⌄ One source at a time, with the quote-per-claim prompt above. Summarizing five sources in one prompt is how claims drift between them. ←PreviousNext→ 3Synthesize across them into a themed comparison⌄ Ask for a table: themes as rows, sources as columns, and an explicit cell for 'does not address this'. The empty cells are often the finding. ←PreviousNext→ 4Identify gaps and disagreements, then the 'so what'⌄ Where sources disagree, report the disagreement rather than letting the model resolve it silently — a split verdict is information. ←PreviousNext→ 5Spot-check the critical facts against the originals⌄ Not every fact: the ones your conclusion rests on. If a number would change your recommendation, open the source and read it yourself. ←PreviousNext→ Pro tip Ask for the strongest counterargument in a separate turn, not as part of the summary. Bundled together, the model tends to produce a counterargument it has already defeated. Keep the source text in the conversation for as long as you are asking questions about it. Once it scrolls out of context, answers quietly shift from reading to remembering. When comparing sources, give each one a short label (S1, S2, …) and require every claim to carry its label. Unlabeled claims are the model's own voice, and they are now easy to spot.
Check yourself 0/3

Key takeaways Feed the sources; never let an important fact come from the model's memory Demand a supporting quote per claim, and sanction 'not stated' so gaps become visible Keep STATED and INFERRED in separate lists — mixed, neither can be checked Resolve citations mechanically. A fabricated one looks exactly right by design Report disagreement between sources instead of asking the model to settle it Spot-check the facts your conclusion depends on, in the original

Copy as Markdown All levels What you'll learn Go from blank page to a strong draft in your voice — fast Give the model the four things it actually needs: goal, audience, format, voice sample Edit in single-purpose passes instead of one vague 'improve this' Repurpose one piece into five, without the flattening AI usually does Never publish a fabricated fact — mark and verify every claim AI is a phenomenal writing partner if you direct it. The goal isn't to push a button and publish — it's to compress the blank-page-to-strong-draft loop, then sharpen with your own judgment. This page is the workflow, the prompts, and the traps.

Six steps. Skip any of them and quality drops sharply. Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Brief it — goal, audience, format, tone⌄ One paragraph. 'A 600-word blog intro for first-time founders, encouraging but not saccharine, no startup jargon. Hook in the first sentence.' Ambiguity in the brief becomes generic AI voice in the draft. ←PreviousNext→ 2Outline first — approve the structure⌄ Anything longer than a few paragraphs: ask for a bullet outline before prose. Kill weak sections at outline stage — they cost seconds to rewrite; a full draft costs minutes and momentum. ←PreviousNext→ 3Draft — one clean pass, don't over-steer⌄ Let it write the whole draft with the brief and outline. Don't interrupt mid-generation with corrections; that produces stitched, incoherent prose. ←PreviousNext→ 4Edit in single-purpose passes⌄ One goal per pass: 'tighten to 400 words', then 'replace abstract claims with concrete examples', then 'cut the throat-clearing opening'. Vague 'make it better' gives you a different mediocre draft. ←PreviousNext→ 5Match your voice — the biggest lever⌄ Paste 300–500 words you wrote yourself. 'Rewrite in this voice — same sentence rhythm, same vocabulary, same restraint.' This single move separates good AI writing from the recognizable AI slop. ←PreviousNext→ 6Verify facts, then publish⌄ Ask the model to mark every stat, quote, name, and source claim with [verify]. Check each one against a primary source. Do not skip. See traps below. ←PreviousNext→

First-draft brief with voice sample CopyOpen in Claude↗ Write a {FORMAT} of {LENGTH} for {AUDIENCE}. Purpose: {ONE-SENTENCE GOAL}. Tone: {THREE ADJECTIVES}. Avoid: {LIST}. Here are 300 words I wrote — match this voice. Same sentence rhythm, same vocabulary, same restraint. Do not "improve" it toward a generic professional voice. <voice_sample> {PASTE A PARAGRAPH OR TWO YOU WROTE} </voice_sample> Mark every factual claim, statistic, quote, or attributed source with [verify] at the end of the sentence, so I can check it before publishing.

Editing pass with visible diff CopyOpen in Claude↗ Edit this text for {ONE GOAL — pick one: clarity, concision, concreteness, rhythm, cutting jargon}. Do not change the meaning or reorder arguments. After the edited version, list every change as a bullet: "removed X", "replaced Y with Z", "cut sentence about W". <text> {PASTE} </text> Ask for the change list. It forces the model to make deliberate edits rather than silently rewriting to its own taste — and it lets you veto any change you disagree with.

Outline before prose CopyOpen in Claude↗ I'm writing a {2000-word essay} on {topic} for {audience}. The argument is {one-sentence thesis}. Before drafting, give me an outline as bullets: section headings, one line of substance per section, plus the transition between sections. No prose yet. Aim for {N} sections. I'll approve or edit the outline; then you draft.

From one piece to five formats — without flattening CopyOpen in Claude↗ Here's a published piece: <source>{PASTE}</source>. Repurpose it into: 1. A LinkedIn post (~150 words) — one specific insight, not a summary. 2. A Twitter/X thread (5–7 tweets) — start with the strongest hook, one idea per tweet. 3. A newsletter blurb (~80 words) — the "why this matters" angle for busy readers. 4. Three email subject lines that would make me open it. Rules: - Do NOT summarize. Each format should stand alone. - Preserve my voice (match the source's rhythm and vocabulary). - Different hook for each — no reused sentences.

"Match my voice" is worthless without a sample. What actually works: Paste real work, not descriptions. "Confident but casual" is fuzzy; 400 words of your writing is not. Pick a sample close to the target task. Voice shifts between formats — your newsletter voice is not your LinkedIn voice. Reject flattening explicitly. Add: "Do not smooth this toward a generic professional voice. Keep the fragments, the aside asides, the unusual word choices." Iterate on tone knobs. After the first draft: "Half a step more direct. Less hedging. Keep the sentence rhythm." If a model still writes in AI-voice after this, either the sample was too short, the request was too generic, or you're on a model tuned toward the mean — try Fable 5 or Sonnet 5 which handle voice-imitation better than default GPT-family styles.

Trap 1 — Fabricated facts, plausibly delivered CopyOpen in Claude↗ The model invents statistics, quotes, source names, book titles, and even URLs. Confidently. Every one of them.Fix: Force a [verify] marker on every factual claim. Never publish an unverified stat or quote. See Hallucinations for the four levels and how to detect each. Trap 2 — Generic AI voice CopyOpen in Claude↗ Balanced sentences. "Not only… but also…". "It's worth noting that…". "In today's fast-paced world". You know it when you see it.Fix: Voice sample + explicit rejection of smoothing. If it slips back mid-draft, paste the offending paragraph back and say "rewrite this specific paragraph in the voice sample I gave you". Trap 3 — Over-editing into mush CopyOpen in Claude↗ Ten small "make it better" passes flatten the piece toward the mean of the model's training data. You started with a distinctive draft and ended with a competent, unmemorable one.Fix: Single-purpose passes only. When in doubt, stop editing. Trap 4 — The em-dash / bullet tell CopyOpen in Claude↗ Excessive em-dashes, three-bullet lists after every claim, "however" between contrasting sentences. Readers now spot this instantly and discount the piece.Fix: Explicit stylistic constraints — "max two em-dashes per section", "prose only, no bullets in this piece". Or write the framing sentences yourself and only ask the model for the middle. Trap 5 — 'Rewrite this' loops CopyOpen in Claude↗ You keep asking "make it stronger" and the model produces different mediocre drafts because you haven't told it what "stronger" means. Rounds of this waste hours.Fix: Name the specific weakness. "The third paragraph is too abstract — give me a concrete example from a real 2020s startup." "The opening is throat-clearing — start with the punchline." Trap 6 — Publishing without human editing CopyOpen in Claude↗ The model wrote a "good enough" draft. You skimmed and published. Two weeks later you notice the awkward transition, the misused word, the paragraph that says nothing.Fix: Print or read aloud before publishing. AI cannot hear rhythm the way you can.
documents.s: The traps that make writers reject AI

documents.t: Task Best default Why Long-form essay, voice-matched Claude Sonnet 5 or Fable 5 Strongest at rhythm, restraint, and voice imitation Fast blog draft, workmanlike prose Claude Sonnet 5 or GPT-5 Fast, competent, cheap Poetry, narrative fiction, distinctive style Fable 5, then hand-edit Better at unusual voice targets SEO/marketing copy with keyword targets Any frontier model + explicit constraints All roughly equivalent; the brief matters more than the model Editing existing prose Sonnet 5 or Opus 4 Best at surgical single-purpose edits Translation / localization See Porting Prompts Across Models Voice preservation across languages is a distinct skill Cross-provider comparison: ChatGPT for Claude Users and Gemini for Claude Users.

You are the editor. Judgment, taste, and accountability stay with you. Disclose AI assistance where it matters — journalism, academia, contracted work with disclosure clauses. Increasingly, readers assume AI involvement in everything; being explicit about what YOU brought builds trust. Do not pass off fabricated quotes or statistics as researched. This has already ended careers in 2024–2025.
Check yourself 0/3

Key takeaways The brief is the biggest quality lever after voice — goal, audience, format, tone, in one paragraph Outline before prose for anything longer than a few paragraphs — kill weak structure cheap Edit in single-purpose passes with visible change lists; never in vague 'make it better' loops A 300–500 word voice sample plus explicit anti-flattening beats every 'write like me' description Force [verify] tags on every factual claim; check them against primary sources before publishing AI drafts, humans edit and ship — read the final draft aloud before you hit publish

Copy as Markdown Intermediate Last verified: 2026-07-25. Methodology (test-driven prompt/agent design, SMART criteria, exact-match vs. LLM-graded rubric) follows Anthropic's official "Develop tests" guide. The concepts here are model-agnostic and apply equally to OpenAI, Gemini, and open-weight models. Confirm against the official source. What you'll learn Understand what an eval actually is — a repeatable test that scores model output against a fixed rubric Know when a vibe check is fine and when only an eval will do Recognize the four eval types you will actually use, and when each applies Build a minimum viable eval — 20 cases, one rubric, one script — in an afternoon Avoid the six traps that make evals lie to you If you take one habit from this site, take this one. Prompt-craft, model choice, tool wiring — none of it compounds until you can measure whether a change made the system better or worse. Once you can, every future decision — pick Sonnet 5 or Fable 5, add a tool, tighten a system prompt, raise the thinking budget — becomes a five-minute check instead of a week of argument. Evals are how you replace "it feels smarter" with a number that survives disagreement.
documents.s: Evals — The Core Skill That Beats Vibes

documents.t: An eval is three things bolted together: A fixed set of inputs — usually 20 to a few hundred cases drawn from real usage. A rubric or ground truth — for each case, what does "correct" look like? A scoring loop — a script that runs the model on every case, compares output to the rubric, and reports pass/fail (or a graded score) plus cost and latency. Everything else — dashboards, LLM judges, CI gates — is optional scaffolding around that core. Rerun that loop on every change. That is the whole game.

Not every prompt needs an eval. Use judgment. Situation Vibe check OK Build an eval One-off script for yourself Yes — A prompt you'll ship to five colleagues Yes (light) If reliability matters Anything user-facing, at any scale — Yes Anything running unattended (agents, batch jobs) — Yes Any decision to swap models or providers — Yes (or you're guessing) Anything where a wrong answer has cost (money, safety, legal) — Yes (non-negotiable) Rule of thumb: the first time you catch yourself saying "does the new version feel better?", stop and build the eval. The next ten changes will pay for it.
documents.s: When a vibe check is enough — and when it isn't

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Exact-match / structural checks⌄ The output must equal a specific string, match a regex, parse as valid JSON, or match a schema. Cheap, fast, unambiguous. Use for classification, extraction, code that must compile, tool calls, structured output. ←PreviousNext→ 2Rubric grading (human or LLM judge)⌄ The output is scored against an explicit rubric — 'is the summary faithful to the source? Y/N', 'is the tone appropriate? 1–5 with anchors'. Use for writing, summaries, explanations, anywhere quality is fuzzy. ←PreviousNext→ 3Reference-based comparison⌄ Compare against a known good answer using semantic similarity, BLEU/ROUGE, or an LLM asked 'does A convey the same information as B?'. Use for translation, paraphrase, retrieval-augmented answers. ←PreviousNext→ 4Trajectory / process eval⌄ For agents: did it call the right tools in a sensible order, without wandering or unsafe steps? Score the trace, not just the final answer. See the agent-specific playbook for the mechanics. ←PreviousNext→ Real systems mix these — a JSON schema check gates a rubric grade, which gates an end-to-end trajectory check. Cheap layers fail fast; expensive layers only run when cheap ones pass.
documents.s: The four kinds of eval you will use

documents.t: You can have a working eval in an afternoon. Skip everything else on this list first. Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Grab 20 real inputs⌄ From logs, support tickets, or your own use. Cover the common easy path, the tricky middle, and two or three cases that already burned you. Twenty is enough to detect a real regression; hundreds are for later. ←PreviousNext→ 2Write pass criteria per case⌄ One sentence: 'output must include the customer's order number and a refund status of pending/approved/denied' — or 'output must be valid JSON matching schema X'. If you can't write it, the case isn't testable — cut or clarify it. ←PreviousNext→ 3Write a 50-line script⌄ For each case: send the input to the model, capture output and token counts, run the grader, record pass/fail plus cost. A CSV of results is fine — you don't need a UI. ←PreviousNext→ 4Establish a baseline⌄ Run today's prompt against the set. Record the score. That is your bar. Every future change is measured against it. ←PreviousNext→ 5Gate one workflow on it⌄ Wire the script into CI or a pre-deploy check. Any change that drops the score fails the build. Now the eval defends itself — nobody needs to remember to run it. ←PreviousNext→ That's it. Everything after this — LLM judges, calibration, dashboards, cost tracking, per-metric slicing — is amortized over an eval that already exists and already blocks bad changes.

Trap 1 — The golden set is fake CopyOpen in Claude↗ Cases invented by the team, not sampled from real usage. The eval passes; users hit inputs the eval never saw.Fix: Mine cases from actual logs. Every prod bug becomes a new case before you fix it. Trap 2 — The rubric is vibes CopyOpen in Claude↗ "Rate quality 1–5" without anchors. Two graders — human or LLM — disagree wildly, and the score bounces on rerun.Fix: Anchor each point on the scale to observable behavior. "5 = every claim traceable to the source; 3 = one unsupported claim; 1 = three or more unsupported claims." Trap 3 — The LLM judge isn't calibrated CopyOpen in Claude↗ You trust a model to grade because it's cheap. Judges have known biases: they prefer longer answers, first options, and outputs echoing their own phrasing.Fix: Have humans grade 30–50 cases. Measure judge-vs-human agreement (Cohen's kappa at least 0.6). Randomize option order. Spot-check verdicts weekly. Trap 4 — The eval overfits CopyOpen in Claude↗ You keep tweaking the prompt until the score maxes out — on the same 20 cases. Prod tanks.Fix: Split into dev and holdout sets. Never look at holdout scores while iterating. Grow the set from real failures, not synthetic variations. Trap 5 — One number, no cost CopyOpen in Claude↗ The score goes up; the token bill doubles. Or latency jumps to eight seconds. You "shipped an improvement" that regressed the product.Fix: Every run reports score, cost per case, and p50/p95 latency together. A change is only "better" if it doesn't quietly regress two of the three. Trap 6 — Model version drift CopyOpen in Claude↗ You lock the prompt but not the model. The provider ships a silent update; your score walks.Fix: Pin the model version explicitly (a specific dated snapshot, not a floating alias). Rerun the eval on every model bump. See Models & Pricing for the currently pinned families.
documents.s: The six traps that make evals lie

documents.t: You don't need any of these to start — a Python script and a CSV are fine — but once you have a working eval, these save time: Anthropic's evaluation guide — the canonical methodology, aligned with Develop your test cases. Start here even if you use another provider. promptfoo — YAML-defined eval suites, works across Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and open models. Good for side-by-side model comparison. Braintrust / LangSmith / Humanloop — hosted eval platforms with UI, cost tracking, and dataset versioning. Useful once you're grading hundreds of cases per week. Custom scripts — still the most flexible option, especially when your grader is deterministic or domain-specific. Whatever you pick, keep the cases in your own repo, versioned. Tooling is fungible; a curated golden set is the asset.

An eval built once buys you model portability for free. The same 20 cases plus grader plus script that scored Claude Sonnet also scores Fable 5, GPT-5, Gemini 3.6, or a local Qwen — with one line changed. That is why anyone doing serious model selection lives inside their eval, not inside benchmark leaderboards. Public benchmarks answer "which model tops SWE-bench?". Your eval answers "which model handles my users' tickets, at my budget, without drift". Only the second question ships product.
Check yourself 0/3

Key takeaways An eval is a fixed set of cases + a rubric + a scoring loop — everything else is scaffolding Twenty real cases with clear pass criteria beat two hundred synthetic ones Score, cost, and latency together — improving one at the expense of the others is a regression Anchor rubrics to observable behavior; calibrate LLM judges against humans Pin model versions; rerun on every provider update — silent drift is real A good eval is portable: it lets you compare Claude, GPT, Gemini, and local models on YOUR task, not benchmarks

Copy as Markdown Intermediate What you'll learn See exactly what changed in July 2026 — categorized entries replace the daily summary in the app, and a new beta header rewires the API Learn how to view, edit, and delete individual entries in Settings without wiping everything Understand the four behavior changes the agent-memory-2026-07-22 header brings to memory_store endpoints, and why the old cursors stop working Meet the memory_store.* webhooks and Dreams — the parts nobody documents Apply five practical patterns for teaching Claude what to remember (and what to forget) For a year, "Claude's memory" meant a single evolving paragraph the model rewrote each day — good for a bio, bad for anything with structure. Between June and July 2026 Anthropic replaced that with an entry-based model: dozens of small, categorized notes Claude reads and writes in real time. Same idea powers the app and the Managed Agents memory API. This page connects them so you understand both surfaces from one mental model. Last verified: 2026-07-24. The agent-memory-2026-07-22 beta header, the memory_store webhook events, and Dreams model support all changed within the last four weeks. Confirm current beta status and pricing on the platform release notes before shipping. Confirm against the official source.
documents.s: Claude Memory 2026 — Categorized Entries, from App to API

documents.t: Both sides work the same way now: many small entries at named locations, each rewritable in isolation. The old model (one blob per user, rewritten wholesale) is gone in the app and has never been the API surface. Once you internalize "entries at paths, listed by prefix, edited one at a time", both surfaces stop feeling like separate features.
documents.s: The mental model that unifies both sides

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 3 1July 9, 2026 — Monthly recap arrives⌄ A new Settings › Reflect surface starts showing topics you spent time on, your most active day, peak hour, and observations about how you work with Claude. Beta on Free, Pro, and Max (web + Claude Desktop). Requires memory enabled. ←PreviousNext→ 2July 10, 2026 — Categorized entries replace the daily summary⌄ Memory becomes a set of individual, categorized entries that Claude reads and updates during conversations, instead of one rolling daily summary. Announced in the Claude Apps release notes. ←PreviousNext→ 3Rollout — Free / Pro / Max, with Team & Enterprise following⌄ Third-party coverage places availability across Free, Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise, but plan-by-plan wording shifts between Anthropic's help center and news posts. When it matters (compliance, audits), verify in-product for your plan. ←PreviousNext→

The old daily summary had a single failure mode: unrelated context leaked into each other. Fix a fact about your work project and Claude might overwrite something about your writing style. Small, categorized entries fix that structurally — each edit is scoped to one lane. Three consequences most users miss: Retrieval is now targeted, not associative. Claude can pull "your communication preferences" without dragging in the rest of your context. Prompts that used to need "remember I prefer X, not Y" to break through the summary now hit an existing entry directly. You can prune surgically. Delete a single wrong entry in Settings instead of wiping everything and re-teaching Claude who you are. The "burn it all down" tax on correcting one mistake is gone. Categories act as an invisible schema. When Claude decides where an entry belongs (e.g. "communication style" vs. "current project"), it's implicitly choosing whether that fact will be recalled in future personal chats, future work chats, or both. Naming things well up front nudges better recall later.

Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Open Settings › Memory⌄ You'll see entries grouped by category (professional context, communication preferences, ongoing projects, and similar buckets). ←PreviousNext→ 2Edit or delete individual entries⌄ Each entry has its own controls. Fix a wrong fact without touching the rest — the whole reason for the redesign. ←PreviousNext→ 3Steer writes in-chat⌄ Ask Claude to remember, forget, or update specific things ("remember I use Bun, not npm") and it will update the matching entry live. ←PreviousNext→ 4Use incognito for one-offs⌄ An incognito chat is excluded from memory writes and chat history. Use it for anything you don't want persisted — sensitive drafts, one-time explorations, credentials you'd rather not have summarized. ←PreviousNext→ 5Check the monthly recap⌄ Settings › Reflect surfaces what Claude has been talking to you about. Skim it to catch memory drift — if a topic you no longer care about keeps showing up, prune the entries. ←PreviousNext→ Watch out Memory is best-effort recall, not authoritative storage. Never treat it as a source of truth for anything you'd audit (contracts, credentials, medication, legal facts). Restate hard requirements in the prompt or in a Project's instructions.
documents.s: View and manage your own entries

documents.t: 1. Set standing preferences explicitly, once CopyOpen in Claude↗ Please remember these as standing preferences for our chats: - Language: Italian for prose, English for code and error strings. - Units: metric. - Coding style: TypeScript strict, no default exports. - Voice: direct, no filler, no closing "let me know if…". Store each as its own entry in the right category. 2. Correct a single fact without a wipe CopyOpen in Claude↗ Update the memory entry that says I use Vercel for hosting — I moved everything to Cloudflare Workers last month. Leave every other project fact alone. 3. Deliberately forget CopyOpen in Claude↗ Delete any memory entries about the "Project Nightingale" launch — that work is finished and I don't want it surfacing in future chats. 4. Audit what Claude thinks it knows CopyOpen in Claude↗ Before we start, list every memory entry you have about me, grouped by category. Flag anything that looks outdated so I can decide whether to keep or delete it. 5. Sandbox exploratory chats CopyOpen in Claude↗ (Open the chat in Incognito.) Don't try to remember anything from this conversation — I'm just exploring a sensitive draft I don't want stored.

The Managed Agents platform exposes memory as memory stores — collections of memories addressed by path, listed with a path_prefix, and paged with cursors. On July 2, 2026 Anthropic shipped agent-memory-2026-07-22, a beta header that changes the semantics enough to break naive migrations. On July 22, 2026 the older managed-agents-2026-04-01 header adopted the same list behavior — so the "new" rules are now the only rules on memory-store endpoints.
documents.s: Part 2 — In the API: memory_stores and the new beta header

documents.t: # What changed Old behavior New behavior under agent-memory-2026-07-22 1 List order Client-controlled via order_by / order Stable, server-defined order. order_by and order are ignored — sorting client-side if you need it 2 depth parameter Free-form integer Accepts only 0, 1, or omitted. Any other value returns 400 3 path_prefix matching Substring match Must end with /, matches whole path segments only 4 Pagination cursors Interchangeable Cursors issued without the new header aren't valid with it. Restart from page 1 when you adopt it Two more gotchas: Header collision. On memory-store endpoints, agent-memory-2026-07-22 replaces managed-agents-2026-04-01. Sending both returns 400. Migrate the memory-store calls only; leave the other managed-agents endpoints on the original header. SDKs already switched. Python 0.116.0, TypeScript 0.110.0, Go 1.56.0, Java 2.48.0, Ruby 1.55.0, PHP 0.36.0, C# 12.35.0, and the CLI 1.16.0 all send agent-memory-2026-07-22 on memory-store calls automatically. If your code passes betas explicitly, replace managed-agents-2026-04-01 there — don't add both.
documents.s: The four behavior changes you must know

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Bump the SDK⌄ Upgrade to at least Python 0.116.0 / TS 0.110.0 / Go 1.56.0 / Java 2.48.0 / Ruby 1.55.0 / PHP 0.36.0 / C# 12.35.0 (CLI 1.16.0). The header switch happens for you on memory-store calls. ←PreviousNext→ 2Drop dead parameters⌄ Remove order_by / order — the server ignores them. If your code sorts on the returned list order, move the sort client-side. ←PreviousNext→ 3Fix depth⌄ Replace any depth other than 0 or 1 with the value that best matches your intent, or omit the parameter. ←PreviousNext→ 4Normalize path_prefix⌄ Ensure every path_prefix ends with a slash. Remove any substring-style prefixes that relied on partial-segment matches — they will silently return fewer results now. ←PreviousNext→ 5Reset pagination⌄ On the first request after upgrade, don't reuse a stored cursor. Start from page 1 and re-derive the next cursor from the new response. ←PreviousNext→ 6Fix explicit betas⌄ If you pass betas manually, replace managed-agents-2026-04-01 on memory-store calls with agent-memory-2026-07-22 — never send both. ←PreviousNext→

Shipped July 22, 2026 alongside the header default: three memory_store.* webhook event types now cover the memory store's lifecycle, and four environment.* events cover the sandbox environment. This is the piece most integrators miss — you can now react to a memory store being created, updated, or removed by an agent run instead of polling GET /v1/memory_stores on a timer. Subscribe on the Managed Agents webhooks endpoint and route the events into your own audit trail or dashboard.
documents.s: Webhooks: react to memory-store lifecycle without polling

documents.t: Announced in the May 6, 2026 release notes and extended on July 10 to support Claude Fable 5 and Sonnet 5, Dreams is a research preview that reads an existing memory store plus past session transcripts and produces a reorganized output memory store: duplicates merged, stale entries replaced, new insights surfaced. Endpoints are gated by the dreaming-2026-04-21 beta header; access is by request. Treat it as the API-side analogue of the app's monthly recap — a scheduled reflection pass that keeps the store from silting up.
documents.s: Dreams: reorganize memory in the background

documents.t: Aspect Claude.ai app Managed Agents API Storage unit Categorized entry Memory at a path Grouping Category (professional context, communication preferences, ongoing projects, …) Path segments (/projects/acme/…) Read/write Live during chat Agent tool calls during a session Human-editable Yes, per entry in Settings › Memory Yes, via memory-store endpoints Wipe Per entry, or all Per memory, per prefix, or delete store Reflection Monthly recap (Settings › Reflect) Dreams (research preview) Isolation Incognito chat Per-agent, per-session memory-store selection Availability Free, Pro, Max, Team, Enterprise (verify per plan) Managed Agents (public beta) Where this lives in the rest of AILmanac: Memory & Context Editing — the client-side memory tool, a different beast: you implement the storage. Memory Across Chats — the beginner's overview of app memory. Agent Memory Architectures — the theory of episodic vs. semantic memory that makes sense of why categorized entries beat a rolling summary. Managed Agents — the harness that hosts the memory-store surface described here.

Pro tip Team and Enterprise: check whether admins can inspect entries. Treat the app memory as data classification 'internal', not 'confidential'. Never let Claude write API keys, tokens, or credentials into entries. If you paste one in a chat with memory on, delete both the message and any resulting entry. Use incognito for legal, medical, or financial one-offs. Nothing prevents the app from summarizing wording later if you don't. Audit periodically. Run the 'list every entry you have about me' prompt monthly and delete anything that no longer applies. On the API side, treat memory_stores as first-class data. Back them up, list-diff them before and after significant runs, and log memory_store.* webhook events to your audit trail.
