What you'll learn Every one of the nine services contacts at least one third-party advertising or tracking service. There is no clean provider in the set. 124 distinct third-party domains, attributed to 44 organisations, 34 of which are advertising or tracking services. 6 of 9 web clients and 3 of 8 Android clients leak conversation-derived artifacts — URLs, titles, prompts, screenshots — to 11 and 2 tracking organisations respectively. 5 web clients disclose conversation permalinks (or the identifiers needed to rebuild them) to 9 tracking organisations. Three of those five do it by default, with no consent needed. 3 of 9 web clients leak the auto-generated conversation title to 9 third parties including Meta, TikTok and DoubleClick. Rejecting non-essential cookies leaves 80.8% of third-party trackers still active. Third-party integration is not the same set on web and on mobile: 11 tracking organisations appear on both client types, 15 are web-only (including Google Tag Manager, TikTok and the consent-management platform OneTrust), and 8 are mobile-only (including Braze). Auditing the website therefore tells you very little about the app, and vice versa.

Ordinary web tracking observes behaviour: which page you loaded, how long you stayed, what you clicked. Conversational AI generates a new class of object — the provider itself manufactures a short, human-readable summary of what you are thinking about, and then that object travels through the same pipes. The paper's Appendix A shows exactly what that summary looks like. Same prompt, three providers: Prompt typed by the user Title generated by ChatGPT by Claude by Grok "What are the symptoms of early-stage Parkinson's disease?" Early-stage Parkinson's Symptoms Early-stage Parkinson's disease symptoms Early Parkinson's Disease Symptoms "My salary is $85k. How much mortgage can I afford in NYC?" Mortgage Affordability in NYC Mortgage affordability on $85k salary in NYC $85k NYC Salary: $280k-$350k Mortgage Look at the bottom-right cell. Grok's title does not merely record the topic — it encodes the answer, including a salary figure and a mortgage range, into a short string. When that string is transmitted to an ad network alongside a stable identifier, the ad network has learned a health condition or a financial profile from a single field. No inference, no modelling, no clickstream reconstruction. The provider did the summarisation for them. Here is what the paper counted leaking, and to how many distinct tracking organisations: Artifact leaked Providers (web) Providers (Android) Trackers (web) Trackers (Android) Conversation URL 5 0 9 0 Conversation ID 2 2 1 1 User prompt 1 1 2 1 Conversation title 3 0 9 0 Conversation screenshot 1 0 1 0 Shared conversation URL 5 0 9 0 Shared conversation ID 0 1 0 1 The asymmetry is worth internalising: the web clients leak the user-facing artifacts (titles, URLs, screenshots) because web trackers execute inside the page's JavaScript context and can simply read the DOM. Mobile SDKs run outside the WebView's document, so they mostly get the conversation ID — but in exchange they get a much richer identifier set, because a third-party SDK inherits the host app's permissions.
documents.s: Why conversation artifacts are a different problem

documents.t: This is the part most coverage misses, and it is the most transferable lesson on the page. Blocking doubleclick.net in your browser does nothing against any of the following. Guided walkthrough1 of 3 1Server-side tag managers (measured on Grok)⌄ Grok's web client loads a Google Tag Manager container configured to route events through a server-side GTM instance (sGTM). A custom event forwards the conversation URL and the chat topic server-to-server to Meta's Conversions API and TikTok's Events API. Because the hop from Grok's infrastructure to Meta and TikTok never touches your browser, no extension can see it, let alone block it. The same payload carries both Meta's _fbp cookie and TikTok's _ttp cookie, which means the two ad platforms can be joined into a single identity for that event. ←PreviousNext→ 2First-party-proxied analytics (measured on Claude)⌄ Claude's web client loads Segment Analytics proxied through a first-party domain, a-cdn.anthropic.com, carrying a Conversion API configuration that forwards user events server-to-server from Anthropic's infrastructure to eleven downstream trackers — the paper names Facebook, LinkedIn, TikTok, Reddit and Google Enhanced Conversions among them — with two shared IDs per event. A blocklist keyed on third-party hostnames sees a request to Anthropic's own CDN and lets it through, by construction. ←PreviousNext→ 3In-app browsing on mobile (measured across the set)⌄ 71% of all distinct endpoints contacted by the mobile clients originate from WebViews — in-app browsing — rather than from native bytecode. It ranges from 98% in Grok to 91% in Perplexity to 71% in ChatGPT. That means the app is loading the *web* tracking stack (Google Ads, Google Tag Manager, TikTok Analytics, X/Twitter Analytics, Meta Pixel were all observed inside WebViews) inside a container where your browser's content blocker does not run at all. ←PreviousNext→ Watch out The generalisable rule: once a provider moves tracking server-side or proxies it through its own domain, client-side blocking is a measurement of the provider's laziness, not of your privacy. The only client-side controls that still bite are the consent signal itself and not generating the artifact in the first place. A fourth mechanism shows up in the CSP headers rather than in live traffic. Content-Security-Policy response headers enumerate the origins a page is authorised to contact, including ones that stayed dormant during the test — a useful lower bound on future behaviour. Across the nine services: Organisation Domains in CSP Number of providers Google Tag Manager googletagmanager.com 6 Google Analytics google-analytics.com 5 Google Ads googleadservices.com 4 Meta Pixel / Conversions API connect.facebook.net, facebook.net 4 Google DoubleClick doubleclick.net 3 TikTok Analytics analytics.tiktok.com 2 Reddit Ads / Analytics pixel-config.reddit.com, redditstatic.com 2 Microsoft Bing bat.bing.com, bing.com 2 Intercom intercom.io, intercomcdn.com 2
documents.s: Three mechanisms that make your ad blocker irrelevant

documents.t: These are the specific, verifiable behaviours the paper documents. Each is a May 2026 observation, not a permanent property.

This is where the study is most useful and most depressing, because it quantifies something everyone suspects. What you'll learn 77.3% of observed transmissions of web identifiers to third parties occur only after the user accepts non-essential cookies. Your choice does something. But 80.8% of third-party trackers remain active even when non-essential cookies are rejected. What your choice removes is the minority. Across all analysed free-tier services, third-party trackers still collect data in 44.4% (4 of 9) of them under a reject-all configuration. Of the three web clients that leak conversation titles, 88.9% of those disclosures happen only on accept — titles are among the artifacts consent actually gates. Ignoring the banner entirely produced no connections beyond those observed under explicit rejection. Clicking the X is, on these nine services, equivalent to rejecting. Subscription tier barely matters. Free and premium accounts contacted largely identical third parties; Claude's mobile free tier was the single clear exception. Two structural observations follow, and they are the ones to remember: The strongest controls are least available to the users most exposed. Persistent consent preferences on the web exist only on ChatGPT's paid tier, while roughly 95% of ChatGPT users sit on free tiers — and OpenAI has announced advertising for free and low-cost users. On mobile, most apps present no cookie-consent equivalent at launch at all, despite exposing similar tracking infrastructure. You cannot reject what you were never asked about. Presence is not proof of purpose. The paper is careful here and so should you be: a third party appearing in traffic does not by itself mean data is being used for advertising. Some SDKs do crash reporting, session replay or in-app payments. Sentry, Datadog and Intercom have obvious operational justifications. The authors also note their methodology cannot separate a provider's own first-party server-side tracking from functional traffic. Read the tables as "these entities receive this data", not "this data is definitely sold".

Every one of the nine services lets you share a conversation, and every one of them serves the shared conversation without requiring the recipient to authenticate. The security model is the unguessability of a UUID in the URL. Table 6 in the paper measures the default posture per provider and tier; the two outliers are Grok, where free and premium conversation permalinks are public by default with an opt-out, and Perplexity, where guest-tier conversations are always public with no opt-out at all. Perplexity is also the only provider that offers a whitelist control on top. The authors then did the thing that turns a theoretical exposure into a measured one. They deployed canary tokens — from canarytokens.org and from a self-hosted canary infrastructure with a generic domain, because some assistants recognise and refuse known canary domains — both pasted directly into prompts and embedded inside uploaded .docx and .pdf files. Then they waited to see who fetched them. Watch out For DeepSeek, Copilot, Mistral and Claude, some canary URLs fired once at submission time, from AWS or GCP addresses — consistent with the provider's own link-preview or retrieval infrastructure. For Grok, they recorded 70 distinct canary activations over hours to days after submission, from 70 IP addresses spanning 48 autonomous systems in 14 countries across 4 continents, with 65.7% of connections originating in the United States. Perplexity repeatedly fetched canary URLs even when the prompt explicitly instructed it not to, from IP ranges belonging to its Perplexity-User crawler on AWS infrastructure in the US. Seventy retrievals from forty-eight different networks, days later, is not link-preview behaviour. It is the signature of a URL that escaped into a pipeline and got crawled. The authors are appropriately cautious — absence of observed access elsewhere is not evidence of absence, since they only see what their own instrumentation catches — but the positive result stands on its own. Grok was also the only service where the authors identified something they classified as a security concern exploitable by an external party, rather than an intentional product decision. That is why xAI got a vulnerability-disclosure email on 2026-04-17 rather than an ordinary research notification. As of 2026-09-10 the paper reports that Grok still uses publicly accessible permalinks and that no official response had been received.
documents.s: Permalinks are not an access control

documents.t: None of this requires research infrastructure. You can reproduce the shape of the finding on any assistant in about twenty minutes, and you should, because the stacks change constantly and the paper is explicitly a point-in-time lower bound. Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Start from a genuinely clean profile⌄ New browser profile, no extensions, no prior cookies. Prior consent state, auth tokens and telemetry artifacts from an earlier session will silently change what fires. This is the step people skip and it invalidates everything downstream. ←PreviousNext→ 2Open DevTools before you open the assistant⌄ Network tab, check 'Preserve log' and 'Disable cache'. Load the assistant, answer the consent banner the way you normally would, then have a short conversation on a topic you would not want inferred. Let the provider generate a title for it. ←PreviousNext→ 3Export the HAR and grep for your own content⌄ Right-click in the Network panel, 'Save all as HAR with content'. Then search the file for the conversation's UUID, for distinctive words from the generated title, and for your email address in plaintext, MD5, SHA-1 and SHA-256. Hashed email addresses are the identifier people miss because they look like noise. ←PreviousNext→ 4Repeat with the opposite consent choice⌄ Fresh profile again, this time flip accept to reject. Diff the set of hostnames contacted. The delta is what your consent choice actually buys you; the intersection is what it does not. ←PreviousNext→ 5Now do the share flow separately⌄ Generate a share link and watch the Network panel during that action specifically. Sharing was where the study found the worst transmissions — screenshots and verbatim prompts — and it is a code path that never runs during ordinary chat. ←PreviousNext→ 6Optionally, plant a canary⌄ Put a canary URL on a domain you control in a conversation and in an uploaded document, and watch your access logs for a week. One hit at submission time is a link preview. Repeated hits from unrelated networks days later are not. ←PreviousNext→ Extract every third-party host and hunt for your own identifiers in a HAR CopyOpen in Claude↗ # Every distinct host the page contacted, by request count jq -r '.log.entries[].request.url' capture.har \ | awk -F/ '{print $3}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn # Any request whose URL or POST body contains the conversation UUID CONV_ID="paste-the-uuid-from-the-address-bar" jq -r --arg id "$CONV_ID" ' .log.entries[] | select((.request.url | contains($id)) or ((.request.postData.text // "") | contains($id))) | "\(.request.method) \(.request.url)"' capture.har # Your email, in clear and in the three hashes trackers actually use EMAIL="you@example.com" for h in "$EMAIL" \ "$(printf %s "$EMAIL" | md5)" \ "$(printf %s "$EMAIL" | shasum -a 1 | cut -d' ' -f1)" \ "$(printf %s "$EMAIL" | shasum -a 256 | cut -d' ' -f1)"; do printf '%s -> ' "$h" grep -c -- "$h" capture.har done

Ordered by how much they move the needle, per the paper's own mitigation discussion. Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Stop generating the artifact — do not share, and revoke old shares⌄ The worst transmissions in the study happen in the sharing code path, and every provider lets you revoke previously shared links. Go through your existing share list now. A permalink you created in 2024 and forgot about is still public on Grok and Perplexity's guest tier, and the canary result shows shared URLs do get fetched. ←PreviousNext→ 2Use incognito / temporary chat for anything sensitive⌄ Most providers now offer a mode where the conversation is not saved to account history. No saved conversation means no persistent permalink and, in several cases, no generated title — which removes the single most information-dense artifact from the pipeline. ←PreviousNext→ 3Reject non-essential cookies anyway, and know what it buys⌄ It removes roughly a fifth of the trackers, and on Claude specifically it demonstrably stopped the Meta Pixel, the Datadog telemetry and the eleven-tracker server-side forwarding. That is a real reduction. It is not privacy. ←PreviousNext→ 4Prefer the web client over the mobile app for sensitive work⌄ Counterintuitive, but: mobile SDKs inherit the host app's permissions and get identifiers the browser never exposes — advertising IDs, SSAID, installation IDs, geolocation — and most apps present no consent mechanism at all. The web client leaks richer conversation content; the app leaks stronger, harder-to-reset identity. ←PreviousNext→ 5On Android, reset and limit the advertising ID⌄ Three of the eight apps transmit the AAID to third parties (Adjust, AppsFlyer, Singular). Deleting the advertising ID entirely — Settings, Privacy, Ads — is stronger than resetting it, because the study shows resettable IDs being transmitted alongside permanent install- and account-level IDs, which lets a tracker re-bind a fresh AAID to the old profile. ←PreviousNext→ 6For genuinely sensitive material, take it off the hosted client entirely⌄ None of the above touches the server-side pipeline. The only architecture that removes the third-party surface completely is a local model or a raw API call from your own client — an API request carries no tag manager, no pixel and no WebView. ←PreviousNext→

The paper's scope note is easy to skim past and it is the part that should worry engineers: the leakage vectors observed here "stem from embedding standard web and mobile tracking directly into conversational interfaces". Nothing about them is specific to a frontier lab. If you have shipped an LLM-powered support chatbot, a custom assistant or a third-party AI wrapper, and your marketing team has installed the usual analytics on the same pages, you have almost certainly reproduced this architecture by accident. Three concrete things to check in your own product: Do you generate conversation titles or summaries client-side? If so, they are in the DOM, and any tag manager on that page can read them. The fix is to keep generated summaries out of the document title, out of <meta> tags, and out of any analytics event payload. Are conversation IDs in the URL path? Then they are in the Referer header of every third-party request the page makes, and in document.location for every script. The study found two providers shipping the global conversation ID to Datadog as an independent parameter, which is enough to reconstruct a permalink. Is your share page publicly readable? Under the ePrivacy Directive's Article 5(3) and the EDPB's Guidelines 2/2023 on its technical scope, URL and pixel tracking, persistent identifiers, and instructing the browser to forward data to a server-side API all require prior informed consent. The CJEU's Fashion ID judgment (C-40/17, paragraph 78) goes further: enabling third-party access is itself a processing decision that triggers your obligations, whether or not the third party ever reads the data.
documents.s: If you build on these APIs, this is your problem too

documents.t: Useful as a model for how this kind of research lands, and as a record of who moved. Date Event 2026-03-23 Authors first notice tracker activity while analysing Perplexity and Grok 2026-04-06 Testing expanded to all major platforms across consent states, tiers and privacy modes 2026-04-13 Findings notified to data protection authorities in the EU and UK 2026-04-17 xAI notified via vulnerability disclosure, specifically about Grok's conversation access controls 2026-05-27 The Spanish DPA (AEPD) cites the work, requesting escalation to an EDPB plenary meeting held 2026-06-06 2026-08-15 OpenAI updates ChatGPT's privacy policy to explicitly mention third-party trackers (causal link unconfirmed by the authors) 2026-09-10 Grok still exposes publicly accessible permalinks; no official response received Check yourself 0/6 Key takeaways All nine major conversational AI services contact at least one advertising or tracking organisation: 124 third-party domains, 44 organisations, 34 of them ATSes. There is no clean option in the mainstream set. Conversational AI creates an artifact class that ordinary web tracking does not have — the provider's own generated title, a compressed natural-language summary of user intent — and 3 of 9 web clients ship it to 9 third parties including Meta, TikTok and DoubleClick. Client-side blocking is structurally defeated three ways: server-side tag managers (Grok to Meta Conversions API and TikTok Events API), first-party-proxied analytics (Claude's Segment via a-cdn.anthropic.com, forwarding to eleven trackers), and mobile WebViews carrying 71% of all mobile endpoints. Consent removes the minority: 80.8% of trackers survive rejecting non-essential cookies, and the strongest control — persistent consent preferences — exists only on ChatGPT's paid tier while roughly 95% of users are on free tiers. A conversation permalink is an unguessable URL, not an access control. Canary tokens proved shared Grok conversations are fetched 70 times from 48 autonomous systems in 14 countries, days after the chat ended. The cheapest real mitigations: revoke old share links, use temporary/incognito chat, delete rather than reset your Android advertising ID, and move genuinely sensitive work to a raw API call or a local model where no tag manager exists. If you ship an LLM feature, you probably inherited this architecture by accident — check for generated summaries in the DOM, conversation IDs in URL paths, and publicly readable share pages.

Prompt like a Butterfly, Sting like a Tracker: A Privacy Analysis of Web and Mobile Conversational AI Agents (PDF) — the primary source for every number on this page. Oliveira, Sanchez, De Santa Olalla Gómez, Serna, Jackevicius, Garcia-Herrero, Girish, Suarez-Tangil and Vallina-Rodriguez; accepted at PoPETs 2027; CC BY 4.0. guinucool/pbst2027 — the open-science artifact repository: third-party classification code, fingerprinting-API detection, PII extraction, the manually labelled third-party domain list, sample Grok HAR captures and an artifact appendix with reproduction instructions. Raw traffic captures are withheld as they contain sensitive data. A visual summary of the paper (Spanish) — the co-author's own walkthrough, useful for the legal framing. Hacker News discussion, item 49890226 — 421 points and 136 comments as of 2026-09-30, including practitioner pushback on methodology and several follow-up reproductions. IMDEA Networks — the research institute behind the measurement work, and a reliable source for follow-up studies in this line. Canarytokens — the free canary-token service the authors used, and the easiest way to reproduce the permalink-access experiment yourself. EDPB Guidelines 2/2023 on the technical scope of Article 5(3) of the ePrivacy Directive — the regulatory text that brings URL tracking, pixels and server-side forwarding inside the consent requirement. Related on AILmanac: ChatGPT's Ad Pixel and the __obi Cookie, What Your Agent Uploads, Agentic Browsers and Same-Origin Risk, Cryptographic Context Injection in Grok.

ChatGPT's Ad Pixel and the __obi Cookie — the other half of the advertising story: how OpenAI's own measurement pixel joins a ChatGPT account to the shopping sites you visit, and why rejecting marketing consent does not stop it. The Private Local AI Stack — the architecture that removes this entire surface, and what you give up to get it. Copy as Markdown Advanced What you'll learn Separate the two egress channels every coding agent has — and understand why only one of them is visible to you Read the Grok Build wire capture: 196 KB of model traffic vs 5.10 GiB of repository upload, from the same session Learn why a permission denial and a "don't train on my data" toggle can both be honored while your repo still leaves the machine Wire-tap your own agent with mitmproxy and a canary repo, and count the bytes per endpoint yourself Compare what Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI and Codex each document sending — and where the documentation ends You almost certainly model your coding agent's privacy like this: it sends what it reads. Approve a file read, that file goes to the model. Deny it, it doesn't. Your prompts and the files in context are the payload; everything else is metadata. That model is wrong for at least one shipping agent, and structurally incomplete for several others. In July 2026 a researcher pointed a proxy at xAI's Grok Build CLI and found that a 12 GB repository left the machine as a git bundle — full history, never-read files, .env contents — through a channel that had nothing to do with what the agent read, while the setting a user would reach for to stop it governed something else entirely. This page is not really about Grok. It's about the channel it exposed, which most agents have in some form, and about the fact that you can check your own in an afternoon instead of trusting a marketing page.
documents.s: What Your Coding Agent Actually Uploads

documents.t: Every agent CLI that talks to a hosted model has Channel A. Some also have Channel B. Channel A — the model turn. Your prompt, the system prompt, tool definitions, and the contents of files the agent actually read. This is the channel your intuition tracks. It's the one permission prompts gate, the one .gitignore-style deny rules affect, the one you can roughly predict from the transcript. It's also small: a working session moves kilobytes to low megabytes. Channel B — the ambient channel. Anything the client uploads on its own initiative, not as part of answering your turn: codebase indexing, session traces, crash reports, usage analytics, feedback bundles. It runs on the client's schedule, not the model's reasoning. It's not in your transcript. It doesn't ask. And because it's driven by a code path rather than an LLM decision, no amount of prompting affects it — telling the agent "do not read any files" constrains Channel A and says nothing about Channel B. Channel B is not inherently sinister. Cursor's server-side index is a Channel B and it's documented in detail. The danger isn't its existence — it's that user-facing controls are almost always designed for Channel A, so people reason about a system with two exits while looking at one.

A researcher publishing as cereblab ran Grok Build CLI 0.2.93 (macOS arm64, commit f00f96316d4b) through mitmproxy on 127.0.0.1:8080 with a trusted CA, against throwaway repos containing planted canary strings. The harness, the captured evidence, and SHA-256 checksums are published as a reproduction repo, so this is a claim you can re-run rather than one you have to believe. What the capture showed: Two endpoints, wildly different volumes. In a single session against a 12 GB repository: Channel Endpoint Bytes Requests A — model turns POST cli-chat-proxy.grok.com/v1/responses 196,705 5 B — repository upload POST cli-chat-proxy.grok.com/v1/storage 5,476,228,005 (5.10 GiB) 82, all HTTP 200 Roughly a 27,800× ratio. That gap is the whole argument: a volume like that cannot be sourced from what the model read. It's sourced from the codebase itself. The uploads went out as ~75 MB chunks (73 of them in the logged run) and the capture was cut off while they were still succeeding, meaning 5.10 GiB is a floor, not a total. The canary that was never read. The agent was prompted, in plain terms, Reply exactly OK, do not read any files. A file at src/_probe/never_read_canary.txt containing a unique marker did not appear in any /v1/responses body — Channel A behaved exactly as instructed. It did appear in an uploaded git bundle recovered from the intercepted /v1/storage request. The researcher git cloned the captured bundle and got the repository back, marker and full history intact. A separate canary, a fake DB password in a .env file, showed up verbatim and unredacted in both channels. The destination was a named bucket. Strings in the binary and staged upload metadata pointed at a Google Cloud Storage bucket, grok-code-session-traces, with object paths of the form gs://grok-code-session-traces/repo_changes_dedup/v2/…. Nothing in the CLI's setup materials described this. Last verified: 2026-07-14. This page quotes facts that change over time — treat the date above as its freshness. Sources: cereblab wire-level analysis (gist + grok-build-exfil-repro), Hacker News threads 48892468 / 48896493, The Hacker News coverage The fix, and the shape of the response. On 2026-07-13 the same unchanged 0.2.93 binary stopped issuing /v1/storage requests across six retests — a server-side flag flip (disable_codebase_upload: true), not a client update. xAI responded on X rather than with a formal advisory: enterprise zero-data-retention customers were said to be unaffected, individual subscribers were pointed at a /privacy command, and previously uploaded data was said to be deleted. Treat the current state as fixed-for-now; treat the class of bug as permanent. The source, later. On 2026-07-14 xAI published the Grok Build harness under Apache 2.0, and the machinery described above is in the tree: xai-grok-shell/src/upload/gcs.rs, whose module docs call the upload helpers "the data-collector helpers," and a DEDUP_GCS_PREFIX = "repo_changes_dedup" constant matching the gs://grok-code-session-traces/repo_changes_dedup/v2/… object paths in the capture above. The wire evidence and the source agree. See Inside Grok Build for what else the published harness shows.

★ "The agent only sends what it reads." False whenever a Channel B exists. Reading is an LLM decision; indexing is a code path. They are not the same subsystem and they do not share a gate. ★ "I denied the file, so it's safe." A permission denial operates at the tool layer — it stops the agent from pulling the file into context. It is not a network egress rule. In the Grok case, a denied file still shipped inside the git bundle. If your threat model needs a file to not leave the machine, the enforcement point has to be the filesystem or the network, not the agent's own permission prompt. ★ "Don't train on my data" ≠ "don't transmit my data." These are two different controls and vendors routinely expose only the first. Grok's "Improve the model" toggle mapped to training consent; with it off, the server still returned trace_upload_enabled: true and the repo uploads continued unchanged. Anthropic's docs draw the same distinction explicitly for Claude Code — the training-data setting and the telemetry/feedback switches are separate knobs with separate env vars. Read every privacy toggle as answering "may you keep it?", never as answering "will you take it?"
documents.s: Three things this breaks that you probably believed

documents.t: You do not need to trust anyone's documentation — including this page. Fifteen minutes and a proxy gives you ground truth for whatever agent you run. Do this on a throwaway repo with fake secrets, on your own machine. Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Install a MITM proxy and trust its CA⌄ mitmproxy generates a local CA on first run. Install it into the system trust store so the agent's TLS calls terminate at the proxy instead of failing. This is the whole trick — agent CLIs are ordinary HTTPS clients and most respect standard proxy environment variables. ←PreviousNext→ 2Build a canary repo⌄ Create a throwaway git repo. Plant a unique marker in a .env file (a fake credential), and a second unique marker in a file you will explicitly tell the agent never to open. Commit both — committed files are what a git-bundle upload would carry. Markers must be strings that cannot occur naturally, so a grep over the capture is unambiguous. ←PreviousNext→ 3Run the agent through the proxy with a null task⌄ Point HTTPS_PROXY at the listener and give the agent a task that requires reading nothing at all. If the agent is only using Channel A, an almost-empty session should move almost no bytes. ←PreviousNext→ 4Count bytes per endpoint⌄ Sum request body sizes grouped by host and path. This is the measurement that matters. A session that reads nothing but moves hundreds of megabytes has a Channel B, whatever the docs say. ←PreviousNext→ 5Grep the capture for your canaries⌄ Search the raw flows — and decompress any archives or bundles you find — for both markers. The never-read marker appearing anywhere in the capture is a positive result: something is uploading files independent of what the model read. ←PreviousNext→ 6Re-run with every privacy toggle set to maximum⌄ Now turn off training consent, telemetry, analytics, indexing — everything the vendor exposes — and repeat. The delta between the two runs tells you exactly what those toggles actually control, which is the question the toggle's label rarely answers. ←PreviousNext→ Minimal wire-tap harness CopyOpen in Claude↗ # 1. proxy + CA (macOS; on Linux use your distro's trust store) brew install mitmproxy mitmdump -w flows.mitm --set confdir=~/.mitmproxy & sudo security add-trusted-cert -d -r trustRoot \ -k /Library/Keychains/System.keychain ~/.mitmproxy/mitmproxy-ca-cert.pem # 2. canary repo mkdir -p /tmp/canary/src/_probe && cd /tmp/canary && git init echo 'DB_PASS=CANARY-AAAA-ENVSECRET' > .env echo 'CANARY-BBBB-NEVERREAD' > src/_probe/never_read.txt git add -A && git commit -m "canary" # 3. run the agent through the proxy, asking it to read nothing HTTPS_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:8080 HTTP_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:8080 \ <your-agent-cli> "Reply exactly OK. Do not read any files." # 4. bytes per endpoint — the number that matters mitmdump -nr flows.mitm \ --set console_eventlog_verbosity=info \ -s <(echo 'def response(f): print(f.request.pretty_host, f.request.path, len(f.request.raw_content or b""))') # 5. did a file you never opened leave the machine? strings flows.mitm | grep -c 'CANARY-BBBB-NEVERREAD' If step 5 returns anything but 0, you have found a Channel B — and you found it yourself, which is the only kind of finding that ages well.

Documentation is a claim; a wire capture is evidence. The gap between them is the entire lesson of this page. Still, the claims differ enough to be worth knowing — and knowing them tells you what to look for when you run the capture. Claude Code. No whole-repo indexing or bundle-upload channel appears in the documented data flow; the agent searches with tools and sends file contents as part of the model turn, so the file contents that leave are the ones pulled into context. Operational telemetry is separate and, per Anthropic's docs, "does not include any code or file paths" (DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1); Sentry error reporting is separate again (DISABLE_ERROR_REPORTING=1). The channels that do carry code are explicit and opt-in: /feedback sends conversation history including code (DISABLE_FEEDBACK_COMMAND=1), and the session-quality survey's transcript-share step uploads a transcript only if you actively choose Yes, with known key and token patterns redacted first. CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC is the single kill switch for the lot. Retention: 30 days for commercial (Team/Enterprise/API), 30 days for consumers who leave model-improvement off and 5 years for those who turn it on; zero data retention exists for qualifying Enterprise accounts. Anthropic does not train on code sent under commercial terms unless the org opts in. Cursor. A textbook documented Channel B: the codebase index is built by chunking your repo, embedding the chunks, and sending embeddings plus encrypted file paths to Cursor's servers. Per the docs, code content is held in memory during indexing and then discarded rather than stored in plaintext, and chunks are decrypted client-side when the agent retrieves them. This is a real whole-repo upload of a derived artifact — a materially different risk profile from a raw git bundle, and materially different from Claude Code's read-what-you-need model. Which of the three you want is a judgment call. Not knowing which one you're running is not. Gemini CLI. Usage statistics are on by default and disabled with privacy.usageStatisticsEnabled: false in settings.json; the docs state that prompt and response content and the contents of files read or written are not logged. OpenTelemetry instrumentation is separate and can be pointed at a collector you control (telemetry.enabled: false to turn it off). Codex CLI. Anonymous client analytics are on by default and disabled via the analytics config flag; OTel export is routable to your own collector, and prompt logging (log_user_prompt) is off unless you enable it. Session transcripts persist locally under CODEX_HOME — see below. Last verified: 2026-07-14. This page quotes facts that change over time — treat the date above as its freshness. Sources: code.claude.com/docs/en/data-usage, cursor.com/docs codebase indexing, google-gemini/gemini-cli docs, developers.openai.com/codex config

Egress is only one direction. Every one of these agents also writes your session — prompts, file contents, tool output, sometimes secrets — to local disk in plaintext, and those files outlive the session. Claude Code stores transcripts under ~/.claude/projects/ for 30 days by default (tune with cleanupPeriodDays). Codex persists history under CODEX_HOME. Grok Build staged its uploads in ~/.grok/upload_queue — reportedly on the order of gigabytes per turn, and under load capable of growing until it filled the disk, which is a denial-of-service bug hiding inside a privacy bug. Consequence: a laptop backup, a synced folder, or a second process with read access to your home directory is an exfiltration path that never touches the network stack you just instrumented. Any secret that entered a session is now on disk in cleartext somewhere you didn't put it.
documents.s: The half nobody checks: your own disk

documents.t: The recurring theme in the Hacker News discussion — hundreds of comments across both threads — was that markdown-level instructions are not a security boundary. CLAUDE.md and its equivalents are guidance to a model, not enforcement against a binary. If a control has to hold against the client, it must live below the client. Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Give the agent a filesystem, not your filesystem⌄ Run it in a container or devcontainer with only the working repo mounted. This is the single highest-leverage change: an agent that cannot see ~/.ssh, ~/.aws, your shell history, your other clients' repos, or your password vault cannot upload them through any channel, documented or not. A separate OS user achieves much of the same with less ceremony. ←PreviousNext→ 2Make egress an allowlist⌄ Deny outbound by default from the agent's container and allow only the model API host it needs. A Channel B you never approved cannot dial out through a closed egress policy. As a bonus, this converts every future undocumented upload channel from an incident into a connection error in your logs. ←PreviousNext→ 3Keep secrets out of the blast radius entirely⌄ The .env in your working tree is the single most valuable file an agent can leak, and it is the one most likely to be committed and therefore carried by any bundle-shaped upload. Inject secrets from a secret manager or the environment at run time; keep them out of the repo and out of the mounted tree. ←PreviousNext→ 4Test the toggles, don't trust them⌄ Run the capture from the previous section once, with all privacy settings maxed. Fifteen minutes buys you a fact instead of a claim — and it's the only step here that would have caught this incident before the researcher did. ←PreviousNext→ 5If you ran an affected tool: rotate, don't reason⌄ Do not try to reconstruct what was and wasn't uploaded. If SSH keys, cloud credentials, or API tokens were reachable in a directory an agent had access to during an exposure window, treat them as disclosed and rotate them. Credential rotation is cheap; a forensic argument about which bytes moved is not. ←PreviousNext→ 6Buy the contract if the code matters⌄ Zero-data-retention and commercial terms are not a substitute for the controls above, but they change what a vendor is permitted to keep and what recourse you have. If you are running an agent over a codebase you cannot afford to leak, the consumer tier is the wrong tier. ←PreviousNext→ Check yourself 0/4

Nothing about this incident was model-specific, and nothing about it required a novel attack. It required a client that did something reasonable-sounding — cache the repo server-side to give the agent better context — without surfacing it, and a settings screen whose vocabulary ("Improve the model") didn't map onto the question users were actually asking. Both of those are extremely common. The agent CLI category is eighteen months old, moving fast, and shipping features that upload code because uploading code makes the product better. Expect more of these. The defensible position is not picking the vendor with the best privacy page; it's building the habit of measuring, and running the thing inside a box that limits what a wrong answer can cost you. If you want the adversarial side of the same problem — untrusted content steering an agent that already has your permissions — read When Coding Agents Get Weaponized and Hardening Autonomous Runs. For how the CLIs differ on everything other than data flow, see Coding Agent CLIs Compared.

Copy as Markdown Intermediate What you'll learn Trace the real escalation path — automated classifier, specialised review queue, trained human reviewer, account ban, law-enforcement referral — and see where the latency actually sits (days, not seconds) Learn the asymmetry OpenAI published and almost nobody quotes: threats to others may be referred to police, self-harm cases explicitly are not Do the retention arithmetic across providers, including the two numbers that survive every privacy control you can toggle Understand why a zero-data-retention contract does not exempt you from the safety pipeline — and why Anthropic's most capable models cannot be used under ZDR at all See what incognito, temporary and activity-off modes actually govern (training and history) versus what they do not (abuse monitoring) Decide, per class of text, which surface it belongs on — and what to do instead when the honest answer is 'none of them' Between August and early October 2026, three conversations with a commercial AI assistant publicly became police matters. One produced a felony arrest. The pattern is not a glitch and it is not new policy — it is the documented operation of an abuse pipeline every major provider runs, described in help-centre articles that almost nobody reads before pasting. The useful question is not "do they read my chats?" — the answer has been yes, in a narrow and specific sense, for years. The useful questions are what triggers a human to look, what a human is authorised to do next, and which of your privacy settings touch that path at all. The third answer is the one that surprises people: mostly none of them.
documents.s: Who Reads Your AI Chats — Safety Review, Police Referral, and the Retention You Can't Delete

documents.t: Last verified: 2026-10-06. Case facts are from contemporaneous reporting and are the subject of pending criminal proceedings; charges are allegations, not findings. Policy figures are from provider documentation current on the verify date and change without notice — re-read the linked help-centre articles before relying on any number here. Confirm against the official source. San Francisco, August 2026. A Claude user allegedly wrote that he had bought an AR-15 and had Anthropic's CEO "in his sights." Per the police report cited by The San Francisco Standard, the messages were sent on Friday 14 August at 2:30 p.m. Anthropic notified SFPD the following Tuesday at 9 a.m. Officers attended Anthropic's office; the subject was not present and, as of that reporting, had not been arrested or charged. He told the Standard he had not been serious. Anthropic's statement: the account was banned and the case referred, and "this is our safeguards process working as intended." Florida, late September 2026. Carli Michelle Heller of Bonita Springs had been using Claude much as one uses a journal. According to the arrest report, on 26 September she wrote that she would shoot up the Lee County Sheriff's Office, and on 27 September that she had obtained a new gun. Automated systems flagged the text, a human review team assessed it, Anthropic reported it, deputies located her at home and detained her without incident. She was charged with making a written threat of violence — a second-degree felony — with a court date in November. Tom's Hardware counted the Florida case as at least the third Claude conversation to reach police since August.
documents.s: What actually happened in the three cases

documents.t: The latency is days, not seconds. Friday afternoon to Tuesday morning is roughly four days. This is a review queue staffed by people, not a tripwire wired to a dispatcher. That cuts both ways: it is not real-time surveillance, and it is also not a system that can intervene in a genuinely imminent event. A human made the call. In both cases the automated classifier only routed. The decision to contact police was made by a trained reviewer reading the text. The thing people find most uncomfortable — an employee read my private journal — is the deliberate design, not the failure mode. Account termination came first. Banning preceded or accompanied referral. If you are ever on the wrong side of a classifier for innocent reasons, the first symptom is losing access, not a phone call.

Every major provider runs some version of this. The vocabulary differs; the shape does not. Guided walkthrough1 of 5 11 — Automated classification on every request⌄ Safety classifiers score inputs and outputs. This runs on essentially all traffic to consumer surfaces and is not something you can opt out of; it is how usage policies are enforced at scale. Scores are data in their own right, and they are retained separately from the conversation — a distinction that matters enormously later on this page. ←PreviousNext→ 22 — Routing to a specialised queue⌄ High-scoring conversations in specific categories are routed out of the normal flow. OpenAI's published description: 'When we detect users who are planning to harm others, we route their conversations to specialized pipelines where they are reviewed by a small team trained on our usage policies and who are authorized to take action, including banning accounts.' Anthropic's Usage Policy states that its Safeguards Team 'will implement detection and monitoring to enforce our Usage Policy.' ←PreviousNext→ 33 — Human review⌄ A trained reviewer reads the conversation. At Google this function is explicit and broader than abuse: a subset of Gemini chats are reviewed by humans, including trained service providers, to assess quality and safety and to address Terms of Service violations. Google's own instruction to users is blunt: do not enter confidential information you would not want a reviewer to see. ←PreviousNext→ 44 — Enforcement⌄ Throttling, suspension or termination. Anthropic's Usage Policy reserves exactly this: 'we may throttle, suspend, or terminate your access to our products or services.' This is the overwhelmingly common outcome and the only one most flagged users ever experience. ←PreviousNext→ 55 — External referral, in a narrow band⌄ Two distinct triggers. Mandatory: Anthropic states that when it detects CSAM, including AI-generated CSAM, or the coercion or enticement of a minor, it will report to the relevant authorities. Discretionary: OpenAI's position is that 'if human reviewers determine that a case involves an imminent threat of serious physical harm to others, we may refer it to law enforcement.' Anthropic's Privacy Policy grounds the same discretion in a good-faith belief that disclosure is reasonably necessary to, among other things, 'prevent serious harm to any person or to property.' ←PreviousNext→

When OpenAI published the passage above, the sentence that followed it got far less attention and is arguably more consequential: OpenAI stated it is "currently not referring self-harm cases to law enforcement to respect people's privacy given the uniquely private nature of ChatGPT interactions." So the published line is drawn at harm to others, not at distress. Someone in crisis about themselves is handled inside the product — crisis resources, model behaviour changes, possibly human review — without a police referral. Someone who writes a threat against a third party is in a different pipeline entirely. If you only remember one thing about escalation thresholds, remember that the line is about who gets hurt, and that it is a policy choice a provider can revise.

This is the section that changes behaviour, because the numbers are longer than almost anyone assumes and several of them are immune to the controls in your settings panel. What Provider Duration Survives you deleting it? Normal conversation you delete Anthropic (consumer) Gone from history immediately, purged from back-end storage within 30 days — Conversation flagged as violating the Usage Policy Anthropic Inputs and outputs up to 2 years Yes Trust-and-safety classification scores for that conversation Anthropic Up to 7 years Yes Data you opted into model improvement Anthropic (consumer) De-identified, up to 5 years in training pipelines Per opt-out at the time Chat read by a human reviewer Google (Gemini Apps) Up to 3 years, disconnected from your Google Account Yes — deleting your activity does not remove it Gemini Apps Activity on Google Auto-delete at 18 months by default (adjustable to 3 or 36 months, or off) — Gemini Apps Activity off Google Temporary chats kept 72 hours to respond to you and protect safety — ChatGPT Temporary Chat OpenAI Not in history, not in memory, not used for training; may be retained up to 30 days for safety — Prompts and completions on a Covered Model Anthropic At least 30 days, mandatory, then auto-deleted — Two rows deserve to be read twice. Seven years of classification scores. The conversation itself may be gone; the structured judgement about it persists for the better part of a decade. A classification score is not a copy of your text, but it is a durable, account-linked assertion that your text scored a certain way on a certain category. For anyone reasoning about long-term exposure, that is the real retention horizon, and it is roughly 85× longer than the 30-day purge window people cite when they say deletion works. Three years that outlive deletion. Google is explicit that human-reviewed chats and their associated metadata — language, device type, location information, feedback — are not deleted when you delete your activity, precisely because they have been disconnected from your account. Anonymisation is what makes the retention defensible and also what makes it permanent from your side: there is no longer an account handle to issue the delete against. Google tries to disconnect reviewed chats before a human sees them, but anything you typed into the message is part of the message.

This is the single most common misconception among developers who believe they have solved the problem contractually. Zero Data Retention for Claude Code on Claude for Enterprise means prompts and responses are processed in real time and "not stored by Anthropic after the response is returned" — "except where needed to comply with law or combat misuse." Anthropic's own documentation spells the exception out: Even with ZDR enabled, Anthropic may retain data where required by law or to address Usage Policy violations. If a session is flagged for a policy violation, Anthropic may retain the associated inputs and outputs for up to 2 years. And separately, on what ZDR never covered in the first place: Anthropic still retains User Safety classifier results in order to enforce our Usage Policy. So the correct mental model is: ZDR removes the storage, not the pipeline. Classification still happens on every request; the scores are still kept; a flagged session still gets a two-year retention. ZDR is an excellent control against routine retention and a poor one against abuse-response retention, which is exactly the retention that matters if something you sent is ever contested.

Anthropic documents these explicitly, and each has bitten someone: It does not cover the web app or Cowork. ZDR for Claude Code covers Claude Code inference. Chat on claude.ai through the same Enterprise interface, and Cowork sessions, follow standard retention. It does not follow the user, only the organisation. ZDR applies to requests that authenticate into a ZDR-enabled org. A developer who signs in with a personal account, or with an API key from a different org, is simply not covered. Anthropic's answer is the forceLoginMethod and forceLoginOrgUUID managed settings — worth deploying if you believe ZDR is load-bearing for you. It does not propagate to new organisations. ZDR is enabled per-org by Anthropic's account team and does not automatically apply to new orgs created under the same account. It does not cover third parties. Data processed by MCP servers and external integrations is outside ZDR entirely. (See What Your Agent Uploads and Securing MCP Servers.)
documents.s: Four more things ZDR does not do

documents.t: Anthropic designates its most capable models — currently Claude Mythos 5.1, Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Mythos 5 and Claude Fable 5 — as Covered Models, which require data retention by default. Prompts and completions are retained for at least 30 days, then automatically deleted, and the retained window is assessed by automated safety systems designed to flag harmful content. The stated reason is the genuinely interesting part, because it is an admission about the limits of per-request filtering: Because "some forms of misuse only become detectable across many requests, these models require safeguards that operate over a retained window of usage data rather than on a single request at a time." A single request that assembles one benign-looking piece of a dangerous whole is invisible to a stateless classifier. Detecting the pattern requires remembering the requests. That is a real security argument, and it means capability and retention are now coupled by design: for these models, you can have the frontier capability or you can have zero retention, not both. ZDR is unavailable for Covered Models in standard configurations; where an org or workspace lacks the mandatory retention, requests for those models are rejected server-side regardless of client configuration, and Claude Code's best alias quietly resolves to Opus instead of Fable. Anthropic has signalled an Enterprise Frontier Safeguards path for eligible customers to use Fable 5 and 5.1 under ZDR for internal business applications, rolling out in autumn 2026 — confirm current status with your account team rather than assuming either way. For the model-side view of this, see the Fable 5.1 Field Guide, which notes the same mandatory 30-day window from the API-behaviour angle: a request from an org without it returns a 400.
documents.s: Covered Models: the capability/retention trade is now explicit

documents.t: Here is the clean separation, and it is the practical thesis of this page. Control Governs Does not govern Anthropic incognito chat Excluded from model improvement even when improvement is on Safety flagging and the retention that follows it ChatGPT Temporary Chat History, memory, training Safety/abuse retention — up to 30 days per OpenAI's FAQ Gemini Apps Activity off Training, human review of future chats, long-term activity storage A 72-hour window kept to respond to you and protect safety Delete conversation Your history, and back-end copies on a purge timer Flagged content, classification scores, already-reviewed chats Zero Data Retention Routine storage of prompts and completions Classification itself, score retention, flagged-session retention Read the right-hand column as a single sentence: consumer privacy controls are training-and-history controls. None of them is an abuse-monitoring control. That is not a gotcha hidden in fine print — it is the only way a usage policy can be enforceable at all. But it does mean the mental model "incognito means nobody sees this" is wrong in a way that matters. One control genuinely does narrow human review: Google lets you turn off the pathway that feeds chats to reviewers, via myaccount.google.com → Data and Privacy → Gemini Apps Activity → Turn off. Future conversations are then not sent for human review and not used for training. Chats already reviewed are still inside their three-year window.
documents.s: What your privacy settings actually control

documents.t: Heller was charged under Florida's written-threats statute, Fla. Stat. 836.10. Its elements are worth reading because they explain how writing to a chatbot can be charged at all. The statute reaches a person who sends, posts or transmits — or procures the sending, posting or transmission of — a writing or other record, including an electronic record, "in any manner in which it may be viewed by another person," containing a threat to kill or do bodily harm, or to conduct a mass shooting or an act of terrorism. It is a second-degree felony. Two observations, offered as reading of the statutory text rather than as legal advice: The text does not require an intended human recipient. It requires a record transmitted in a manner in which it may be viewed by another person. A conversation stored on a provider's servers and readable by that provider's reviewers is not obviously outside that language. This is precisely the gap between what a user feels they are doing (writing privately) and what the statute describes (transmitting a viewable electronic record). Intent is still an element. Florida pattern elements require that the defendant intended the threat as a true threat — the doctrinal line that separates a prosecutable threat from hyperbole or venting, and the obvious terrain for a defence. "I was just venting to a chatbot" is a factual argument about intent, not a safe harbour created by the medium. If you need the statute itself, it is published by the Florida Senate; the link is in the sources. If you are in actual legal trouble, talk to a lawyer, not a field guide.

The honest decision procedure, by class of text. Class of text Right surface Why Ordinary work, code, writing Any hosted assistant The pipeline exists but is irrelevant to you Confidential business data Commercial/Enterprise tier with the right terms; ZDR if you qualify Routine retention removed; abuse retention remains Regulated data (health, financial) BAA/HIPAA-configured enterprise deployment Contractual, not just technical, protection Security research touching violence, weapons, exploits Hosted is fine — but supply context in-band Reviewers read text, and context is what distinguishes research from intent Journalling, crisis, intrusive thoughts, ideation Local model, or a human The one class where the pipeline is genuinely adverse to the user's interest That last row is the Florida case in one line. A chat assistant has the affordance of a diary — private-feeling, always available, never bored — and none of its properties. If you want the affordance, run the model on your own machine, where the pipeline does not exist because there is no server. A journal that no classifier ever sees CopyOpen in Claude↗ # one-time: install Ollama, then pull a small local model ollama pull llama3.2 # a private journalling session — no network, no review queue, no retention ollama run llama3.2 Everything in that session stays on your disk. See Run Models Locally with Ollama for the full setup and The Private Local AI Stack for the architecture that removes the hosted surface entirely. The other practical move: when your legitimate work genuinely does involve violence, weapons, self-harm or exploitation as subject matter, say so in the conversation. A classifier scores text; a human reviewer reads it. Stated context is the only thing in your control that changes what the reviewer concludes. Give the reviewer the context a classifier cannot infer CopyOpen in Claude↗ Context for this conversation, stated up front: I am a [threat analyst / security researcher / novelist / clinician / trust-and-safety engineer] working on [specific artefact: a tabletop exercise, a published paper, chapter 14 of a manuscript, an abuse-detection ruleset]. I need to discuss [violent / self-harm / weapons / exploitation] subject matter as material to be analysed, depicted or detected — not planned. My output is [a report / fiction / a detection rule], not an operational plan. Please keep that frame for the whole thread, and tell me if a request of mine crosses from analysis into operational detail so I can rephrase it. That last line is the useful half. It asks the model to act as a cooperative boundary-keeper rather than leaving you to guess, and a thread containing an explicit refusal-and-rephrase exchange reads very differently to a reviewer than one that does not.

Three over-corrections to avoid, because the discourse around these cases produced all three: It is not continuous surveillance by humans. The human step is reached by a small fraction of conversations routed by classifier, in specific categories. The default experience of every one of these pipelines is that nobody ever reads your chat. It is not new. Content classification plus a human abuse queue plus a narrow legal-referral clause is the standard architecture of every large communications platform, and has been for two decades. What is new is the intimacy of the input — people tell an assistant things they would never post — and the fact that the retention exceptions are now long and written down. It is not unique to one provider. Every table in this page has entries for Anthropic, OpenAI and Google because all three publish the same basic design. Choosing a provider on this axis means comparing specific documented numbers, not vibes. The one real axis of choice is hosted versus local, and Choosing a Model Provider is the page for the rest of that decision. Check yourself 0/6

Anthropic Privacy Policy — section 3, "Recipients and Third-Party Data Sources", is the clause permitting disclosure to government authorities and law enforcement on a good-faith belief it is reasonably necessary to, among other grounds, prevent serious harm to any person or property. Anthropic Usage Policy — the Safeguards Team detection-and-monitoring commitment, the throttle/suspend/terminate enforcement language, the mandatory CSAM reporting obligation, and the scope statement covering anyone who can submit inputs including via resellers and passthrough access. How long do you store my data? — Anthropic privacy centre — the source for immediate removal from history, the 30-day back-end purge, the 5-year de-identified training-pipeline retention, and the critical pair: up to 2 years for flagged inputs and outputs, up to 7 years for trust-and-safety classification scores. Is my data used for model training? — Anthropic privacy centre — the opt-in framing for model improvement, the incognito-chat exclusion, and the statement that conversations flagged for safety review may be used to improve detection and enforcement including training models for the Safeguards team. I have a zero data retention agreement with Anthropic. What products does it apply to? — which products ZDR covers, and the explicit statement that Anthropic still retains User Safety classifier results in order to enforce the Usage Policy. Zero data retention — Claude Code docs — the primary source for the "except where needed to comply with law or combat misuse" carve-out, the 2-year flagged-session retention under ZDR, the table of what ZDR does not cover (claude.ai chat, Cowork, third-party integrations), the per-organisation and forceLoginOrgUUID routing caveats, the features disabled under ZDR, and Covered Model availability. Covered Models — Anthropic support — the model list (Mythos 5.1, Fable 5.1, Mythos 5, Fable 5), the at-least-30-days mandatory retention assessed by automated safety systems, the cross-request-detection rationale, and the Enterprise Frontier Safeguards path for ZDR-eligible customers. Gemini Apps Privacy Hub — Google — human reviewers including trained service providers, the up-to-three-years retention for reviewed chats that survives deleting your activity, the 18-month default auto-delete, the 72-hour window when activity is off, and the explicit instruction not to enter confidential information. Helping people when they need it most — OpenAI — the post containing the specialised-pipeline and law-enforcement-referral language, and the sentence excluding self-harm cases from referral. (The passages are widely quoted; the page blocks automated fetching.) Temporary Chat FAQ — OpenAI help centre — what Temporary Chat removes (history, memory, training) and the safety-retention window of up to 30 days. Also blocks automated fetching; figures here are as reported from that article. Anthropic called SFPD over threat against CEO — The San Francisco Standard, 4 September 2026 — the Friday-to-Tuesday timeline, Anthropic's "safeguards process working as intended" statement, and the user's own account. A Florida Woman Used Claude as a Diary — Decrypt, 5 October 2026 — the Florida case: dates, the automated flag, the human review team, the arrest and the charge. Anthropic reports Florida woman's Claude 'diary' threat — Tom's Hardware — the count of at least three such conversations reaching police since August 2026. Fla. Stat. 836.10, "Written threats to kill, do bodily injury, or conduct a mass shooting or an act of terrorism" — The Florida Senate — the statutory text, including the "in any manner in which it may be viewed by another person" element and the second-degree-felony classification. Copy as Markdown All levels Plain-English definitions, no prior knowledge assumed. Skim it, or search for a term you hit elsewhere. Review the essentials as flashcards — tap to flip:
An AI set up to take actions in a loop — it reads a goal, calls tools, sees the results, and repeats until done. Claude Code is an agent for your codebase.
The company that makes Claude.
A way for your software to talk to Claude programmatically, instead of typing in a chat window. See Your First API Call.
A live, runnable output (an app, chart, or document) that Claude renders in a side panel on claude.ai, separate from the chat.
Asking the model to reason step by step before answering, which improves accuracy on hard problems.
The family of AI models (and apps) made by Anthropic. "Claude" can mean the chat app, the models, or the brand depending on context.
Anthropic's agentic command-line/IDE tool that can read and edit your codebase, run commands, and use tools. See What Claude Code Is.
A plain-text file where you give Claude Code persistent instructions about your project — its highest-leverage customisation.
Automatically condensing older conversation turns into a short summary when the context window fills, so a long session can keep going without losing the thread. See Context Management.
Deliberately deciding what goes into the model's context window — instructions, examples, retrieved data — to get the best result. The discipline behind prompting, RAG, and memory.
The maximum amount of text (measured in tokens) a model can consider at once — your prompt plus its reply. Exceed it and the oldest content drops off.

A control on newer Claude models for roughly how much the model thinks before answering. Match the tier to the task instead of maxing it out — you pay for thinking in latency and cost. See Extended Thinking & Effort.
A list of numbers representing the meaning of a piece of text, so software can find things that are similar in meaning (not just matching keywords). Powers semantic search and RAG.
A repeatable test of AI output quality, so you can tell whether a change made things better or worse.
Including a few worked examples in your prompt to show the model the pattern you want.
Further-training a model on your own examples to specialise it. Usually a last resort — try prompting and RAG first.

Instructing the model to answer only from the context you provide — and to say "I don't know" when the answer isn't there. The main prompt-level defense against hallucination. See the Pattern Library.
Rules and limits that keep an AI's behaviour safe and on-task — e.g. permission rules, "run tests before done", or human approval for risky actions. See Securing Agents.
When a model states something false but confident. The core skill is verification. See Hallucinations.
In Claude Code, a command that runs automatically at a lifecycle event (e.g. after every file edit) to enforce formatting, gates, or safety.
The act of running a model to get an output (as opposed to training it).

The date after which a model has no training data — it genuinely doesn't know what happened later unless you supply the facts in your prompt. Claude's cutoff is published in each model's release notes. This is why asking about very recent events without context can produce outdated or invented answers; the fix is to paste in the relevant facts or use a tool that retrieves live information.
How long you wait for a response. Bigger models are usually slower; streaming improves perceived latency by showing output as it's generated.
The kind of AI behind Claude: trained to predict the next chunk of text, which turns out to be enough to write, code, summarise, and reason. See What Is an LLM?.
An open standard for connecting AI to external tools and data (databases, GitHub, browsers). An "MCP server" exposes a tool; Claude can call it. See MCP.
A model that handles more than text — e.g. images and PDFs as input.
In Claude Code, a preset that changes how Claude communicates (e.g. concise, explanatory, learning) without changing what it can do. See Output Styles.
In Claude Code, how much it can do without asking — from prompting on every action to auto-accepting edits. The main speed-vs-safety dial. See Permissions.
A read-only Claude Code mode that researches and proposes a plan before touching any files — you approve before it acts. See Plan Mode.
What you send the model: your instructions, question, and any context.
Reusing the unchanged front part of a prompt across calls to cut cost and latency. See Prompt Caching.
An attack where malicious instructions hidden in content the AI reads (a web page, a document) try to hijack it. See Prompt Injection.
Fetching relevant snippets from your data and adding them to the prompt so the model answers about them. See RAG.
A mode where the model spends extra compute "thinking" before answering, for harder tasks. On newer models you tune it with effort.
A packaged capability (instructions + optional scripts) that Claude loads on demand when relevant. See Skills.
A /-prefixed shortcut in Claude Code — built-in (like /clear) or your own reusable prompt — that triggers a defined action. See Slash Commands.

Sending the model's output token by token as it's generated, instead of waiting for the whole response. To a user it looks like the model is typing in real time; to a developer it means processing a stream of chunks instead of one response object. It dramatically improves perceived latency on long outputs and lets you start rendering before the model finishes. See Streaming.
Getting results in a strict, machine-readable shape (e.g. JSON matching a schema) instead of free text — so other software can rely on them. See Structured Output.
A separate Claude instance with its own context and tools, used to delegate part of a task (e.g. research) so the main session stays focused.
The high-level instructions that set the model's role and rules for a whole conversation — your most powerful steering lever.
A setting (on some models) controlling randomness: low = focused and repeatable, high = varied and creative.
The unit models read and count in — roughly ¾ of a word in English. Pricing and context limits are measured in tokens. See Tokens & Context.
Letting the model call functions you define (search, calculator, your API) and use the results. See Tool Use.

Asking the model to do a task with no examples — just instructions. Most everyday prompts are zero-shot. Contrast with few-shot, where you include worked examples to guide format or style. Zero-shot is fine for straightforward tasks; add examples when the model keeps missing the output shape you want. Missing a term? Add it — glossary entries are a perfect first contribution.

Copy as Markdown All levels Two small conventions make AILmanac easy to navigate and easy to trust. Master them once, and every page becomes faster to read and easier to rely on. What you'll learn Read the four level badges and know which pages are written for you Spot a freshness stamp and interpret an old date correctly Tell evergreen pages from volatile ones at a glance Know where every model fact lives — the single source of truth

Every page starts with a badge telling you who it's for. Here are all four, exactly as they appear: Beginner No prior knowledge assumed. Start here if you're new. Intermediate You've used AI a bit and want to go deeper. Advanced Building things — agents, the API, custom setups. All levels Useful at any level. Badges rely on text, not just color, so they work for everyone (including screen readers and color-blind readers). Skip what's above your level — or stretch into it when you're ready. Pro tip Want the pages strung together in a sensible order for your reader type? Follow a Learning Path. The Learning Paths string pages together in a sensible order per reader type.

AI moves fast. Anything that changes — model names, prices, limits, UI labels, beta features — is a volatile fact, and on AILmanac those carry a stamp like this: Last verified: 2026-08-10. This is what a freshness stamp looks like. The date is when a human last checked it; the link is the official source that always wins. Confirm against the official source. How to read what you see: Evergreen pages (concepts like "what is an LLM") don't carry a date — they don't go stale, so a date would be noise. Volatile pages show the date so you know how current the specifics are. An old date isn't a bug — it's honesty. It tells you to double-check that particular fact rather than assume. Watch out When the date looks old, don't treat the specific number or label as gospel — open the linked official source and confirm. The source always wins over the page.

Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Read the badge first⌄ Glance at the badge under the title. If it's above your level, skip it for now or stretch in when ready; if it matches you, dive in. ←PreviousNext→ 2Check for a date stamp⌄ No stamp means the page is evergreen and won't go stale. A stamp means the page carries volatile facts. ←PreviousNext→ 3Judge the date⌄ A recent date means the specifics are current. An old date is a signal to verify, not a sign the page is broken. ←PreviousNext→ 4Follow the source link when it matters⌄ For anything you'll act on — a price, a limit, a model name — open the official source linked in the stamp. It always wins. ←PreviousNext→

A guide that's confidently out of date is worse than no guide. These conventions let us be complete without pretending nothing changes — and let you calibrate how much to trust any given line. Copy as Markdown All levels AILmanac is a free, community-built almanac for getting the most out of Claude — and any AI. An almanac is a reference you come back to: complete, plain-spoken, and kept current. That's the goal here. What you'll learn Understand what AILmanac is — and what it deliberately is not Find the level that fits you: beginner, intermediate, or advanced Pick your fastest way in and start reading in under a minute

Everyone, on purpose — and we tell you the level of every page so you never feel lost or talked down to: Level This is you if... Beginner You've barely used AI and want a guaranteed first win. Intermediate You use Claude already and want noticeably better results. Advanced You build with Claude Code, the API, agents, and MCP.

There are excellent resources already (see the Landscape Map). AILmanac is not a link dump and not a copy of the official docs. It is: Opinionated — we tell you the one recommended way, then the alternatives. Level-tagged — every page is badged so you read what's right for you. Template-rich — copy-paste starters you can use in 30 seconds. Honest about freshness — facts that change (model names, prices, features) carry a "last verified" date and a link to the source.

:::warning The official docs are the source of truth When AILmanac and the official Anthropic documentation disagree, the official docs win. AI tools change fast; we work hard to stay current, but always confirm anything critical against the source we link to. ::: We also don't store your data, can't see your account, and won't make decisions for you on high-stakes work — see Responsible Use.

documents.t: Claude.ai is the no-setup starting point for everyone. You also get it on mobile (iOS/Android) and by voice — great for capturing ideas on the go. Power it up with Projects, custom instructions, and Artifacts.
Claude Code works inside your project. It reads, edits, runs commands, and fixes tests — acting on your files with your permission.

documents.t: The API and Agent SDK let your own software call Claude programmatically, so you can ship AI features, automations, and agents.

What you'll learn Open Claude and ask your first real question (no setup needed) Write a prompt the way a sharp colleague would want it: goal, length, audience, tone Refine an answer with plain-language follow-ups (iterative refinement) Adopt the one safety habit that matters: verify before you trust :::tip Add a screenshot here This page is the beginner floor — it deserves annotated screenshots or a short GIF.
